37. Mr. Islam then submitted what is the assurance that the Election Commission will not pass any order arbitrarily. The short answer to this contention is that the order of the Election Commission is not immune from challenge before the Tribunal which can grant any relief in terms of Rule 45.

38. Before we deal with the aspect as to the nature and extent of the jurisdiction under Rule 70 we would like to consider some of the decisions of the Supreme Courts of the sub-continent.

39. In Mohinder Singh Gill and another Vs. The Chief Election Commissioner A.I.R. 1978 (SC) 851. The Indian Supreme Court noticed Section 58 and Section 64A of the Representation of the People Act wherein the Legislature envisaged the necessity for the cancellation of poll and ordering of re poll in particular polling stations where situation may warrant such a course. It was observed: "where provision is made in the Act to deal with situations arising in a particular polling station, it cannot be said that if a general situation arises whereby numerous polling stations may witness serious mal-practices affecting the purity of the electoral process, that power can be denied to the Election Commission to take an appropriate decision".

40. The Court considered that 'Election covers the entire process from the issue of notification under Section 14 of the Representation of the People Act to the declaration of the result under Section 66 of the Act. When a poll that has already taken place has been cancelled and a fresh poll has been ordered, the order therefore, with the amended date, is passed as an integral part of the electoral process. It is an order during the course of process of election. The court considered the argument of arbitrary exercise of power and concluded:

"If during the process of election, at an intermediate or final stage, the entire poll has been wrongly cancelled and fresh poll has been wrongly ordered that is a matter which may be agitated after declaration of the result on the basis of the fresh poll, by questioning the election in the appropriate forum by means of an election petition in accordance with law. The petitioner, then, will have a remedy to question every step in the electoral process and every order that has been passed in the process of the election including the countermanding of the earlier poll."

But the court pointed out writ petition challenging the cancellation coupled with re-poll "amounts to calling in question a step in 'election' and is here fore barred by Article 329(b)". P.K. Goswami, J: giving his view observed Election is a long, elaborate and complicated process and, as far as we can see, the rule of audi alteram partem, which is in itself a fluid rule, cannot be placed in a strait-jacket for purposes of the instant case. It has also to be remembered that the impugned order of the Election Commission could not be said to be a final pronouncement on the rights of the parties as it was in the nature of an order covering an unforeseen eventuality which had arisen at one stage of the election. The aggrieved party had all along a statutory right to call the entire election in question, including the Commissioner's order, by an election petition under Section 80 of the Act, for the trial of which an elaborate procedure has been laid down in the Act. Then, as has been stated, there is also a right of appeal under Section 116A.

The learned Judge then made a cautious observation:

"Justice and fair play have often to be harmonised with exigerieies of situations in the light of accumulated totality of circumstances in a given case having regard to the question of prejudice not to the mere combatants in an electoral contest but to the real and larger issue of completion of free and fair election with rigorous. promptitude. Not being adequately informed of all the facts and circumstances, this Court will not make the task of the election court difficult and embarrassing by suggesting guidelines in a rather twilight zone."

41. The Pakistan Supreme Court, however, took the view that writ jurisdiction is not totally barred in election matters in exceptional case it may be available. In Akbar Ali Vs. Raziur Rahman Khawaja and others 18 D.L.R. (SC) 426 when the Presiding Officer had acted wantonly in cancelling SIX ballot papers of the respondent which were free from any defect, the Court observed If an election authority or tribunal acts in this fashion whether under the National and Provincial Assemblies Act or the Electoral College Act the decision in Miah Jamal Shah's case would not be an authority for the view that their decisions are sacrosanct and may not be called in question in the High Court." The Court further observed The decision in Miah Jamal Shah's case is not to the effect that an untenable interpretation of law by the Commissioner or the Election Tribunal acting under Section 60 of the Electoral College Act which may amount to excess of jurisdiction or failure to exercise jurisdiction is not susceptible to interference by the High Court.

42. Thus the arguments of the learned Counsels can be summarised by saying that one group of learned Counsels namely, Me. S.R.Pal, Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Dr. Kamal Hossain and Mr. T.H. Khan have taken the view that the power conferred by Rule 70 is a necessary inherent power for conducting the election while other group of learned counsels namely, Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, Mr. Mainul Hosain and Mr. Amirul Islam have taken view that the respective functionaries must be allowed to perform their duties without any interference by the Election Commission.

43. Considering the law which we have surveyed in the foregoing paragraphs it has been noticed that the Election Commission has been given the power from start to finish to oversee that the elections arc organised, held and conducted in accordance with law. Rule 70 has conferred upon it the power to review any order passed by the designated authority. Rule 29 shows that when the poll is adjourned the Presiding Officer will inform the Returning Officer and the Returning Officer shall - (a) Immediately report the circumstances to the Election Commission; (b) appoint, as soon as may be, with the approval of the Election Commission, a day for a fresh poll; and (c) fix a place or places at which and the hours during which such fresh poll shall be taken,

44. It was argued by the learned Counsel particularly Mr. Amirul Islam that it is the Returning Officer who shall take the decision for fresh poll and fix the date. He will merely inform the Election Commission and the approval of the Election Commission is necessary for fixing a date only and not for the purpose of taking a decision for fresh poll. This decision is to be taken by the Returning Officer himself.

45. A bare reading of the rule docs not permit us to construe Rule 29 Sub-Rule 2 in that fashion that has been argued. On the contrary it is the Election Commission which will take the decision whether there are reasons for ordering fresh poll and the Returning Officer shall fix the date when the poll is to be held.

46. Again it has been argued that the declaration of the Presiding Officer as to the person who got highest number of votes is final and the Presiding Officer is only to prepare the statement in Form "J[TA]" and in case of Chairman Election the Presiding Officer sends to the Returning Officer who consolidates the results and upon consolidation by the. Returning Officer the Election Commission is obliged to publish the result and it has no other option

<u>47. This argument cannot be accepted because the overall responsibility for holding the election and to see that it is conducted justly honestly and fairly is that of the Election Commission itself. To deny such power is to encourage the muscle power that has been demonstrated in the writ petitions when in the morning one declaration was made by the Presiding Officer and in the afternoon he reported that there had been no election at all. Even in some cases it has been found that the. Presiding Officer and the Returning Officer were forced, coerced or persuaded to declare the result in the "TA" Form and "L" Form whereas information has been lodged with the Election Commission by competent responsible quarters that there had been no election at all. If the argument is allowed it will mean whatever happened it will be sufficient without appealing to the voters if Presiding Officer and Returning Officer arc wooed and kept in good humour, That is no election and that is no democracy. Election is needed 10 sustain democracy and a perverse election or voterless election destroys democracy. Hence, the power of review given in Rule 70 is of necessity an important one for holding elections honestly, justly and fairly. This power as we have noticed is neither new nor an innovation. We have quoted Section 109 of the Electoral College Act to show that such power was also given in the previous Act. For the prima facie purpose of such re-poll is to restore a detailed poll process and to complete through the "Salvationary effort of a re-poll". To quote K. Iyer, J: "whether in fact or law, the order is validly made within his powers or violative of natural justice can be examined later by the appointed instrumentality, viz., the Election Tribunal." (A.I.R. 1978 SC. 851 at page 867).</u>

48. Reading the entire law and the rules we have come to this conclusion that the real and larger issue is completion of free and fair election with rigorous promptitude. Hence, election being a long, elaborate and complicated process for the purposes of electing public representatives it is not possible to lay down guidelines by any court because all the exigencies cannot be conceived humanly nor the vagaries of people contesting the election can be fathomed. In a dispute the issue is to be raised and evidence adduced for adjudication by a competent Tribunal. This function has been given to the Election Tribunal and to nowhere else. The Election Commission has been given power to decide certain matters but such enquiry will not come within the purview of judicial enquiry because the power to decide judicially is different from deciding administratively. By taking resort to extraordinary jurisdiction for a writ the High Court Division will be asked to enter into a territory which is beset with the disputed facts and certainly by well-settled principles it is clear a writ court will not enter into such controversy.

<u>49. On consideration of all aspects of the matter, our conclusions are as follows:-</u>

<u>(1) Under rule 70 read with Section 24 of the Ordinance the Election Commission has been vested with plenary supervisory and discretionary jurisdiction to oversee that an election is conducted honestly justly and fairly and in accordance with the provisions of the Ordinance</u>

<u>and the Rules.</u>

<u>(2) In so doing it may pass any order, unless specifically barred, including an order for re poll acceptance/ consolidation of result review etc. on the basis of materials before it. The observance of the rule of audi alteram partem though desirable in some circumstances is not an invariable pre-condition for the validity of such order.</u>

<u>(3) The jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution cannot be invoked except on the very limited ground of total absence of jurisdiction (coram non-judice) or malice in law to challenge any</u>

<u>step in the process of election including an order passed by the Election Commission under Rule 70 because:</u>

<u>(a) the real and larger issue of completion of free and fair election with rigorous promptitude for timely emergence and functioning of elective bodies must take precedence over settlement of private disputes.</u>

<u>(b) all election disputes must wait pending completion of the election and be taken to the special forum created under the Election Law itself for their resolution.</u>

<u>(c) almost invariably there will arise dispute over facts which cannot and should not be decided in an extraordinary and summary jurisdiction of writ.</u>

50. Civil Appeal No. 40 of 1988.

A.F.M. Shah Alam Vs. Mujibul Huq and others.

In this case the Presiding Officer submitted his report on 10.2.88 stating that the poll was peacefully held. He also sent a "TA" Form which shows Mujibul Huq, the petitioner received highest votes. But the Election Commission directed re-poll. This was challenged before the High Court Division. It was pointed out by the Respondent that the Presiding Officer himself by his subsequent report Annexure "M" series stated that the disturbances had taken place in the center and when the second election took place on 14.4.88 again there was disturbance. The Election Commission's order for re-poll for the third time which took place on 24.6.88 and this time Respondent No.3 secured highest votes: The High Court Division took the view that the petitioner had challenged the order of re-poll itself and the fact that the re-poll itself took place subsequently twice, "does not mean that the challenge has been given a go-bye" and then concluded that after submission of the result by the Presiding Officer the Election Commission has got no authority to cancel the result submitted by the Presiding Officer and there is no law authorising the Election Commission to order a re-poll, The High Court was clearly in error in not keeping in view the scheme of enactment and the well-settled principles empowering such high powered body namely, the Election Commission for taking necessary steps for ensuring fresh and fair election. In view or the principle laid down above the decision or the High Court Division is set aside and the appeal is allowed. Writ is re-called. No cost.

51. Civil Appeal No.4 of 1989.

Khurshed Alam Vs. Humayun Kabir Salim & others.

Leave was given to consider the correctness of the order made in Writ Petition No. 329 of 1988 wherein the learned Judges made the Rule absolute after selling aside the Election Commission's order for re-poll, In view of the principle we have laid down above it is held that the High Court Division was in error in coming to such conclusion. The appeal is therefore, allowed and the order of the High Court Division is set aside. Writ is recalled. No cost

52. Civil Appeal No.5 of 1989.

Taslimuddin Vs. Md. Abdul Quader Sarker & others.

Here the Presiding Officer submitted election results held on 10.2.88 to the Returning Officer who consolidated the result. This result was accepted by the Election Commission by an order dated 31st March, 1988. The High Court Division, however, in Writ Petition No.705 of 1988 made the Rule absolute after setting aside the order of the Election Commission and took the view that the Election Commission's order directing the Returning Officer to accept the result submitted by the parties on obtaining affidavits from them is not a legal order and accordingly the order of the Election Commission was set aside. The learned Judges it seems presumed that the Presiding Officer cancelled the election and as such no result can be published by the Returning Officer. It has been pointed out that in Writ Jurisdiction the High Court Division will not go into the disputed question of fact and since the decision of the High Court Division was based on such disputed question, there is no hesitation in saying that such decision cannot be sustained. In the result, this appeal is also allowed. Writ is recalled. No cost.

53. Civil Appeal No.2 of 1989 with Civil Petition For Special Leave to Appeal No.23 of 1989.

The election was held on 10.2.88 but the Election Commission directed re-polling in Shahab Ali Academy Centre and for acceptance of the result of Dattar Bazar High School Centre. The High Court Division took the view that the Election Commission cannot invalidate the results when it was declared by the Presiding Officer and accordingly made the Rule absolute in part. Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal No.23 of 1989 arose out of the other part of the case. We have given our anxious consideration and have concluded that both the orders of the Election Commission are free from infirmity for the reasons mentioned in foregoing paragraphs and therefore it is within the jurisdiction of the Election Commission to pass the aforesaid order. In the result, the appeal is allowed but the petition is dismissed. The High Court Division's order in respect of Shahab Ali Academy Centre is set aside and the writ is recalled. No cost.

54. Civil Appeal No.3 of 1989.

Abdus Sattar Vs. Bangladesh Election Commission &others The Election Commission directed fresh poll in two centers namely, Shatugaon Primary School Centre and Ghilabdu Mission Primary School Centre because of disturbances in the two polling stations by its order dated 2nd April, 1988 was challenged by filing writ petition No. 528 of 1988 and the High Court Division made the Rule absolute and set aside the Election Commission's order for re-poll. As we have said that whether there are disturbances or not that is within the jurisdiction of the Election Commission so as to pass order for re-poll. This order could be challenged before an Election Tribunal. But certainly the High Court Division jurisdiction is not attracted under Article 102 of the Constitution. This appeal is also allowed. The order of the High Court Division is set aside. Writ is recalled. No cost.

55. Civil Appeal No. 38 of 1988.

The Election Commission directed re poll in all the four centers. Admittedly election was held only in one center but the Election Commission directed cancellation of the result and holding for fresh poll in all the four centers. When this was challenged in Writ Petition No.655 of 1988 the High Court Division took the view that after the Presiding Officer declared the result of the election in appropriate form and forwards the same to the appropriate authority, the Election Commission cannot cancel the result. When there was no election in three centers and the only center where so-called election was held which was marked by disturbances there is no hesitation in saying that the Election Commission was within jurisdiction to order re-poll in all the four centers. The High Court Division has fallen into error in passing the impugned order.

The appeal is also allowed. The order of the High Court Division is set aside. Writ is recalled. No cost.

56. Civil Appeal No.29 of 1988.

In this case election was held in three centers out of four centers. It seems Kalimuddin filed a petition before the Election Commission. The Election Commission passed the order on 31.3.88. Writ Petition was filed on 10th April, 1988. The Rule was made absolute and the High Court Division observed We hold that the order of re-poll passed by the Election Commission is without any lawful authority and of no legal effect" and then the High Court Division added a significant order "the order of the Election Commission is set aside without prejudice to the rights of the parties that might be decided elsewhere," Such observation could be found in other cases also. It shows clearly that the High Court Division is passing an order at the intermediate stages. It cannot open another round for the parties "to be decided else where", obviously the Tribunal. As we have mentioned in the foregoing paragraphs that such an order is not contemplated for ensuring election which is to be conducted by U1e Election Commission.

In the result, therefore, the order of the High Court Division is set aside and the appeal is allowed. Writ is recalled. No cost.

57. Civil Appeal No.17 of 1989.

The Election Commission directed fresh poll in one Centre namely, Uttar Sartha Primary School Centre. The High Court in Writ Petition No.257 of 1988 set aside the Election Commission's order. The question is whether the Election Commission had power directing re-poll. Since we have found such power is preserved for the exercise of jurisdiction, there is no hesitation in saying that the High Court Division was wrong in its conclusion. The appeal is also allowed. Writ is recalled. No cost.

58. Civil Appeal No. 8 of 1989

Saifuddin Ahmed Chowdhury Vs. Bangladesh Election Commission and others.

The Election Commission directed fresh election in two centers Jorkaran Dak Bungalow and Fultali Primary School. The High Court took the view that after declaration of result by Returning Officer the Election Commission's power under Rule 70 was exercised illegally. It is unfortunate that the High Court Division without comprehending the scheme of the Act for vesting the Election Commission with necessary powers for ensuring that the election is conducted honestly, justly and fairly had passed the order which is erroneous.

In the result, this appeal is allowed. Writ is recalled. No cost.

Before parting with these cases, we would like to put on record our appreciation-for the valuable assistance rendered by the learned Counsels.

End.

full_judgment:
Kazi Ebadul Hoque, J.: In these Rules Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and others have been asked to show cause as to why acquisition of petitioner's lands in question should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and of no legal effect Those Rules are disposed of by this judgment as common questions of fact and law are involved in them.

2. Case of the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 554 of 1992 is as follows:

The petitioners are owners of 19 kathas of lands of CS Plot Nos. 12 and 13 of Mouza Dhanmondi having their two-storied residential building on the northern side of that land and the mosque and grave of their predecessor late Colonel MA 'Rashid to the southern side thereof. Respondent No. 3, Chairman Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakhya, in short, RAJUK required some land for construction of the link road connecting Green Road with Mirpur Road and the Planning Commission in its meeting dated 5.11.88 approved the scheme for 100 feet wide link road over the said building of the petitioners. Government on 12.11.89 informed the respondent No.1 Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka that subject to approval of Central Land Allocation Committee, in short CLAC proposal of RAJUK for 6.28 acres of land including 2.95 acres of private land approved for 80 feet wide link road with 6 feet wide footpath on both sides instead of 100 feet wide link road to save valuable land. Thereafter respondent No. 1 stated LA Case No. 40 of 1989-90 for acquisition of 2.95 acres of land belonging to the petitioners and others and issued notices and compensation payable to the petitioners for acquisition of their land and building was assessed on 14.11.89 by respondent No. 1. Thereafter construction of the said link road was ceremonially opened by the President on 30.12.89. CLAC in its meeting dated 12.2.90 approved allocation of 6.28 acres land including, 2.95 acres of private land. Thereafter the petitioner No.1 informed the respondent Nos. 1 and 3 that if the proposed link road is shifted towards the north petitioners' building as well as more private lands can be saved utilizing more Government khas land as per directive of the Planning Commission. Thereafter second revised drawing was prepared by RAJUK saving petitioners' building and sent proposal dated 9.4.90 to the Government to-obtain approval of the CLAC on the basis of 'the revised-drawing to save petitioners building by releasing some land from acquisition and by acquiring some land afresh and the same after approval by the respondent No. 4 on 10.4.90 was sent to the respondent No. 2 for obtaining approval of the CLAC. At that stage respondent No.3 being influenced by illegal occupants of Government khas lands to the north sent proposal dated 27.5.90, with revised third drawing dated 9.5.90 to respondent No. 3 shifting the link road to the southern side of petitioners building requiring 6.36 acres of land including 4.66 acres of private land. Petitioners filed objection to the said revised proposal dated 27.5.90 on the ground that almost entire land of the petitioners will be acquired and ground floor and entrance of petitioners building will be submerged by the earth work of the link road. Respondent No. 2 by summary dated 1.6.91 sought approval of the Acting President to the scheme. But by letter dated 14.8.91 Director President's Secretariat requested respondent No. 2 to supply particulars of khas land available near the proposed 80 feet wide link road and other particulars. But without furnishing the said particulars respondent No.4 prepared fourth revised plan dated 24.9.91 including therein petitioners building and some land to the south and as per the said drawing 6.40 acres of land including 4.68 acres of private land was required for the said link road and only small area of khas land was included in that plan, and RAJUK in its meeting dated 25.9.91 approved the same. Thereafter by letter dated 2.10.91respondent No. 3, requested respondent No. 4 to take up the matter with respondent No. 2 for allocation of the land by CLAC and to direct respondent No. 1 for requisition of land as the Prime Minister desired early implementation of the scheme arid there after respondent No. 2 took up the matter with CLAC which in its meeting dated 2.11.91 approved the allocation of 4.67 acres of private land as per revised drawing. Thereafter by letter dated 17.11.91 respondent No. 2 called back summary dated 1.6.91 from the Acting President's Secretariat, Thereafter on the representation dated 10.10.91 and 22.10.91 by a welfare society formed by the illegal Occupants of the Government khas land respondent No: 4 by letter dated 18.11.91 informed Prime Minister's Secretariat that necessary action in the matter was taken. Thereafter respondent No. 3 at the instance of interested quarters by letter dated 31.11.91 informed the respondent No. 2 that it is desirable to construct the link road as per 3rd revised drawing dated 9.5.90 falsely stating that CLAC in its meeting dated 2.11.91 allocated land as per third revised drawing dated 9.5.90. There after on 23.11.91 respondent No. 2 prepared and sent summary for the approval of the Prime Minister sending the 3rd instead of the 4th revised drawing and the Prime Minister approved the same on 25.11.91. Thereafter on 26.11.91 respondent No. 2 gave approval for acquisition of 4.66 acres of land under section 5(1) of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance. 1982 though till then no notice under section 3 of the said Ordinance was issued and formalities under section 4 thereof for hearing objection were not complied with. Notice under section 3 of the said Ordinance was issued on 28.11.91 after approval dated 26.11.91 depriving the petitioner’s opportunity to me objection and hearing in the matter. Petitioners received notice dated 19.12.91 under section 6 of the said Ordinance in the last week of December, 1991 acquiring their land without specifying the portion sought to be acquired. Petitioners also came to learn about notice dated 28.011.91 in the last week of December, 1991 after enquiry and obtaining a photo copy thereof. Thereafter petitioner No. 1 filed appeal to the Prime Minister to acquire land as per drawing dated 9.1.89. Comments having been sought -upon the said representation respondent No.3 came to the project site and assured the petitioners that steps are being taken to revise the acquisition line. But in spite of such assurance steps are being taken to construct the link road by the southern side of petitioners building as per drawing dated 9.5.90 and thereby frustrating petitioners appeal to the Prime Minister, Petitioners having no other alternative than to move this court.

3. Case of the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 661 of 1992 is as follows: Petitioner No. 1 is the owner of four-storied building on 5 kathas of land on the north western portion of CS plot No. 67 of Mouza Dhanmondi and petitioner No. 2 is the owner of two-storied building on 6 kathas of land on the north eastern side of the said plot No. 67. Respondent No. 2 by memo dated 26.11.91 gave approval to the acquisition of 4.66 acres of private land before compliance of formalities under section 4 of the said Ordinance and such approval under section 5(1) of the said Ordinance could be given only after hearing objection under section 4 of the said Ordinance but notice under section 3 of the said Ordinance was issued on 28.11.91. By taking wrong starting point from the northern side of CS plot No. 67 acquisition line has been shifted 25 feet south at the instance of interested persons. Without issuing any notice on the petitioners' fixing the demarcation line staff of the respondent Nos. 1 and 3 demolished the boundary walls of the petitioners on 4.12.91 and trying to put their buildings within the acquisition, though as per the revised drawing their lands do not come within the acquisition line. Notice dated 28.11.91 under section 3 of the said Ordinance was for collateral purposes at the instance of interested quarters. Petitioners filed objection on 8.12.91 and raised objection to demolition of their boundary walls and acquisition of their land situated on the further south side of the original acquisition line and also objected to the mode of survey conducted by the surveyors of the respondent Nos. 1 and 3 and requested for joint survey. Accordingly, on 24.12.91 a summary was made and claim of petitioners found correct and the survey made before issuing acquisition notice was wrong and the surveyor of the respondent No. 1 could not fix the demarcation pillar as per his survey due to opposition from the persons on the northern side of the link road and non-cooperation of the surveyors of respondent No. 3. Notice dated 28.11.91 under section 3 of the said Ordinance was suppressed and after demolition of their boundary walls the petitioners came to know about the acquisition. During pendency of their objection dated 8.12.91 respondent No. 1 issued notice dated 19.12.91 under section 6 of the said Ordinance showing acquisition of some land of the petitioners and their buildings thereon. Issuance of notice dated 19.12.91 before disposal of their objection and demolition on their boundary walls within the time for filing objection was malafide and for collateral purpose.

4. Case of the petitioners in Writ Petition No. 1059 of 1992 is as follows: Petitioner No.1 is the owner of about one bigha of land situated on the northern side of CS plot No. 12 of Mouza Dhanmondi and petitioner No. 2 is the owner of about 10 decimals of land in the south eastern side of CS plot No. 158 of Mouza Raza Bazar. Being unduly influenced by interested persons acquisition proceeding was started by issuing notice dated 28.11.91 under section 3 of the said Ordinance to acquire 24 decimals of land of the petitioner No. 1 and 10 decimals of land of the petitioner No. 2 for collateral purpose and in violation of the provisions of the said Ordinance and approval under section 5(1) thereof was given before issuing notice under section 3 thereof and hearing objection under section 4 thereof. In terms of the original plan only 0.05 acres of land of the petitioner No. 1 and 0.03 acre of land of petitioner No. 2 fell within the acquisition line. Petitioners came to learn about the proposed acquisition as per the 2nd revised drawing dated 9.5.90 in the 2nd week of January, 1992 and then they went to the office of the respondent No. 6 and obtained copies of notices under sections 3 and 6 of the said Ordinance. Thereafter on 22.1.92 petitioners filed objection against acquisition of their land as per revised plan and requested to construct the road as per original plan but no hearing was given to the petitioners. But without disposing of their objection and without payment of compensation to them respondents cannot construct the road.

5. Case of the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 1060 of 1992 is as follows: The petitioner is owner of about one bigha of land situated to tire northern side of CS plot No. 24 and north-eastern side of CS plot No. 67 of Mouza Dhanmondi. At the instance of interested quarters respondent No. 3 shifted the acquisition line of the land required for construction of the link road to further south on the basis of revised drawing dated 9.5.90 which was never approved by CLAC on 2.11.91 but CLAC approved the revised drawing dated 24.9.91. But respondent No. 2 by memo dated 26.11.91 gave approval for acquisition of 4.66 acres of private land under section 5(1) of the said Ordinance before compliance of formalities under section 4 thereof and notice under section 3 thereof was issued on 28.11.91 illegally for collateral purpose at the instance of interested quarters. As per the revised drawing dated 9.5.90 an area of 0.33 acre out of 0.36 acre of land of the petitioner falls within the acquisition line. Petitioner after coming to know about the proposed acquisition as per revised drawing dated 9.5.90 submitted on 24.12.91 a representation to the respondent No. 4, Additional Deputy-Commissioner (LA) Dhaka to reject the proposal of RAJUK as per revised drawing dated 9.5.90 as the acquisition was not in public interest but to benefit some interested quarters. Thereafter the petitioner went to the office of the respondent No. 6 and got copies of notices under sections 3 and 6 of the said Ordinance and filed another representation to the respondent No. 6 to drop the acquisition proceeding as per revised drawing. The respondent No. 6 without disposing of the objection of the petitioner and payment of compensation to the petitioner possession of the land cannot be taken over.

6. These Rules are being contested by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 jointly filing one set of affidavit-in-opposition and supplementary affidavit-in-opposition and respondent No. 3 by filing another set of affidavits-in-opposition denying the material allegations. Their case, in short, is as follows: An area of 2.95 acres of private land was acquired in LA Case No. 40 of 1989-90 by respondent No. 1 on receipt of approval for acquisition of the same and out of the same 2.41 acres of land was handed over to the RAJUK. Thereafter on 24.5.90 petitioner No. 1 made representation to the President to save her building and grave of her late husband from acquisition. Hence revised plan was prepared by the respondent No. 3 considering the objection of the petitioners to save their building and grave keeping in view engineering aspect and traffic facilities in the matter to make the road straight as far as practicable. 6. 36 acres of land was required for the link road including 2.95 acres of private land. But as a result of decision in 62 writ petitions 1.71 acres of private land was added increasing the area from 2.95 acres to 4.66 acres of private land. Neither the building nor the mosque nor the grave will be affected by the revised plan dated 9.5.90 which was approved and being implemented. According to the said revised plan, link road will pass keeping the building of the petitioners and the mosque and the grave on both sides of the said road. Ground floor and entrance of petitioners’ building will not be affected in any manner. CLAC allotted 6.40 acres of land in its meeting held on 2.11.91. CLAC having allocated .04 acre of land more than the required 4.36 acres respondent No. 3 by letter dated 21.11.91 informed respondent No. 2 about the said correction. Respondent No. 1 received only two drawings one dated 9.1.89 and the order dated 9.5.90 for the purpose of acquisition. Memo dated 26.11.91 issued by the respondent No. 2 intimating approval of the Government for acquisition of land was not the final decision as contemplated under section 5(1) of the said Ordinance. Rather it was the initial decision and as such words.  “১৯৮২ সালের ২ নং অধ্যাদেশের ৫(১) ধারার অধীনে” were inserted inadvertently in that memo dated 26.11.91 and the said memo dated 26.11.91 does not disclose of any objection under section 4 of the said Ordinance nor there was any such objection before respondent No. 2 and as such memo dated 26.11.91 is not a decision under section 5(1) of the said Ordinance and the petitioners cannot take advantage of the irrelevant insertion of the same. After receipt of the said memo respondent No. 1 served notice dated 28.11.91 under section 3 of the said Ordinance. Petitioners did not file any objection under section 4 of the said Ordinance but the petitioner No. 1 of WP 2554/92 filed a petition on 22.1.92 in response to notice dated 19.2.91 under section 6 of the Ordinance claiming compensation for the acquired land after service of notice under sections 3 and 6 of the said Ordinance correctly and according to law correctly writing the quantity of land acquired. Revised drawing was prepared and approved considering traffic problem, engineering aspect of construction of the link road, advantage and disadvantages of the people of the, locality and the affected persons, and in public interest and there is no malafide or partiality in the matter at the instance of any interested quarters. Petitioners of WP No. 2554/92 have no cause of action for the writ petition after filing of petition by the petitioner No. 1 for compensation in respect to notice dated 19.12.91 and the same is to linger the acquisition proceeding and to stop construction of the link road. Revised alignment was not made on the representations dated 10.10.91 and 22.10.91 of interested persons. CLAC did not approve drawing dated 24.9.91 but it approved drawing dated 9.5.90. Notice under section 3 of the said Ordinance was issued on 28.11.89 for acquisition of 1.32 acres of part of CS plot Nos. 8, 12, 15, 23, 24 and 65 of Mouza Dhanmondi and duly served in accordance with law in the locality as per the revised alignment but hearing objection was not necessary as the petitioners did not file any objection under section 4 (1) of the said Ordinance. No objection under section 4(1) having been filed by the petitioners and the area acquired by notice under section 3 of the said Ordinance being only 1.32 acres-less than than 10 bighas-there was no question or submitting report or obtaining approval of the Government. The petitioners cannot now object to the acquisition of their land. Similarly, petitioner No. 2 of Writ Petition No. 661 of 1992 filed another application on 4.1.92 to the respondent No. 6 claiming compensation for her acquired building at the present market rate.

7. Petitioners have filed affidavits-in-reply to the affidavits-in-opposition filed by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 as well as respondent No. 3.

8. Mr. SR Pal, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners, in some of the petitions, submitted that land proposed to be acquired as per the notice under section 3 of the Ordinance No. 2 of 1982 and decided to be acquired as per notice under section 6 thereof is vague and not specified and as such there cannot be any acquisition on the basis of such vague notice. He further submitted that objection to be filed under section 4 of the said Ordinance is a substantial right and the petitioners have been deprived of that right by not serving the notice under section 3 of the said Ordinance depriving the petitioners of their valuable right to file objection to the proposed acquisition and an opportunity to be heard in the matter.

9. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners in some other petitions, submitted that Government gave approval to the acquisition of the land under section 5 of the said Ordinance before issuance of notice under section 5 of the said Ordinance depriving the petitioners of the opportunity to file objection and to be heard in the matter. He further submitted that by excluding Government khas land thereby shifting the acquisition line to the south on the land of the petitioners being unduly influenced by the unauthorised occupiers on such khas land in violation of the approval of the CLAC smacks of malafide and as such the whole acquisition proceeding is bad in law.

10. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, learned Advocate for the respondent No. 3, submitted that the proposed acquisition was for public purpose and in public interest for facilitating traffic by opening a link road to reduce congestion in the city and the petitions have been filed with malafide intention to delay the execution of the project in spite of shifting the acquisition line to the south after considering their objection to save their residential building.

11. Mr. AF Hasan Ariff, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent Nos. 1 and 2, submitted that notices under sections 3 and 6 of the said Ordinance were-duly served according to the mode of service provided under rule 4 of the Acquisition of Immovable Property Rules, 1982 and the area to be acquired has been specifically mentioned in the said notice with specification of the land. He further submitted that petitioners having not filed any objection within 15 days of service of the said notice and some of them having claimed compensation long after such notice allegation of depriving them of any opportunity to be heard has no basis. Under memo dated 26.11.91 no approval under section 5(1) of the Ordinance was given as will be evident from the letter dated 9.8.91 of the respondent No.6 in reply to which the said memo dated 26.11.91 was sent.

12. Admittedly LA Case No. 40 of 1989-90 was started by the respondent No.6, Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) Dhaka and 2.95 acres of land was acquired for construction of link road connecting Green Road with Mirpur road by the respondent No.3. RAJUK and after delivery of possession in 2.41 acres of the said acquired land to the RAJUK construction of the said link road was formally opened by the then President on 30.12.89. At this stage petitioner No. 1 of Writ Petition No. 554 of 1992 filed representations to the respondent Nos. 1 and 3 as well as to the President for saving her building and grave of her late husband from acquisition. But she has not annexed copy of the said representation with the writ petition to show what statement she made therein. However, the fact remains that to save the two storied building of the petitioners of Writ Petition No. 554 of 1992 the drawing of the proposed link road was revised but that drawing having created a big curvature in the said road alignment another revised drawing was prepared on 9.5.90 shifting the road alignment to the southern side of the petitioners' said two-storied building. This proposal with the revised drawing dated 9.5.90 was placed before the Acting President with summary dated 1.6.91 but the representation of the petitioner No. 1 having been sent to the RAJUK again the said road alignment was changed as per revised drawing dated 24.9.91. Petitioners contended that the proposal as per the revised drawing dated 24.9.91 was approved on 2.11.91 by, the CLAC but the respondents contend that the proposal as per revised drawing dated 9.5.90 was approved on 2.11.91 by CLAC. It appears from letter dated 21.11.91 sent by the respondent No. 3 to the respondent No. 2 that decision in the CLAC meeting held on 2.11.91 was not correctly recorded and in place of 4.67 acres of private land it will be 4.66 acres and total land will be 6.36 acres instead of 6.40 acres and the road should be constructed as per the alignment shown in the summary sent to the Acting President on 1.6.91. Thereafter summary dated 1.6.91 was called back from the Acting President's Secretariat and summary dated 23.11.91 was sent to the Prime Minister for her approval of the Scheme by acquisition of 4.66 acres of private land as per revised plan dated 9.5.90. It is admitted by the petitioners that this proposal was approved by the Prime Minister on 25.11.91 and fresh notice dated 28.11.91 under section 3 of the said Ordinance was issued for acquisition of 1.32 acres of land comprising parts of CS plot Nos. 8, 12, 15, 23, 24 and 67 of Mouza Dhanmondi after receipt of the approval of the respondent No. 2 dated 26.11.91 by the respondent No. 1. We are to see now whether approval of CLAC is a legal requirement for the acquisition of the said land.

13. It appears from Bangladesh Gazette published on 6.5.1976 that by resolution dated 27.4.76 Ministry of Land Administration, Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives (Land Administration and Land Reforms Division) formed Central Land Allocation Committee for approving proposals for allocation of land in the Dhaka City with Minister-in-Charge of the said Ministry as its Chairman, but this resolution does not state under what provision of law CLAC was formed. There is no provision in the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 requiring formation of CLAC and obtaining approval from CLAC for acquisition of land for public purpose or public interest. So it can be safely concluded that formation of CLAC and its approval is not a legal requirement but it has been formed for administrative convenience as a matter of policy to regulate acquisition of land under the said Ordinance. It appears from the said letter dated 21.11.91 of the respondent No. 3 that correction of decision of CLAC dated 2.11.91 was made with the approval of the Minister of State in charge of the Ministry of Land who was Chairman of CLAC. Subsequently summary sent to the Prime Minister pursuant thereto on 23.11.91 was approved by the Prime Minister on 25.11.91. Prime Minister being Executive Head of the Government if with her approval decision of the CLAC was changed then we find no ground to take exception to the same.

14. It is a fact and not denied that the respondent No. 6 issued notice under section 3 of the said Ordinance on 28.11.91 after receipt of the approval dated 26.11.91 from the respondent No. 2 along with the revised drawing dated 9.5.90. It is also admitted that as per this revised drawing dated 9.5.90 road alignment passed by the southern side of the said two-storied building and northern side of the grave and mosque over the vacant land of the petitioners of Writ Petition No. 554 of 1992 saving their residential building and grave from acquisition as prayed for. Thus we find nothing objectionable on the part of the, respondents in changing the road alignment as per revised drawing dated 9.5.90. To save the said building construction of the road in question was stopped for more than 2- and half years. When the petitioner No. 1's said building has been spared on her own prayer can she turn round now and claim that 'spare my valuable vacant land and take my building'. One cannot be allowed to blow hot and cold at the same breath. Law does not permit one to reprobate and approbate at the same time. We, therefore, find nothing malafide in the decision of the respondents to acquire additional land as per revised plan dated 9.5.90 excluding the said two-storied building, grave and mosque. Rather it is clear that the petitioners have not come with clean hands to challenge the acquisition in question.

15. There is also no merit in the submission that more private land is being acquired in a malafide manner leaving aside Government khas land to the northern side after clarification made in the affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 that as a result of decision in 62 writ petitions area of khas land was reduced.

<u>16. Petitioners in all the Rules alleged that no notice under sections 3 and 6 of the said Ordinance was served. But the contesting respondents denied the allegations and asserted that these were duly and legally served. Under Rule 4 of the Acquisition of Immovable Property Rules, 1982 such notices are to be served by affixing the same at convenient places on or near the property sought to be acquired displaying copies of such notices on the notice boards of some specified offices. In these Rules photostat copies of the said notices have been annexed by the petitioners. But they asserted that they obtained the same from the office of the respondent No. 6. No such copy could be legally obtained from any Government office. Had they obtained certified copies and annexed the same with this petition then it could be ascertained when they obtained the same. But it is difficult to ascertain from the photostat copies in the absence of any endorsement thereon when those were supplied and by whom and if at all those were supplied to the petitioners. In such circumstances when photostat copies of those notices were produced by the petitioners it can naturally be inferred that these were served in the locality in the manner prescribed by law. Moreover, when the petitioners were accessible upto the President's Secretariat and could obtain photostat copies of all the confidential official documents annexed to the petitions can it be believed that they were unaware of the fresh acquisition proceeding which they have now challenged as illegal on the ground of depriving them an opportunity to me objection and to be heard in the matter by suppression of those notices.</u>

17. It appears from the Annexure 2 to the Affidavit-in-opposition of the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 in Writ Petition No. 554 of 1992 that petitioner No. 1 filed an application to the respondent No. 6 on 22.1.92 only claiming fair compensation for the acquired property. Similarly, it appears from Annexure 1 to the affidavit-in-opposition filed by respondent Nos. 1 and 2 in Writ Petition No. 661 of 1992 that petitioner No. 2 filed an application to the respondent No. 6 on 4.1.92 only claiming compensation according to the prevailing market rate for the acquired property. It further appears from Annexures N and N(I) to the Writ Petition No. 1059 of 1992 that the petitioners filed objection to the acquisition of their land to the respondent No. 6 on 22.1.92. Similarly, it also appears from Annexure N to the Writ Petition No. 1060 of 1992 that the petitioner filed objection to the acquisition of her land to the respondent No. 6 on 7.1.92. Thus it is clear that the Petitioners of Writ Petition Nos. 554 of 1992 and 661 of 1992 did not raise any objection before the respondent No. 6 against acquisition of their property. Now it does not lie in their mouth that they have been deprived of a substantial right of objection to the acquisition of their land and hearing in the mater. As regards the objections filed by the petitioners in Writ Petition Nos. 1059 and 1060 of 1992 it is clear that those objections were filed after service of notices under section 6 of the Ordinance and not within the prescribed period of 15 days after service of notice under section 3 of the said Ordinance. As they did not file those objections within the prescribed period before service of notice under section 6 of the said Ordinance it also does not lie in their mouth that they have been deprived of any such right. It is no doubt true that if objections are filed within the prescribed period of time then the objectors are entitled to be heard in the matter and the respondent No. 1 is under legal obligation to submit a report for decision of the government if the land exceeded 10 bighas, and to the Divisional Commissioner if the land did not exceed 10 bighas. Since no objection was filed by the petitioners within the prescribed period of 15 days of service of notice under section 3 of the said Ordinance the respondent No. 1 decided to acquire the land in question and issued notice under section 6 of the said Ordinance for requisition of the lands in question after 21 days of issuance of notice under section 3 of the said Ordinance. We are; therefore, of the view that the respondent No. 1 did not violate the provision of section 4 of the said Ordinance in acquiring the lands in question by notices under section 6 of the said Ordinance.

18. From Annexure 3 to the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition it appears that by letter dated 9.8.90 respondent No.6 sent a detailed report to the respondent No. 2 in reply to the letter dated 1.8.90 of the respondent No. 2 explaining the details for purpose of acquisition of the land as per the revised drawing possibly dated 9.5.90 requiring 4.66 acres of private land. After receipt of that letter from the respondent No. 6 the respondent No.2 by letter dated 26.11.90 (Annexure M to Writ Petition No. 554/92) informed the respondent No. 1 that the Government approved the proposal for acquisition of 4.66 acres of private land under certain conditions. Thus, it is clear that this was an administrative approval pursuant to the approval of the Scheme by the Prime Minister on 25.11.91 and not any decision for acquisition of land under section 5(1) of the said Ordinance as wrongly mentioned in the said letter. Therefore, we find no merit in the submission on behalf of the petitioners that Government decided to acquire their land before issuing notice under section 3 of the said Ordinance depriving them opportunity to file objection and to be heard in the matter.

19. Notices under section 3 of the said Ordinance dated 28.11.91 shows that an area of 1.32 acres of land from part of some plots have been proposed to be acquired for construction of link road from Green Road to Mirpur Road and objections invited within 15 days of service of the said notice. Similarly, notices under section 6 of the said Ordinance dated 19.2.92 show that definite area of land from specified part of a plot has been decided to be acquired and possession to be taken over. Petitioners obtained and annexed photostat copies of all the drawings of the link road including the drawing dated 9.5.90 under which lands of the petitioners have been decided to be acquired. Thus it is clear that the petitioners understood the identity of the land which has been decided to be acquired from them. So we do not find any defect in the said notices to declare the acquisition proceeding without lawful authority on the ground that the land is not clearly identifiable. When a map or drawing is prepared before the acquisition of land, showing part of the plots to be acquired and in the notice under section 6 of the Ordinance location of the part of the plot with area to be acquired is clearly mentioned as done in the instant LA case under challenge then it cannot be said that the land to be acquired is vague and not identifiable.

20. Decision in the case of Sufia Khatun Vs. Secretary, Revenue reported in 20 DLR (SC) 18 relied on by the learned Advocate for the petitioners in support of his submission that the notices under sections 3 and 6 of the said Ordinance having not specified the part of the land the entire acquisition proceeding is void has no manner of application in the facts and circumstances of the rules under judgment.

In the result all the Rules are discharged without any order as to costs. Orders of stay stand vacated.

End.
