full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the principal opposite party-petitioner is directed against the judgment and order passed by District Judge, Chandpur on 31-10-93 in Election Tribunal Appeal No. 6 of 1993 allowing the appeal on contest without cost declaring the election of the elected candidate (present petitioner) as void and the applicant opposite party No. 1 being duly elected chairmen of No. 10 Tamta Union Parishad setting aside the judgment and order passed by Assistant Judge and Election Tribunal, Chandpur on 31-5-93 in Election Tribunal Case No. 1 of 1993 dismissing the case on contest without cost.

2. The opposite party No. 1 being applicant filed Election Tribunal Case No. 8 of 1992 in the Court of the Assistant Judge and Election Tribunal, Chandpur impleading the present petitioner as opposite party along with others for a declaration that the election of the returned candidate namely; present petitioner, of No. 10 Tamta Union Parishad held on 3-2-92 as void after counting the ballot papers of 2 centres namely; Waruk High School Centre under Ward No. 2 and Dopolla Janata High School Centre under Ward No. 3 and for declaring the applicant as duly elected chairman of the said Union Parishad on the allegations; that the applicant-opposite party No. 1 along with 6 others contested for the post of Chairman of No. 10 Tamta Union Parishad held on 3-2-92. The applicant opposite party No. 1 had the symbol of “আনারস” and the opposite party petitioner had the symbol of “চাকা” the other contesting candidates had other symbols. In the Union Parishad there were 3 Wards having 7 polling centres. During the time of polling in two centres namely, Waruk High School Centre under Ward No. 2 and Dopolla Janata High School centre under Ward No.3, the opposite party petitioner resorted to illegal activities in collusion with his associates and the Presiding Officers of those two centres and managed to cast false votes in his favour of absentee voters and of persons who were already dead in spite of protest of the agents of the applicant. Consequently there were no fair and peaceful election in those two centres and that the agents of the applicants were also driven out from those centres. After the polling was over, on counting it was found that the applicant secured 651 votes in Waruk High School Centre and opposite party petitioner secured 1544 votes and was declared elected. On the following day i.e. 4-2-92 the applicant came to know about the result from the Office of the Returning Officer and found 100 votes were taken out from the side of the applicant and illegally shown to have cast in favour of the opposite party petitioner. Furthermore, in Dopolla Janata High School Centre also opposite party petitioner resorted to illegal activities in the same manner in collusion with the Presiding Officer and his associates. It was further alleged that on verification and scrutinising all the connected papers and recounting the ballot papers of those 2 centres it will appear that the opposite party petitioner in collusion with the Presiding Officer and his associates resorting to illegal activities managed to get himself elected which materially affected the election result

3. The petitioner being the opposite party contested the case by filling written objection denying all material allegations made in the application contending, inter alia; that the election was held in a peaceful manner and fairly and that after proper counting of votes cast in favour of the contesting candidates the opposite party petitioner was duly declared as elected Chairman of the said Union Parishad. There was no rigging as alleged by the applicant. In Waruk High School Centre out of 4476 votes only 2477 votes were cast and after counting it was found that the opposite party petitioner secured 1644 votes and the applicant secured 451 votes. At Dopolla Janata High School Centre 1220 votes were cast out of 2084 votes where the opposite party-petitioner secured 528 votes and applicant secured 371 votes. It was further stated that Waruk High School Centre is situated by the side of Comilla-Chandpur Road and the Deputy Commissioner and the Superintendent of Police used to visit that centre occasionally during the polling time and there was no disturbance. None of the agents of the applicant put any objection at the time of counting before the Presiding Officer alleging that 100 votes of the applicant were illegally made invalid and more than 100 votes were taken out of him and shown cast in favour of the opposite party-petitioner and in fact 131 votes were invalid there and not 31 votes as alleged by the applicant

4. The learned Election Tribunal who held the trial considering the evidence, facts and circumstances dismissed the case by his Judgment and Order dated 8-9-92.

5. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order the applicant preferred Election Tribunal Appeal No. 4 of 1992 in the Court of the District Judge and Election Appellate Tribunal, Chandpur. The learned District Judge and Election Appellate Tribunal, Chandpur after hearing allowed the appeal by his order dated 27-4-93 setting aside the judgment and order of the Election Tribunal and sent back the case on remand to the trial Court directing to recount the ballot papers of two centres namely Waruk High School Centre and Dopolla Janata High School Centre with a further direction that after recounting the ballot papers of those two centres, if the Tribunal feels it necessary, he will allow both the parties to adduce evidence and then decide the case.

6. Election Tribunal on receiving the case back on remand re-numbered it as Election Tribunal Case No. 1 of 1993. Thereafter, on 23-5-93, in presence of both the parties and also the learned Advocates of both the parties, opened the gunny bags containing the ballot papers of those two centres and re-counted again. The Election Tribunal thereafter finishing the re-counting and considering again the evidence on record dismissed the case.

7. Being aggrieved by this judgment and order the applicant again preferred Election Tribunal Appeal No.6 of 1993. Learned District Judge and Election Appellate Tribunal, Chandpur, who heard the appeal, by his judgment and order dated 31-10-93 allowed the appeal declaring the applicant as Chairman elected of No. 10 Tamta Union Parishad and set aside the judgment and order of the Election Tribunal dismissing the case.

8. As against that the opposite party- petitioner moved this court and obtained this Rule.

9. Mr.  A Baset Majumder, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submitted that only case of the applicant in the election petition was for re-counting and there was no mention of any double seal on any ballot papers. In Ext. 'Ka' it was a prayer for re-counting and all other rest allegations are vague and unspecified. He submitted that recounting of ballot papers is not specifically provided under the Election Rules but it can be exercised by the inherent power of the Tribunal, if it is found that there was a prayer made in writing by any party to the presiding officer for re-counting at the time of counting after the poll. He submitted that there is nothing to show from the contents of the election petition or from any evidence on record that any such prayer was made before the Presiding Officer of the disputed 2 centres for recounting of the ballot papers at the time of counting after the poll. He further showed from the election petition that grievance made therein was only that out of 200 votes of the applicant 100 ballot papers were spoiled and rest 100 were shown cast in favour of the opposite party petitioner. The learned Advocate further submitted that when there is nothing to show on record that any grievance or prayer in writing was ever made by the applicant or by his agents to the Presiding Officer for recounting on any allegation made in the Election Petition, recounting by the Tribunal cannot be held. In support of his contention he referred the case of Md. Shahajan vs. Md. Sadeq and others reported in 38 DLR (AD) 275 relevant para 13, wherein their Lordships have held that:

"In election cases, it is often found that a defeated candidate brings a number of allegations including vague charges of his opponent influencing the Presiding Officer, but ultimately fails to prove, or abandons, all the allegations and insist on only recounting of the ballot papers. On recounting, it is found that the result has gone in his favour by some mysterious means. That is why recounting of the ballot papers by a Tribunal long after the election should not be resorted to simply on mere asking by an interested party. Ballot papers have special sanctity of their own and their secrecy should not be infringed by reopening the sealed packet unless the recounting becomes indispensably necessary to determine the dispute. When recounting would become so necessary depends on circumstances in each case. In the absence of clear justifications, no recounting should be ordered or made. Some finality must attach to counting of votes. Ground work for recounting must be prepared; recounting should be refused if no prayer for recounting had been made to the Presiding Officer who is alone empowered to recount on the spot either on his own motion or on requests of any candidate. Recounting of ballot papers by the Tribunal is not specifically provided in the election rules, but it falls within the inherent powers of the Tribunal to decide the election dispute."

Mr. A Baset Majumder next argued that on remand the learned Election Tribunal after re-counting the ballot papers of the disputed 2 Centres, in presence of both the parties and their learned Advocates, dismissed the Election Petition on proper consideration of evidence, facts and circumstances on clear finding that the applicant made no grievance on 4-2-92 knowing the result of Waruk High School Centre and that at the time of recounting double seals on 187 ballot papers were found on Symbol “চাকা” created subsequently and that no remarkable discrepancy was found after recounting the ballot papers of Dopolla Janata High School Centre. The learned Appellate Tribunal on total disregard of the provisions of law and on wrong assessment of the evidence on record passed the impugned judgment and order declaring the applicant as chairman of No. 10 Tamta Union Parishad setting aside the judgment and order of the Election Tribunal cannot be sustained in law.

10. Mr. NH Khondaker, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the applicant opposite party No.1 submitted that the instant application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not maintainable. In support of his contention he referred to the Union Parishad Election Rules 13(4) which is as follows: "If any election petition is filed with the Tribunal calling in question the validity of any election, the deposits concerning that election shall neither be refunded to the candidate nor it shall be forfeited to the Union Fund till it is finally disposed of ." Mr. Khondaker by Annexure, 'I' issued by the Returning Officer dated 23-11-1992, annexed in his application for vacating the order of stay, showed that the opposite party petitioner Md. Humayun Kabir withdrew his security deposit of Taka 1,000.00 and submitted that the revision is the continuation of the election case and since the opposite party petitioner withdrew the security money before the final disposal of the matter, the instant revisional application is incompetent. Mr. NH Khondker submitted that the lower Appellate Court, being the final court of facts on proper consideration of the evidence on record, rightly passed the impugned judgment and order declaring the applicant as elected Chairman and it cannot be disturbed in revision. In support of his contention he referred the case of Jashimuddin Kanchan vs. Md. Ali Ashraf, reported in 42 DLR (AD) 289 wherein their Lordships have held that" finding based on due consideration of evidence was beyond the scope of revisional court to interfere with. "He next referred the case of Fakhruddin Mia and another vs. Mohammad Khodabaksh Sheikh, reported in 29 DLR (SC) 268 wherein their Lordships have held "High Court can interfere under section 115 where the lower Court's decision is based on conjecture. Finding based on facts is binding on the High Court both in its exercise of the revisional powers as also of its appellate power Mr. Khondaker also referred the case of Muktad Hossain Majumder vs. Abul Bashar Majumder and others, reported in 38 DLR 41 wherein it has been held Election Tribunal under Local Government Ordinance 1984, is not a civil Court, an appeal to the District Judge against the decision of Election Tribunal will be governed by the provisions of the Civil Procedure Code and submitted relying on those decisions that the Election Appellate Tribunal as Appellate Court on proper consideration of the evidence on record passed the impugned judgment and order and there is nothing to interfere. Mr. NH Khondaker, the learned Advocate, next submitted that by adopting unfair means the opposite party petitioner in collusion with the Presiding Officer and his associates managed to cast false votes on false personation of the persons who were already dead or out of the country and also created violence, in consequence of which the election result was materially affected. In support of his contention he referred to the case of Abdul Hannan vs. Election Tribunal, Cox's Bazar, Chittagong and another, reported in 31 DLR (AD) 191 wherein their Lordships have held that Election result when alleged to be materially affected, to be ascertained according to law of secrecy to be observed to a certain extent but not at the cost of defeating purpose of election. He next referred the case of Moulana Abdul Haque vs. Fuzlul Hoque and others, reported in 38 DLR 401 wherein it has been held that;

"Power to reopen ballot boxes and recount of votes (by the Election Tribunal) not provided for either in the Local Government (UP) Ordinance or the Union Parishad Election Rules, 1983 but just an outcome of the judicial decisions as clearly laid down from time to time. The principles stated in the judgments of the Higher Courts of law for recounting of votes underline certain conditions, such as, the Tribunal felt the necessity of counting the votes to satisfy itself as to correct counting by the Presiding Officer or that the issue raised in the election petition cannot be determined without recounting."

He also referred the case of Nadar Ali Khan vs. AKM Ahmedullah Chowdhury and others, reported in 39 DLR 193 wherein a Single Bench of this Court has held that;

A single corrupt practice by or on behalf of a candidate if proved sufficient for declaring the election void.

12. Mr. NH Khandaker lastly, contended relying on the decisions referred above by him, that the instant revisional application is not maintainable. Furthermore, the learned Election Appellate Tribunal, being final court of facts, on proper consideration of evidence on record and relevant law passed the judgment and order impugned before this court and there is nothing to interfere.

13. In reply to the first contention of Mr. NH Khondaker the learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr. A Baset Majumder submitted that the Election Rule l3(4) relates only with the final decision of the Election Tribunal. The Local Government (Union Parishad) (Amendment) Ordinance 1984, Ordinance (XLIV of 1984) provided for an appeal against the judgment and order of the Election Tribunal which is as follows:

(4) Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Election Tribunal may, within thirty days of the announcement of the decision, prefer an appeal to the District Judge within whose jurisdiction the election dispute was held; and the decision of the District Judge on such appeal shall be final.

"No bar or embargo has been put by this Ordinance debarring filing any revisional application against any order of the Election Appellate Tribunal if the security deposit is withdrawn prior to filing of revisional application before this court. The amendment of the Rule under Ordinance XLIV Rule 2(4) provides that District Judge's judgment and order on appeal shall be final and the finality ends on appeal and, as such, the revisional application is quite competent."

14. Heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and perused the record.

15. Regarding the first contention raised by Mr. NH Khondakder on maintainability of this instant revisional application I find that the Union Parishad Election Procedure and Rules 13(4) provides that the deposit concerning the election shall neither be refunded to the candidate nor it shall be forfeited to the Union Fund till it is finally disposed of Subsequently in pursuance of Ordinance No. XLIV of 1984 by amendment an appeal has been provided under Rule 2(4) which is as follows:

"Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Election Tribunal may, within thirty days of the announcement of the decision, prefer an appeal to the District Judge within whose jurisdiction the election in dispute was held; and the decision of the District Judge on such appeal shall be final".

So finality of the Election Tribunal Proceeding comes to an end after the decision of the appeal. Furthermore, nowhere in the Rules there is anything to show that after withdrawal of the security deposit preferring a revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the appellate order, which ended in finality, is a bar. I find no substance in the submissions of Mr. NH Khondaker, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1

16. On careful perusal of the impugned judgment as well of the trial Court, it appears that there are certain admitted facts. The applicant having the symbol of “আনারস” contested for the post of Chairman of No.10 Tamta Union Parishad along with 6 others having various symbols including the opposite party petitioner who had the symbol of “চাকা” There were 3 wards in that Union Parished having 7 centres and the election was held on 3-2-92 and the present petitioner was declared chairman elected. Opposite party No.1 being applicant filed the Election Petition No. 8 of 1992. The learned Election Tribunal who held the trial dismissed the case. On appeal the Appellate Court sent back the case on remand directing the Election Tribunal to recount the ballot papers of two centres namely; Waruk High School and Dopolla Janata High School Centres again with a further direction that, if he feels, evidence may be taken and thereafter to write out a proper judgment. Accordingly the trial Court on 23-5-93, in presence of both the parties and also the learned Advocates of both the sides, opened the gunny bags containing the ballot papers of both the  centres for re-counting. After re-counting negligible difference was found in Dopollah Janata High School Centre with respect to the used and unused ballot papers In Waruk High School Centre it was found that symbol “আনারস” secured 444 votes, symbol secured 1450 votes, symbol “হরিণ” secured 2 votes symbol “চেয়ার” secured 60 votes, symbol “মোমবাতি” secured 51, votes, symbol “ছাতা” secured 115 votes and symbol “হাঁস” secured 16 votes. Amongst the 117 previous spoiled ballot papers 17 were found valid which were added to other symbols. But out of 195 ballot papers there were several seals in 8 ballots of different candidates and in 187 ballots seals were put both in symbo “আনারস” and “চাকা” Naturally, a question arose whether the counting after poll was made along with double seals earlier or double seals were put subsequently at any point of time. Though it is the case of the applicant that in Waruq High School Centre opposite party petitioner secured 1541 votes but on recount it came down to 1450. It was the allegation that 31 votes were spoiled and 100 valid votes were included making it 131 votes. There is no evidence on record to show that 100 votes of the applicant were valid but on scrutiny in 100 ballots the Tribunal found that there were no seals.

<u>17. In the application dated 4-2-92 before the Returning Officer no objection was raised regarding those double seals but the fact remains that no objection regarding casting of false votes or putting double seals in the ballot papers were raised nor any prayer was made before the Presiding Officer for recounting. In the instant case the Election Tribunal itself could not say and was not in a position to say whether the double marks were put during election or the acts of some interested persons afterwards. In such a position their Lordships of the Appellate Division, on the similar facts, have held in the case reported in 38 DLR (AD) 275, 276 that; "When the Tribunal itself was not in a position to say whether the double marks were post-election acts or were the doings of the respective voters, election of the returned candidate should not have been interfered with. It is not a case of benefit of going to a defeated candidate feeling aggrieved like the accused in a criminal case. Here, presumption is in favour of the returned candidate, whose election shall not be declared a nullity unless the Tribunal "is satisfied" as laid down in Rule 49, that the election has been materially affected by some illegal acts or contravention of some Rules. "In this particular case opposite party petitioner was declared elected and challenging the declaration applicant opposite-party No. 1 filed Election Tribunal Case No. 8 of 1992 which was dismissed and against that an appeal was preferred being Election Tribunal Appeal No. 4 of 1992. The learned Appellate Tribunal after hearing assessed the evidence on record in its entirety and felt it necessary for ends of justice that the recounting should be made with respect to the two centres namely; Waruk High School Centre and Dopolla Janata High School Centre and sent back the case on remand to the Tribunal. Accordingly, the tribunal after re-counting again declared the opposite party petitioner as the successful candidate. As against this judgment and order Tribunal Appeal No. 6 of 1993 was preferred. On perusal of the impugned judgment and order it appears that the case was sent back on remand to the Tribunal only for recounting the ballot papers of 2 centres named aforesaid, the learned appellate tribunal committed an illegality in reopening the whole case and assessing the evidence again in its entirety and passed the impugned judgment and order contradicting his earlier findings totally ignoring the dispute in question. On careful consideration of the evidence and the impugned judgment and order, it appears that the learned Appellate Tribunal on conjecture found that though the applicant secured 112 votes more than the opposite party petitioner the Presiding Officers in collusion with Assistant Presiding Officer by putting double seals on 187 ballot papers declared the opposite party petitioner elected and that the Election Tribunal by his judgment and order dated 31-05-93 also illegally declared him elected. This finding appears to me is based on no evidence on record and as such, his decision cannot be sustained in law.</u>

<u>18. Admittedly no written prayer was filed before the Presiding Officer for recounting of the ballot papers on any allegation of malpractice and admittedly the tribunal did not find that the election has been materially affected by any corrupt practice or violation of any Election Rule, the appellate tribunal committed an illegality in not at all considering these legal aspects of the matters. Furthermore, the tribunal itself when was not in a position to say whether the double marks on ballot papers were post-election acts or were the subsequent doings of the respective voters, the election of the petitioner cannot be interfered with. In such a position the presumption is always in favour of the returned candidate which cannot be declared a nullity unless the tribunal "is satisfied" as laid down in Rule 49, that election has been materially affected by some illegal acts or contravention of some Rules. In view of the principles laid down by their Lordships in the aforesaid decision reported in 38 DLR (AD) 275, 276, exactly on the similar facts, the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned appellate tribunal is liable to be set aside.</u>

19. There is no dispute regarding the principles laid down in the decisions referred by the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1 but those are quite distinguishable and are not applicable in the instant case. The learned Advocate failed to show anything that there was any ground for recounting which the applicant-opposite party No. 1 prepared from the very inception by filing any application to the Presiding Officers or the election was affected materially for malpractice or violation of any election rules. The learned Advocate also failed to show that the Election Tribunal committed any illegality in dismissing the election case of the applicant twice and declaring the petitioner as chairman elected in contravention of any election rules.

<u>20. Recounting of votes by the Election Tribunal not provided under the Election Rules but an outcome of judicial decisions of Higher Courts but in the absence of clear justification recounting should not be ordered. Furthermore, there must be preparation of grounds for re-counting from the time immediately polling is over and that when no prayer for recounting was made initially to the Presiding Officer the prayer for recounting cannot be allowed. Admittedly in the absence of these requirements of law, the appellate Tribunal committed an illegality in sending the case back on remand for recounting of votes of two centres, consequently the judgment and order passed by him impugned before this court is liable to be set aside.</u>

21. In view of the discussions and decisions referred above I find that the learned Appellate Tribunal committed an illegality in setting aside the judgment and order of the Election Tribunal and declaring the applicant opposite party No. 1 as elected Chairman of No. 10 Tamta Union Parishad, and cannot be sustained in law and is liable to be set aside.

22. In the result the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The judgment and order passed by District Judge and Election Appellate Tribunal, Chandpur on 31-10-93 in Election Tribunal Appeal No. 6 of 1993 is hereby set aside and the judgment and order passed by Assistant Judge and Election Tribunal, Chandpur on 31-5-93 in Election Tribunal Case No. 1 of 1993 is hereby restored and affirmed.

The order of stay granted earlier by this court is hereby vacated.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and is directed against the judgment and order dated 14.9.89 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Chandpur, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 3 of 1989 reversing those dated 31.12.83 of the Assistant Judge, Matlob Upazila in connection with an application for temporary injunction under Order 39 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure in Title Suit No. 32 of 1988.

2. Short facts giving rise to this Rule are as follows:

The plaintiffs-petitioners instituted the above suit in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Matlob Upazila within the district of Chandpur praying for permanent injunction against the defendant opposite parties so that defendant No. 1 through the disputed LA Case No. 4/87-88 cannot acquire plaintiffs Kha schedule land out of Ka schedule land as described in the plaint for alleged development of Farajikandi Complex of defendant No. 2 and that defendant No. 2 may not go into the possession of the suit-land and/or break any door or window of the house of the plaintiffs situated thereon and also may not interfere with their peaceful possession over the same in any way. The plaintiff's case briefly is, that they acquired the suit-property by way of purchase and exchange in all 1.73 acres of land and then dug up a tank thereupon in plot No. 1368, measuring 0.92 acre and plot No. 1369, measuring 0.56 acre and also constructed a house upon the suit-plot No. 2126, measuring 0.25 acre of land; that they also planted trees upon the banks of the tank and continued rearing fishes in the tank by spending huge amount of money; that their predecessor-in-interest Kadam was a refugee from India and that the defendant No. 2 started an orphanage house named Farajikandi Complex, but he in collusion with the Land Acquisition Officers and others without serving any notice upon the plaintiffs illegally proceeded with the acquisition of the schedule-lands to make the plaintiffs homeless, though the said land is not necessary for the aforesaid complex; that the defendants were trying to forcefully take possession of the suit-lands. Hence the above suit by the plaintiffs for permanent injunction.

3. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed written statement to contest the suit by denying the material allegations made in the plaint and also by raising some questions of law including the question of maintainability of the suit, the same being hit by sections 43 and 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. II of 1982). Similarly, defendant No. 2 filed another written statement to contest the suit by making similar averments in his written statement including the question of maintainability of the suit. After the institution of the suit, the plaintiffs filed an application under Order 39 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for temporary injunction till disposal of the suit by restraining the defendant No. 1 from acquiring the said Kha schedule lands of the plaintiffs through the process of the disputed LA Case No. 4/87-88 and from delivering possession thereof to defendant No. 2 and also from interfering with the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs in the suit-lands and from breaking any door and window of their house. The defendant No.1 as well as defendant No. 2 filed two separate written objections against the application for temporary injunction by making almost the similar averments to the effect that the statements made in the application for temporary injunction are false, imaginary and concocted and there is no cause of action for the application and that the application for temporary injunction is not maintainable in view of the bar under section 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982 and it has been further contended in the written objection that in the Farajikandi Complex of Matlob Upazila, there are about 300 orphans being brought up and given education and the main source of income of that orphanage was a tank measuring 4 acres of land which was acquired by the Government in the year 1986 for construction of Meghna Dhona Goda Bandh by the Government, as a result, the orphanage fell in serious pecuniary hardships and hence the Executive Committee of the Orphanage in a meeting held on 4.7.87 decided to make a prayer for acquisition of the land concerned for digging out another tank over about 4/5 acres of land including the complex's other lands measuring 2.50 acres to make an alternative source of income for the orphanage, and accordingly, the Deputy Commissioner, Chandpur was approached who being satisfied with the requirement of the Complex-Defendant No. 2 started the acquisition process of the lands including the suit land of the plaintiffs. The proposal for acquisition of the said lands was accepted and finally Government also approved the same. Meanwhile, the Deputy Commissioner issued notices under section 3 of Acquisition and Requisition of the Immovable Property Ordinance 1982 and published the same according to law and thereafter another notice under section 6 of the said Ordinance was also published and served. It has been further alleged in the written objection that on enquiry no pond was found on Plot Nos. 1368 and 1369 as claimed by the plaintiffs and no trees allegedly planted on the bank of the said tank were also found and further there was no earth filling in Plot No. 2126 by the plaintiffs by spending any money as alleged and there was no suppression of the notice of LA Case No. 4/87-88 as alleged and that the plaintiffs did not raise any objection against the acquisition when the notices were served under section 6 of the Ordinance and that the contesting defendants did not hire or procure any lathial to forcibly take possession of the suit-land as alleged. The learned Assistant Judge after hearing the parties and on consideration of the facts of the case and the averments made in the application for temporary injunction and also the written objection, framed the following points for determination;

1. Whether there was any prima facie case for injunction in favour of the plaintiffs.

2. Whether the balance of convenience and inconvenience was in favour of the plaintiffs.

3. Whether the plaintiffs would suffer irreparable loss if no temporary injunction is granted.

The learned Assistant Judge on consideration of the materials on record and the facts of the case found that the plaintiffs have prima facie case only in respect to Plot No. 2126 measuring .25 acre and not in respect of other plots of the suit land and also found the balance of convenience and inconvenience in favour of the plaintiffs and regarding the 3rd point about the irreparable loss he decided it in favour of the plaintiffs and ultimately held that the plaintiffs are entitled to get .temporary injunction only in respect of plot No. 2126 measuring .25 acre of the suit land and accordingly granted temporary injunction in-part in a modified form against the contesting defendant No. 2 on contest and ex parte against others by his judgment and order dated 31.12.88. Being aggrieved by the same, the contesting defendant No. 2 Farajikandi Complex preferred an appeal being Misc. Appeal No. 3 of 1989 before the District Judge, Chandpur, which was transferred to the court of the learned Subordinate Judge Chandpur for disposal who after hearing both the sides was pleased to find that the learned Assistant Judge failed to correctly understand and appreciate the provisions of sections 43 and 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance by which civil Court's jurisdiction has been excluded from calling in question any order passed or action taken by the Requisitioning or Acquisitioning Authority under the said Ordinance and also there is a clear bar against granting any injunction in respect of the requisitioned or acquisitioned property and considering that point alone, the learned Subordinate Judge has allowed the appeal and set aside the order of temporary injunction granted by the learned Assistant Judge. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge, the plaintiffs moved the present revisional application and obtained the present Rule.

<u>4. Mr. Md. Lutfor Rahman Mandol, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiffs-petitioners, has submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge misconceived and misconstrued the provisions of section 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 and also failed to appreciate the above provisions of law in the facts and circumstances of the present case and committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision which has occasioned a failure of justice by setting aside the impugned order of temporary injunction granted by the learned Assistant Judge in favour of the plaintiffs-petitioners. His further submission is that the exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil Court by section 44 of the aforesaid Ordinance should be deemed not to be absolute, if the order passed or any action taken under the said Ordinance is a collusive and malafide one and for collateral purposes, then it will be an order or action without jurisdiction and in that case in spite of the bar in section 44 of the Ordinance, the civil Court shall have jurisdiction to examine the propriety of the impugned order or the action in exercise of the power vested in it under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the instant case his main grievance is that no notice under section 3, 6 or 7 of the aforesaid Ordinance has been served upon the plaintiff in the LA Case though their ownership over the suit land is not disputed. In order to show non-service of the said notices, upon the plaintiffs, they have filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure with a supplementary affidavit along with some annexures relating to issuance of notices in the relevant land-acquisition case, of course at a very belated stage after conclusion of the hearing of this Rule by which they have advanced a prayer for calling for the records of LA Case to see whether notice as required under the law was at all served upon the plaintiffs. It has been further contended on behalf of the plaintiffs that the suit plot No. 2126 has not been included in the sketch map of the LA Case prepared by the Acquisitioning and Requisitioning Authority for the Farajikandi Complex, but in spite of that, the said plot has been brought under acquisition process and this action of the Acquisitioning and Requisitioning Authority is palpably malafide and illegal and hence without jurisdiction that being the position, the civil Court has jurisdiction to entertain the suit to examine the propriety of the LA Case and pass the order of injunction in favour of the plaintiffs being satisfied with the other requirements for granting temporary injunction. In support of his contentions, the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-petitioners has referred to a number of decisions some of which may be cited here namely, the decisions reported in 9 DLR 26, 17 DLR (SC) 515, Law Reports Appeal Cases 1969 Vol. II page 147, 37 DLR (AD) 161, 34 DLR (AD) 222 and AIR 1940 PC 105.</u>

5. Mr. Zillul Haque, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant opposite party No. 1 the Farazikandi Complex, on the other hand, has contended that there is no illegality in the impugned order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in appeal and the same has not occasioned any failure of justice. His further contention is that the civil Court's jurisdiction has been expressly and clearly barred by section 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 and hence neither the suit nor the application for temporary injunction out of the same is at all maintainable in law and so far the allegation of non service of notice upon the plaintiffs-petitioners, it appears that for the first time this question of fact has been raised before this court while exercising revisional jurisdiction, with an attempt to show that the order passed or action taken in the process of the acquisition of the suit lands under the aforesaid Ordinance is a malafide one. The learned Advocate for the opposite party, on the other hand, submits that the notices as required under the law were duly published and served. He has further submitted that neither in the plaint nor in the application for temporary injunction, the question of non-service of notice or any malafide action on the part of the Acquisitioning or Requisitioning Authority has been alleged and in the plaint of the suit, no prayer for setting aside any malafide order or action as now alleged has been made. The suit is only for permanent injunction against the defendants without any prayer for declaration of plaintiffs title or interest in the suit land. There is also no prayer for any declaration that any order passed or action taken under the said Ordinance is malafide, unlawful or without jurisdiction. Next, Mr. Haque contends that the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly found that the judgment and order of the trial Court in the matter of temporary injunction is illegal and without jurisdiction due to the bar of sections 43 and 44 of the said Ordinance also due to misreading of some material document, namely the sketch map of the LA Case, which very well shows that the suit plot No. 2126 measuring 0.25 acre is already included in the sketch map as prepared for the acquisition of the lands under the LA Case in question. The learned Advocate for the Opposite Party seriously objected to the filing of the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the supplementary affidavit by the petitioner after conclusion of the hearing of the case and he has also contended that there is no scope for entertaining such application or affidavit to determine a question of fact as to the service of notice in the LA Case without urging such point at the trial Court. He has further argued that the question of jurisdiction is a very vital matter and the statute ousting jurisdiction of civil Court must be strictly construed and in this connection he has referred to a decision in the case of Abdul Waheed Khan Vs. Bhawani and others reported in AIR 1966(SC) 1718. As to the application of Section 44 of the Ordinance, the learned Advocate for the opposite party has referred to a decision in the case of Ali Jan Khan & ors. Vs. Bangladesh & ors reported in 37 DLR (AD) 161. By drawing our attention to the provisions of section 44 of the said Ordinance, he has submitted that not only in a suit but also in an application against any order passed or any action taken under the said Ordinance, civil Court's jurisdiction has been barred and also granting of any injunction has been prohibited in clear term by any court in respect of any order passed or action taken or to be taken under the said Ordinance. Therefore, his submission is, that in any view of the matter, granting of injunction by the Assistant Judge was barred under the law; hence it was without jurisdiction and the learned Subordinate Judge has very rightly held that the impugned order of the Assistant Judge is wholly illegal and without jurisdiction and accordingly set aside the same.

<u>6. I have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the application and all other relevant papers available in the case-record including the impugned order of the learned Assistant Judge. Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure is the section relating to the jurisdiction of a civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure and it reads as follows:</u>

<u>"The Courts shall (subject to the provisions herein contained) have jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suits of which the cognizance is either expressly or impliedly barred".</u>

<u>In interpreting this section, it has been held in numerous decisions of the highest Court of this sub-continent that exclusion of jurisdiction of a civil Court should not be readily inferred. On a plain reading of the section, it appears that a civil Court has jurisdiction to try all suits of civil nature excepting suits of which their cognizance has either expressly or impliedly been barred by law. By way of interpretation of the above section of the Code in different cases, it has been further held that even if there is an express bar of civil Court's jurisdiction in respect of cognizance in a matter but if the order passed or action taken by any authority or person is a malafide one, in such cases in spite of such bar, the civil Court shall have jurisdiction to entertain a suit as because an order passed or action taken which is malalide one and consequently it is an order or action deemed to be without jurisdiction and in such cases, the civil Court shall not lose its jurisdiction to see whether the order passed or action taken, is in conformity with the law in question. In this regard we may look into some of the decisions as cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioners, one in the case of Province of East Bengal Vs. Dewan A Ali reported in 9 DLR 26, it has been held by their Lordships of a Division Bench as follows :</u>

<u>'The mere presence of an alternative machinery is not by itself sufficient to oust the jurisdiction of the civil Courts; even the existence of express provision in that behalf coupled with the alternative machinery may not always have the effect of completely ousting the said jurisdiction in all cases, e.g., where assessment is made in respect of an item of income which is not assessable under taxing Act, civil suit would lie to recover it, inasmuch as the officer making the assessment had jurisdiction to make it.</u>

<u>The bar created by section 65 of the Bengal Agricultural Income Tax Act will be operative only when the subject matter of the suit is a matter which falls strictly within the competence of the taxing authorities to determine, and that too only if no question of fraud or abuse of the machinery provided by the Statute is involved".</u>

<u>"It is also well-settled that even if jurisdiction is so excluded, the civil Courts have jurisdiction to examine into cases where the provisions of the Act have not been complied with, or the Statutory Tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure". This decision is based on the famous case of Secretary of State Vs. Mask & Co (PC) reported in 67 IA at page 222."</u>

<u>In the case of Abdul Rauf and others Vs. Abdul Hamid Khan and others reported in 17 DLR (SC) 515, it has been held as under.</u>

<u>"A malafide act is by its nature an act without jurisdiction. A malafide order is a fraud on the statute. It may be explained that a malafide order means one which is passed not for the purpose contemplated by the enactment granting the power to pass the order, but for some other collateral or ulterior purpose."</u>

<u>In the case of the Secretary of State Vs. Mask & Co. as reported in 67 IA 222 as well as in AIR 1940 (PC) 105, it has been held as follows:</u>

<u>"The exclusion of the jurisdiction of the civil Courts is not to be readily inferred but such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied. Even if jurisdiction is so excluded, the civil Courts have jurisdiction to examine into cases where the provisions of the Act have not been complied with, or the statutory tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure".</u>

<u>The jurisdiction of the civil Court in the instant case has been expressly barred under section 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 which reads as follows:</u>

<u>"Section 44. Bar to jurisdiction of Court: Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Ordinance, no Court shall entertain any suit or application against any order passed or any action taken under this Ordinance, and no injunction shall be granted by any Court in respect of any action taken or to be taken in pursuance of any power conferred by or under this Ordinance."</u>

<u>A bare reading of the section shows that the jurisdiction of the civil Court has been clearly and expressly barred from entertaining any suit or application against an order passed or action taken under this Ordinance; but question is whether in spite of such bar, if it is found that any malafide order is passed or action taken with an ulterior motive for any collateral purpose, in that case, the civil Court will be barred from entertaining any suit or application. In view of the above decisions, the civil Court shall not totally be incompetent to examine the propriety and legality of such malafide order or action, particularly to examine whether such order has been passed or action taken is or was in accordance with the law in question. In the instant case, of course, no final order of acquisition appears to have been passed. In the midst of the process of acquisition, the plaintiffs have instituted the suit simply praying for permanent injunction without challenging any order or action of the Acquisitioning or Requisitioning authority as malafide or without jurisdiction; of course, the grievances now raised before this Court are, inter alia, that no notice of acquisition of the suit-land under sections 3, 6 or 7 of the said Ordinance has been served upon the plaintiffs-petitioners and that the acquisition process has been started with ulterior motive only to oust the plaintiffs petitioners from the suit-lands and that there is no requirement of the suit-land for the purpose of the Complex in question. But to consider and verify the above submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners, there is no sufficient materials before Court. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has tried to introduce some papers by a supplementary affidavit after the conclusion of the hearing of this case, to show the non-service of notices upon the plaintiff-petitioners, but the matter relates to a question of fact which having not been raised before the trial Court, I don't think it proper to allow it to be raised here and take into consideration the supplementary affidavit at this stage in revision in an interlocutory matter. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has also filed an application under section 151 CPC with a prayer for calling for the records of the LA Case in the same way after conclusion of the hearing of this case which also I do not think proper to entertain at this stage in connection with an interlocutory matter for temporary injunction. The suit is still pending before the trial Court, the plaintiff-petitioners, if they so desire, may however make such prayer before the trial Court and produce the papers annexed to the supplementary affidavit before the trial Court. I have perused the application for temporary injunction of the plaintiffs and the order passed thereon by the learned Assistant Judge. It appears that the trial Court partly allowed the prayer for temporary injunction in favour of the plaintiffs with respect to only Plot No. 2126 on the basis of a finding that the said plot does not appear in the sketch map prepared for showing the quantity and plots of lands required for acquisition in connection with the complex, but on scrutiny of the sketch-map, it is found that the suit-plot is very well within the sketch-map comprising the lands required for the said acquisition. Hence, it is clear that the learned Assistant Judge absolutely on a wrong view of the sketch map in respect of Plot No. 2126 of the suit-land allowed the application for temporary injunction in part. The learned Subordinate Judge has of course not examined that part of the finding of fact of the Assistant Judge, but absolutely on a question of law holding that the application for injunction is barred under section 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, allowed the appeal on the contesting defendant and set aside the judgment and order of the trial Court. From a simple reading of section 44 of the Ordinance, it appears to me that power of granting injunction by any Court in respect of any order passed or action taken or to be taken in pursuance of the power under the said Ordinance has been expressly taken away and the learned Subordinate Judge appears to have rightly taken the view that the application for temporary injunction in the instant case is not at all maintainable, as the same is hit by section 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982 and he has rightly observed that the Assistant Judge has misconceived the facts of the case and also the provision of sections 43 and 44 of the said Ordinance. Section 43 is an indemnity clause in the said Ordinance which reads as follows:</u>

<u>"43 Indemnity–No suit prosecution or other legal proceeding shall lie against any person for anything which is in good faith done or intended to be done in pursuance of this Ordinance or any order or rule made thereunder".</u>

<u>This indemnity clause relates to any person by whom anything is done under this ordinance in good faith or intended to be done in pursuance to the Ordinance or any order or rule made thereunder, in such circumstances, no suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding would lie against him. This is not with regard to any legal bar in respect of the jurisdiction of the civil Court regarding any order or action of any authority or person. The legal bar in respect of such matter is found in section 44 of the said Ordinance. For the reason stated above, I am of the view that there is no illegality in the impugned order of the learned Subordinate Judge and the same has not occasioned any failure of justice. Hence, no inference is called for by this Court in Revision.</u>

7. In the result, the Rule is accordingly discharged without any order as to costs.

Let the lower court's records be sent down at once will a copy of this judgment.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and order dated November 28, 1991 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 343 of 1987).
full_judgment:
MH Rahman, J.: The appeal and the two petitions were heard together and are now disposed by this judgment. The appeal, at the instance of the Government, is directed against the High Court Division's judgment and order dated November 28, 1991 passed in Writ Petition No. 343 of 1987, striking down an acquisition notification.

2. In their Writ Petition before the High Court Division respondent Nos. 1-3, was her men by profession, challenged the acquisition asserting, inter alia, that as owners in possession they have been using the case land from time immemorial, as the vacant northern portion of their ancestral homestead, for washing and drying clothes. In the first week of January, 1985 they came to know that the Authorised Officer and Land Acquisition Officer, Dhaka in June, 1984 issued a notice under section 3 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. II of 1982) for acquisition of their said lands in LA Case No. 49/1983-84 for extension of Darul Ulum Ahsania Madrassa. The notice was suppressed and not served on them. On January 21, 1985 the respondents filed an objection before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA), Dhaka, but having had no response thereto they filed another objection petition on February 6, 1985 before the Joint Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, but that objection petition was rejected without giving any hearing to them. On April 6, 1985 the respondents filed another objection petition before the Minister of Land Administration and Land Reforms who was pleased to direct the Land Reforms Commissioner to enquire into the matter. After an open and on the spot enquiry into the matter the Commissioner submitted his report clearly holding that the case land was not essential for the alleged purpose of acquisition and that there was sufficient vacant space in the Madrassa premises as well as in the adjoining area which could be acquired for extension of the Madrassa in question. By an order dated June 6, 1985 the respondents were informed that the Government decided not to acquire the case land of the petitioners and requested the Additional Deputy Commissioner to annul all actions taken in this regard and that if the requiring body still insisted on acquisition of land, alternative sites should be selected. In spite of the aforesaid decision of the Government the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, proceeded with acquisition of the case land and published the impugned notification on November 6, 1986 finally acquiring the case land.

3. The appellant's case is, that the respondents land was validly acquired for a public purpose and that on reconsideration the order dated June 4, 1985 was cancelled by the Government by another order dated September 9, 1985, and, thereafter, the acquisition proceedings were completed by issuing the impugned Notification dated November 6, 1986.

4. The High Court Division did not accept the respondents two main contentions that the purpose for which the property was acquired was not a public purpose and that the subsequent Government decision not to proceed with acquisition was malafide. It, however, accepted the respondents new submission, made at the time of the hearing, that the requiring body having not deposited the compensation money within 6 months from the date of decision of the Government to acquire the property all proceedings in respect of acquisition stood abated under section 12.

5. The High Court Division held that the time for payment for compensation began to run from January 5, 1985 when the decision to acquire the property was made and notice under section 6 was signed. On May 28, 1985 the requiring body was asked to deposit the money, but the requiring body made the deposit on February 17, 1986. The High Court Division observed that "it can at best be said that the acquisition proceeding remained stayed" from the period from June 4, 1985, the date of annulment of acquisition, to September 22, 1985, the date of communication to the Deputy Commissioner cancelling the annulment. It was held that even excluding that period from June, 4, 1985 to September 22, 1985 the deposit made by the requiring body on February 17, 1986 was not made within six months from the final decision to acquire the property on January 5, 1985.

6. Mr. Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Additional Attorney-General, at first urged that the Government's decision dated June 4, 1985 to annul the acquisition proceedings had the effect of wiping out the previous proceedings, and by the subsequent order dated September 4, 1985 a fresh acquisition proceeding was started after annulment, and hence either September 4, 1985 or September 22, 1985 when the order was communicated to the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka ought to have been taken as the starting point of limitation of six months for deposit of compensation and as the deposit was made on February 17, 1986 by the requiring body within the period of six months specified in section 12 there was no contravention of that section.

7. Knowing well that the acquisition proceeding was not, in fact, started by issuing fresh notices of acquisition, etc. the learned Additional Attorney-General did not press the above contention. Instead, he submitted that the High Court Division erroneously upheld the petitioner's contention, made impromptu during the hearing, about violation of section 12 of the Ordinance, when there was no such averment either in the petition or in the affidavit-in-reply of the writ petitioners. It was submitted that the respondents had all along been challenging the order of acquisition and for their own fault no compensation could be paid in time.

8. Mr. Fazlul Karim, the learned Counsel for respondents Nos. 1 to 3, however, urged that under section 15 of the Ordinance there must be an agreement and deposit of compensation money with the acquiring authority before any notice for acquisition of property for a non-Government requiring body like a private Madrassa can be made and that the belated deposit of fund for compensation by the requiring-body indicates that there had been no agreement between the Government and the requiring-body before the notices for acquisition were issued. This plea, not urged before, does not call for any scrutiny. The requiring-body may be asked to deposit the compensation money only after the decision to acquire is finally made by the Government. Sub-section (1) of section 12 reads as follows:

"12. Abatement or Revocation of Acquisition Proceedings: (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Ordinance, where in any case compensation has not been paid or deposited within a period of six months from the date of decision of the Government, the Divisional Commissioner, or the Deputy Commissioner, as the case, may be, for acquisition of the property under section 5 or the proviso to section 4(3) (b), as the case may be, for no fault of the person interested, all proceedings in respect of such acquisition shall, on the expiry of that period, stand abated and a declaration by the Deputy Commissioner to that effect shall be published in the official Gazette. (The period of six months was substituted by one year by section 2 of Act XVI of 1987)"

9. The expression "compensation has not been paid or deposited within six months from the date of decision" for acquisition in sub-section (1) of Section 12 is to be understood with reference to section 10.

10. Section 10 provides for payment of compensation:

"(1) On making an award under section 7, the Deputy Commissioner shall, before taking possession of the property, tender payment of the compensation awarded by him to the persons entitled thereto according to the award, and shall pay it to them unless prevented by some one or more of the contingencies mentioned in sub-section (2).

(2) If the persons entitled to compensation do not consent to receive it, or if there be no person competent to receive the compensation or, if there be any dispute as to title to receive the compensation or as to the appointment of it, the Deputy Commissioner shall keep the amount of the compensation in a deposit account in the Public Account of the Republic which shall be deemed payment for the purpose of taking over possession of the property without any prejudice to the claim of the parties to be determined by the Arbitrator…………..

<u>11. The provision of section 12 will come into play only when the compensation is not paid to the persons interested or not kept in a deposit account in the Public Account of the Republic under sub-section (1) of section 10. Under section 12 no obligation as such is placed on the requiring body to deposit compensation within six months from the date of decision for acquisition.</u>

12. From annexure 'E' to the writ petition it appears a notice under section 6 was served upon the persons interested in the property to appear before the authorised officer by January 22, 1985 for stating the nature of their interest in the property and the amount and particulars of their claims to compensation for such interest. Instead of appearing before the authorised officer on January 22, 1985, the petitioners filed a day before, on January 21, 1985 an objection petition before the Joint Secretary. The writ petitioners, always busy with their successive petitions objecting to the acquisition, had no occasion to complain about non-payment of compensation. It was because of the writ petitioners the process of making award and payment of compensation stalled.

13. There could be no averment and there is none, in the writ petition that no compensation was paid under sub-section (1) of section 10 or there was any occasion for deposit of the compensation in a deposit account in the Public Account of the Republic as per provision of sub-section (2) of that section the question of invoking section 12 does not arise. It is only in case of non-compliance of the provisions of section 10 the question of abatement or revocation of the acquisition proceeding will arise. The learned Judges of the High Court Division totally failed to examine this aspect of the matter and erroneously invoked section 12 and wrongly directed the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka to record an order to the effect that the acquisition proceeding stood abated.

14. In the result, Civil Appeal No. 20 of 1993 is allowed, but without any order as to cost.

15. No further order is necessary in Civil Petition No. 58 of 1992, filed by the requiring body, and, is accordingly disposed of.

<u>16. The petitioners in writ petition before the High Court Division filed civil petition for leave to appeal No. 58 of 1993 on February 22, 1993. The petition is time-barred by 354 days. On the top of the paper book it is described as civil petition, but on the cause list it is mentioned as cross petition for leave to appeal. The petitioner's explanation for the delay is that on February 6, 1993 they received the notice of granting leave in the appellant's leave petition No. 85 of 1992 and thereafter they filed the cross petition on February 22, 1993. There is no provision for filing cross petition for leave to appeal before this Court. Their explanation for condonation of the delay is not satisfactory. Civil Petition No. 58 of 1993 is dismissed as time-barred.</u>

Mustafa Kamal, J.: I agree with the judgment given by my learned brother MH Rahman J. I would like to add the following:

18. There is an all-round confusion as to the meaning of section 12. The owner of the land, the acquiring authority and the requiring body (it is a body other than the Government) are all harbouring the impression that an acquisition proceeding will abate under section 12 if the requiring body has not "paid" or "deposited" the compensation` money within a period of one year from the date of decision of the Government. That is not so.

<u>19. Under section 15, when any property is proposed to be acquired for any person other than the Government, such person shall enter into an agreement with the Government in a prescribed form before a notice under section 3 is published. The Deputy Commissioner has to tender and pay compensation to "the persons interested", before taking possession, to be assessed in terms of sections 8 and 9. The payment of compensation is regulated by section 10. It is either "paid" in terms of section 10(1) or "deposited" in terms of section 10(2). It is this "payment" and "deposit" in section 10 which is attracted in section 12, not the deposit of compensation by the requiring body. Reading all the sections together, sections 8, 9, 10, 12 and 15, it is clear that abatement will take place if the acquiring authority fails to "pay" or "deposit" compensation in terms of section 10 within one year from the date of decision of the Government (which is section 5 in the case of acquisition). The requiring body, therefore, will deposit the consideration money with the Government well ahead of expiry of one year from the date of decision of the Government, but within what date, is a subject matter of agreement between the Government and the requiring body under section 15. This is their internal arrangement, but legal consequence of abatement will follow only when the Government fails to "pay" or "deposit" compensation in terms of section 10.</u>

End.

Moulana Mokhtar Ahmed ------ Appellant 
Vs.
Mohammadul Huq Usmani & ors  ------ Respondents.
case_source: From the judgment dated 25-8-86 passed by the High Court Division, Circuit Bench, Chittagong, in Civil Revision Case No.187 of 1986.
full_judgment:
A.T.M. Afzal, J.- This appeal by special leave, at the instance of the elected chairman of No. 6 Jhilonza Union Parishad, Cox's Bazar arises from judgment and order dated 25 August 1986 passed by the High Court Division (Circuit Bench, Chittagong  in revision upholding the decision of the Election Tribunal), confirmed in appeal, declaring the election of the petitioner void and further declaring respondent No. 1 as Chairman of the said Union Parishad.

2. Chairman election for the aforesaid Union Parishad was held on 7.1.84. Appellant secured 4263 votes and his nearest rival respondent No. 1 secured 4236 votes. Thus the petitioner was declared elected by a margin of 27 votes.

3 Respondent No. 1 brought an election petition under Section 26 of the Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance 1983 before the Election Tribunal, Cox's Bazar making various allegations against the petitioner and in the matter of conducting the election and in counting of results. It was alleged that there was widespread adoption of unfair means, undue persuasion and influence, bribery and disorderly conduct near the polling station, that there was collusion between the presiding officers and the appellant, failure to maintain secrecy of voting breach of official duties, etc. and casting of votes in the name of dead persons and absentee voters. It was further alleges that the counting of votes was done under insufficient light and amid disturbed condition, that objection was raised demanding recounting of votes of all the centers but the said recounting was never done in spite of assurance given by the election officials.

4. The appellant contested the election petition by filing a written objection denying all the material allegations made by the respondent.

5. Several witnesses were examined on either side and documents proved in support of respective cases. During the pendency of the election petition as many as three Munsifs came in and acted as Election Tribunal at Cox's Bazar and finally the case record having been transferred by the Election Commission to the Upaziia Munsif, Chakaria, the judgment was delivered by the Election Tribunal, Chakaria on 23.12.85.

6. As to the allegation of illegality of irregularity in the conduct of the election the Tribunal found that they were not proved by proper evidence and the issue was answered in the negative. On the basis of recounting of ballots at the Tribunal, however, it was found ultimately that the respondent secured two votes more than the appellants. The Tribunal observed that the election result was materially affected by recounting before the Tribunal and it, therefore, declared the election of the appellant void and further declared the respondent as Chairman of the Union Parishad concerned.

7. The appellant unsuccessfully took an appeal against the decision of the Tribunal and then an unsuccessful revision against the appellate order.

<u>8. Coming to this Division with a prayer for leave to appeal, submissions were made disputing and raising question as to the recounting of ballots by the Tribunal which appeared to merit consideration as the appellant was unseated by a margin of two votes only by a process of recounting long after the election.</u>

<u>9. At the hearing of the appeal, however, Mr. T.H. Khan, learned counsel for the appellant frankly submitted that he does not dispute the authority and jurisdiction of the Election Tribunal to take recourse to recounting of ballots in a proper case. Indeed it is too late in the day to take exception to such jurisdiction of the Election Tribunal after all the pronouncements made by this court which have been noticed by the Appellate Tribunal and the High Court Division. Mr. Khan does not also seriously dispute that in the instant case, there was sufficient basis and evidence for allowing the prayer made on behalf of the respondent for re-counting of votes. Mr. Khan is obviously conscious of the findings made by the Tribunal in this behalf which read as follows In the above circumstances and facts the recounting by the Tribunal is not illegal and irregular, since the counting of the votes by the presiding officers were challenged and allegations made in the plaint", (Election Tribunal).</u>

10. The District Judge in appeal found; "Thus from the statements in the petition before the Tribunal and the statements of the P.Ws. recorded by the Tribunal it appears that the respondent petitioner has been able to prove that the counting of the ballot papers were not properly done and that some of the valid ballot papers were excluded from counting in favour of the respondent-petitioner and some invalid ballot papers were counted in favour of the appellant O.P. In the above circumstances. it has been clearly established that there were sufficient grounds for the Election Tribunal to dispose of the matter after recounting of the ballot papers."

11. Mr. Khan, however, raised objection as to the procedure adopted by the Tribunal in recounting the votes intermittently by different presiding officers of the Tribunal for more than a year and to the use of the consolidated result sheet (order dated 31-12-84) and ether notes (as in the order sheet ) kept with the record by preceding Munsifs, by the Election Tribunal which ultimately delivered the judgment on the basis of the records which were not prepared by it. We have examined order sheet of the Tribunal carefully in order to see if the result of the counting can be said to have become doubtful because of the procedure followed in the case to which objection has been taken.

12. It may he pointed out at the outset that it is not correct to say that the recounting went on for over a year. As a matter of fact the recounting began following the application by the respondent on 29 8.84 and concluded by Mr. Humayun Rashid, Munsif who left his office by the end of 1984. Before leaving he recorded the results of the recounting in his order dated 31.12.84. It is found from the Tribunal's judgment that the appellant wens on appeal against the order dated 31.12.84 and the same was dismissed by the District Judge, Even then the appellant went on filing applications against every order that was not to his advantage and the Tribunal upon hearing the parties and on the basis of record disposed of each objection giving reasons.

13. In the order dated 31.12.84, the Tribunal while bringing on record the result of the recounting mentioned that the ballot papers of four Centre’s, namely, Moktarkul Suratia Madrasa, Cox's Bazar College Centre, Madhya Jhilonja Primary School and South Kharulia Primary School were not examined minutely to see whether there was official seal or mark on the back of the ballot papers and the final judgment would be pronounced after doing that job. Order dated 24.3.85 shows that the aforesaid unfinished job was done on that date in presence of the party's lawyers and the Tribunal again recorded the results of recounting for all the seven centres where election was held. It has been clearly mentioned in the said order that only the valid and legal ballots have been counted in making the record of counting. It is found that the appellant by filing an application on that day prayed for re- consideration of "some ballots" of South Kharulia Primary School centre only which were rejected on the ground of "double seal" (later order shows it was "double mark" and not "double seal"). Thus the appellant, it seems, had no other grievance as to recounting except reconsideration of certain ballots of only one centre as aforesaid. Respondent raised objection to the prayer made and the Tribunal fixed 4.4.85 for hearing of the matter. Upon hearing on that date the Tribunal in its order dated 8.4.85 stated that the appellant claimed that there was valid seal On his symbol খেজুর গাছ on the disputed ballots but it is found upon scrutiny that there was seal on the symbol of another candidate which were however more indistinct than the former. The disputed ballots were again examined in presence of the parties and the tribunal mentioned in its order that no difference between the seals was visible by naked eye and it was held that the said ballots were correctly declared invalid. It was also mentioned in the said order that no proof was available of any post-election tampering of election materials. It seems that the appellant raised some new and further objections as to certain ballots and the Tribunal considered and rejected them.

<u>14. It will be seen that the succeeding Munsifs worked on the basis of the consolidated result sheet (order dated 31.12.84) and from time to time dealt with the applications as and when filed by the parties, particularly by the appellant raising objection for leaving out certain ballot papers from counting in his/their favour. We have found nothing illegal or irregular in the order sheet following the order dated 31.12.84. Each and every application filed thereafter has been considered properly and rejected on merit. The Tribunal in its final judgment has objectively disposed of each and every objection raised by the appellant in the matter of not counting particular ballot/ballots in his favour and counting some in favour of the respondent. No objection can be taken to the use of the matters on record of the case by the succeeding Munsifs because the law clearly provides for such use.</u>

15. Mr. Khan faintly raised an argument that the election materials were tam, pared with before recounting and as such result of the recounting could not be relied upon. In the order sheet of the Tribunal there is nothing to show that any objection was taken as to the alleged tampering of the election materials before recounting began. It is true that some gunny bags were in torn condition. The Appellate Tribunal upon noticing the evidence observed that;

"So it is presumed that the authority took all possible steps for protection and preservation of the bags containing the election materials for protection from subsequent mischief as the authorities were informed of the apprehension of the mischief beforehand and to keep the gunny bags in the same condition as those were just after the counting of ballot papers by the Election authorities. It may also be presumed that the torn condition of the gunny bag was there from the very beginning and that it was not done by either of the parties with malafide intention.

So, the presumption of the mischief committed by the respondent-petitioner as alleged by the appellant O.P, is not at all supported and established by the papers on record."

16. It appears from the order sheet that the counting was done on all the days in the presence of the parties, their lawyers and the Presiding Officers and both sides enthusiastically took part in tile process of re-counting, They were filing application after application in respect of particular ballot paper/papers either for counting in their favour or alleging illegal rejection. As already seen, each application was disposed of on merit and with reason. After all this long exercise before the Tribunal in the matter of re-counting, Mr. Khan has lightly refrained from arguing that a valid ballot paper was not counted in favour of the appellant or that an valid ballot paper was counted in favour of the respondent.

17. In view of the discussion above we find no substance in the contention ultimately raised by the learned counsel for the appellant and thus no scope to interfere legally with the impugned order upholding the concurrent decision of the Tribunal below, unfortunate it may seem though that the decision in the case turned on two marginal votes only.

18. The appeal is accordingly dismissed without any order as to cost.

End.
