parties:
Md Shajahan ------ Appellant 
vs
Md Sadeq & another ------ Respondents
case_source: From the judgment and order dated 16-7-1985 passed by the High Court Division, Comilla Bench, in Civil Revision No. 102 of 1985.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed J : Appellant before us is a defeated candidate for election to the office of Chairman of Yakubpur Union Parishad in the district of Feni. The election was held on 28 December 1983 and respondent No. 1 was declared elected by the Returning Officer with a small majority of 17 votes (2326-2309=17). The appellant challenged the election by an election Petition under the Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance, 1983, before the Munsif-cum-Election Tribunal, Daganbhuiyan, bringing a number of allegations which related to the election to the election held in one of the three Polling Stations, namely Dudmukha High School Centre, the election held in the other two Polling Stations remaining unchallenged. The allegations were that the returned candidate, respondent No.1, had adopted unfair means, such as, he had influenced the Presiding Officer who rejected some of his valid votes as invalid and accepted some invalid votes of the returned candidate as valid votes, that votes of some dead and absence voters were cast in the election and that the Presiding Officer at first declared a result which showed him (appellant) the winner, but later on, submitted a different result to the Returning Officer and consequently he was defeated in the election. To be specific on this point, his allegation was that he had obtained 498 votes and the respondent had obtained 1100 votes, but in his report to the Returning Officer the Presiding Officer stated that the appellant got 444 votes and the respondent got 1135 votes.

2. The Tribunal after hearing the parties and considering the evidence adduced by them rejected all the allegations as baseless excepting the allegations as to the actual counting of votes by the Presiding-Officer. The Tribunal recounted the ballot-papers in presence of the parties. The Tribunal did not find any truth in the allegation that the appellant had got 498 votes as against 1100 votes of the returned candidate, but found the numerical counting of the Presiding-Officer correct. But from 444 votes of the appellant the Tribunal rejected one vote as invalid, and from 1135 votes of the returned candidate the Tribunal rejected 68 votes as invalid on the common ground of "double marks". With such rejection of 69 votes the appellant's overall total came to 2308 and that of the respondent was reduced to 2256. That is, the appellant got 52 votes more than the returned candidate.

3. The Tribunal, however, did not declare the appellant elected in spite of his majority of 52 votes, but declared the election held in this Polling Station 'void' and directed a fresh election there keeping undisturbed the results of the two other Polling Stations so that those results could be added to the result to be obtained from the fresh election in the disputed Polling Station for final determination of the question as to election of Chairman of the Union Parishad.

4. This order of the Tribunal was challenged by both the parties by two separate appeals before the Election Appellate Tribunal (District Judge). This appellant in his appeal, Appeal No. 3 of 1984, contended that in view of his majority of 52 votes, the Tribunal ought to have declared him elected. The respondent, on the other hand, in his Appeal No. 4 of 1984, challenged the re-counting which was, according to him, based on arbitrary and illegal rejection of his 68 votes which were found perfectly valid on the spot by the Presiding Officer in presence of both the parties. The Appellate Tribunal did not consider the propriety of the 'recounting', but decided the appeals on a different ground. It was that the 'M' Form relating to ballot-paper account was not prepared by the Presiding-officer and submitted by him to the Returning Officer though the provision for preparation and sub-mission of 'M' Form was mandatory under the Election Rules. The Appellate Tribunal held that the 'M' Form was not submitted to the Returning Officer by the Presiding Officer by the Presiding Officer who thereby contravened the mandatory provision in rule 40 of the Election Rules, 1983 and concluded that independent of any other questions, contravention of the mandatory provision as to Form 'M' vitiated the election and on that ground maintained the Tribunal's order for re-election in the disputed centre and dismissed both the appeals.

5. This appellate order was challenged by the appellant before the High Court Division by an application under section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code. The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division having heard both the parties came to certain findings which are summarized below:

The partial re-election as directed by the Tribunal is not sustainable in law as election of the returned candidate as Chairman of the Union Parishad was also not declared void and set aside. (the Tribunal, it may be mentioned, though declared the election of the disputed Centre 'void' did not declare the election of the returned candidate void as a whole, but maintained it). The order for fresh election in one of the three centres is contradictory in term in that there cannot be election in one part of the Union so long the returned candidate's election as Chairman for the whole of the Union has been upheld. There is no definite and clear finding by the Tribunal that there was any divergence between the result declared by the presiding-officer on the spot and the he submitted to the Returning-officer. The is no basis for the Appellate Tribunal's findings that the 'M' Form was not prepared and submitted to the Returning officer, by the. Presiding-officer in that the Tribunals own order in the Order-sheet showed that 'M' Form had been submitted by the Presiding officer to the Returning-officer in a separate which was contained, along with other packets, in the gunny bag.

The learned Single Judge, on these findings and also relying upon rule 49 which provides that the Tribunal shall not declare the election of a returned candidate void unless it is satisfied that the result of the election has been materially affected, set-aside the order as to fresh election and dismissed the election petition with the result that the election of the returned candidate was finally upheld.

6. Leave was granted to consider whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division while setting-aside the Tribunal's order for fresh election in one of the three Centre, correctly appreciated our decision in the case of Mofazzal Hossain vs Election Commissioner, (1976) 28 DLR (AD) 51 and rightly applied the principle enunciated therein to the instant case.

7. To appreciate the real question involved in this appeal a brief review of the facts relating to election of the disputed Centre is necessary. As has been stated above, contest between the two candidates was narrowed down to the question of recounting of the ballot-papers only, all other allegations brought by the appellant having fallen through. It was found by the Tribunal, and we find correctly, that the election was held peacefully in a very congenial atmosphere and that the counting of votes by the Presiding. Officer was also held in a peaceful manner. The question, therefore, is whether the 'counting was correct and valid, valid in the sense that only valid votes were included and invalid votes were rejected and further that the rejection of the 69 ballot-papers as "invalid" was made according to law. Report of the Presiding-officer submitted to the Returning-officer shows the following result of the counting:

Appellant 		-444

Respondent 		-1135

Invalid votes 		-41

Total: 	        	 1620

But according to the allegation of the appellant made in his election-petition 'the result initially declared by the Presiding Officer is:

Appellant		-498

Respondent	-1100

Invalid		-22

Total: 		 1620

On re-counting the Tribunal found the following:

Appellant 			- 443

Respondent 			-1065

Invalid (original) 		- 41

Invalid (declared

by the Tribunal) 		- 69

Challenged votes 		- 2

Total: 				 1620

8. It should be noted that the total number of ballot-papers used in this Centre, both valid and invalid, was 1620 in all the three stages as shown above. The allegation of the appellant that he, had got 498 votes and the respondent had got 1100 was not found correct by the Tribunal for the Tribunal also found the appellants votes to be 444 from which however the Tribunal rejected one on the ground of "double-marks." The Tribunal also found 1135 votes for the respondent but from this figure the Tribunal rejected 68 votes on the ground of "double-marks"; all other things and figures were found intact. That is, so far as the numerical counting is concerned, the Presiding Officer's figure perfectly tallies with the figure found by the Tribunal on recounting in presence of the parties. Now, it 68 votes of the respondent which had been found valid by the Presiding Officer on the spot were rightly rejected as invalid by the Tribunal then the result of the election in this Centre was materially affected and consequently, the whole of the Chairman's election was also materially affected; and in that case election of the returned candidate must be declared void. Fresh 'election may however be held only in the disputed Centre. The Tribunal, though ordered fresh election in the disputed Centre, did not declare election of the returned candidate void but kept it intact. This is clearly illegal.

9. Mr Ishtiaque Ahmed, learned Advocate for the appellant, has tried to convince us that it is a mere omission on the part of the Election Tribunal to declare election of the Chairman voids and that at best it is an irregularity which may be corrected even at this stage. Had it been a mere omission in the Tribunal's judgment omission could have been supplied and election of the respondent could have been set-aside by us maintaining the Tribunal's order for re-election in the disputed Centre. It is to be seen whether it is a mere omission on the part of the Tribunal. The Tribunal gave serious consideration to the question whether the election of the returned candidate should or should not be set-aside and recorded its reason for not setting-aside the respondent's election but for maintaining it. The reason was that the Tribunal was not sure whether the" double-marks" on the 68 ballot-papers of the respondent were post-election manipulations or were in existence at the time of counting of those ballot-papers by the Presiding Officer, on the spot. If these were post-election manipulations, that is, after dispatch of the ballot-papers by the Presiding-officer and before the recounting by the Tribunal after a time gap of about 9 months, then the returned candidate could not be saddled with its responsibility and the rejection of these votes would be wholly illegal and improper. But if those double marks were there from before, that is, those markings bad been made by the respective voters, out of ignorance or for some other reasons, then their rejection by the Tribunal would be perfectly justified and the order for re-election must be upheld. So it should be seen how the Tribunal dealt with this question which is the only point for consideration in this appeal, and for that purpose, in the whole of the election petition.

10. The Tribunal has considered three probable reasons for the "double marks". One is that the double marks were there in the ballot-papers at the time of the counting by the Presiding-officer, but these ballot-papers' though invalid, were dishonestly accepted as valid by the Presiding-officer or his Assistants; or due to inexperience and inefficiency on the part of these officers these ballot-papers were counted in favour or the respondent; or there were no such double-marks but these were acts of malicious hands for the purpose of tampering with the otherwise valid ballot-papers of the respondent done after they were sent out by the Presiding Officer. It is, therefore, clear that the Tribunal itself could not come to any definite finding whether these" double markings" were made by the respective voters while casting votes or were post-election acts or some other persons. In view of this position, neither the election of the returned candidate has been declared void nor has the appellants been declared elected in place of the returned candidate though he was found by the Tribunal to have obtained 52 votes more than his opponent. The Tribunal, as appears from its elaborate judgment considered this point and directed fresh election in this Centre 'in the interest of justice". It is in view of this position that we find that the omission to declare the respondent's election 'void' is not a mere omission in the judgment of the Tribunal but we find that it is due to the fact the Tribunal was itself not satisfied that the double markings on the 68 ballot papers of the returned candidate were in existence at the time of the counting by the Presiding Officer.

11. Dr Kamal Hossain, learned Advocate for the respondent, has submitted that the appellant in his election petition did not make any prayer for recounting the ballot papers and that after about two months he filed an application for amending the election-petition so as to include therein a prayer for recounting the ballot-papers. The learned Counsel has also referred to a GD Entry in this connection made by the respondent to the Police on 29-3-84 to the effect that he was apprehending that election materials, particularly the ballot-papers, which were in the custody of the Returning Officer, might be tampered with at the instance of his opponent. It appears that the election-petition was filed on 8-2-84, a GD Entry as referred to was made on 29-3-84, a petition for amendment of the election-petition for the purpose of recounting was made on 21-4-84 and that the ballot-papers were recounted by the Tribunal on 28-9-84, Mr. Ishtiaque Ahmed explains that the petition for recounting is a mere formality for, the allegation of improper counting by the Presiding Officer was specifically made in the election-petition but the prayer for recounting was not made as it was implied in the petition itself and that immediately after the election the appellant had sent an application to the Election Commissioner for arranging recounting of the ballot papers.

<u>12. It appears that all election materials were dispatched in sealed packets by the Presiding Officer on the same night following 28 December 1983 immediately after the counting was completed, and that from that time till the recounting was held, after about 9 months, the respondent for the Presiding Officer had no connection with the ballot-papers. It during this period the "double marks" had been put on the ballot papers, as the Tribunal itself suspected, rejection of those 68 ballot-papers will be clearly unwarranted the improper. Rejection of these ballot-papers will be proper only if it is proved that the doubt-marks were pre-counting acts of the voters themselves-Now, in this case, is there any scope to hold that the double marks' were in existence at the time counting of votes by the Presiding Officer? 'Double marks', as has been explained by the Tribunal, mean marks made on more than one space in a ballot-paper each space being earmarked for only one candidate. 'Double marks' indicating a vote for more than one candidate were only one candidate is to be elected in such a glaring defect that it cannot escape notice of the parties or their representatives in whole presence the ballot- papers are counted. Had 68 ballot-papers bearing 'double marks' been counted in favour of the respondent the election agent of the appellant would have certainly raised objection. Secondly, the 'allegation' would have been taken as a specific ground by the appellant in his election petition in which a number of vague and baseless allegations were made. The Presiding Officer, OPW 8, while deposing before the Tribunal stated that he had counted the ballot papers thrice for his satisfaction as to correct counting.</u>

<u>13. In Election cases, It is often found that a defeated candidate brings a number of allegations including vague charges of his opponent influencing the Presiding Officer, but ultimately fails to prove, or abandons, all the allegations and insists on only recounting of the ballot-papers. On recounting, it is found that the result has gone in his favour by some mysterious means. That is why recounting of the ballot-papers by a Tribunal long after the election should not be resorted to simply on mere asking by an interested party. Ballot papers have special sanctity of their own and their secrecy should not be infringed by reopening the sealed packet unless the recounting becomes indispensably necessary to determine the dispute. When recounting would become so necessary depends on circumstances in each case. In the absence of clear justifications, no recounting should be ordered or made some finality must attach to counting of votes. Ground work for recounting must be prepared; recounting should be refused if no prayer for recounting had been made to the Presiding Officer who is alone empowers to recount on the spot either on his own motion or on requests of any candidate. Recounting of ballot- papers by the Tribunal is not specifically provided in the Election Rules, but it falls within the inherent powers of the Tribunal to decide the election dispute. In the instant case, the appellant or his representative did not request the Presiding Officer for recounting the ballot- papers. The Tribunal found that the election was held and the ballot-papers were counted in an orderly manner all-though and no objection was raised on the spot before the Presiding Officer as to the counting of the ballot papers. In the circumstances, the learned Single Judge rightly relied upon the decision in the case of Nurul Islam vs Munsif, Election Tribunal, 28 DLR (Dhaka) 373. In that decision it was observed, among other things, that a ballot-box containing ballot-papers must be regarded as a sacred thing whose secrecy should not be disturbed on a mere prayer of a defeated candidate when he has failed to prove any of its allegations of mal-practices against his opponent or the election officials. In the instant case when the Tribunal itself was not in a position to say whether the double marks were post-election acts or were the doings of the respective voters, election of the returned candidate should not have been interfered with. It is not a case of benefit of doubt going to a defeated candidate feeling aggrieved like the accused in a criminal case. Here, presumption is in favour of the returned candidate whose election shall not be declared a nullity unless the Tribunal "is satisfied" as laid down in rule 49 that the election has been materially affected by some illegal acts or contravention of some rules.</u>

14. In the result, we find no reason to interfere with the High Court Division's order reversing the Tribunal's order and dismissing the election-petition. The appeal is, accordingly, dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:

case_source: From the Judgment and Order dated 21.1.85 passed by the High Court Division, Chittagong in Civil Revision No. 128 of 1978.
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, C.J---This appeal arises. from Civil Revision No. 128 of 1978 decided by a Bench of the High Court Division, Chittagong (Mr. Justice Fazle Husain Mohammad Habibur Rahman and Mr. Justice Md. Abdul Jalil) on 21st January 1985.

<u>2. Appellants who are plaintiffs filed O.S. No. 19 of 1977 in the 3rd court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong impleading respondent No. 1 as defendant No. 1 along with other defendants for a decree for establishment of title and confirmation of possession with a prayer for permanent injunction and alternately for khas possession on setting aside order of requisition of the suit property under suction 3 of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 8948. Plaintiffs also filed an application under Order 39, rules 1 and 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for temporary injunction restraining defendants from dispossession them till the disposal of the suit.</u>

3. Plaintiffs predecessor purchased the suit land in 1929 and had been in possession on payment of Government revenue P.S. khatian stand in the names of plaintiff who made construction of a one-storied building on the land of R.S. plot No. 6889 which is situated in the Bazar area. Plaintiffs are carrying on groceries business there.

4. Defendant No. 1 became the owner and possessor of 94 sataks of land by virtue of a wakf deed dated 17th October 1963 executed by Mr. A. RM. Shamsul Huda in favour of a Madrasah named Mosharul Ullum Gouchia, Senior Madrasah which was constructed on a portion of the land and the remaining hurl was around the Madrasah. The Madrasah was close to the suit land and building of R.S. plot No. 6889.

5. Defendant No. 1 became owner and possessor of more than 0.37 ½  sataks of land in ajmali possession around the Madrasah. He had purchased it by sale deed dated 8th and 10th February 1965. As Vice-Chairman of Manupur Union Parishad, he had some political influence and by using it managed to obtain a letter of recommendation from the Ministry of Education for requisitioning the suit and without making any enquiry whatsoever and ascertaining the real facts the Ministry had issued the letter of recommendation Defendant Nos. 2 and 5; the requisitioning authority, by suppressing the fact of possession of access land by the Madrasah and defendant No. 1, stated in their proposal that the land in possession of Madrasah was only '60 sataks In reality the Madrasah has been in actual khan possession of '94 sataks, and defendant No. 1 in possession of 37 ½  sataks of land Further, property in question was requisitioned before, the same was actually approved by the Government. Also, the requiring body stated in its proposal for requisition that the laud was necessary for extension of existing Midrasah building but the older for requisition was pas ed for vocational training centre. No notice as enjoined by law was served upon the plaintiffs. All these acts revealed the malafides of defendants. Plaintiffs filed Miscellaneous Requisition Appeal No. 26 of 1976 to the Additional Commissioner defendant No. 5 who, without considering the real facts, dismissed the appeal. Plaintiffs then filed the aforesaid suit to protect their right to property.

6. Defendant No. 1 and defendant Nos. 2-6 filed written objections against plaintiffs' petition for temporary injunction Defendant No.1  also flied an application under Order 7, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint on the ground that the suit is barred under section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act.

7. The learned Subordinate Judge heard the application for temporary injunction and the application under Order 7, rule 11, C.P.C. together. He allowed the temporary injunction and rejected the application under Order 7, rule 11, C.P.C. on finding that.—

"(a) the defendant No. 1, the Superintendent of Manupur Mosharul Ullum Gouchia Senior Madrasah was the person who initiated the proposal for requisition;

(b) she purpose of requisition as shown in different proposals appear to be contradictory;

(c) there is nothing on record to show that the proposal of defendant No. 1 was verified in the locality by an authority before issuing approval to requisition;

(d) Copy of report or inspection of A.D.C. Chittagong in Misc. Reqn. Appeal No. 26/76 also furnishes some materials... . the requisition is not for the interest of the Madrasah rather for the self interest of the Superintendent. The A.D.C. on local inspection opined that there is no justification for requisition and acquisition of land for Madrasah,"

8. Defendant No. 1 preferred Civil Revision No. 128 of 1978 before the High Court Division, Chittagong. The learned Judges of the High Court Division, after hearing the parties, set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge who had rejected the application under Order 7, rule 11, C.P.C. for rejection of the plaint.

9. Against the judgment of the High Court Division, plaintiff-applicants moved this Court and obtained special leave to appeal inters as follows:

Mr. M.H. Khondker, Counsel for the plaintiff-petitioners contended that the learned Judges of the High Court Division were wrong insofar as they, while rejecting the plaint under Order 7. rule 11 C.P.C., failed to notice that section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 offers  no bar against filing the suit in the Civil Court for determining the question as to whether the order of requisition itself was illegal, ultra, wires without jurisdiction and Malafide. He referred to the following cases:

1) Secretary of Sates vs.Musk & Co. 44 CWN 70=1A IR 1940 PC 105;

2) Mian Mohammed Latif  vs. Province of West Pakistan, 221 DLR 98 SC=PLD 1970 SC 180;

3) Abdul Raul. Vs. Abdul  Hamid 17 DLR .15 SC at p. 519.

Incidentally, he mentioned that as the High, Court Division has rejected the plaint, the order of rejection being a decree under section 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the plaintiff petitioners have a right of appeal but as no right of appeal to the Appellate Division in such cases has been granted by Constitution of Bangladesh the petitioners have preferred this application for special leave to appeal against the order rejecting the plaint.

Leave is granted to consider the points raised."

10. Question which arises for determination is whether, in view of the bar imposed by the provisions of section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act the Civil Court had any jurisdiction to entertain the suit. Mr. S.R Pal, Counsel for the appellants, submitted that the plaintiffs suit being for declaration of title and confirmation of possession alternatively for Etas possession and for a decree for declaring the order of requisition and all proceedings thereunder illegal, malafide and without jurisdiction, plaintiffs' prayer (d) in the plaint was not barred under section 14A of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act. Prayer (d) in the plaint in Title Suit No. 19 of 1977 is as follows:

"(d) A decree for declaring that requisition order and the proceeding thereunder are all illegal ultra vires, without jurisdiction, fraudulent, malafide, concocted, made not in good faith brought about undue influence and fraud be passed."

The learned Counsel submitted that the Subordinate Judge was right in holding that the Civil Court has jurisdiction to enquire if the requisition in question is for public purpose, whether there is any malafide in the order of requisition and whether the provisions of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 has been complied with". Accordingly, the learned Subordinate Judge was right in not throwing out the plaint in limini. In support of his contention that the Civil Court have jurisdiction to examine the question whether the order of requisition was a nullity being illegal, ultra vires, without jurisdiction and malafide, the learned Counsel cited the following decisions:

1) Secretary of State Vs. Mask & Co., 44 CWN 70=AIR 1940 PC 105;

2) Mian Mohammad Latif Vs. Province of West Pakistan, (1970) 22 DLR 98 SCE PLD 1970 SC 180;

3) Abdul Rauf Vs. Abdul Hamid, (1965) 17 DLR 575 SC at p. 519.

11. Mr. Pal further submitted that the learned Judges of the High Court Division were wrong in holding that "we do not find any element of malafide intention or malice on the part of any of the defendants" without reversing the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that "the requisition is not for the interest of the Madrasah rather for self-interest of the Superintendent. The A.D.C. on local inspection opined that "there is no justification for requisition and acquisition of land for the Madrasah."

12. As against the submissions of the appellant, Counsel, Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, Counsel for the respondent No. 1, submitted that since the requisition was for public purpose and passed by a competent authority in accordance with law, it cannot be challenged on the ground of nullity or want of jurisdiction or malafide in view of the bar imposed by section 14A of the Act. Proper enquiries were made before requisitioning the property. The Madrasah is admittedly an educational institution which imparts religious, general and vocational education. The purpose of requisition, quantum of land and the particular land required bad been approved by the Ministry of Education. There is no malafide in requisition of the suit land. Even if the Madrasah owned other properties it would not render the order of requisition void.

13. Before proceeding to consider the respective contentions of the learned Counsel, we may refer to the provisions of section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act. It provides: "

"14A. Except as expressly provided in this Act, no Civil Court shall entertain any suit or application against any order passed or any action taken under this Act and all suits and appeals pending in any such Court against any order passed or any action taken under this Act shall abate with effect from the date of coming into force of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property (Amendment) Ordinance, 1963."

14. It is not the grievance of the plaintiff-appellants that in passing the requisition order the authority has not complied with the procedure for requisition as provided in the Act. It is also not their case that the purpose for which the land had been requisitioned was not a public purpose. It appears that being aggrieved by the order of requisition they moved the appropriate authority for setting it aside on the ground of malafide but to no avail. Being unable to obtain any relief from them plaintiff-appellants filed the aforesaid suit. Among other reliefs claimed, their prayer (d) in the plaint as quoted above is for declaring the order of requisition void on the ground of malafide.

15. Facts relating to malafide have been stated in paragraph 5 of the plaint. Paragraph 5 is as follows:

“ That it will not be out of place to mention here in this connection that the defendant having an affable face out-side out having serpentine heart within has become the owner and possessor of '94 sataks of land on 17.10.63 by virtue of Wakf Deed on the day by one A.D.M. Shamsul Huda in favour of Madrasah named Mozharul Ullum Gouchia Senior Madrasah of which defendant No. 1 is the Superintendent as the fortune has favoured such a man. After the execution of the Wakf, the Madrasah house was constructed on a portion of the land and the remaining land stands round about the said Madrasah house. This Madrasah house has been constructed just close to the suit land building on R.S. 6889. Besides this '94 sataks of land the defendant has become owner and possessor of more than '37 ½  sataks of land in ejmali possession against each plot by virtue of the purchase by the sale deeds dated 8.2.65 and 10.2.65. In that way the defendant No. 1 has managed to bring under his control about 13 ½  sataks of land in the disputed locality. The remaining lands besides the land covered by the Madrasah house the defendant No. 1 has possession there in khas."

16. According to appellants counsel, the learned Subordinate Judge was right in rejecting the application 'ruder Order 7, rule 11; C.P.C. for rejection of the plaint in the aforesaid title suit by looking into the plaint whether there are sufficient facts relating to malafide requiring Court's finding thereof. But the point can only be determined conclusively if after taking evidence, both oral and documentary, the allegations are proved. This could be done at the trial which, unless the Civil Court tad jurisdiction to entertain the suit, could not be held. According to the learned Counsel the allegations were not bare statements of Malafide without 3 particulars.

17. Paragraph 5 of the plaint as quoted above has given particulars of malafide. In this connection Mr. Pal also referred to the following report of inspection of A.D.C., Chittagong in Miscellaneous Requisition Appeal No. 26 of 1976 to which reference was made by the learned Subordinate Judge in his judgment:

"He reported that according to the owners and many other present on the occasion, the requisition is not for the interest of the Madrasah rather for self interest of the Superintendent. The A.D.C. on local inspection opined that there is no justification for requisition and acquisition of land for the Madrasah.

18. Mr. Pal submitted that hi these circumstances and in view of specific allegations in the plaint, the bar of section 14A of the Act will not operate. According to him, the learned Judges of the High Court Division should, therefore, have looked into the plaint and decided in favour of the plaintiff-appellants. On the contrary, he contended the learned Judges of the High Court Division went beyond the scope of their jurisdiction in rejecting the plaint.

19. Rejection of plaint is governed under the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. Thus, Order 7, rule 11, C.P.C. provides:

11. The plaint shall be rejected following cases:

(a) where  it does not disclose a cause of action;

(b) where the relief claimed is undervalued and the plaintiff. on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so,

(c) where the relief claimed is property valued, that the plaint is written anon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp paper with in a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so;

(d) where the suit appears from the state meat in the plaint to be barred by any law."

20. Defendant No. 1 is the Superintendent of the Madrasah filed an application under the aforesaid provisions of law for rejection of the plaint, his contentions, among others, being that the suit land was requisitioned under the provisions of the (Emergency) Requisition' of Property Act, 1948 and that according to clause (d) of Rule .11 (quoted above) the suit is barred under section 14A of the aforesaid Act.

21. Malafide as alleged by the plaintiff appellants is a question of fact which has, therefore to be established on proof Ordinarily the Court decides upon it after taking evidence and hearing the parties. No difficulty would seem to arise determining upon any allegation of malafide raised in a suit. Bat where a suit is not initially maintainable or barred by any law can such allegation be  merely looked  into and without taking evidence can it be held that the bar against such suit becomes inoperative on the allegation of malafide made in the plaint. If in such circumstances the answer is in the affirmative, provisions relating to the bar of suits would be rendered, nugatory.

<u>22. Under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure any Civil Court has jurisdiction to try all suits of a civil nature excepting suit of which their cognizance is either expressly impliedly barred Pakistan Supreme Court held that the question as to whether the act of an executive or administrative officer or a quasi judicial or judicial tribunal is without jurisdiction illegal and not binding on a party, being a matter of a civil nature is always to be decided by which such jurisdiction may have been taken away Vide, Abdul Rauf Vs Abdul Hamid (1965) 17 DLR 515 SC.</u>

<u>23. In the aforesaid case, when determining whether certain orders and proceedings taken under the Frontier Crimes Regulation Were without jurisdiction, being malafide, Pakistan Supreme Court observed;</u>

<u>"There is in this case art attack on the proceeding on the ground of malafide too. A malafide act is by its nature an act without jurisdiction. No legislature when it grants power to take action or pass an order contemplates a malafide exercise of statute it may be explained that a main tide order means one which is passed not for the purpose contemplated by the enactment granting the power to pass the order but for Some other collateral or ulterior purpose."</u>

<u>24. This is a well-known proposition of law which this Court has yet no occasion to depart from or express any disagreement with it. The point, however, is whether any bar of suit imposed by the legislature can be disregarded to make such suit which is so barred, maintainable in order to try an issue on male. Elide alleged in the plaint. It may, at least in some cases, be seen that hardship, or even injustice, may result if, in spite of  evident truth in the allegation of malafide, the suit is held to be not maintainable because there is a bar against such suit in the statute concerned ant, seeker of justice in a court of law should become aware, if not already so, that justice is done according to law. A Judge may have sympathy for a litigant's suffering due to technicalities of law made by the legislature, still in view of the express legislative intention, he must follow the "hands-off doctrine'. Otherwise chaos and anarchy would prevail leading to all sorts of complexities and confusion, Whatever the legislature says, unless it is contrary to the Constitution, its mandate, either express or implied, has been obeyed by Court. We are aware of the principle stated by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the well-known case of Secretary of State Vs. Mask AIR 1940 PC 105. The principle as stated in the judgment is.—</u>

<u>It is settled law that the exclusion of the jurisdiction of the Civil Courts is not to be readily inferred. but that such exclusion must either be explicitly expressed or clearly implied. It is also well settled that even if jurisdiction is so excluded, the Civil Courts have jurisdiction to examine into cases where the provisions of the Act have not been complied with, or the statutory tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure.</u>

25. This case undoubtedly lays down a great principle of law which has been consistently followed by the Superior Courts in this sub-continent. It will, however, be seen that facts and law in the present case are entirely on different lines which, therefore, do not attract its application to them. Similar is the position in respect to the decision reported in Mian Muhammad Latif Vs Province of West Pakistan  PLD 1970 SC 180. Here lack of competence of the requisition authority or non-conformity with the provision  of the Act or violation of the fundamental principles of judicial procedure is not the appellant's grievance.

26. Reference was made by Mr. Pal to the case of Muhammad  Latif against West Pakistan PLD 1970 SC 180 where in spite of provisions of law imposing bar of suits, the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that since the allegation was that the impugned order was a nullity in the eye of law, the jurisdiction of the Civil Court was not barred.

27. It may, however, be mentioned that according to the provisions of law ousting the jurisdiction of the Civil Court as contained in section 11 of the Sind Revenue Jurisdiction Act, 1876 the bar was not absolute. It was provided that ordinarily  a party in revenue matters should exhaust all his remedies by way of appeal before invoking the aid of the Civil Court.

28. In our opinion, section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act has, in clear and unmistakable terms put an express embargo on entertainment of any suit or application against any order or action under the Act Not only this, if any suit or appeal was pending fin before the enactment of this section (this section was inserted by EA, Ordinance No. XIII of 1963) against any order or action under the Act it was to abate.

<u>29. As to the allegation of malafide, since we are of the opinion that no Civil Court is competent to entertain any suit so as to try such issue it would be inappropriate for us to make any comment on whether there has been lack of bonafide in passing the impugned order. If such suit was entertain able the allegation regarding malafide could have been examined. Shine the Act itself provides remedy in the Act itself and the appellant took advantage by taking recourse to such remedy, he may not have any cause for grievance. Moreover, malafide was attributed not to the authority concerned but was directed primarily against respondent No. 1 who is merely Superintendent of the Madrasah and the Superintendent is a paid employee who got no personal interest in the property and that extension of the Madrasah is part of approved plan for vocational training and that the plaintiffs land is necessary for the, plan which is undoubtedly a public purpose.</u>

In the facts and circumstances of the case as stated above, the appeal is dismissed. There will however, be no order as to costs.

Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J:—I regret that I could not subscribe to the views expressed in the judgment of my Lord the Chief Justice.

31, Facts in short are as follows: Plaintiff-appellants filed a suit being OS No. 19 of 1977 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong, praying for a decree for establishment of title, confirmation of possession with permanent injunction, alternately, for khas possession and declaring requisition of the suit property as bad in law. He also prayed for temporary injunction till the disposal of the suit.

32. Plaintiff is in possession of the suit property since 1929 and in 1975 he constructed one storeyed building which is adjacent to the bazar area and conducting his business of groceries etc. ever since. By a wakf deed dated 17.10.1963 .94 sataks of land was donated in favour of Madrasah named Mozharul Ullum Gouchia Senior Madrasah by Wakf. Defendant No. 1 is the Superintendent of the Madrasah. The Madrasah house was constructed on a portion of the land and the remaining land is still vacant. This Madrasah is very close to the suit land. Defendant himself purchased another .37½  sataks of land in 1965. Thus defendant No. 1 become owner of 1.31½  sataks of land. It is alleged that defendant No. 1 exhorted his influence in the Ministry of Education and obtained recommendation from the said Ministry for requisitioning of the land of the plaintiff. This requisition was challenged unsuccessfully. Hence the plaintiff brought the suit as aforesaid.

33. Defendant No. 1 filed a petition under Order 7, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that the suit is barred under section 14A of the Registration Act. The trial court rejected this petition on the finding that there was no enquiry by any authority before requisitioning the suit land and the report of the A D.C. Chittagong showed that the requisition was not for the interest of the Madrasah rather it was for the self-interest of defendant No. 1. It was observed:

"The A.D.C. on local inspection opined that there is no justification for requisition and acquisition of land for Madrasah."

In this view of the matter, the petition under Order 7, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure was dismissed.

On revision, the High Court Division took the view that the requisition was made by the competent authority for a public purpose and observed:

"But in our opinion even if there are other properties for the Madrasah, it will not render void the order of requisition which was made by the requisitioning authority admittedly after inquiry."

As for the other reliefs the High Court noticed that the plaintiffs' cause of action for the entire suit is based on the requisition order and if the suit does not lie the plaintiffs have no cause of action for the other reliefs. In this view of the matter. "The entire plaint is liable to be rejected under Order 7, rule 11 C.P.C." and accordingly after setting aside the order of the trial court the first miscellaneous appeal was allowed and the rule was made absolute.

Leave was granted to consider the question whether in a proceeding when the plaintiffs alleges malafide the plaint is liable to be rejected under Order 7, rule 11 C.P.C.

34. The plaintiffs challenged the order of requisition and that is his main grievance no doubt. He alleged malafide in the requisitioning of his property and for that purpose he brought the suit The question is whether the court is barred from entertaining the suit in view of section 14A of the i.e question Act.

<u>35. It has been well settled that when power is given to do something that power must be exercised in accordance with law itself. The plaintiffs alleged that Madrasah had sufficient land for the purpose of the extension of the Madrasah. He alleged in his plaint that the defendant initiated the requisition proceeding out of grudge and ill motive and the requisitioning authority had requisitioned the suit property without any inquiry. The trial court had recorded the finding that there was no inquiry before requisitioning the property in question. On the face of such finding it is beyond comprehension as to how the plaint itself was rejected under Order 7, rule 11 C.P.C.</u>

36. Order 7, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for rejection of the plaint :

(a) where it does not disclose a cause of action :

(b) where the relief claimed in undervalued and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to correct the valuation within a the to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so :

(c) where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so :

(d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law.

It seems that the High Court " Division rejected the plaint on clause (a), in other words, that the plaintiffs have no cause of action since the plaint does not disclose of  action independently of the requisition order. So, the plaint is required to be rejected.

37. With respect the reasoning’s does not appear to be convincing, In this Court the argument was advanced on section 14A of the Requisition Act and the appeal was disposed of on the main ground that the suit is burred under section 14A of the Requisition Act and even the malafide cannot be investigated, in as much as, such suit initially is not maintainable and expressly such suit has been barred, It has been argued that the express legislative  intention clearly shows 'hands off' doctrine  although no authority was cited for such proposition.

<u>38. It is needless to mention if anything have been settled over the decades then it is the proposition that power conferred by or under any law must not be exercised malafide or for collateral purpose. The malafide act is an act without jurisdiction. No legislature grants power for malafide exercise of it and when such malafide is alleged in fact the Civil Courts have the power to investigate and give decision thereon. It is unnecessary to cite long line of decision On this point.</u>

39. To refer to a few eases from the long line, it will be seen that in the case of Abdul Raul and others, reported in 17 DLR, (SC) 515 the then Supreme Court of Pakistan was considering a similar provision (sec. 60 of the Frontier Crimes Regulation) as in Sec. 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act providing for ouster of jurisdiction of the Civil Court. In that case certain proceedings were challenged in the civil court, inter alia, on the ground of malafide. Civil Court declined jurisdiction in view of the ouster clause but the High Court on appeal set aside the order and remanded the case holding that the court had jurisdiction to try the suit. The High court’s order was approved by the Supreme Court and appeal dismissed and explaining the conditions in which an ouster clause s to the jurisdiction of civil court is attracted it made the following observation:-

"The decision of the question whether the Civil Court had jurisdiction in the present case would depend on whet oar the impugned orders and proceedings were without jurisdiction. There is in this case an attack on the proceeding on the ground of malafide too. A malafide act is by us nature and act without jurisdiction. No legislature when it grants power to take action or pass an order contemplates a malafide exercise of power. A malafide order is a fraud on the statute. It may be explained that a malafide order means one which is passed not for the purpose contemplated by the enactment granting the power to pass the order., but for some other collateral or untie or purpose."

In the case of Federation Pakistan vs Saeed Ahmed PLD 1974 (S.C) 151 (168) Hamoodur Rahman. C.J. explained that a malafide act and coram non judice  stand on the same footing and no ouster clause in any enactment howsoever widely couched can save them from judicial scrutiny. His Lordship said:

"Indeed malafide acts stand on the same footing as acts done without jurisdiction. Similarly coram non judice also stand on the same footing because these words. would literally mean that they have been done by an authority or body exercising judicial or quasi-judicial powers which was not properly constituted even under the law under which it was set up and that its decision is not a decision of a competent authority. If this be so then such acts do not also qualify for validation and they have not been saved from scrutiny by the ouster, dense, no matter how widely that ouster clause may be worded."

40. This Division in the case of Khondker Ehteshamuddin  @ Iqbal 33 DLR (AD) 154 agreed with an approval the aforesaid proposition of law by holding that, "Of course when a Martial Law Court or Tribunal has acted without jurisdiction or such Court or Tribunal is not properly constituted, that is to say, is coram non judice, or has acted malafide, the power of the superior Courts under Article 102 of the Constitution in an appropriate case may be exercised."

41. That sec 14A provides no absolute bar has been found by the High Court Division  itself upon  a reference to the decision reported in 17 DLR 263 which reads thus:

"A suit would only lie in this behalf, if the impugned A order is wholly outside the purview of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, otherwise the validity of any act done under the said Act cannot be challenged in a suit or in any other manner except as allowed under section 14A quoted above in other words.

In order to prosecute an independent suit, it must he shown that the impugned order cannot be passed or that the order does not amount to an order under the Act, that is to say, the order itself is incompetent. There is, however, a vital distinction between an order which cannot be made or which cannot be described as an order made under the Act and an order made by a competent authority for a valid purpose (when the purpose of the order is an essential clement of its validity but tainted with some irregularity or illegality far non observance of some provision of the Act. In the former case a suit will lie, but in the latter eventuality the grievance can only be agitated under Section 14A."

42. This principle is grounded on the theme that if you tinker with rights on any supposed intendment of the legislature then you will be closing the door for doing away the little protection that has been left to the individual. To hold to the contrary is to say that the Civil Court will have no jurisdiction to investigate whether the action has been taken for collateral purpose or malafide. That will mean arbitrariness.

43. Syed Ishtiaq Abmed has not for a moment disputed the correctness of the exposition of the law as noticed above. His submission, however, is that the allegations of malafide are not against the requisitioning authority as such but against the respondent No.1 who only represents the requiring body. His second line of argument is not supported by any authority though, that the second part of section 14A abating all pending actions indicates that the legislature intended a total bar to Civil Court's jurisdiction no matter whether the action is challenged on grounds of rmlafide or coran non judice.

<u>44. As to the second submission, we find ourselves unable to agree in the absence of any authority or principle in that behalf. Consistent judicial view on malafide and coram non judice is so well-established that to hold otherwise on some supposed intention of the legislature would be to deny an universally accepted sound principle of law.</u>

<u>As to the first submission, it is not correct to say that there is no allegation of malafide against the authorities, True, the burden of the allegation as in the plaint is against the respondent No. 1 but then the main theme in the plaint is that the order of requisition was passed for a collateral purpose and thus malafide in nature. The High Court Division committed a manifest error in deciding the matter fully as if it were deciding a suit. It may be that ultimately the plaintiffs cannot prove malafide as alleged in the suit but the plaint cannot be rejected outright under Order 7, rule 11 C.P.C. upon entering into the question at issue on the basis of facts to be proved by evidence.</u>

<u>45. In the case of Ali Jail Vs Bangladesh 37 DLR (AD) 161 this Court considered the question as to the correctness  of the rejection of the plaint under Order 7, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the matter of requisition under Emergency (Land and Building) Requisition Ordinance, 1982. In that case requisition was made for the public purpose. Section 5 provides that the decision of the Government shall be the conclusive evidence that the property is needed for a public purpose. When the requisition was challenged by way of suit, the trial court rejected the plaint under Order 7, rule 1 J of the Code of Civil Procedure, in view of section 44 of the Ordinance, which bars such suits. The appellate court below took the view that the trial court ought not to have rejected the plaint without deciding' whether the purpose was fur the public purpose. The High Court Division. in revision, took the view if from the pleading it can be seen that the purpose does not appear to be in public interest the civil court's jurisdiction is not ousted by section 44 of the Ordinance.</u>

<u>This Court upheld this view and observed:-</u>

<u>"So far the acquisition and requisition proceeding is concerned. we are satisfied that the acquisition was for the public purpose and the law as provided in the Ordinance had been fully complied with. Once it is held that the land bad been acquisitioned validly for public purpose section 44 barring the jurisdiction of a Civil Court comes into play and in this view of the matter there is no hesitation in saying that the High Court Division correctly restored the order of trial court."</u>

<u>46. In the Ordinance of 1982 section 5 provided conclusive evidence clause. Even then this Court had approved the view of the High Court Division if from the pleadings it can be seen that the purpose does not appear to be in public interest the Civil Court's jurisdiction is not ousted by section 44 of the Ordinance." On the other hand in the Requisition of Property Act 1948 there is no such conclusive evidence clause. Section 14A bars the jurisdiction of the Civil Court "except as expressly provided in this Act." In other words, the remedy there has been given by way of appeal against the order of requisition and even after such appeal if the aggrieved party can show that the requisition was malafide or for collateral purposes, the Civil Court is not barred from perusing the pleading to come to the conclusion whether the purpose was the public purpose or not. The outright rejection of the plaint under Or. 7, rule 11 C.P.C. deprives the court from scrutinising as to whether the purpose is a public purpose. Moreover the trial court had recorded a finding in this case that there had been no enquiry by the authorities as to the necessity of requisitioning. In 37 DLR (AD) 161 the finding was that the requisition was for public purpose. But in this case that is lacking. On the face of such finding the rejection of the plaint was illegal, if the Court does not even peruse the plaint and rejects it outright the door for arbitrariness is opened and whatever little right a citizen is left with is reduced to a shadowy substance. It is no consolation to say that the plaintiff had a remedy by way of appeal, which in fact he availed of unsuccessfully inasmuch as the plaintiff being dissatisfied with order of 'Caesar to Caesar' brought the Suit and obtained a prima facie finding of fact from the trial court that the requisition was done for collateral purpose. There is no public purpose in robbing Peter fur paying Paul. In this View of the matter, the opinion is that the rejection of the plaint under Order 7, rule II was clearly misconceived and contrary to the rulings laid down by this Court. I would allow the appeal without costs.</u>

M. H. Rahman, J.- I have gone through the judgments written by my Lord, the Chief Justice and my learned brother Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.; I concur with the Judgment of my Lord, the Chief Justice.

A. T.M Afzal, J- I have gone through the judgments written by my Lord, the Chief Justice and my learned brother Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J. I concur with the judgment of Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.

Order of the Court

By the majority decision the appeal is dismissed, There will, however, be no order as to costs.

Tapan Kumar Chakraborty, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
Deputy General Manager, Rupali Bank Ltd ----- Petitioner
Vs. 
Shah Jalal and others ----- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
This Rule under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against an order of remand.

2. The relevant facts giving rise to this rule in brief are, that opposite party No. 1, as plaintiff, brought Title Suit No. 225 of 1985 in the First Court of Munsif, now Assistant Judge, Barisal seeking, inter alia, a declaration that the order of termination of his services dated 17.9.81 was void, illegal, malafide and without jurisdiction and that he was very much in service with all rights and privileges attached to his office. The suit was. contested by defendant No. 1, General Manager (Administration) Rupali Bank, Dhaka, contending, inter alia, that the suit was barred under sections 19 and 25(b) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act. During the hearing of the suit the defendant, however, filed an application praying for dismissal of the suit on the ground that the suit being in the nature of relief exclusively triable by the Administrative Tribunal under the provisions of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980, the Civil Court has no jurisdiction to entertain it. The plaintiff opposed the application by filing a written objection. It was contended by him that the Rupali Bank with other specified banks was brought within the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal on 25.9.84 by "Ordinance No. LX of 1984 and as the cause of action of the suit arose on 24.9.81 which was much earlier than the date of the incorporation of the bank in the Schedule of the Act, the Administrative Tribunal has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. Thereupon the learned Munsif took the view that the suit is exclusively triable by the Administrative Tribunal and hence the Civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. Accordingly, he dismissed the suit. Being aggrieved the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 104 of 1986 to the learned District Judge, Barisal. The appeal was, on transfer, heard by the learned Subordinate Judge of that place. He reversed the decision and sent back the case to the Trial Court for fresh decision. It is against this order the contesting defendant has obtained the present rule.

3. It is submitted on behalf of the petitioner that Article 117(2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh provides that when an Administrative Tribunal is established no court shall entertain any proceeding or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal and since the instant suit was brought after the incorporation of Rupali Bank in the Schedule of the Act and it relates to the terms and conditions of an employee of the Rupali Bank the Civil Court shall have no jurisdiction to entertain the same. In reply, the learned Advocate for the opposite party contends that the statutory period of six months limitation as provided in the second proviso to section 4(2) of the Act having elapsed long before the incorporation of the bank in the Schedule of the. Act by the Administrative Tribunal Ordinance 1984 the Tribunal could not be said to have any jurisdiction over the subject matter of the suit. According to him, the said proviso clearly shows that the Administrative Tribunal would be incompetent to entertain any case unless it is film before it within six months from the date of the impugned order and as in the instant suit the plaintiff has called in question the order of his termination which is dated 17.9.81, that is, 4 years before the Administrative Tribunal got jurisdiction to try such cases, Article 117(2) of the Constitution shall have no application to the suit. He maintains that there is nothing in the Administrative Tribunal Act to indicate that the legislative intent is to take away the vested right of a person retrospectively beyond six months of the impugned order.

4. Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 provides for establishment of one or more Administrative Tribunals to exercise jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to or arising out of the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic or of any statutory public authority. Section 2(a) of the Act defines statutory public authority as an authority, Corporate body specified in the Schedule of the Act. Rupali Bank under which opposite party No. 1 had been serving was incorporated in the said Schedule on 25.9.84. As a result, matters relating to the terms and conditions of service of persons in the service of the Bank were brought within the purview of the Act on and from that date.

5. Under sub-section (1) of section 4 an Administrative Tribunal is vested with exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine applications made by any person in the service of the Republic or of any statutory public authority in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights, or in respect of any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic or of any statutory authority. Sub-section (2) provides that if a person in the service of the Republic or of any statutory public authority is aggrieved by any order or decision in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights or by any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic or any statutory public authority, he can make an application to the Administrative Tribunal under sub-section (I). This provision is subject to two provisos.

6. The second proviso is relevant for our purpose. It says that no such application shall be entertained by the Administrative Tribunal unless it is made within six months from the date of making or taking of the order, decision or action concerned or making of the decision on the matter by the higher administrative authority, as the case may be. In view of this proviso the Administrative Tribunal shall have no jurisdiction to entertain an application unless it is filed within six months of the impugned order.

<u>7. The Govt. in exercise of its power under section 3 of the Act, established an Administrative Tribunal for the country effective from 1.2.1981. Rupali Bank in which the plaintiff had been serving being not originally included in the schedule the said tribunal had no jurisdiction over the subject matter under the law as it stood then. By Ordinance No. LX of 1984 which came into force on 25.9.84 the said Bank was incorporated in the schedule of the Act. As a result the Administrative Tribunal got jurisdiction to hear matters relating to the terms and conditions of service of the said Bank on and from that date. But in view of the second proviso to sub-section (2) of section 4 it shall have no power to entertain an application unless the same is filed within six months of the impugned order. In the instant suit the impugned order was made on 17.9.81 which was much earlier than the date of incorporation of the Bank in the Schedule of the Act i.e. 4 years before the Administrative Tribunal got its jurisdiction to entertain such a case. Consequently, the case is undoubtedly beyond the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal. That being so, the suit does not come within the mischief of Article 117(2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh which provides that where any Administrative Tribunal is established no Court shall entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such Tribunal.</u>

8. My view finds support from the decision in the case of Md. Shahabuddin Vs. Janata Bank & others 41 DLR 94. In that case one Md. Shahabuddin, who was a member of the Clerical Staff, Chak Bazar Branch, Barisal of the same Janata Bank, brought a suit in 1986 challenging an order of termination of his service from the bank made on 17.9.81. A question came up for decision before the High Court Division as to whether the suit would be maintainable in view of the existence of the Administrative Tribunal having exclusive jurisdiction over the matter. A Division Bench of this Court held that the plaintiffs cause of action having arisen on 17.9.81, that is, 4 years before the Administrative Tribunal got jurisdiction to try such a case, the Civil Court shall retain jurisdiction to entertain and try such a case. For the above reasons, I do not find that the learned District Judge has committed any error in holding that the Civil Court is competent to hear the suit.

9. The learned Advocate for the petitioner, however, sought to argue that the suit is barred under section 25(1)(b) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act. This point was not urged before the Courts below. Moreover, there is a specific issue on the point pending adjudication. In the circumstances I am not inclined to allow the petitioner to argue it at this stage, particularly when the suit has been sent back to the Trial Court for fresh trial observing the following:

"The matter was decided at the stage of fixing peremptory hearing of the suit without taking any evidence. Though as many as five issues were framed but the suit was dismissed without taking evidence on the disputed issues.

So, this is a fit cause for sending the suit on remand to dispose of the suit on merit giving chance to the parties to adduce evidence afresh and to come to a fresh decision by the Trial Court on very independent issues without making any piecemeal of them".

The Rule is, accordingly, discharged without cost.

End.

lawyer:
S R Pal, Senior Advocate, instructed by Syed Sakhawat Ali, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Appellants. 
Md. Fazlul Karim, Advocate instructed by Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Narendra Nath Basu Roy and another ------ Appellant.
 Vs.
Municipal Committee Mymensingh ------ Respondents.
case_source: From the Judgment and decree dated 12th June,1984 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka Bench, in S, A, No, 402 of 1975.
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J.—This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and decree passed by the High Court Division in SA No. 402 of 1975.

<u>2. Plaintiff-respondent instituted Title Suit No. 106 of 1966 in theist Court of Subordinate Judge. Mymensingh, against the defendant-appellants praying for declaration of title to the land in suit appertaining to C.S. Plot No. 95 of Mouza Mymensingh town bearing Municipal holding No. 231 (present holding No. 66 and 66A) and for recovery of khas possession after demolishing the structures standing thereon.</u>

3. Plaintiff's case was that the land belonged to the Municipality of Mymeasingh Sailendra Nath Basu was an employee of the Municipality He took lease of the suit land for residential purpose for a period of 9 years from 1921. Lease was renewed from time to time and Sailendra Nath Basu paid rent upto 1956. Then he left Pakistan leaving the land in suit in the custody of his constituted attorney Mr. Ashutosh Datta Roy, an Advocate and his younger brother Natendra Nath Basu defendant No. 1. Defendant. No. 2 is the wife of defendant No. 1 She applied for mutation on 11-3-58 claiming to have purchased the suit land on the basis of a kabala dated 9-2-57 executed by the said Sailendra Nath Basu. The plaintiff contended that since Sailendra Nath Basu had no saleable interest the said kabala was fraudulent and collusive and defendant No. 2 has acquired no, interest thereunder. The defendants had constructed some pucea structures on the land without the consent and approval of the Municipality. As such the defendants are liable to remove the same. It is farther contended that Mymensingh Municipality is the owner of the land and the defendant are the trespassers.

4. Defendants 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement  denying the claim of the plaintiff. Their case was that the suit land was khas land of Maharaja Shashi Kinta Acharyya Chowdhury and appertained to the landlord’s khatian No. 95 of Mymensingh town. Then the Mymensingh Municipality had been entrusted by the Zaminder for protecting the land on behalf of the superior landlord and accordingly, the Municipality was nothing more than the custodian of the land belonging to the proprietor Zamindar. It was leased out to  Saileedra Nath Basu for 9 years and pucca structures were constructed with the knowledge and approval of the Municipality and the superior landlord and the defendants possessed the suit land openly and adversely. They further pleaded that after the acquisition of the rent receiving interests the said land vested in the Government and the defendants had become tenants directly under the Government and the Government had also recognised them.

5. The trial court upon consideration of the evidence and facts and circumstances of the case dismissed the suit holding that the Municipality was a lessee under the Maharaja by a patty which could not be substantiated by the production of it and in this context it was held. ; '"The Municipality was only the trustee of the Maharaja with regard to the land in suit". Next it was found that the defendants raised some pucca structures in violation of the terms of the lease "their possession as adverse to the knowledge of the Municipality which as such both of them acquired tenancy right by adverse possession". Lastly, it was found "that after the wholesale acquisition the Government has recognised the defendant as tenant." In this view of the matter, the suit was dismissed.

Plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 403 of 1963 and the learned Additional District Judge after bearing the parties concurred with the findings of the trial court and dismissed the appeal.

6. Plaintiff filed second appeal being Second. Appeal No. 402 of 1975.  The learned Single Judge of the High Court Division allowed the appeal and decreed the plaintiff's suit in part after setting aside the judgment and decree of the appellate court below. The High Court Division found that the defendants did not acquire tenancy right in the suit land under the Government.

7. Leave was granted to consider the question whether after the wholesale acquisition of the rent receiving interest by the Government Sailendra who took lease of the suit land in 1921 became a tenant under the Government.

Mr. S.R. Pal, learned Counsel, appearing for the defendant-appellants, contended that the High Court Division was wrong in holding that upon the wholesale acquisition of the rent receiving. interest by the Government the defendants  did not acquire any tenancy right. The learned Counsel argued that since the land originally, belonged to Maharaja, a rent receiver, after the acquisition of the rent-receiving interest Government became the owner of it, and consequently by operation of law the defendants became tenants of the Government and as such the suit is not maintainable.

8. The argument is .attractive but does not stand scrutiny. It is that the land originally belonged to the Mymensingh Maharaja. He gave this land to the Municipality sometime in the late 19th century and since then it become the land of the Municipality. Lease was granted to Sailendra in 1921 by the Municipality for 9 years and it was renewed from time to time upon 1956.

9. The Bengal Municipal Act 1932 provided the constitution of the Municipally and it provided further that the Municipality is a legal person which could sue and be sued. See section 15(2). It could also own land and dispose of it. See sections 91 & 95 of the Bengal Municipal Act 1932. It. can acquire and dispose of property. It can acquire land within or outside municipality compulsorily through the Government. See section 98(1). It is unfortunate that the appellate court found the entrustment" of the and of Maharaja to the Municipality which neither as a fact was proved nor could it be so because by operation of law land vested in the Municipality and it became owner.

10. Sailendra was an employee of the Municipality and lease was granted to him initially for 9 years in 1921 which was extended upto 1956, From 1921 to 1956 Sailendra was a non-agricultural tenant of the Municipality and a tenant is estopped from denying tile title of his landlord. Now to examine the contention of Mr. Pal that the land originally belonged to a rent-receiver and that the acquisition of rent receiving interest by General Notification dated 14th April, 1956 it became the property of the Government. The General Notification reads as follows

"For acquisition of rent-receiving interest. Notification No. 4835 LR, dated the 2nd April 1956:-

"In- exercise of the power conferred by sub-section (1) of section 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (East Bengal Act No. XXVIII of 1951), as amended by the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance 1956. (East Bengal Ordinance No. III of 1956) it is hereby notified, for the information of ail concerned that the Governor is pleased to acquire, with effect from the 14th April, 1256, all interests of all rent-receivers in their respective estates, taluks, tenures, holdings and tenancies situated in the district of '" ... including their interests in all sub-soil and rights to minerals in such estates taluks , tenures, holdings and tenancies except the interests and rights which have already been acquired by and have already vested in, the Provincial Government under the provisions of the said Act." For acquisition of khas lands.

Notification No. 4839-L.R. dated the 2nd April, 1956:-

"In exercise of the power conferred by sub-section (2) of section 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (East Bengal Act XXVIII of 1951) as amended by East Bengal Slate Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 (East Bengal Ordinance III of 1956), it is hereby notified, for the information of all concerned that the Governor is pleased to acquire, with effect from the 14th April, 1956, all lands in the khas possession of all rent receivers situated in the district of .. other than the classes of lands coming under clauses (a) and (b) of sub-section (2) of section 20 and other than such lands as have already been acquired by, and nave already vested in, the Provincial Government under the provisions of the said Act".

11. When Mr. Pal was asked whether it was a estate of Maharaja or khas land he frankly conceded that the land in question would not answer the description either as the estates, taluks, tenures, holdings or tenancies or khas land. Since none of these descriptions of the land of the Municipality fit ill it does not come within the mischief of the law and the general notification.

<u>12. The Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 expressly excludes any land vested "in or in the possession of any local authority". See section 85A clause (3). Therefore, the defendants could not take resort even to the provision of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act. The reason is simple, because the application of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act would saddle the Municipality with certain legal obligations and as such the legislature expressly omitted the operation of such act insofar as any land vested in or in the possession of any local authority.</u>

<u>"so that the advantages which it gives and the dis-advantages which it imposes may not come into operation with regard to such land". (18 DLR 618 (622).</u>

<u>13. It is undeniable fact that the land vested in the Municipality since 1932 and therefore, the defendant were only tenants of the land belonging to the Municipality by taking a temporary lease for nine years which however was renewed from time to time. The teamed Courts below unfortunately did not approach the facts of the case from the correct legal aspect. The High Court Division repelled the contention that after the wholesale acquisition by the Government the defendant has become a tenant under the Government and that the Maharaja has lost his paramount interest. This contention was repelled by the High Court Division by saying "the plaintiff is very much the owner of the suit land and cannot be denied any relief in the suit on the ground that it has lost its title," Mr. Pal argued that the question was not answered in the judgments of the courts below as to how this suit land vested in the Municipality and how it is exonerated from the provision of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The answer is what we have given already that by the general notification affecting the rent receiving interest and the khas land of the rent receiver, the land which has vested with the Municipality since 1932 was not affected and therefore, the contentious of the defendants do not hold good, And. secondly the defendants' plea of adverse possession, as noticed already, has no substance. The trial court found that the defendants had constructed pucca structures in violation of the terms of the kabuliyat and these structures were raised some 20/25 years back. The view was taken that their possession "was adverse to the knowledge of Municipality' and in these circumstances "the Municipality was with the right of collecting cent and tax only as in the meantime the defendant 1 and his brother acquired tenancy right by adverse possession." The appellate court below though affirmed the judgment and order of the trial court took the view that the questions of adverse possession does not arise in this case and concluded that Sailendra continued to be a tenant by holding over.</u>
