It appears from the first paragraph of the above notification that this enhanced rate of pension as at Annexure-A' to the notification was only applicable to pensioners retiring from service on or after 1.6.85 and not to those who had retired from service prior to 1.6.85. Similarly, the subsequent notification as at Memo No. অম/বিধি-১/৩ পি-২৮/৮৫/৬২ dated 5.7.89 the pensioners who had retired prior to 1.6.85 were excluded from its benefit.

50. Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed has argued that the object of the enhancement of the rate of pension by these two notifications was obvious and that was to render sustenance to the retired government servants in view of rising costs of living and the diminishing value of currency on account of uncontrollable inflation.

51. The learned Additional Attorney-General has not seriously disputed the proposition that the enhancement of the rate of pension was aimed at providing sustenance to the retired government employees.

<u>52. It is palpable that these two notifications divided the pensioners with reference to the particular date that is, those who had retired prior to 1.6.85 and those who retired subsequent to 1.6.85. Has this classification any relation with the object sought to be achieved by these two notifications, that is, providing sustenance to pensioners in view of the rising cost of living?</u>

<u>We find that this classification on the basis of the date of retirement has hardly any nexus with the object sought to be achieved by these two notifications, that is, making provision for sustenance of the retired government employees in the face of the rising cost of living.</u>

<u>As such, we find that this classification, on the basis of the date of retirement, between those pensioners who had retired prior to 1.6.85 and those who retired subsequent to 1.6.85 for the purpose of applicability of these two notifications has been arbitrary and, therefore, repugnant to the very concept of equality and equal protection of law as enshrined in Article 27 of the Constitution. This offending portion whereby the government employees who had retired prior to 1.6.85 were denied the benefit of the enhanced rate of pension as provided in these two notifications must, accordingly, be deemed to be unconstitutional as violative of Article 27 of the Constitution and knocked down.</u>

53. We are not unaware that the government granted certain dearness allowances to the pensioners retiring prior to 1.6.85 and the learned Additional Attorney-General placed before us the notifications whereby dearness allowances were granted to them. These are Notification No. MF(Regn I-I) 3P-28/82/73 dated 21.7.86 and Notification No. অম/(অবি) প্রবি-২/মন্ডা-২/৮৭/১২৪ dated 27.7.1987. We have heard the learned Additional Attorney-General to say that in the light of granting dearness allowance the pensioners are not entitled to any further increase in pension. We have already found that the exclusion of the pensioners from the benefits of Notification Nos. MR(Regn-1)-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 অম/বিধি-১/৩ পি ২৮/৮৫/৬১ dated 5.7.89 have been violative of Article 27 of the Constitution and, as such, the offending portion is liable to be knocked down as a result of which the pensioners will be legally entitled to the benefits of these two notifications. By allowing the benefits of dearness allowance the pensioners cannot, therefore be deprived of their legal right to get the benefits of these notifications.

54. The learned Additional Attorney-General's contention that all financial measures must contain effective date is a general proposition of law, but, for the matter of that, it cannot be argued that if fixing of such effective date violates any provision of the Constitution or any Fundamental Right enshrined in the Constitution this Court cannot intervene to undo the violation.

55. The learned Additional Attorney-General has also submitted that to direct the government to calculate pension of the pensioners retiring prior to 1.6.85 according to Notification No. MF(Regn 1) 3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 and Notification No. অম/বিধি-১/৩ পি ২৮/৮৫/৬১ dated 5.7.89 will tantamount to legislation in the way of amending those notifications and this the Court cannot undertake. We are not legislating by declaring the offending portion of the notifications as unconstitutional. We are merely interpreting a measure in the light of the Constitution and cutting down its offending portion being unconstitutional while retaining the rest of it and that is what is precisely the constitutional duty cast upon this Court by Article 102

56. The respondents must, accordingly, be directed to calculate the pension of all pensioners according to the rate as at the Annexures to these two notifications irrespective of their dates of retirement. It must also be remembered that the retired government employees would also be entitled to the benefit of dearness allowance allowed to them from time to time.

57. Mr. Ahmed has high-lighted the apparent inequity of the effect of calculating pension on the basis of the last emoluments drawn by the government employees and as an example he has cited the case of a Secretary retiring before 1.6.85 and getting a net pension of Taka 900.00 per month and a Secretary retiring on or after l. 7.91 getting a net pension of Taka 4000.00 per month. Similarly, he cited the case of an employee in the lowest scale of pay who retired before 1.6.85 and getting a pension of Taka 94.5 per month and the employee retiring from the same post on or after 1.7.91 getting a net pension of Taka 612.00 per month. We have no doubt that the effect of calculating pension on the basis of the last emoluments drawn has resulted in great inequity between government employees retiring from the same post as a result of upward revision of pay in view of the rising costs of living and depreciation of the value of currency. But, a legislative enactment or a governmental action cannot be knocked down as unconstitutional even if it results in inequity, is even shocking to the conscience and apparently unjust, unless such enactment or such action is violative of any provision of the Constitution in the former and the Constitution or any other law in the latter. As such, this inequity and unconscionable effect cannot be rectified by this Court by applying Article 27 of the Constitution. Probably, it is for the government to remove such inequity by implementing one of the Fundamental Principles of State Policy enshrined in Part II of the Constitution, particularly, Article 15 (d) of the Constitution, So far as the case of the pensioners is concerned.

58. This Rule is, accordingly, made absolute in part.

59. The words occurring in the first paragraph of Notification No. MF (Regn 1) 3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85, "retiring from service on or after 1st June, 1985" are hereby struck down as unconstitutional being violative of Article 27 -of the Constitution. It is hereby directed that the pension of all pensioners, irrespective of their date of retirement, be calculated according to the Pension Table as at Annexure-A to this notification and also according to Notification No. অম/বিধি-১/৩ পি ২৮/৮৫/৬১ dated 5.7.89. In order to remove all doubts it is also directed that with effect from 1.6.85 the pension of all pensioners retiring before 1.6.85 is at firstto be calculated on the basis of the last pay drawn by them according to the rate as at Annexure-A to Notification No. MF (Regn 1) 3P-28/85/60 dated 10.8.85 and Notification No. অম/বিধি-১/৩ পি ২৮/৮৫/৬১ dated 5.7.89 and then the actual amount surrendered by them at the time of commutation of their pension shall be excluded from the amount worked out according to the above calculation and their net pension shall be the balance payable with effect from the respective dates on which these two notifications were given effect to. The Dearness Allowance that had been allowed to the pensioners from time to time shall be payable in addition to the above net pension worked out according to the above calculation.

60. The respondents shall implement this judgment within 6 (six) months from this date.

61. Considering the circumstances of the case, the parties are directed to bear their respective costs.

Certificate under Article 103(2)(a) of the Constitution as prayed for by the learned Additional Attorney-General and also by Mr. Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, is granted as, in our opinion, this case involves substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, particularly Article 27 thereof.

End.

case_source: From the judgment and Order dated 4-3-1985 passed by the High Court Division, Dhaka in Writ Petition No. 20 of 1985.
full_judgment:
Fazle Munim CJ: This appeal arises from Writ Petition No. 20 of 1985 decided by a Bench of the High Court Division, Dhaka (Mr. Justice Abdul Matin Khan Chowdhury and Mr Justice Amin-Ur-Rahman Khan) on 4th March 1985.

2. Facts of the case are: On 28th December, 1983 the election of the Chairman of Ketharia Union Parishad No. 6 (Ka) within Banskhali Upazila, District Chittagong was held in which respondent No.3 was declared elected as Chairman on 23rd January 1984. Appellant and respondent No. 3 contested the election. The Union Parishad consists of three Wards, Ward No. 1 having two voting centres and the other two Wards had only one each. Appellant secured 2202 votes, respondent No. 3 secured 2,462 votes. Respondent No. 3 was, therefore, declared Chairman.

3. Appellant filed Election Petition on 7th February 1984. On 9th April 1984 respondent No. 3 appeared before the Tribunal and prayed for adjournment of the case for filing written statement. Time was allowed but respondent No. 3 did not file any written statement. Prayers for adjournments were made by respondent No. 3 on 19th April 1984 and 29th April 1984. As respondent No. 3 did not file the written statement the Tribunal granted time for doing so till 8 May 1984. From that date respondent No. 3 did not take any steps in the matter and accordingly the Election Tribunal fixed date for ex-parte hearing of the election case on 9th May, 1984. As respondent No. 3 did not take any step in the case, the Election Tribunal look up the case for ex-parte hearing. Appellant who appeared before the Election Tribunal was examined and in his examination- in-chief he stated the illegalities and irregularities committed by respondent No. 3 as well as the person in-charge of conducting the election of Ward No. 3.

The Election Tribunal, respondent No. 2 allowed the election case and declared the election held in Ward No. 3 of the aforesaid Union Parishad as invalid. Further, he directed for holding of a fresh election in the Ward within 30 days from the date. The election of respondent No. 3 as Chairman was also declared invalid.

4. On 20th May 1984 the Election Commission directed for holding of fresh election in Ward No.3 in pursuance of the order passed by respondent No. 2 on 9th May 1984.

Accordingly on 7th June 1984, election was held in Ward No. 3. Respondent No. 3 participated in the election. Appellant secured 1,103 votes and respondent No. 3 got 413 votes.

5. On 20th June 1984 the result of the fresh election of the Union Parishad declaring the appellant as Chairman of the Union Parishad, was published in Dhaka Gazette, Extraordinary. On 24th June 1984 the appellant was sworn in as Chairman and since then he has been conducting the affairs of the Parishad. On 9th July 1984 the Local Government (Union Parishads) (Amendment) Ordinance, 1984, Ordinance No. XLIV of 1984 was promulgated and published in the Gazette. By this Ordinance section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) (Amendment) Ordinance, 1983, Ordinance No. LI of 1983 was amended as follows:

"2, Amendment of section 29, Order LI of 1983-In the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 (LI of 1983), in section 29, for sub-section (3) the following shall be substituted, namely:

(3) Save as provided in sub-section (4), the decision of an Election Tribunal on an election petition shall be final.

(4) Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Election Tribunal may, within thirty days of the announcement of the decision, prefer an appeal to the District Judge within whose jurisdiction the election in dispute was held; and the decision of the District Judge on such appeal shall be final:

Provided that in the case of a decision announced before the commencement of the Local Government (Union Parishads) (Amendment) Ordinance 1984 (XLIV of 1984) such appeal may be preferred within thirty days of such commencement."

6. On 14th July 1984 respondent No. 3 in pursuance of the aforesaid provisions of the amended Ordinance preferred an appeal before the District Judge, Chittagong who constituted the election Appellate Tribunal. In his memorandum of appeal respondent No. 3 did not state that a fresh election in Ward No. 3 had already been held on 7th June 1984 and that he had also participated in the election. On 24th February 1985 the Election Appellate Tribunal, respondent No.1 allowed the appeal filed by respondent No.3 and set aside the order dated 9-5-84 passed by the Election Tribunal, respondent No. 2, and sent back the case on remand to it for fresh disposal of the case in accordance with law.

7. Appellant moved the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution read with Constitution (Partial Revival) (Second) Order, 1985, and the Chief Martial Law Administrator's Order No. 1 of 1985. It was contended by him that the order passed by the Election Tribunal on 9th May 1984 had already been executed on 7th June 1984 by holding a fresh election and that he had been declared as the elected Chairman of the Union Parishad. Further, respondent No. 3 was given sufficient opportunity to file his written statement in the Election Tribunal Case on as many as five times but he did not take any step. On 4th March 1985 High Court Division summarily rejected the petition.

Being aggrieved the appellant moved this Court and obtained special leave to appeal to consider the contention that the High Court Division erred in law in applying the Ordinance No. XLIV of 1984 inasmuch as, it did not give any retrospective effect and, as such, the decision of the Election Appellate Tribunal was without jurisdiction.

<u>8. It appears that respondent No. 3 did not file an election petition against the ex-parte order of the Election Tribunal passed on 9th May 1984 directing the holding of a fresh election in Ward No. 3. Election Commission, it appears, directed the holding of election in Ward No. 3 within 8th June 1984. Accordingly election in Ward No. 3 was held on 7th June 1984 in which respondent No. 3 participated. Though appellant was declared elected Chairman no election petition was filed by respondent No. 3 against this election.</u>

9. From a reading of the unamended provisions of sections 29 of the Ordinance, it appears that a person who felt aggrieved by a decision of an Election Tribunal had the following remedy:

"(I) An election Tribunal shall, upon receipt of an election petition give notice thereof all the contesting candidates at the election to which the petition relates.

(2) Subject to any rules made in this behalf, the Election Tribunal shall, after giving the contesting candidates an opportunity of being heard and taking such evidence as may be produced before it make such orders as it may think fit."

These two sub-sections remained but sub- section (3) of section 29 which provided,

"Save as provided in sub-section (4), the decision of an Election Tribunal on an election petition shall be final."

was substituted by new sub-sections (3) and (4) as quoted above was added by the amending Ordinance No- XLIV of 1984.

<u>10. From the facts as stated above, it appears that respondent No. 3 did not file an election petition before the Election Tribunal after the result of the election held in Ward No. 3 were announced on 7th June 1984. Had he filed such election petition and was aggrieved by the decision on the Election Tribunal he could have exercised his right to appeal under the provisions of Ordinance No. XLIV of 1984. In consequence of his omission to do so he could not exercise his right of appeal granted by section 4 of the amending Ordinance. Prior to making this omission respondent No. 3 also did not file an election petition before the Election Tribunal when it passed an ex-parte order on 9th May 1984 directing the holding a fresh election in Ward No. 3. If respondent No. 3 wants to exercise his right of appeal against this ex-parte order it would be time barred- under the provisions of section 4. Moreover, according to provisions of section 3 the ex-parte order passed by the Election Tribunal has become final. In such a predicament, that is, there being no election petition against the ex-parte order of Election Tribunal passed on 9th May 1984 which has become final and there being also no election petition against the election held on 7th June 1984, respondent No. 3 cannot claim to prefer an appeal under the provisions of section 4 of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance 1983 as amended by Ordinance No. XLIV of 1984.</u>

11. For the reasons stated above it appears that the learned Judges were wrong in not declaring that the Election Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal preferred by respondent No. 3 against the exparte order of the Election Tribunal.

12. In the result, the appeal is allowed. Judgments and Orders of the High Court Division and the Election Appellate Tribunal are set-aside and that of the Election Tribunal is restored. There will, however, be no order as to costs.

Shahabuddin Ahmed J: I have gone through the judgment proposed to be delivered by my Lord, the Chief Justice. I agree that the appeal should be allowed and the Election Tribunal's decision should be restored, but as my reasoning’s are a little different from those of my Lord, the Chief Justice, I am giving my reasons separately.

14. Facts of the case have already been stated in detail in the judgment of my Lord, the Chief Justice. Appellant and respondent No. 3 along with another contested an election for the office of Chairman of the Ketharia Union Parishad which was held on 28-12-83. Respondent No. 3 was declared elected on 23 January 1984 and he also took oath of office, but on 7 February 1984 the appellant filed an election petition before the Election Tribunal and Munsif at Banskhali, Chittagong, bringing some allegation of mal-practices against respondent No. 3, particularly an allegation that respondent No. 3 had canvassed for votes and entertained voters within the prohibited area of the Polling Booths. On receipt of notice of the election petition respondent No. 3 entered appearance and took as many as three adjournments for filing written statement in answer to the allegations made against him, but did not file any written statement. On the date finally fixed for the purpose that is, on 8 May 1984, he did not file written statement nor he took any step in the matter whereupon the Tribunal fixed the matter for ex-parte hearing on the following day, and on that day the Tribunal allowed the election-petition ex-parte and set-aside the election of the Union Parishad in part, that is to say, the Tribunal set-aside the election held in Ward No. 3 only, maintained the results of the election held in the other two Wards, and directed fresh election in Ward No. 3 so that the result of the election held in the other two Wards could be amalgamated with the result of the fresh election to be held. In pursuance of this decision, fresh election was held in Ward No. 3 on 7 June 1984 and the Returning Officer after consolidating the results of election of all the three Wards of the Union declared the appellant elected Chairman: His election was notified in the official gazette and he took oath of his office on 24 June 1984.

15. On 9th July 1984, section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 was amended and by this amendment sub-section (4) was inserted in section 29. This sub-section provides for appeal against any decision of the Election Tribunal within 30 days from the date of decision; and in the case of any decision given before this amendment, it is provided that appeal might be filed against such a decision also within 30 days from the date of the amendment. Respondent No. 3, in pursuance of this amendment, filed an appeal on 14 July 1984 before the District Judge and Appellate Election Tribunal, challenging the ex-parte-decision of the Tribunal dated 9 May 1984 taking the ground that the ex-parte decision was improper having been given without giving him any opportunity to defend himself in the election petition and further that in the said ex-parte decision there was no finding by the Tribunal that the election was materially affected by non-compliance with any rules or violation of any mandatory provisions of law.

16. The Appellate Election Tribunal heard the appeal in presence of both the parties and, by his judgment dated 25 February 1985, allowed the appeal, set-aside the ex-parte decision of the Tribunal along with the fresh election held in Ward No.3 and directed rehearing of the election-petition on a finding that respondent No. 3, the elected Chairman, had not been given any opportunity to file written statement against the election-petition. The appellant challenged this order of the Appellate Election Tribunal by a writ petition, but the learned Judges of the High Court Division summarily rejected the petition. As against this order of the High Court Division leave was granted by us on 24 March 1985 to consider, among other things, whether the amended law got any retrospective effect in respect of a decision of the Election Tribunal which has been implemented before the amendment.

<u>17. Mr Fazlul Karim, learned Advocate for the appellant, addressed us on questions of law and fact particularly, he contended that the amended provision of the Ordinance namely sub-section (4) of section 29 has got no retrospective effect in respect of a decision of the Tribunal which has already been implemented. He has pointed out that the ex-parte decision of the Tribunal dated 9 May 1984 setting aside the election in Ward No.3 and directing a fresh election there was executed by holding a fresh election on 7 June 1984 whereupon the appellant took oath of office. Contention of Mr Fazlul Karim is that though a decision of the Tribunal announced before the amendment could be appealed against, but when such a decision has already been implemented, appeal against it is not contemplated by the amendment which, he argues, contemplates only decisions which, though announced earlier than the amendment, have not yet been implemented. The ex-parte-order dated 9 May 1984 having been implemented, he argues, it stands outside the ambit of the subsequent Amendment. To appreciate this point section 29, both before and after the Amendment, ill quoted below;</u>

<u>Before amendment.</u>

<u><u>"29. Trial of election petitions.-(l) An Election Tribunal shall, upon receipt of an election petition, give notice thereof to all the contesting candidates at the election to which the petition relates.</u></u>

<u>(2) Subject to any rules made in this behalf, the Election Tribunal shall, after giving the contesting candidates an opportunity of being heard and taking such evidences as may be produced before it, make such orders as it may think fit.</u>

<u>(3) The decision of the Election Tribunal on an election petition shall be final and shall not be called in question in or before any Court."</u>

<u>After amendment.</u>

<u><u>"29. Trial of election petitions.-(l) An Election Tribunal shall, upon receipt of an election petition, give notice thereof to all the contesting candidates at the election to which the petition relates.</u></u>

<u>(2) Subject to any rules made in this behalf, the Election Tribunal shall, after giving the contesting candidates an opportunity of being heard and taking such evidence as may be produced before it, make such orders as it may be think fit.</u>

<u>(3) Save as provided in sub-section (4) The decision of an Election Tribunal on an election petition shall be final.</u>

<u>(4) Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Election Tribunal may, within thirty days of the announcement of the decision, prefer an appeal to the District Judge within whose jurisdiction the election in dispute was held; and the decision of the District Judge on such appeal shall be final;</u>

<u>Provided that in the case of a decision announced before the commencement of the Local Government (Union Parishads) (Amendment) Ordinance, 1984 (XLIV of 1984), such appeal may be preferred within thirty days of such commencement."</u>

<u>18. It should be noted that under the unamended law a decision of the Tribunal on an election petition, whether might have been the decision, was final and could not have been challenged in any Court. Keeping in view this position, the law was amended which not only made the Tribunal's decision appealable in prospective cases, but also .i t provides for appeal against a decision announced before the amendment. Had the Legislature intended that a decision which has already been implemented be- fore the amendment would remain unaffected by the amendment, it would have expressed this intention in clear specific words. In the absence of any such express provision in the amendment, it is very difficult to read in it a line of demarcation between a decision which has been implemented and one which has not been so implemented. What I find in the language of sub section (4) of section 29 is that under the unamended law, all decisions of the tribunal, even if they were illegal or grossly improper, remained immune from any challenge and that in order to enable a person aggrieved by such decisions the amendment was brought about and this Amendment in its second part, expressly provided for appeal against all these decisions. A Legislature which got power to enact a law, also got power to enact retrospectively; in sub section (4), this intention as to retrospectively of effect has been expressed in express and clear language. As such the contention of Mr Fazlul Karim in this respect is rejected.</u>

<u>19. Mr Fazlul Karim next contends that in the fresh election held in Ward No. 3, respondent No. 3 participated and, as such, he is stopped from challenging the election. Contention of respondent No. 3 is that he did not participate in the fresh election nor is he interested in the fresh election; secondly, whether he participated or not in the fresh election, he got statutory right, under the amended law, to challenge the earlier decision of the Tribunal setting aside his election ex-parte against which there was no provision for appeal at that time. That decision, it is contended, is the root of the trouble. Election held in Ward No. 3, it should be noted, is not an election for the whole of the Union, but it is an election in part as the results of election held in the other two Wards of the Union. were maintained and kept intact so as to be amalgamated with the result of the fresh election in the disputed Ward. In such an election no fresh candidate can contest, no nomination paper is necessary and the election is limited to the existing candidates namely, those who had participated in the election which have been maintained by the Tribunal. As in the instant case, election in Ward No. 3 shall be held as a matter of course in order to complete the process of election started on 28-12-1983. In such an election a candidate, who already participated in the election of the other two Wards, got no option but to participate, and in case he does not participate, he will face the consequence; or it may be that if his votes already obtained in the undisturbed part of the election i.e. in other two Wards in this case, exceed the highest number of votes obtained for the whole of the Union by another candidate he will be declared elected even if he did not participate in the disputed fresh election. In these circumstances, participation of respondent No. 3 in the fresh election in Ward No. 3 is immaterial and in the eye of law he is a candidate in respect of the whole of the Union. His participation in the fresh election in Ward No. 3 will not stand in his way to challenge the ex-parte decision setting aside the main election held on 28-12-1983.</u>

20. Mr Fazlul Karim next contends that after the fresh election was held in Ward No. 3, the respondent, did not challenge it by filing an election petition. Yes, he could have filed an election petition if he had been aggrieved by that fresh election; but he got no grievance against that election, for this election might have been held peacefully and lawfully. But his grievance being the earlier ex-parte decision against him, his right to appeal therefrom, given by subsequent law, is not affected by non-filing of election petition against the fresh election. I am, therefore, clearly of the view that the appeal against the Tribunal's ex-parte decision dated 9 May 1984 is quite maintainable. Now I shall enter into the merits of this appeal.

<u>21. The Appellate Election Tribunal found that respondent No. 3, elected chairman, was not given any opportunity to defend himself by filing a written statement. This finding I am afraid, is not supported by materials on record. The election petition was filed on 7 February 1984 and notice thereof was issued on the following day fixing 29 February 1984 for appearance. Respondent No. 3 appeared before the Tribunal long before that day; he appeared on 8 February 1984 in response to a separate notice to show cause why temporary injunction would not be issued by the Tribunal restraining him from functioning as Chairman till disposal of the election petition. In that connection he showed cause and this matter took about eight weeks and ultimately temporary injunction was refused. Respondent filed an application on 9 April 1984 for adjournment to file written statement the election petition; his application was allowed and the matter was adjourned to 19 April 1984; but he did not file written statement on 19 April and prayed for further time which was also granted till 29 April 1984. On that day also he did not file any written statement but prayed for another adjournment which was granted till May 1984. On that date neither did he file any written statement not did he take any steps. Thereupon the Tribunal set the matter for ex-parte decision on the following day, and accordingly, on that day, 9-5-1984, the Tribunal examined the petitioner (appellant), perused his election petition and found the allegations against respondent No.3 to be true. In the circumstances, the order allowing the election petition ex-parte is perfectly justified. In an election matter the person against whom specify allegation of malpractices has been brought must be prompt in denying the allegation by filing written statement. On his part simple denial of the allegation may be sufficient since the burden of proof of the allegation lies upon the petitioner. Failure of respondent No. 3 to submit written statement, considered along with the evidence adduced by the appellant, provided sufficient materials for disposing of the election petition ex-parte.</u>

22. Mr. Jamiruddin Sircar, learned Advocate for the respondent, contends that in the ex-parte order there is no finding that the election was materially affected. It is true that under rule 48 of the Election Rules, the Election Tribunal shall not declare an election void unless he finds that the election has been materially affected by non-compliance of any provisions of the law, but in the impugned decision no such finding has been given in specific words. But from the evidence adduced by the petitioner-appellant which remained unchallenged, the allegation in the election petition and dialatory tactics adopted by respondent No. 3, it is clearly found that the election was materially affected in Ward No. 3 by certain acts of respondent No. 3 in violation of rules. In view of this position the Tribunal's decision directing fresh election in Ward No. 3 should not have been interfered with in appeal. The observation of the Election Appellate Tribunal that respondent No. 3 was not given any opportunity to file written statement got no basis whatever. Thus, on merit, I find that the Tribunal's decision should not have been reversed. This should have been corrected by the High Court Division by hearing the Writ Petition on merit.

In the result, the appeal is allowed. The Order of the Election Appellate Tribunal as well of the High Court Division is set-aside and that of the Tribunal is restored.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued on an application filed under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against the judgment and order dated 28.4.86 passed by the District Judge, Cox's Bazar dismissing the Election Tribunal Appeal No. 1 of 1986 and affirming the judgment and order dated 23.12.85 passed by the Election Tribunal (Munsif) Chakaria in Election Tribunal Case No. 1 of 1985.

2. The opposite party Mohammadul Huq Usmani filed an application under section 26 of the Local Government (Union Parishad) Ordinance 1983 before the Election Tribunal, Cox's Bazar calling in question the election of the chairman of No. 6 Jhilonzi Union Parishad praying for declaring the election of the present petitioner as void and for declaration of the present opposite party as elected chairman with alternative prayer for declaring the election as a whole void. The said application was registered as Election Tribunal Case No. 10 of 1984 it was later on transferred to the Munsif, Chakaria as Election Tribunal and was renumbered as Election Tribunal Case No.1 of 1985. The case of the present opposite party who was the petitioner before the Election Tribunal, is as follows:

3. The petitioner and opposite party along with others contested the election of chairman of No. 6 Jhilonza Union Parishad, Cox's Bazar held on 7.1.84 in which the symbol of the opposite party Mohammadul Huq Usmani was 'Bullock Cart' and the symbol of the present petitioner Moulana Mokhter Ahmed was 'Date Tree'. There were widespread adoption of unfairness, bribery, undue persuasion and influence, disorderly conduct near the polling station, failure to maintain secret of voting, breach of official duties etc. at the instance of the respondent No.1 (the present petitioner) in all the polling stations and thereby the present petitioner was illegally declared elected showing to have secured 4263 votes in total and the present opposite party No. 1 was shown to have secured 4236 votes in all i.e. the petitioner Moulana Mokhter Ahmed was shown to have secured 27 votes more than opposite party No. 1. It was also alleged that there was recording of votes of dead and absentee voters by false personation in favour of the elected candidate. The counting of votes was held in insufficient light amidst disturbance created by hundreds of undesirable persons in spite of objection raised by the opposite party No. 1 and his polling agent. He also demanded recounting of the votes of all the centres and he was assured that the recounting would be held in the Thana Council on the next day in his presence and in presence of his agent and the returning officer but no recounting was held.

4. The present petitioner as respondent No. 1 in the said case contested the same by filing a written objection denying the material allegations and contending, in substance, that the election was held in a fair atmosphere and he was duly declared elected as he secured the highest number of votes. It was further contended that there was sufficient light at the time of counting and the counting was held properly in presence of the agents of the candidates and that all the provisions of Election Rules were duly observed. The petitioner apprehending tampering with election materials by the opposite party No.1 in collusion with the concerned official, sent telegrams to the Chief Election Commissioner and other authorities requesting them to keep the election bags in safe custody.

The petitioner of the Tribunal case examined eight witnesses including himself and the respondent No.1 the present petitioner examined six witnesses.

5. At the instance of the petitioner of the Tribunal case an order was passed for recounting of the votes. Thereafter the Election Tribunal held the recounting of the votes and after recounting the present petitioner was found to have secured two votes less than the present opposite party No. 1.

6. The learned Election Tribunal after considering the evidence on record and the facts and circumstances of the case and the result of the recounting allowed the case and declared the election of the present petitioner (respondent No.1) Moulana Mokhter Ahmed as void and also declared the petitioner of the election case i.e. the present opposite party No.1 Mohammadul Huq Usmani as elected chairman of No.6 Jhilonza Union Parishad by a judgment and order dated 23.12.85.

7. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and order the respondent No.1 Moulana Mokhter Ahmed preferred Election Tribunal Appeal No.1 of 1986 in the court of the District Judge, Cox's Bazar and the learned District Judge after hearing dismissed the appeal on contest and affirmed the judgment and order passed by the learned Election Tribunal by a judgment and order dated 28.4.86. Against the said order the appellant obtained the present Rule.

8. Mr. Ameirul Kabir Chowdhury, the learned advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the learned District Judge failed to consider the deposition of the D.Ws. most of whom are official witnesses including the Presiding Officers of the relevant centres and also misconstrued the deposition of P.W. 4 and committed an error of law in not holding that the order for recounting passed by the learned Tribunal is illegal which has occasioned a failure of justice. He further submits that the gunny bags containing the ballot papers having admittedly been found in torn condition, the learned appellate Court should have drawn adverse inference against the opposite party No. 1 and should have presumed that the contents of the gunny bags were not in original condition and there was possibility of those being tampered with and those should not have been recounted in such circumstances. He further submits that there is no allegation of bias against the accused Presiding Officers and that as the learned Tribunal found that the election was held properly the order of recounting wag not justified.

9. Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1 submits that without recounting the election petition could not have been disposed of and as such the learned Tribunal rightly recounted the votes on cogent reasons assigned by it and that the Election Tribunal has jurisdiction to recount the votes under certain circumstances and those circumstances did exist in the present case and so the learned District Judge committed no error of law in affirming the order of the learned Tribunal. He further submits that the case has been decided on the basis of concurrent findings of facts arrived at by both the courts below and there is no error of law calling for interference in revision.

10. Mr. Amirul Kabir Chowdhury, has referred to the case of Nurul Islam Talukdar Vs. Munsif of the 4th Court, Chittagong reported in 28 D.L.R. 375 wherein it was held by a Division Bench of this court:-

"In the instant case, the Tribunal acted with material irregularity when it proceeded to examine the ballot papers ignoring the broad facts that the gunny bags containing the election papers were tampered with having a number of stitched up holes. Again when on discovery of apparently tampered ballot papers, so many in number, examination of the presiding officers was indispensably necessary in the interest of justice, but he arbitrarily refused to examine them and thereby failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in him." It was further held:-

"When the ejection was held in a peaceful atmosphere and scrutiny and counting of ballot papers were made in an orderly manner, without any objection from any quarter, reports of the Presiding Officer as to the due performance of their duties must be accepted."

11. In the instant case there is no finding of any tampering with the ballot papers save and except that the gunny bags were found torn and so the principle enunciated in the aforesaid case has no application to the present case. Moreover, in the present case the Presiding Officers were examined.

12. Mr. Amirul Kabir Chowdhury, further submits that depositions of the witnesses were not at all considered by the court passing the order of recounting. Mr. Chowdhury also referred to the case of Manik Chowdhury Vs. Election Tribunal reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 305 wherein it was held that a Tribunal cannot recount votes interfering with the election result unless a case of improper counting by the Presiding Officer is made out. There is no dispute that the Election Tribunal has jurisdiction to recount the votes under certain circumstances specially when the dispute cannot otherwise be decided without recounting of the votes. In this connection Mr. A.K.M. Shafiqur Rahman draws my attention to the case of Afzal Khan Vs. Election Tribunal reported in 32 DLR (AD) 187 wherein it was held by the Appellate Division ;-

The jurisdiction of counting eminently lies elsewhere and even the Election Tribunal cannot count the ballot papers unless the recounting becomes a necessary part of the case itself which has been brought on the basis of certain allegations of corrupt and illegal practices. It is well settled that if recounting of ballot papers is a material issue before the Tribunal in connection with an election petition which cannot be determined without such recounting, then only the Tribunal has got power to reopen the ballot boxes and recounting the ballot papers provided sufficient foundation has been laid to come to the finding that the recounting is indispensably necessary for adjudication of the election petition".

13. In the case of Abul Bashar Vs Habibur Rahman Mia and others reported in 31 D.L.R.CAD) 297 it was held –

"We have no manner of doubt that in an appropriate case the Election Tribunal has authority to make a recounting of the votes in order to satisfy itself that the counting made by the Presiding Officer on the basis of which the result of the election has been declared was properly made,".

14. In the case of Nur Hossain Vs Election Tribunal reported in 27 DLR (AD) 117 it was held;-

"In the instant case the parties led evidence before the Tribunal which also heard the lawyers of the parties. In view of the allegations of improper and incorrect counting of the ballot papers he recounted them in the presence of the parties and their lawyers and then rejected certain ballot papers as being ambiguous for having been otherwise invalid and accepted those which were unambiguous following the provision of Rule 40 (3) (b) of the Rules. Since the High Court Division found that the Tribunal had scrutinized and recounted the ballot papers in accordance with the relevant rules in the presence of the parties and their lawyers without any objection from them, there is no scope for interference in the matters, even though the Tribunal did not assign reasons for distinguishing the ambiguous from the unambiguous ballot papers".

15. In the one of Kafezuddin Mia Vs. Election Tribunal reported in 27 DLR (AD) 118 it was held that the ballot papers recounted in presence of the parties who has no objection regarding formal proof cannot be raised after closure of the evidence that failure to demand recounting before the Presiding Officer and giving up demand before the Returning Officer is no bar for recounting by the Tribunal. It was further held:-

"We agree with the learned judges of the High Court Division that the ballot papers had been rightly treated as proved since they were admitted in evidence without any objection by the petitioner, who participated not only in the counting but also in the verification of the result of the count. An objection as to admissibility of a piece of evidence cannot be allowed to be taken after the closure of evidence".

It was further held:-

the contention that the judgment of the Tribunal does not contain reasons for acceptance or rejection of certain ballot papers is unjustified. The Tribunal rejected certain ballot paper as being ambiguous or having been otherwise invalid because of defects, such as of double sealing. Certain ballot admittedly cast in favour of the respondents Abut Hossain, and whose validity could not challenge, were again accepted and counted in favour of Abul Hossain, having been discovered in bags containing ballot papers relating to some other candidates. It cannot be disputed that the count by the Presiding Officer, had affected the result of the decision".

16. In the instant case the learned Tribunal found that the conducting of the election was done properly in accordance with the procedure of election but it also found after discussion and consideration of the evidence on record and the facts and circumstances of the case, that the counting of the votes were held ill insufficient light. The Tribunal also found that at the time of recounting most of the Presiding Officers were present before the Tribunal who identified the election materials and both the parties as well as their appointed learned Advocates were present at the time of recounting before the Tribunal. It also found that without recounting it was not possible to dispose of the case. The learned District Judge came to the finding that the contention raised by the petitioner of the Tribunal case cannot be set at rest without recounting the ballot papers. He also discussed the evidence on that point and held :-

"From the statements in the petition before the Tribunal and the statements of the PWs. recorded by the Tribunal it appears that the respondent petitioner has been able to prove that the counting of the ballot papers were not properly done and that some of the valid ballot papers were excluded from Counting in favour of the respondent petitioner and some invalid ballot papers were counted in favour of the opposite party."

<u>17. In the above circumstances it has been clearly established that there were sufficient grounds for recounting by the Election Tribunal in order to dispose of the matter. The learned Tribunal in his judgment assigned reasons for recounting the ballot papers and also considered the objection raised by the present petitioner. The petitioner filed an application for vacating the order of recounting and it was rejected after hearing on contest.</u>

<u>18. Hence I find that the learned Appellate Court did not commit any error of law in affirming the decision of recounting by the Election Tribunal and the Election' Tribunal had authority to recount the votes under the circumstances of the case. In appears that the recounting was held in presence of both the parties and their lawyers and after recounting the Election Tribunal came to the finding that the present opposite party Mohammadul Huq Osmani got 3 (three) votes more than the present petitioner Moulana Mukhter Ahmed. One vote was disputed at the time of recounting and it was excluded and the no result was that Mohammadul Huq Osmani got two votes more than Moulana Mukhter Ahmed.</u>

19. Some of the gunny bags containing the ballot papers were found in torn condition and the learned appellate court found that the torn condition of the gunny bags was from the very beginning and it was not done by either parties and that the presumption of the mischief as alleged was not supported and established by the papers on record, although both the parties apprehended tampering with the election materials and both of them informed the Chief Election Commissioner and other authorities to keep the election papers in safe custody. However, there :is no specific case of tampering of any particular ballot paper or papers while those were in custody after the election was over. Mr. Chowdhury, however, submits that some ballot papers having double seals were wrongly excluded from the petitioner’s votes. The learned court below found those to have been rightly excluded. Mr. Chowdhury's contention that the deposition of DWs. were not considered and the deposition of P.W.4 was misinterpreted cannot be a ground for 'interference with the concurrent finding of facts arrived at by both the courts below based on evidence on record. Moreover the Presiding Officers were present at the time of recounting.

<u>20. It is true that a court or Tribunal when decides a case must consider the evidence of both the parties to come to a correct decision but in the present case it was not done. But in the facts and circumstances discussed above I am of the opinion that no prejudice has been caused for non-consideration of the evidence in question.</u>

21. In view of the facts and circumstances discussed above I find no error of law to have been committed by the learned District Judge in affirming the judgment and order of the learned Election Tribunal declaring Mohammadul Huq Osmani an the Chairman and declaring the election of Moulana Mukhter Ahmed as void.

The Rule is therefore discharged without any order as to costs.

Mr. Amirul Kabir Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the petitioner intends to move the Appellate Division against this order and prays for stay of operation of this order to enable him to move the Appellate Division. The prayer is allowed. Let the operation of this order be stayed for four weeks from date.

End.

Vs.
The Post Master, (1st Class), Faridpur Head Post Office, District-Faridpur and 4 others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Nurul Huque Bhuiyan : This Rule Nisi by the petitioner under Article 102 of the Constitution calls upon the respondents to show cause as to why the respondents should not be directed to implement the order given by the Administrative Appellate Tribunal on 23.4.87 in Appeal Case No. 44 of 1986 and allow the petitioner to join his duties.

2. The facts leading to this Rule, in short, are that the petitioner when working as Postal Operator at Head Post Office at Faridpur was charge-sheeted on 3.12.84 for misconduct. The charge-sheet was served upon him on 9.12.84. In reply to the charge-sheet the petitioner submitted his written statement on 25.2.85. Thereafter a second show cause notice was served upon him on 23.4. 85 to which the petitioner replied but the Post Master, Faridpur Head Office, the respondent No. 1 by his Memo. No. F1-1/84-85 dated 22.5.85 passed an order of compulsory retirement of the petitioner from service.

3. Against the said order of compulsory retirement dated 22.5.85 the petitioner moved an appeal before the Post Master General, Southern Circle, Khulna, the respondent No. 3 who by his order dated 19.10.85 dismissed the appeal of the petitioner.

4. Against the order of the said Post Master General, dated 19.10.85 the petitioner preferred Administrative Tribunal Case No. 231 of 1985 before the Administrative Tribunal who by his order dated 12.6.86 dismissed the case.

5. Against the order of the Administrative Tribunal date 12.6.85 the petitioner filed appeal Case No. 44 of 1986 before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal by order dated 23.4.87 allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and order appealed against and the petitioner was discharged from the departmental proceeding and the charge-sheet and the order of compulsory retirement from service as passed upon the petitioner on 22.5 85 was set aside.

6. After the aforesaid order of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal was passed on 23.4.87 the petitioner went to resume his duty at his place of posting at Head Post Office, Faridpur but he was not permitted to resume his duty because respondent No.1 by the impugned Memo. No. F1-1/Tribunal-1/85 dated Faridpur 4.2.84 BS corresponding to 19.5.87 (Annexure-B) started further inquiry against the petitioner on the self-same occurrence under section 11(3) of the Government Servants (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1985 and put the petitioner under suspension. Thereupon, the petitioner moved the Writ Petition in this Court and obtained the present Rule.

7. The respondent No. 1, the Post Master, Faridpur Head Office, District Faridpur filed an affidavit-in-opposition denying the material allegations made in the writ petition and stating inter alia, that to implement the order of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal the petitioner was required to get redress before the Administrative Tribunal under the provisions of Rule 7 of the Administrative Tribunal Rules, 1982, that as the petitioner was in the service of the Republic he was debarred from invoking the writ jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution and that the petitioner had alternative remedy before the Administrative Tribunal and as such the Rule was liable to be discharged.

<u>8. Mr. AJ Muhammad Ali, the learned advocate appearing for the petitioner, has submitted that the impugned order contained in the memo. Dated 19.5.87 under the signature of respondent No. 1 is in violation of the cardinal principle of law that no one should be vexed twice for the same offence and is also in contravention of Article 35(2) of the Constitution and as such is malafide, bad in law, illegal and is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.</u>

9. Mr. Delwar Hossain, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing for respondent No. 1, has submitted that the writ petition in this Court is not maintainable under Rule 7 of the Administrative Tribunal Rules, 1982 as the petitioner's remedy was to file an application before the Administrative Tribunal for implementing the decision or the order of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal dated 23.4.87 according to the procedure laid down in the said Rule 7 but the petitioner failed to exhaust that remedy before moving the writ petition in this court. In support of this submission the learned Advocate for the petitioner has relied upon the case of Sailor Rahman Vs. Bangladesh and others, 41 DLR 538.

<u>10. The Rule 7 of the Administrative Tribunal Rules, 1982 runs as follows:</u>

<u>"7. Execution of decisions and orders of a Tribunal—A Tribunal shall, for the purpose of execution of its decisions or orders, follow, as far as practicable, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (V of 1908) relating to the execution of a decree."</u>

11. Under the provisions of Rule 7 of the Administrative Tribunal Rules, 1982 the Administrative Tribunal, we think, can execute, auctioning as an executing Court, its own decisions or orders and also the decisions or orders of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal following the provisions of Civil Procedure Code relating to execution of a decree. The petitioner therefore has a remedy under Rule 7 of the Administrative Tribunal Rules, 1982 before the Administrative Tribunal to implement the decision or order of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal dated 23.4.87. The petitioner has been given a further remedy under section 10A of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 which runs as follows :

"10A. Contempt of Tribunal—(1) The Administrative Appellate Tribunal shall have power to punish for contempt of its authority or that of any Administrative Tribunal, as if it were the High Court Division of the Supreme Court."

<u>12. The petitioner failed to avail of the remedies under rule 7 of the Administrative Tribunal Rules, 1982 and under section 10A of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 and so he cannot avail of the remedy under Article 102 of the Constitution. The present writ petition therefore is not maintainable. This view finds support in the said case reported in 41 DLR 538 wherein it has been held :</u>

<u>"As of today the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 is a self-contained and composite legislation. Both the execution of the decisions and orders of a Tribunal and violation thereof are well taken care of by the legislation. It does not need the additional umbrella of this Court's jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution for implementation of decisions and orders of the Administrative Tribunal.</u>

<u>Besides, it, in spite of the existence of Rule 7 and section 10A of the Act, it is made a practice to additionally invoke the jurisdiction of this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution for purposes of implementing a decision and order of the Administrative Tribunal, then the affected parties ill themselves be the losers."</u>

In the above circumstances, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.
