full_judgment:
KM Hasan J: This Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause why the impugned order passed by the Ministry of Land Administration, Government of Bangladesh, Respondent No.1 as evidenced by Annexure G to the petition moved in Court today, should not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and to be of no legal effect

2. The facts are, in short, that the petitioners are the owners or co-sharers of an area of 5.79 acres of land bearing RS Plot Nos. 12650, 12651, 12652, 12716, 12717, 12718, 12719, 12720, 12721, 12722, 12723, 12724, 12727, 12728, 12729, 12730, 12731, 12732, 12673 in Mouza Chandgaon Police Station Panchlaish at present Chandgaon, Chittagong

3. The land was requisitioned with the intent to acquire the same for creating residential plots by Chittagong Development Authority (CDA), by order dated 28-5-64, issued under section 3 of the Requisition of Property Act, 1948. A notice was issued by the Respondent No.2 under section 5(3) of the said Act, for filing objections by the owners of the land on 6-7-68. It is claimed in the petition that the petitioners objected but no one paid any heed and the case lands were acquired under land acquisition case No. 138 of 1962-63. A part compensation was made, though at a very low rate, . and received by the land owners but no final payment has been made nor any final notification issued vesting the said land in the Government.

4. It is further stated in the petition that as the requisition of the case land was in excess of the requirement for the project for which it has been requisitioned, a part of it was not used for the last 26 years by the Chittagong Development Authority. The respondents neither took possession of it nor used if for the purpose it was requisitioned.

5. It is claimed that the said requisition not only threatened to drive out the petitioners from their home and hearth but their family graveyard was also requisitioned which is contrary to the provisions of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance. Several representations by the petitioners were made to the Ministry of Land Administration to relieve them from their sufferings.

6. With the approval of the Cabinet and on obtaining the opinion of the Ministry of Law and Justice, the Ministry of Land Administration gave a general direction to all the Secretaries concerned by Memo No. DA-72/84/514 dated 30-8-84 (Annexure- B) informing that a decision had been taken that if an acquired land was left unused beyond any justifiable time then it should be released in favour of the original owner without referring to the requiring authority or organisation for whose use the land was acquired.

7. By a further memo No. DA-72/84/26-acqn dated 9-12-84 issued by the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms, the Government of Bangladesh reaffirmed the earlier policy for surrendering the unused lands for their utilisation for productive purpose (Annexure-C). Based on the policy of the Government, the said Ministry vide a Memo dated 22-5-86 asked the Deputy Commissioner concerned to send considered opinion whether to release the requisitioned case land in favour of the original owners (Annexure-D).

8. On 13-9-89 the petitioners made a representation to the respondent No. 2 the Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong in which they mentioned that though the land was requisitioned for creating residential plots but the same had not been used for the said purpose. The petitioners further requested the respondent No. 2 to release the unutilised land to the original owners (Annexure-E).

9. The Additional Deputy Commissioner (LA) Chittagong vide his memo No. 739/LA dated 27-5-90 addressed to the Secretary, Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reform informed that all lands acquired by the Chittagong Development Authority could not be used for the purpose for which they were acquired, one of which is the disputed case land. The Additional Deputy Commissioner recommended that the case land may be released in favour of the original owners who are poor and still residing there.

10. Despite this recommendation the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reform declined to consider the release of the land vide its letter dated 24-9-90 (Annexure-G) stating that there was no scope for such consideration. Since then the petitioners made several representations and tadbirs but without any success. On 14-12-91 the petitioners' lawyer served a demand of justice notice to the respondents asking them to review and/or rescind the letter dated 24-4-90 but no action was taken.

11. The petitioners being aggrieved by the order (Annexure-G) moved this Court and obtained this Rule.

12. The Rule is contested by Respondent Nos. 2, 3, and 4 by filing two separate affidavits- in-opposition denying material allegations. Their common case is that the development of the project for the residential purpose at Muradpur under CDA scheme No. 26/61-62 has received approval of the Government as per section 36 B(I) of the Chittagong Development Authority Ordinance, 1959 vide memo No. 11 dated 4-1-63. The case property comprising an area of 5.79 acres of land of mouza Chandgaon along with other properties were acquired by the Government in LA Case No. 138/62-63 for creating a residential area. The total area thus requisitioned comes to 100.13 acres of land out of which 5. 79 is the disputed land.

13. The respondent No. 2 Deputy Commissioner, Chittagong after observing all the 'formalities required by law handed over vacant possession of 100.13 acres including the disputed area of 5.79 acres of land to the CDA on 6-12-66 and 31-12-68. This chunk of land comprising of 5.79 acres is separate and not contiguous to the rest of the requisitioned land. On 23-4-77 the entire 5-79 acres of land was allotted to the Bangladesh Steel and Engineering Corporation for construction of multistoried residential buildings for its workers and possession was also delivered to the said Corporation on 10-5-78. As the Corporation failed to start construction in time, CDA cancelled the said allotment and took back possession of the entire land allotted to it. After that, the CDA prepared a scheme to develop the land into a residential area by dividing it into small plots for the low income group. The Government gave its approval to the scheme and included the scheme in the revised Annual Development Programme of the year 1991-92 and allotted Taka 10 lakh for the development work under this scheme for the same period. It is further stated that the CDA had already completed development works under the scheme and is soon going to start allotment of plots as per rule.

14. It is further stated in the affidavit-in- opposition that the compensation for the lands thus requisitioned was assessed under LA Case No. 138/62-63 based on the prevailing market price of the land in the vicinity then. Therefore, adequate compensation was made over to the original owners as per relevant provisions of Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948. It is further stated that no homestead and graveyard were acquired and the land in question is being used based on the Annual Development Programme.

15. It is also stated in the affidavit- in-opposition that as the land in question is being used for the residential purpose the question of releasing the same does not arise. No order was ever issued for the release of the project land by the relevant Ministry, i e the Ministry of Land. In fact, the respondent No 1, the Ministry on a careful consideration of the development activities of the CDA refused to release the case land from requisition (Annexure-G).

16. The grounds taken by the petitioner in the writ petition are that, the impugned order (Annexure G) has been made violating the policy of the Government (Annexure-D). The case land has not been acquired, nor vested, nor full compensation paid, nor used for the purpose for which it was acquired. The land has not yet been vested in the respondents and the petitioners' legal right over the case property is still subsisting as no notification has yet been published in the official Gazette under section 5(7) of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948. The case land includes homestead of the petitioner and family graveyard and thus keeping the land under requisition and declining to derequisition the same by the respondents is a violation of the fundamental right of the petitioners. The (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 is ultra vires of the Constitution as it does not provide a clear guideline in it for payment of compensation and, as such, it is incompatible with Articles 36 and 42 of the Constitution. Lastly, the land admittedly having not been used for the purpose for which it was requisitioned for a long period of twenty eight years the continuation of the requisition is not sustainable beyond the life of the Ordinance which was of temporary nature.

17. The respondents, on the other hand, assailed the arguments of the petitioners by submitting that the writ petition is not maintainable as the petitioners have no locus standi to file this writ petition. The allegations involve disputed questions of facts which cannot be decided in writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution.

18. Mr. M Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate for the petitioners, has argued that the requisition and acquisition process of the case land had started in the year 1964, more than twenty eight years back, but so far only part compensation has been paid and the full payment has remained unpaid. Moreover, the compensation is so low that it cannot be considered adequate. But from the record it appears 90% of the compensation money assessed has already been handed over to the original owners and only 10% is yet to be paid. It also appears that the compensation is assessed under LA Case No. 138/62-63 on the basis of the prevailing market price then There is no evidence on record to show that any objection was raised by the petitioners while accepting the 90% of the compensation. Now, after twenty-eight years we do not find any reason for this court in its writ jurisdiction to enter into the disputed question of adequacy or inadequacy of the compensation assessed.

<u>19. By referring to Article 42(1) and (2) of the Constitution Mr. Islam next challenged the very vires of (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 on the ground that no clear guideline for payment of compensation has been provided in it. Article 42 guarantees that no person shall be deprived of his property by way of acquisition, nationalisation and requisition save by authority of law that provides for compensation and specifies the principle on which, and the manner in which the compensation is to be assessed and paid. We however do not find any substance in the contention of the learned Advocate that the Act does not provide guideline for payment of compensation. Section 5(B) of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 provides that when a property is requisitioned under section 5(3) with a view to its permanent acquisition, the owner of the property shall be offered or paid in advance before possession is taken over, compensation to the extent of either 100% for structure and building and 90% for lands of the provisional estimate. From annexure F to the writ petition we find that the owners of the case land had already accepted 90% of advance compensation. Moreover, section 7 of the said Act lays down the manner and principle for payment of compensation for immovable property. Sub-section (aaa) of section 7 further provides for arbitration in case of non-acceptance of compensation by the land owners and sub-sections c, cc, d and e of section 7 lay down how an arbitrator shall proceed in calculating the market value of the land requisitioned. From the record it does not appear that the original owners went for arbitration complaining the adequacy of the compensation.</u>

20.  The next point urged by the petitioner is that the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 under which the case land was requisitioned was a temporary law that had already come to an end. It has not been endowed with a new life by a later Act. Therefore, any proceeding under the Act of 1948 such as LA Case No. 138/62-63 has also come to end. As a result the said proceeding should stop and no further steps under sections 5, 6 and 7 of the Act of 1948 can now be taken regarding the case land as it is too late for the Government to proceed with the acquisition of the land and publish in the official Gazette a notice to the effect that the Government has decided to acquire the requisitioned property of the petitioners.

21. The learned Advocate then submits that section 47 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immoveable Property Ordinance 1982 should not be considered to have given life to the said LA proceeding. This section is to the effect:

"Special Savings Relating to Expired EB Act XIII of 1948. Notwithstanding the cessation of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 (EBA XIII of 1948), on the expiry of the period of its operation, all proceedings and matters, including all notices, notifications, and orders, relating to requisition or acquisition of any property or compensation or award in respect of any property requisitioned or acquired and all applications and appeals pending before any authority, arbitrator or court under that Act shall be continued, enforced, heard or disposed of as if that Act had not ceased to have effect and were continuing in operation."

<u>22. According to him, section 47 is not meant for an acquisition proceeding like LA Case No. 138/62-63 that has come to an end, but meant for an application or an appeal that was pending before any authority, an arbitrator or a court under the Act of 1948. A scrutiny of section 47 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Act, 1982 will show that the saving clause also relates to the Act of 1948 giving life to all proceedings and matters including all notices, notifications and orders relating to requisition and acquisition of any property under the said Act 'as if that Act had not ceased.' Therefore, it will not be correct to conclude that no further steps can now be taken under section 5(6) and 5(7) of (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948, to complete acquisition of the case land. In our view, the acquisition proceeding is still subsisting and may be completed by publishing Gazette notification, if the Government so desires.</u>

<u>23. Mr. Amirul Islam then argues that the impugned order Annexure G has not been passed with lawful authority as it contains refusal by the Land Ministry to derequisition the case land despite recommendation by the Deputy Commissioner, the statutory authority under the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948. He submits that under section 5(5) of the said Act the Deputy Commissioner is the authority to hear all objections from the land owners whose lands have been requisitioned and make recommendations on their objections. He then points out that such a recommendation by the statutory authority to derequisition the case land had been made by Annexure F, a letter written by the Deputy Commissioner (LA) to the Secretary Ministry of Land. In spite of that, in reply to a letter written by the petitioner No. 1, Alhaj Abul Bashar, praying for derequisition of the case land, the Secretary Ministry of Land simply refused to derequisition the case land. A copy of the same letter was also sent to the Deputy Commissioner (Annexure-G). This letter, according to the learned Advocate not only disregards the recommendation of the statutory authority but goes against the policy of the Government to derequisition the unutilised land as contained in Annexure C, a memo issued by the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms.</u>

<u>24. A scrutiny of the section 5(5) will show that the Deputy Commissioner is only authorised to make a recommendation that is not binding either on the requiring body or on the concerned Ministry. In fact, the Deputy Commissioner has no authority to release any property from requisition. Similarly, letters and memos (Annexure C) issued by the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms only contain the policy of the Government and are addressed to the Secretaries of different Ministries of some other concerned authorities. It is an inter-ministerial matter not creating legal duty upon the requiring authority and the concerned Ministry to derequisition the unutilised land in question. Article 102 of the Constitution can be invoked only when the petitioner's right has undisputedly accrued either under the Constitution or any legal instrument and such right has not been given effect to. In other words, the petitioners are being deprived of the benefit of such right. This letter is not a legal instrument creating legal right for the petitioners over the case land. It only lays down the policy of the Government without any force of law and without creating any legal right. Therefore, we do not find infringement of any legal right invoking protection under Article 102 of the Constitution.</u>

<u>25. A reading of Annexure-C, specially its last paragraph, shows the Government's concern about the unutilised lands that are lying with the requiring authorities, after completion of projects, for which they were requisitioned. It urges the requiring bodies to return those lands to the owners if they are not used within a reasonable time. Otherwise, it states that such lands would be released by the Government in favour of the original owners without referring the matter to the requiring authority or Ministry for whose use the lands have been requisitioned or acquired. A long time has lapsed since the issuance of the letter but the Government has not taken any step in that direction. On the other hand it appears that the Ministry that issued the letter for return of unused lands had itself refused to release the case land by Annexure G. It may be noted here that the Ministry that issued the said letter and the Ministry that refused to release the case land are the same. The Ministry of Land and the Chittagong Development Authority are very much the relevant authorities to decide what land they may return for being excess and unutilised land It has been held in the case of Badal Rani Misra vs. Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR (AD) 68 (relevant para-12).</u>

<u>"The question relating to the release of requisitioned land, it is not disputed, falls within the administrative function of the requisitioning authority and if the said authority, having regard to the facts in the instant case that the order of requisition of the plots was passed by it upon approval of the proposal of the requiring body by the Government considered it necessary to seek approval of the Government before passing an order of release of the same, it does not appear how that discretion called for interference by the High Court and how the High Court could pass an order of release under the Requisition of Property Act."</u>

26. In view of the above decision we do not find any illegality committed by the requisitioning authority in refusing to derequisition the case land. Therefore, we are not inclined to direct the Government to derequisition the case land measuring 5.79 acres on the petitioners' submission that the same is outside the project and its requisition was in excess of the requirement under the project

<u>27. The learned Advocate for the petitioners then raises the point that the case land has not yet been vested in the Government The original owners are still the legal owners of the case land. Non vesting of the land even after 28 years of requisition shows that the case land is not required for the purpose for which it was acquired. Therefore, the case land should be derequisitioned and returned to the original owners. Here by referring to Sat yam Co-operative Housing Society Ltd. vs. Calcutta Improvement Trust AIR 1989 263 Mr. Amirul Islam argues that the petitioners are well within their right to challenge the requisition for long and inordinate delay by the acquisition authority in concluding the acquisition proceeding. We have gone through the decision and, in our view, the decision referred to is not applicable in the instant case as the facts and circumstances are different. In that case certain land was purchased by a Housing Society and after getting clearance from Calcutta Improvement Trust it started construction of five apartment buildings for its members. While the construction was in progress and a substantial part was completed the Society was asked to stop work and was informed that the acquisition proceeding in respect of the land was pending for a long time. Under the circumstances the Court held that inordinate delay on the part of the acquisition authority can be a cause of action. This is not the case here. Petitioners came to know about the requisition immediately on requisition of the property but neither objected nor went for arbitration rather accepted a substantial part of the compensation.</u>

28. Under the (Emergency) Requisition Act 1948 the statutory vesting is completed with handing over of possession and publishing in the official Gazette, a notice to the effect that the government has decided to acquire the requisitioned property. In the instant case no such Gazette notification has yet been published justifying the petitioner's claim that statutory vesting in the Government is not completed. The whole acquisition process is a long one and stretches over many years. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the government has suggested that this court may fix a time for publication of a Gazette notification. In this  connection he has referred to an unreported decision held in Writ Petition No. 1004 of 1980 where this Court has given such a direction. We have already observed that the acquisition process is not yet complete. Therefore, we do not think, a direction from us to the Government to publish Gazette notification is necessary at this stage.

29. From the facts of the case Mr. Amirul Islam argues that except 5.79 acres of land, rest of the lands requisitioned have already been acquired, but the case land has not been acquired as it is not within the proposed development project. It is a chunk of land separate from the rest. From the record it appears that the case land was handed over to the Steel and Engineering Corporation by the requiring body for a housing project of the said Corporation. But subsequently, it was taken back when the Corporation failed to start the project. The respondents claim this as the reason for the delay in starting their own project. The respondents also submit that under the Emergency Requisition Act 1948 there is no bar to use any requisitioned property for a purpose other than the purpose for which it is requisitioned. We find substance in this argument. We have already taken the view that the acquisition process is not yet concluded and continuing and therefore we are not inclined to hold that the case land was not included in the original project.

30. The petitioners also claim to be in possession of the case land where according to them they have their homestead and family graveyard. On the other hand, it appears that by the requisition process the possession of the case land had already been handed over to the requiring body and work on it to develop it for residential purpose has already been undertaken. In paras 1 & 2 of the writ petition the petitioners have admitted that certain plots (the numbers of which are given) including the plots covering the case lands are requisitioned by the authority. This is again admitted by the petitioner No. 1 in his application dated 13-1-89 (Annexure E) to the Deputy Commissioner, praying for derequisition of the case land. Handing over of the case land to the requiring authority after its requisition can also be ascertained from Annexure (iii), the possession certificate, issued under the LA Case No. 138 of 1962/63. In support of the petitioners' possession of the case land the petitioners relied on Annexure-F' a letter dated 26-5-90 written by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, to the Secretary, Ministry of Land in which it is stated that the petitioners are in possession of the case land. Therefore, it appears that a disputed question of fact as to who is in possession of the case land is involved and this Court in its writ jurisdiction does not intend to enter into any disputed question of fact.

31. Mr. Kamal-ul-Alam, the learned Advocate for the Respondent No. 4 (CDA), has submitted that this application is not maintainable inasmuch as the petitioners are not aggrieved persons and because it involves disputed questions of facts as to whether the petitioners are successors-in-interest of the original owners from whom the land had been requisitioned and whether they are in possession or not. It appears from the record that the order of requisition has never been denied nor it was challenged either under sub-section 1 or 2 of section 5 of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948. On the other hand, this petition was filed originally by 59 petitioners though some others were substituted later. Out of 59 petitioners only petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 have given their father's name. Other petitioners have simply stated at the end of the list of their names that all the petitioners are from Faridapara PS Chandgaon, District Chittagong. The writ petition does not mention the name of the fathers of the petitioner Nos. 3-59. The petitioners also do not specifically state to which particular area of the 5.79, acres of the case land each petitioner is laying claim. Not even the title deeds of the original owners are annexed to the writ petition in support of the petitioners' claim for ownership. Whether the petitioners are the genuine heirs of the original owners remains a disputed question of fact and cannot be decided without evidence.

32. On this vague claim of ownership we cannot exercise our writ jurisdiction. Moreover, we find that the requiring body CDA has already allotted plots to petitioner Nos. 1 and 3. It may also be noted here that the impugned order, Annexure-G, is addressed to petitioner No. 1, Alhaj Abul Bashar only and not to other petitioners. Therefore we find that the petitioners are not aggrieved persons.

33.  The petitioners claim also suffers from laches and delay. The case land was requisitioned in the year 1964 and the writ petition was filed in 1992, almost after 28 years. It seems to us that the writ petition under Article 102 has been filed after an inordinate delay during which lot of changes have taken place regarding the disputed land. Under the circumstances this Division Bench is loath to exercise its writ jurisdiction. The statement made by the petitioners that during this time they have been trying elsewhere for the derequisition of case land is vague and without material. Save the recommendation of the Deputy Commissioner in 1990 based on an application dated 13-9-89, (Annexure-E), by the petitioner No. 1 no other material has been given. From this it appears that it is only around later part of 1980 the petitioner No. 1 woke up to file an application for himself and others for derequisition of the case land. Extraordinary remedy provided by writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution is a speedy relief meant for the vigilant not for indolent. It is by now well settled that laches and delay disentitles one to seek remedy before writ jurisdiction.

In view of the above, we find that the petitioners cannot get any relief. The Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

case_source: From the Judgment and Order dated 18th January 1984 passed by the High Court Division, Comilla Bench, in Civil Revision No. 184 of 1983
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed J : In this appeal by special leave the question for determination is whether the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division rightly interfered with the appellate Court's Judgment holding that the respondent are tenants of the plaintiff-appellant and that they are stopped from questioning the appellant's title in the suit-premises. The order impugned of the High Court Division is dated 18 January 1984 in Civil Revision No. 184 of 1983 arising out of Title Appeal No. 87 of 1977 of the Additional Court of Subordinate Judge, Noakhali.

2. The suit land is a Chandina-bhiti with a construction thereon in Maijdee town. One Gagan Ali was admittedly its owner in possession. In fact, he had only the possessory right therein. Case of the plaintiff-appellant is that Gagan Ali sold the premises to him by a registered sale-deed dated 8 December 1953 (Exhibit 1) and delivered possession to him. Thereafter, he possessed it by inducting different tenants, one Hashmatullah (PW 4) being one such tenant. After the tenancy of Hashmatullah was terminated the appellant inducted into the premises as tenant one Kala Miah by a registered Agreement dated 31 August 1964 corresponding to 15 Bhadra 1371 BS (Exhibit 3). Kala Miah continued his tenancy on payment of rent till his death and on his death his sons and other heirs. Who are the main defendants in this suit, held over possession as tenants but they defaulted in payment of rent. The appellant therefore, filed the suit namely OC Suit No. 886 of 1973, in the First Court of Munsif, Noakhali, for realization of arrears of rent from January 1972 to October 1973 at the rate of RS 45/- per month and also for eviction of the defendant tenants on whom notice of eviction was already served under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act.

3. Defendant No.1, (respondent No.1) son of Kala Miah contested the suit denying the appellant's title altogether and setting up a rival claim of title himself on the basis of purchase from one Mohammadullah. He contended that the original owner, Gagan Ali, did not sell the premises to the appellant under any kabala, like Exhibitl, but Gagan Ali made oral transfer of his interest including possession of the suit-land to Mohammadullah and that it is Mohammadullah who, by an unregistered agreement dated 2-6-64 (Exhibit Ka) sold the premises to him on receipt of consideration of Taka 600 and since then he has been possessing it as of his own right. He denied that his father Kala Miah was a tenant under the appellant or that he got the premises by inheritance from his father and, as such, no question of his holding over as a tenant of the appellant arose.

4. The learned Munsif on consideration of the evidence both oral and documentary held that Kala Mia was not a tenant under the plaintiff, that defendant No. 1 has been possessing the suit property on the basis of his purchase from Mohammadullah who, on his turn, had purchased it from Gagan Ali and that there was no landlord-tenant relationship between the plaintiff and the defendants and on these findings he dismissed the suit by judgment dated 8-5-74. The plaintiff preferred an appeal but the appeal was dismissed by the sub-ordinate Judge against whose decision the plaintiff filed a revisional application being Revision Case No. 387 of 1981 before the High Court Division and the latter, on allowing the application, remanded the appeal to the Subordinate Judge for rehearing. Thus after re-haring the appeal the learned Sub-ordinate Judge by his Judgment dated 2-4-83 allowed the appeal, reversed the trial Court's judgment and decreed the suit finding, among other things, that the plaintiff got title from Gagan Ali by the Sale deed Exhibit 1, that the plaintiff inducted Kala Mia, father of defendant No. 1, as tenant by the registered Agreement, Exhibit 3, that on the death of Kala Mia his heirs including defendant No. 1 held over possession as tenants but defaulted in the payment of rent. This decision of the appellate Court was again challenged by defendant No.1, in revision namely Civil Revision No. 184 of 11983 and the learned Single Judge, by the impugned judgment, reversed the appellate Court's decision and restored that of the trial Court.

5. Mr Asrarul Hossain, learned Advocate for the appellant, has seriously assailed the decision of the learned Single Judge, particularly his interference in revision with the finding of facts arrived at by the lower Appellate Court on the question whether the respondents were tenants by holding-over' under the appellant. The learned Advocate has criticised the learned Single Judge for, what he terms, illegally rejecting the appellant's documentary evidence including a clear admission of the respondent that he was a tenant under the appellant and also for the view taken by the learned Single Judge that in the absence of satisfactory proof of payment of rent the respondent was not a tenant of the appellant whose registered instruments including the registered Lease Agreement have been arbitrarily rejected. The learned Advocate contends that in view of creation of the tenancy in favour of Kala Mia, father of the respondent, the latter was estoppel from questioning the appellant's title under section 116 of the Evidence Act.

<u>6. The law on the subject, that is, land-lord-tenant relationship, is a settled law. It has been expounded in section 116 of the Evidence Act, which is quoted below for proper appreciation in this case:</u>

<u>116. No tenant of immovable property, or person claiming through such tenant, shall, during the continuance of the tenancy, be permitted to deny that the landlord of such tenant had, at the beginning of the tenancy, a title to such immovable property; and no person who came upon any immovable property by the license of the person in possession thereof shall be permitted to deny that such person had a title to such possession at the time when such license was given."</u>

<u>The estoppels as described in this section are known as tenant's estoppels or estoppel by contract. This estoppel is founded upon a contract between the tenant and the landlord. It provides that when a person enters into possession of immovable property as a tenant of another person the neither he nor anybody claiming through his shall be permitted during the continuance of the tenancy to deny the landlord's title however defective that title might be. This necessarily implies that in case the tenant sets up a claim of title in himself he shall first surrender possession to the person from whom he had taken it. This principle of law has been nicely expounded by Jessel MP in Re Siringer's Estate, page 384 LR 6 Ch 9 in the following works:</u>

<u>"Where a man having no title obtains possession of land under demise by a man in possession who assumes to give him a title as tenant, he cannot deny his deny his landlord's title. This is a perfectly intelligible doctrine. He took possession under a contract to pay rent so long as he held possession under the landlord, and to give it up at the end of the term to the landlord, and having taken it in that way he is not allowed to say that the man whose title he admits and under whose title he took possession has not a title. That is a well-established doctrine. That is estoppels by contract."</u>

<u>Sometimes it is found that after entering into possession as a tenant a person, from some motive, defaults in the payment of rent and when the question of eviction is raised he takes the plea that he is not a tenant for there is no evidence that he ever paid rent to the landlord. Such a device cannot carry him anywhere in view of the basic principle that once he is found to have entered into possession as tenant non-payment of rent shall not be interpreted as non-existence of the tenancy. Payment of rent is one among many other proofs of a tenancy. Mere non-payment of rent does not terminate the tenancy or make the possession of the tenant adverse to the landlord, as has been rightly held in the case of JM Singh vs Baldeo Singh, 49 IA 299. This position is based on the footing that once relation of landlord and tenant is established it is presumed to continue, and the burden of proving that it has ceased is on the person who alleges it to have ceased. Section 116 in express language precludes the tenant from questioning his landlord's title during the continuance of the tenancy: this section however does not debar him from doing so after it is shown by him that the landlord's title has been lost or extinguished since then. But if he himself claims title he must first surrender possession to the person from whom he had taken the lease. Again, if the landlord determines the tenancy on any ground but the tenant continues to stay on still the tenant will be stopped from questioning the landlord's title unless he restores possession to the landlord who had put him into possession.</u>

<u>7. Mr TH Khan, learned Advocates for the respondent does not dispute this proposition of law particularly when the question has finally been decided by the Privy Council in the case of Currimbhoy & Co vs Creet, AIR 1933 (PC) 29. But his contention is that in the instant case the appellant filed to prove that the respondent was his tenant by holding over or that his father Kala Mia, had been a tenant under the appellant; on the contrary, he contends, evidence has been led by the respondent to show that he had got possession of the land by purchase in his own name and by his own right and that his father was not a tenant of the appellant, that he did not inherit it on his father's death and, as such, there was no question of holding over. This argument clearly takes us back to the disputed facts between the parties, whether Kala Mia was a tenant under the appellant and, if so, whether Kala Mia's heirs including defendant, respondent No. 1 continued in the tenancy. Since these question had been decided finally by the appellate Court they could not be reopened and reagitated in revision unless it is shown that the findings had not been made on due consideration of all material evidence according to established principles of assessment of evidence. As such, the evidence both oral and documentary requires to be reviewed.</u>

8. Registered Agreement Exhibit 3 is the evidence of creation of a tenancy by the appellant in favour of Kala Mia at a monthly rent of Taka 45. The learned Single Judge has observed that through this exhibit is a registered Agreement. It does not by itself prove the tenancy. What appears to be meant by this observation is that the Agreement even if genuine might not have been acted upon. The respondent questioned the execution of the Agreement and also alleged that it was not acted upon. So far as the execution is concerned, besides PW 1 (the appellant), PW 5 a Deed- writer has deposed that he had written this Agreement, which was executed in his presence. As to whether it was acted upon, besides the evidence of PW 1, there is the evidence of a number of witnesses including PWs 2, 3 and 4 PW2 is Kala Mia's son-in-law, that is, he is brother-in-law of the respondent (defendant No-1); he has supported the appellant's case that Kala Mia was a tenant under the appellant and resided in the house carrying on cloth- business there. Evidence of PW 2 was sought to be discarded on the ground that he married a stepsister of defendant No.1 and as such he is hostile to him. But there is no evidence whatever that there was any clash of interest or enmity between defendant No.1 and PW 2; and if there were any strained relationship between them, it appears, it is due to the fact that PW 2, through a relation, came to the Court to depose against his disclosing the truth and not supporting his claim of rival title by the unregistered Agreement (Exhibit Ka) which has been challenged by the appellant to be antedated PW 3 is an independent witness. He is a practicing lawyer having residence near the suit premises. He claims to know both the parties. He has stated that the premises belonged to the appellant who possessed it through different tenants and that he saw Kala Mia possessing it as a tenant of the appellant PW 4, Hashmatullah, says that the possessed the premises as tenant of the appellant before the structure was destroyed by fire, that is, prior to Kala Mia's tenancy. On consideration of evidence the lower Appellate Court held that the Agreement, Exhibit 3, was not only genuine but it was acted upon. Case of the respondent (Kala Mia's son) is that his father did not take the tenancy, but he himself purchased the premises from one Mohammadullah who is DW 2 Mohammadullah's evidence is that he sold it to the respondent by the unregistered Agreement, Exhibit (Ka" as already stated on 2-6-64, that is, about three months earlier than Kala Mia's registered Agreement, Exhibit. If Exhibit 'Ka' is relied upon, the we find two tenants simultaneously for the same premises, one is the father and the other is the son Case of the appellant is that Exhibit Ka is a fraudulent and antedated document. Even if it were not fraudulent and antedated, still the broad fact remains that under this Agreement no interest passed to Kala Mia's son unless it is shown that Mohammadullah had any right, title or interest in the premises himself. Mohammadullah claims title from Gagan Ali Bepari, but there is no paper to show that Gagan Ali Bepari had transferred the premises to Mohammadullah. Secondly, Gagan Ali Bepari could not have made such transfer in 1964 as he had already transferred his entire interest in the premises to the appellant by an earlier registered Sale-deed 8-12-53, Exhibit 1. The claim of the respondent that he purchased it from Mohammadullah is negative by Exhibit 1 read with the supporting oral evidence. Evidence of Mohammadullah has been challenged on another ground; his elder brother PW 4 Hashmatullah has deposed that he had taken lease of the premises from the appellant as a month to month tenant by a registered Agreement dated 13-6-55 (Exhibit 3A) and continued their till the structure was gut- ted by fire in 1964. He has further deposed that Mohammadullah, his younger brother, was at that time a mere student. Thus it appears that Mohammadullah, respondent's vendor, was not even a tenant in the premises but his elder brother was the tenant. To avoid that question of validity of the alleged transfer of the property by Mohammadullah to him, the respondent went to the extent of denying the genuineness of appellant's title under, Exhibit 1, the registered sale-deed and it has been argued that this Sale-deed was either fraudulent or it was not acted upon. To counter this contention evidence, both oral and documentary, has been led by the appellant. It is that after the purchase under Exhibit 1, and when Hashmatullah was a tenant, the premises was sold in auction for recovery of some public dues and it is the appellant who got the sale set aside. In this connection the appellant filed an order of the Board of Revenue setting aside the sale at his instance. That order is Exhibit 5 dated 30 January. 160. PW 3, the lawyer, has supported the appellant's case saying that he was engaged by the appellant in the proceedings for setting aside the auction sale under Exhibit 5 the learned Single Judge has observed that this document got no direct bearing on the issue in question. If the tenancy of Kala Mia is in question, this document is not so much relevant, but if the appellant-land-lord's title is challenged, this document is very much relevant. We therefore find that the respondent with a view to boosting up his story of purchase from Mohammadullah, who was nobody to make any such transfer, raised out of motive the dispute about the appellant's original title under Exhibit 1, by the registered sale-deed, executed by Gagan Ali Bepari. Curiously enough, it is Gagan Ali Bepari from whom Mohammadullah claims title by oral purchase at a subsequent- date. In the circumstances, the appellate Court's finding that both Exhibits 1 and 3 are genuine documents and were acted upon is a finding based on proper consideration of evidence and as such this finding was not open for re-opening in the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division.

<u>9. Mr Asrarul Hossain has laid considerable stress on Exhibits 4 and 4(a) which purportedly contain an admission of the respondent (defendant No.1) that he was a tenant under the appellant. These exhibits are certified copies of two applications of the respondent to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) praying for settlement to the suit-premises from the Government, the ultimate owner. Both the appellant and the respondent (defendant No.1) prayed for settlement from the Government in 1973 where upon two separate cases were started which ended ultimately in favour of the appellant, obviously in view of the appellant's possessory right from Gagan Ali Bepari for a long time. The question raised here, however, is not as to who got the settlement from the Government, in both these applications, Exhibits. 4 and 4(a), filed about six years after his father Kala Mia's death, the respondent (defendant No.1) stated that he was a tenant of the appellant, Haji Abdus Sattar, who by misrepresentation had created the tenancy though he had no title, that because of this defect of title, he was offering himself as a candidate for settlement in view of the fact that he had been running a cloth-shop in the premises for a long time. This is a clear admission and it estoppel him from denying the appellant's title in the premises. To wriggle out of this tight comer, he has contended that the documents exhibits 4 & 4(a) are not correct copies of his applications to the Revenue Authorities. The learned Single Judge has observed that these copies of the applications were not legally proved, that they are private documents and further that attention of the respondent was not drawn to the statement contained in these supplications, and as such the question of binding him with the statement therein does not arise. This observation, we find, got no legal or factual basis. For these are certified copies of applications to the Additional Deputy Commissioner for settlement, who after necessary endorsement, incorporated them into the record of the Settlement Case and issued certified copies thereof in accordance with law the originals of the applications cannot be produced or obtained by anybody unless a Court calls for them. These certified copies were filed as exhibits in this suit in presence of respondent who them raised objection, but the Court ignoring his objection marked them as exhibits 4 and 4(a). Again, while deposing in Court as DW 1 he himself drew his attention to these documents stating in his examination-in-chief that these were not true copies his applications to the Additional Deputy Commissioner. In the circumstances, there was no necessity for drawing his further attention to them during cross-examination. As to the authenticity of these certified copies, the respondent did not apply to the Court to lodge in complaint under section 195 CrPC against the appellant on a charge of forgery who produced or filed in evidence these documents in a judicial proceeding Such a complaint may be filed under section 195 (1) (c) CrPC even now if the respondent dares to move the Court for that purpose. These documents issued and certified to be true copies by an authorised officer of the Government are admissible in evidence. The statement contained therein as described above is an admission within the meaning of section 20 of the Evidence Act and the respondent is bound by his admission that he was a tenant of the appellant who allegedly got no valid title to the premises.</u>

<u>10. Mr TH Khan, learned Advocate for the respondent, has tried to make out a case of total non-payment of rent and has contended that in the absence of reliable evidence that rent was ever paid to the appellant it cannot he said that any tenancy was created or the Agreement Exhibit 3, purportedly creating the tenancy was acted upon. Evidence in this connection is that Kala Mia paid rent so long be was alive and after his death his heirs, the defendants, became irregular in payment of rent and ultimately stopped it. PW 2 has stated that Kala Mia during his life-time had engaged him to AD-14 look after his cloth-shop and to pay rent for the premises and that the respondent paid rent for 14 months at a time by Exhibit 6. He has also deposed that he had been authorised in writing by his father in-law to act as his Assistant in the cloth-business (Exhibit 13). These two documents have been seriously challenged as fabrication for the purpose of the suit, PW 2 has, of course, denied the suggestion as to fabrication of Exhibits. 6 and 13; but the payment of rent for 14 months at a time and non-production of any receipts for payment of rent for the earlier period create suspicion in the genuineness of the receipt Exhibit 6. But I have already observed at the beginning that mere non-payment of rent does not snap landlord and tenant relationship and that non-payment of rent will not enable a tenant to question landlord's title unless he discontinues the tenancy and restores possession to the landlord. If mere non-payment of rent is taken as proof of non-existence of landlord and tenant relationship grave consequences will follow, for an unscrupulous tenant upon entering a premise as a tenant will deliberately as a convenient time. Mr TH Khan has contended that there is no evidence of the respondents holding over and that if the evidence as to payment of rent by Exhibit 6 is rejected no tenancy under the appellant exists. Answer to this contention is contained in the principle enunciated already in paragraph 6 above. It is that once a tenancy is created, it will be presumed that it is continuing, unless it is shown that it has ceased. The tenancy was created in favour of Kala Mia on whose death his heirs (including defendant No.1) continued to possess the premises. This is "holding over." For without Kala Mia's tenancy they could not have entered upon possession particularly when the claim of independent title by purchase has fallen through. They say that they did not pay any rent to the appellant but such non- payment of rent hardly improves their case, for the tenancy continues even if payment of rent is not made.</u>

<u>11. Lastly Mr TH Khan has drawn our attention to our decision in the case of Abdus Sattar vs Suresh Chandra Das, 32 DLR (AD) 170 and has contended that a monthly tenancy is not heritable. In that case it was observed:</u>

<u>"A tenancy-at-will is determinable at the will of either landlord or tenant and is a personal relation between the original landlord or tenant and is determined by the death of either of them."</u>

<u>It is obvious that such a tenancy is not heritable in the sense that on the death of a tenant his heirs are not under any legal obligation to pay rent to the landlord or to continue the tenancy, in the same way, as the landlord is not bound to keep the lease alive. Both the parties are at liberty to discontinue the tenancy. If the heirs of late tenant continue to stay on, but do not pay rent they shall not be permitted to say that the landlord has no title and in case they themselves claim title they must first of all restore possession to the land-lord an act which has not been done in this case. As such they have been rightly held to be tenants by holding over.</u>

<u>12. In the result, the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment of the High Court Division is set aside and that of the appellate Court is restored. As to costs, though the conduct of the respondent (defendant No. 1) is reprehensible, calling for costs of the appeal, but since he got two judgments in his favour, we refrain from awarding any cost against him.</u>

End.
