case_source: An Application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.
full_judgment:
A.M. Mahmudur Rahman, J : The petitioner obtained this Rule Nisi under Article 102(2) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh as revived by Proclamation (Partial Revival) (Second) Order, 1985 read with the Proclamation (Amendment) Order No. 1 of 1985 calling upon the respondent Nos. 1-3 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated February 11, 1986 passed by the respondent No. 4 as per Annexure L to the petition declaring the Respondent No. 3 senior to the petitioner should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

2. Facts leading to this rule, in brief, are that Respondent No. 3 Mohammad Ali was appointed a work-charge driver in the Urban Land Development and construction of Public Housing on 9.7.65. Subsequently on creation of the Urban Development Directorate by the Government he was appointed as a contingent driver on 10.9.65 and was appointed on regular basis with effect from 13.4 69. The petitioner Fazlur Rahman Chowdhury was appointed contingent driver in the said Directorate on 21.2.67. By notification No. S-/2M-31/72-946 dated 28.9.1983 the Ministry of Public Works and Urban Development converted the contingent establishment of the Urban Development Directorate into regular establishment from the date of its creation and the post of contingent drivers were made regular posts and the contingent drivers were sought to be absorbed in the regular post with effect from their initial appointment. That respondent No. 2, the Director of the Urban Development Directorate by his Memo No. P-54/65 (P.T)-1650 dated 20.8.1984 found the petitioner to be senior to respondent No. 3 (Annexure-E) but thereafter, by Memo No. Sha-2/2p-3/84/237 dated 4.11.1984 the Ministry of Public Works directed the respondent No. 2 to declare the respondent No. 3 senior to the petitioner. The respondent No. 2 on receipt of the said Memo by his Memo No. P-54/65(part) 2841 dated 2.4.12.1984 declared respondent No. 3 as the junior most driver in the said Directorate and declared him surplus. Thereafter the Deputy Secretary (Administration-1) of Public Works by his Memo dated 13.2.1985 informed the respondent No.2 the decision of the Government that respondent No. 3 was senior to the petitioner and was to be declared surplus ( Annexure-H to this petition) and in compliance thereof the respondent No. 2 declared the petitioner as surplus on the ground that he was junior most driver in the Directorate by his order dated 2 5.2. 85 (Annexure-1).

3. Thus the legal race was set in motion and the petitioner challenged the propriety of the said order of the respondent No. 2 dated 25.3.85 before the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka in Case No. 38 of 1985.The Administrative Tribunal, however, after hearing the case declared the order dated 25.2.1985 of the respondent No. 2 as unlawful and of no legal effect and set aside the same by his judgment dated 4.6.1985.

4. The respondent No. 3 took an appeal against the aforesaid order of the Administrative Tribunal being Appeal No. 37 of 1985 to the' Administrative Appellate Tribunal, the respondent No. 4. Respondent No. 4, however, after hearing both the parties and examining the relevant orders relating to seniority of the petitioner and the respondent No. 3 found that the respondent No. 3 was appointed as contingent driver before the petitioner Fazlur Rahman Chowdhury at the relevant time and was senior to him. And upon such finding the respondent No. 4 set aside the order passed by the Administrative Tribunal.

5. The petitioner has challenged the order of the respondent No. 4, declaring the respondent No. 3 senior to him on the ground that respondent No. 4 upon an erroneous interpretation of Memorandum No. Estb/Ri/S-46/72/55 dated 21.4.72 and Memorandum of SGA/RI/IS-33/69/71 (350) dated 28.3.69 Annexure M and M(1) to this petition issued by the Government passed the impugned order without any lawful authority.

6. Mr. Shafiq Ahmed, the learned Counsel appeared on behalf of the petitioner while Mr. M.M. Haque, the learned Deputy Attorney General represented the respondent No. 1 and Mr. Shamsul Huq Chowdhury, the learned Advocate represented the respondent No. 3.

7. Mr. Shafiq Ahmed submitted that the respondent No. 4, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal was wrong in taking its view that the respondent No. 3 was senior to the petitioner in that although respondent No. 3 was appointed on 16.9.65 in the contingent establishment but subsequently he lost the contingent character of his post on 13.4.1969 on being appointed on a regular basis. On the other hand, the petitioner was appointed as a contingent driver on 21.2.1967 & he remained in that post as such. Therefore, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that the petitioner was senior to the respondent No.3 in the contingent post.

<u>8. The question whether respondent No. 3 was senior to the petitioner or not has to be decided on perusal of evidence & interpretation of the relevant orders of the Ministry of Public Works and the Urban Development Directorate. This point was decided by the respondent No. 4, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal after examining the evidence and interpreting the decisions of the Government as contained in the Memo No. S.C.A/RI/16-33/6 9/71 (350) dated March 28, 8969 of the Services and General Administration Department and Memo No. Estb/RI/S-46/72/55 dated April 21, 1972 of the Secretary, Establishment Division of the Ministry of Cabinet Affairs and other orders relating to the point in issue.</u>

<u>This Court in exercising the jurisdiction under Article 102(2) is not empowered to declare an order or act of a person or authority as has been passed without lawful authority & of no legal effect on the ground that the same was passed upon an erroneous interpretation of Certain laws, rules and orders in a writ of certiorari. This Court .exercising such jurisdiction can declare an act done or a proceeding taken by a person performing the function of the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority to have been done or taken without lawful authority and is of no legal effect on the ground that the person or the authority acted without jurisdiction and/ or the order passed is malafide.</u>

<u>In the petition before us the authority of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal has not been challenged on the ground of want of jurisdiction & or malafide.</u>

<u>Where it is found that a person or an authority is vested with a jurisdiction to do certain act and in exercise of that jurisdiction it does the same whether wrongly or rightly the act done or the proceeding taken cannot be interfered with on the ground of erroneous decision of law if that authority is properly constituted and acted within it's province.</u>

<u>This view of ours finds support in the case of Nasiruddin Vs. Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others reported in 33 D.L.R. (AD) 216. At page 221 of the report the learned Chief Justice has expressed in the following manner:</u>

<u>"It is to be observed that when an authority is Vested with a jurisdiction to do certain acts and in the exercise of that jurisdiction he does it wrongly or irregularly the action can be said to be done within the purported exercise of his jurisdiction".</u>

9. A similar view has also been expressed in the case of Jamil Huq and others Vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 34 D.L.R. (AD) 125 wherein it has been held that when it is found that the tribunal is constituted properly then the proceeding or action taken by the said tribunal cannot be interfered with and irregularities or illegalities committed by such Tribunal or authority will not affect its jurisdiction. We may also profitably refer to the case of Cohens Vs. Vergina back in 1821 which was considered in the case reported in 34 D.L.R. 125 (AD). To quote the learned Chief Justice we may refer the observations noticed in 34 D.L.R. (AD) in the following manner.

"We have no more right to decline that exercise of jurisdiction which is given than to usurp that which is not given. The one or the other would be treason to the Constitution".

10. As in the aforesaid judicial pronoun cements of high authority the extent of jurisdiction of this Court in a writ of certiorari have been instructively laid down we have no hesitation to hold that the respondent No. 4 in this case acted within its jurisdiction and when it acted within its jurisdiction its action is immune from attack under Article 102(2) of the Constitution as revived by Proclamation (Partial Revival) (Second) Order of 1965 read with Proclamation (Amendment) Order No. 1 of 1965. In this view of the matter, we are unable to persuade ourselves to declare the impugned order passed by the respondent  No. 4 as has been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect on the ground that it acted without lawful authority in declaring the respondent No. 3 senior to the petitioner on an erroneous interpretation of the notifications aforementioned. Learned Deputy Attorney General raised an important question in this Rule regarding its maintainability. Now let us consider the contention. The learned Deputy Attorney General submitted that for the reason of sub-article (5) of Article 102 of the Constitution the order passed by the respondent No. 4 is not amenable to judicial review by this court under Article 102 of the Constitution. In other words, the jurisdiction of this Court exercising the power under Article 102 of the Constitution has been ousted by sub-article (5) to question the propriety of the order of the Administrative Tribunal as well as the Respondent No. 4. He placed before us the Constitution (Partial Revival) (Second) Order, 1965 and referring to sub-Article (a) of section 2 submitted that such ouster has also been protected by substituted sub-Article (5) of Article 102 of the suspended constitution. He submitted that Administrative Tribunal has also been excluded by substituted sub-article (5) from the expression "Person" occurring in Article 102 of the Constitution. On the other hand, the learned Counsel for the petitioner drawing our attention to the substituted sub-article (5) of Article 102 of the Constitution submitted that in clause (c) of the substituted sub-article (5) there is no reference to Article 117 of the Constitution which authorizes establishment of the Administrative Tribunal. But reference to Article 117 finds place in the original sub-Article (5) of the Article 102 of the Constitution, So, according to him substituted sub-Article (5) has not made the Appellate Tribunal an excepted person and as such the propriety of the order passed by the respondent No. 4 is subject to judicial review under Article 102 of the Constitution.

<u>11. We have closely examined the contention of the learned Deputy Attorney General as well as the learned Counsel for the petitioner in this respect.</u>

<u>It is true, that, in the substituted sub-Article (5) of the Article 102 no reference to Article 117 of the Constitution was made. But then under this original sub-Article (5) the Administrative Tribunal was to be established under Article 117 of the Constitution and substituted sub-Article (5) in clause (c), it appears, speaks of Administrative Tribunal. That being the position we have no hesitation to hold that the Administrative Tribunal as referred to in substituted sub-Article (5) is the Administrative Tribunal which was established under Article 117 of the Constitution. Now, the question falls for determination is whether-there is a complete ouster of the jurisdiction of the Court in exercising of an extra- ordinary jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution for the reason of the said ouster provision in the Constitution itself. From the language of sub-Article (5) it is clear that the Administrative Tribunal is not a person within the meaning of Article 102 (2) of the Constitution, But by such provision ipso facto it can-not be read into Article 102 that there is a complete ouster of the jurisdiction of the Court to examine the question. The power of the High Court Division is not totally ousted by such Constitutional provision as contained in the substituted sub-Article (5) of Article 103. This court exercising jurisdiction under Article 102(2) can, of course, examine the propriety or otherwise of an act of such a person or an authority when it acts malafide or the order is coram non judice.</u>

<u>12. There is a long line of decisions in support of this view of ours. In the case of Kb. Ehteshamuddin Ahmed lqbal Vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 33 D.L.R. (AD) 154 his Lordship Ruhul Islam, J, who delivered the main judgment, has observed "As a normal practice in a constitutional set-up in exercise of writ jurisdiction, the superior Courts are competent to examine the propriety of the proceedings or action taken by an inferior tribunal, but the position is altogether different in the case of Martial Law Court or Tribunal acting within the ambit of the Martial Law Regulations. Of course, when a Martial Law Court or Tribunal has acted without jurisdiction or such court or Tribunal is not properly constituted, that is to say, is coram non judice or has acted malafide, the power of the superior courts under Article 10.3 of the Constitution in an appropriate case may he exercised".</u>

<u>In the case of Jamil Huq Vs. Bangladesh reported in 34 D.L.R. (AD) 125 the learned Chief Justice observed : "......that any order or action of the excepted authority mentioned in sub-Article (5) of Article In is immune from challenge in writ jurisdiction, subject to the rule laid down by this Division in the case of Khondker Ehteshamuddin Ahmed alias Iqbal Vs. State, 33 D.L. R. (AD) 154, in that the order is coram non judice or malafide".</u>

<u>In Kh Ehteshamuddin Ahmed in a separate judgment his Lordship B. H. Chowdhury, J. has considered the decisions of various courts and his Lordship referred to the case of Federation of Pakistan Vs. Syed Ahmed reported in P.L D. 1974 (SC) 151 and being in agreement noticed the following observation made by Hamoodur Rahman, C. J. :-</u>

<u>"Indeed malafide acts stand on the same footing as acts done without jurisdiction. Similarly coram non judice also stand on the same footing because these words would literally mean that they have been done by authority or body exercising judicial or quasi-judicial powers which was not properly constituted even under law under which it was set up and that its decision is not a decision of a competent authority. If this be so then such acts do not also qualify for validation and they have not been saved for scrutiny by the ouster clause, no matter how widely that ouster clause may be worded".</u>

13. In the present case as no case of want of jurisdiction or of malafide on the part of the respondent No. 4 was urged by the learned Counsel for the petitioner we are not inclined to examine the same in order to strike down the impugned order on that count.

14. In view of the aforesaid discussions, we have got no hesitation to hold that the impugned order is immune from judicial review and cannot be struck down by this court in exercise of extraordinary jurisdiction under Article 102(2) of the suspended Constitution. Therefore, we hold that this rule must fail. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

SULTAN HOSSAIN KHAN, J.-- I agree.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Decree No. 103 of 1962.
lawyer:
Abdul Quayum, Advocate ----- For the Appellant
Md. Obaidur Rahman Mostafa, AAG ----- For the Respondent
parties:
Khorshed Ahmed Chowdhury ----- Appellant
Vs. 
Government of Bangladesh & others ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
Abdul Bari Sarker J: This appeal is directed against the Judgment and decree passed by Mr. Ali Ahmed, Subordinate Judge, Barisal in Title Suit No. 22 of 1961.

2. The suit is for declaration that the khas lands of the plaintiff-Wakf Estate measuring 422.41 acres of khas lands as detailed in schedules A-H have not been legally acquired as excess land as the 70 members of the five families of the name of the wakif Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury, were entitled to retain 700 bighas of khas land under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the order of the Revenue Officer dated 22.2.56 and Circle Officer dated 23.2.56, allowing only 348.80 acres as Khas land of the plaintiff-wake estate, in illegal, null and void.

3. The plaintiffs case is the late Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury was a very rich man and he executed and registered the wakfnama dated 14th Ashar, 1337 BS vide Ext.1 with respect to the suit lands. There were tenants with respect to some part of the suit land and the income from the tenanted land would exceed Tk. 10,000.00. Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury had 422.41 acres of khas land in his possession. The wakfnama was duly enrolled with the Wakf Commissioner and its number is 1261. As per the provisions of the Wakf Deed, the wakif Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury was the sole Motwalli till his death. Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury died on 18th Poush, 1341 BS leaving 4 sons namely Fazle Ali Chowdhury, Khorshed Ahmed Chowdhury, Nazir Ahmed Chowdhury and Najibul Hoque Chowdhury. As per the terms of the wakfnama the above 4 sons of Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury were to act as Mutwalli for 2 years only by rotation and in case of death of any son, the son of the deceased would act as Mutwalli. The total income from the wakf estate of Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury from both the tenanted and Khas land was Tk. 30,000.00 per annum. In the Wakfnama, it is stipulated that each son of the wakif Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury would get 60 mds, of paddy and cash of Tk. 2,000.00 annually, The heirs of Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury have got 70 members in 5 families. The Wakf was created for religious, "charitable and pious purposes in conformity with the Wakf Validating Act XI of 1910. It is alleged that no special notification under section 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was served for acquiring the Khas land of the Wakf Estate and the above orders are illegal, ultra vires, etc, and the officers of the government have been acting without jurisdiction in acquiring the lands. It is alleged that the number of the members in the 5 families of late Abdul Jabbar is 70, they are entitled to retain bighas of Khas lands in their possession and the Revenue Officer and the Circle Officer have acted illegally and without jurisdiction in acquiring the plaintiff's land in the manner done by the impugned orders dated 22.2.56 and 23.2.56 respectively. The plaintiff was, therefore, obliged to file the present suit for declaration.

4. Defendant No. 1, the then Province of East Pakistan, contested the suit by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, on the grounds that the disputed Wakf is an Wakf-ul Awlad and as such the khas lads of the Wakf Estate has been quite legally and rightly acquired by the impugned orders. The allegations and statements made in the plaint arc not true and the same are denied by the defendant. It is contended in the written statement that the plaintiff and other heirs of late Abdul Jabbar the Wakif have got no right, title and interest in the suit lands which are Wakf properties and they are only the beneficiaries of the wakf.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge framed the following four (4) issues:

1: Are the orders of Revenue Officer and the Circle Officer dated 22.2.56 and 23.2.56- respectively in Misc. Case No. 24 of 1355 under section 44 of the BSA and T Act illegal and without jurisdiction?

2: Has there been any proper and valid notice under section 80 of the CPC?

3: Is the suit barred by limitation?

4: What relief, if any, is the plaintiff entitled to?

6. He dismissed the suit, deciding all the issues against the plaintiff.

7. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate for the appellant, has taken us through the impugned judgment, the evidence and other materials on record. He frankly submitted that the present case will be guided by the principle laid down by the Hon'ble Appellate Division in the case of Bangladesh Vs. Shamsuzzoha Nurul Amin Chowdhury and others, reported in 28 DLR (AD) 195, as the facts of the present case are more or less similar to the facts of the above reported case. We have gone through the above case reported in 28 DLR (AD) 195. In that case, their Lordships of the Appellate Division have given interpretation of the law laid down in section 20(5)(i)(c) and (ii) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which runs as follows: (5) (i) Nothing in sub-sections (1) and (2) and (3) of this section shall apply-(c) to so much of the lands held under debutter, wakf, wakf-al-al-aulad or any other trust as is exclusively dedicated and the income from which is exclusively applied to religious or charitable purposes without reservation of pecuniary benefit for any individual. (ii) "Where, under any debutter, wakf, wakf-al-al-aulad or any other trust, the income from the lands covered by such trust is partly dedicated for religious or charitable purposes and partly reserved for the pecuniary benefit of any individual, only such portion of the lands, as may be selected in accordance with the rules to be made in this behalf by the Government, shall come within the purview of sub-clause (c) of clause(i)".

8. It is not disputed that the wakfnana Ext. 1 is a Wakf-al-al-aulad as contemplated under section 20(5)(ii) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such, the wakf property in suit, are liable to be acquired under the above section of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. By the impugned order dated 22.2.56 reproduced in at pages 24-26 Part II of the paper-book, the Revenue Officer allowed 45.36 acres of land to be retained as khas land to meet the expenditure of the charitable deeds mentioned in the wakf deed and 36.39 acres to be retained as Khas land as wakf-al-al-aulad under section 20(5)(ii) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act by making the following observation:

"Examined the accounts of income and expenditure with the original account which has been audited and checked by the Inspector of Wakf each year. It appears from the accounts attached herewith that the Mutawalli spends Rs. 2,50-1-0 on an average per annum on religious and charitable purposes. On verification it is proved that the Mutawalli actually spends the amounts for religious and charitable purposes. He is, therefore, entitled to be allotted so much of the khas land which will cover the expenditure above and this will be done under section 39(3)(a)(b) of EBSA and T Act of 1950. According to the provision of the section above, the annual net income per acre is calculated at Rs. 56-7-0 as shown in the calculation chart attached herewith. The total expenditure is then determined to Rs. 2,560-7-0 and the net annual profit to Rs. 56-7-0. So 45.36 acres of land is required to meet with the expenditure. The Mutawalli has declared his exercise his option to select land. He may, therefore, be allotted under rule 37 of EBSA Rules, 1951, 45.36 acres of land to retain in his khas possession as Wakf Lillah as shown in Schedule 'B'. This is a mixed big type of Wakf and the Mutawalli 33.06 acres of Khas land and maximum area of 3.31 acres for his homestead which actually covers more i.e 36.37 acres as Wakf-al-al-aulad. As he had declined to exercise his opinion to retain lands he may, therefore, be allotted under Rule 37 the area of 36.39 acres of land to be retained as Wakf-al-al-aulad under section 20(5) (ii) of EBSA and T Act, 1950 vide Schedule 'C'. After allotting all other lands of Wakf Lillah and Wakf-al-al-aulad there are more area of 348.87 acres of lands which may be declared as an excess of the prescribed limit as shown in Schedule 'D' annexed herewith".

9. In interpreting the section 20(5)(ii) of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, their Lordships of the Appellate Division in para 14 of the above referred case, observed as follows:

"In our opinion any wakf-al-al-aulad which is dedicated partly for charitable purpose and partly for individual benefit or wholly for benefit of any individual, the Khas land of such wakf-al-al-aulad estate should be retained on the footing of the living heirs representing the wakf estate on the date the section came into operation. The heirs of the wakif in the aggregate will represent the wakf estate in their representative capacity but not in their personal capacity. Calculated on this basis, the wakf-al-al-aulad estate will retain as much as it will be possible to retain above 100 bighas by as many number as the heirs will be in existence above ten."

10. In para 20 of the same Judgment, their Lordships further observed as follows:

"According to our judgment, the heirs of the wakf will represent the wakf estate and land will be allotted to the wakf estate on that basis. The land so allotted will be khas land of the wakf estate. If some land in excess is left over on calculation, it will vest in the Government, but the compensation money for the excess land will be wakf and the mutawalli will be bound to re-invest the same in any other suitable property."

11. In the present case, the plaintiff claimed that there were 70 members in the 5 families of the heirs of the wak if Mr. Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury and as such they are entitled to retain 700 bighas of Khas land. The learned Subordinate Judge, it appears, did not at all consider this aspect of the case and no issue was framed on the subject. Although the plaintiff's positive case is that they are entitled to retain 700 bighas of Khas land as the individuals in the 5 families of the wakif Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury are 70 in number.

12. It may be pointed out that under section 20(2) of the EBSA and T Act a rent receiver may, inter alia, retain in his Khas possession 100 standard bighas of land or 10 bighas for each member of his family whichever is greater. This provision regarding the limit of retainable Khas land was amended and changed. The original ceiling of 100 bighas was raised to 375 bighas by section 4 of Ordinance No. 15 of 1961. But that has again been reduced to 100 bighas by section 5 of PO 98 of 1972. In view of the above position of law and the decision of their Lordships held in the above reported case, it is clear that the Revenue Officer did not comply with the provision of law regarding the area of retainable Khas land by the plaintiff and the learned Subordinate Judge has miserably failed to appreciate the plaintiff's case regarding the area of land, retainable by them on the basis of individual member of the heirs of 5 families of the wakif.

13. It is not possible for us to decide here as to the actual number of members in the families of the heirs of late Abdul Jabbar Chowdhury, specially when the learned Subordinate Judge did not at all discuss the point. We therefore, find no other alternative than to send the suit on remand to the Trial Court for framing an issue as to the number of the members of the families of Late Abdul Jabbar and to allow them to retain Khas lands at the rate of 10 standard bighas per member of the families of the heirs of late Abdul Jabbar, as laid down by their Lordships in the above case and also in section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act., discussed above.

14. The learned Subordinate Judge held that there was no proper and valid notice under section 80 CPC and the suit is bad on that account also. In deciding issue No. 2 regarding service under section 80 CPC the learned Subordinate Judge observed as follows:

2. "It is contended by the learned lawyer for the defendant that no proper and valid notice under section 80 of the CPC has been served upon the defendant No. 1 in this suit. Section 80 of the CPC provides that notice under the signature of the person issuing the notice and containing the names of the parties and the cause of action should be served on the Collector when Province is the defendant. In the present suit no copy of such notice has been produced. So assuming that notice under section 80 CPC was actually sent to the Collector, it cannot be said that it was valid and proper notice under section 80 CPC. Moreover PW 4 Azizul Gaffar Chowdhury, the original plaintiff says in his deposition that he sent the notice under section 80 CPC to the Collector by his signature and he (PW4) cannot say what was the contents of the said notice. Plaintiff has filed postal receipt Ext. 3 and the postal acknowledgement receipt No. 4 in order to prove that the notice under section 80 CPC has been duly served upon the Collector. But with reference to Ext. 4 it appears that one Kiron Chandra Guha, pleader, Amanat Ganj Barisal has signed the alleged notice, PW 2 pro-defendant No. 3 also cannot say what has been written in the notice under section 80 CPC. Notice under section 80 is mandatory. So it is incumbent on the plaintiff to prove that proper, sufficient and valid notice under section 80 CPC was served upon the proper authority. But on the material on record as stated above I am unable to hold that valid and proper notice was served upon the defendant No. 1. Hence I hold that there has not been any valid and proper notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure in this suit."

<u>15. In para 26 of the plaint, it is stated that notice under section 80 CPC was served upon the Collector, Bakerganj representing the Province of East Pakistan on 5.2.60 and the postal and acknowledgment receipt are admittedly filed in Court which are marked as Exts. 3 and 4 respectively. From Exts. 3 and 4, it is clear that the notice was sent to the Collector, Bakerganj and it was received by his office, In para 20 of the written statement, it is stated that there was no valid or proper notice under section 80 CPC. The defendant did not deny the service of notice. Their contention was that the notice was not valid or proper. The defendant did not say in which respect, the notice is not valid or not proper. Section 80 CPC does not contemplate the validity or invalidity of notice among proper notice. Absence of service of notice cannot be a ground for dismissal of the suit, as it is evident from 80 CPC itself. Section 80 CPC runs as follows:</u>

<u>80.(1) "A suit may be instituted against the Government or against a public officer, in respect of any act purporting to be done by such public officer, in his official capacity, after the expiration of two months next after notice in writing has been delivered to or left at the office of,—</u>

<u>9* 	* 		*		 * 		*</u>

<u>(b) (i) in the case of a suit against the Government other than a suit relating to the affairs of the Railway, a Secretary to the Government or the Collector of the District.</u>

<u>(ii) in the case of a suit against the Government relating to the affairs of the Railway, the General Manager of the Railway and in the case of a public officer, delivered to him or left at his office stating the cause of action, the name, description of place of residence of the plaintiff and the relief which he claims; and the plaint shall contain a statement that such notice has been so delivered or left.</u>

<u>(2) Where any such suit is instituted without delivering or leaving such notice as aforesaid or before the expiration of the said period of two months or where the plaint does not contain a statement that such notice has been so delivered or left, the plaintiff shall not be entitled to any costs if settlement as regards the subject-matter of the suit is reached or the Government or the public officer concedes the plaintiffs claim, within the period of two months from the date of the institution of the suit:</u>

<u>Provided that in a suit instituted without such notice, the Court shall allow not less than three months to the Government to submit its written statement."</u>

16. We are of the opinion that although the plaintiff did not file any copy of the notice served on the respondent, the plaintiff nonetheless properly served the notice upon the respondent as contemplated under section 80 CPC and the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge's finding on the issue against the plaintiff is not correct. We, therefore, set aside the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge regarding issue No. 2 and decide the issue in favour of the plaintiff-applicant.

17. As regards the point of limitation, the learned Subordinate Judge found that the suit is governed by Article 14 of the Limitation Act which provides the limitation of 1(one) year from the date of any order concerned.

<u>18. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate for the appellant contends that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in holding that Article 14 is applicable in the present case. He submits that in the present case, Article 120 is applicable. In support of this contention, he put reliance on a decision reported in 21 DLR 492. As already stated, that the present suit is a suit for declaration and not for setting aside the impugned order and, as such, the suit is governed by Article 120 which provides limitation for 6 years. The impugned order was passed on 22.2.56 and 23.2.56 and the suit was filed on 12.8.60 i.e. within 6 years from the date of the impugned orders. The suit was thus filed within time. We, therefore, decide the issue No. 3 in favour of the plaintiff-appellant by setting aside the finding of the Trial Court on this issue.</u>

19. Mr. Obaidur Rahman Mostafa, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, filed a petition before us at the time of hearing of the appeal, alleging that in view of section 2 of PO 90/72, the appeal shall abate. Section 2 of PO 90/72 runs as follows:

"2. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on the commencement of this Order, all suits, appeals, application and other legal proceedings pending or continuing or deemed to be pending or continuing in any court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (EB Ord. No. III of 1956), or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act, or of the acquisition of any property made by any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate, and all orders including orders of injunction and other interlocutory orders, passed in such suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings shall cease to have any effect; and no court shall entertain, and no person shall bring, any fresh suit, appeal, application or other legal proceedings in which the legality or validity of any such law or acquisition is challenged or called in question."

<u>20. Mr. Abdul Quayum, the learned Advocate for the appellant, contends that the above provision of PO 90/72 is violative of the fundamental right of the plaintiff as laid down in the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and, as such, it is void. He further contends that even assuming that the above PO is a good piece of law, in that case also the present suit does not come within the mischief of the above provision of the PO 90/72 which prohibits suits challenging the legality and validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or "of the acquisition of any property made by any provision thereof", as the suit property has not yet been acquired by the Government and it was in the process of acquisition when the suit was filed, He submits that the parties were asked to maintain status-quo with respect to the acquisition of the suit properties by order dated 24.6.60 by the Trial Court. From the perusal of the record of the Trial Court, it appears that the contention of the learned Advocate is correct. It seems that the plaintiff-appellant is still in possession of the suit properties or at any rate this suit property was not finally acquired by service of notice as required under section 44 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It may be pointed out that the process of acquisition became final only after publication of the notification in the official Gazette under sub-section 2 of section 43 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, declaring that the compensation assessment roll has been finally published. The property vests in the Government only after the above notification as laid down in section 44 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in published. Without entering into the investigation as to whether PO 90/72 is violative of the provisions of the Constitution, we are of opinion that the present case does not come within the mischief of section 2 of PO 90/72 and the appeal or the suit is not liable to abate. In view of the above facts and circumstances and the legal position discussed the appeal is allowed. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge are hereby set aside.</u>

The suit is sent back on remand for fresh decision after framing issue, as to the number of members in families of the heirs of the wakifs according to law and in the light of the observations made above. The learned Subordinate Judge should dispose of the suit as early as possible.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. A.Y. Salehuzzaman, Deputy Attorney-General ------ For the Defdt-Petitioner. 

Mr. M. Gholam Rabbani, Advocate ------ For the Pltff- Opposite Party Nos. 1 & 2. 

Mr. Mohammad Ali, Advocate ------ For the Defdt- Opposite Party No.3.
parties:
Government of Bangladesh & ors ------Petitioners
vs.
Basaratullah, being dead his heirs and successors Fazle Karim & ors ------Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J.:- This Rule obtained under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against the judgment and decree dated 20.6.87 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 23 of 1986 allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and decree dated 31.8.85 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 147 of 1984. The trial Court dismissed the suit and the appellate Court below decreed the suit.

2. The opposite party No.1, while alive, and his wife, the opposite party No. 2, instituted the aforesaid suit as plaintiffs on the averments, inter alia, that a piece and parcel of land measuring 6.76 acres of C.S. Plot Nos.1145, 1170, 1171, 1350, 1351, 1352 and 1416 of mouza Khilgaon, formerly P.S. Tejgaon, now Motijhcel, Dhaka was and is owned by them which was requisitioned in L.A Case No. 63/59-60 by a notice dated 21.6.60 under section 3 of the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 for the defendant-opposite party No. 3, the Railway Board. The requisitioning authority tool over possession of the suit land from the opposing parties on 21.6.60. The suit land was requisitioned with the object of permanent acquisition, but no notice under section 5(1a) and (3) was served "either in the locality or on the plaintiffs as required by law for acquisition". An Additional Deputy Commissioner (Development) passed an order to serve fresh notices on the opposite parties under the said sections, being satisfied that no such notices were served before, but the file mysteriously disappeared. On 13.9.67 the successor Additional Deputy Commissioner noting that an injustice will be committed by depriving the opposite parties of due compensation, passed an order to serve fresh notices on the plaintiff opposite parties. But the officers concerned having dragged their feet in the matter of serving fresh notices the plaintiff opposite parties were constrained to file a' suit being Title Suit No. 36 of 1968 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Dhaka against the defendant-petitioners and the opposite party No. 3 challenging their claim of acquisition of the suit land without service of legal notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) of Act-XIII of 1948. The present defendant-petitioners contested the suit by filing a written statement and by asserting that the said notices have been duly served upon the plaintiff-opposite parties. By his judgment and decree dated 8.7.69 the learned Munsif decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff-opposite parties. The learned Munsif came to the conclusion that notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) of the said Act were not served on the plaintiffs and as such there was no valid acquisition of the disputed property.

3. Against the said judgment and decree the defendant-petitioners preferred Title Appeal No.28 of 1970 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka who by his judgment and decree dated 24.5.71 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment and decree of the learned Munsif. The plaintiff-opposite parties thus became entitled to fresh notices for valid and legal acquisition of the suit land.

<u>4. Instead of issuing fresh notices the defendant- petitioners formulated a fraudulent device to serve a copy of the alleged original notice under section 5(1) dated 21.6.60 putting a fresh date of issue in the notice under section 5(1a). This alleged copy of the old original notice under section 5(1) of the said Act was served on 23.4.73 directing the plaintiff-opposite parties to appear before the concerned authority on 30.12.60 to object to the acquisition proceedings, if any. This action was fraudulent and absurd on the face of it. The defendant-petitioners also served a fresh notice under section 5(3) of the said Act on the same day, i.e. 23.4.73 upon the plaintiff-opposite parties giving 7 days' notice to object to the acquisition of the suit land. The statute requires the concerned authority to give notice of 15 days to state the owners' objection. But in the notice served on 23.4.73 the plaintiff-opposite parties were asked to file their objections on 30.4.73; i.e. within 7 days. This notice was also an illegal, invalid and void notice.</u>

5. The plaintiff-opposite parties made representations against such wrong actions before various authorities including Mr. Mirza Golam Hafez who was the Minister-in-Charge of the Ministry of Land Administration & Land Reforms. After a detailed discussion of facts and law involved in the matter, he came to the view that there had been no legal or valid acquisition of the suit property as no notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) were served. Upon the Minister's order an opinion was obtained from the Ministry of Law which also opined that fresh notices under section 5(la) and 5(3) were required to be served for valid acquisition of the suit property. Thereafter, Mr. Abdul Haque took over charge as Minister of Land Administration and Land Reforms, but before passing any written order in the matter he went out of office. His successor Mr. Md. Ismail passed an order simply rejecting the plaintiff-opposite parties representation. The plaintiff-opposite parties then submitted a representation on 12.3.82 to the then President of Bangladesh. Subsequently they made a representation on 4.6.82 to the Chief Martial Law Administrator and submitted all relevant papers. They received a communication in January, 1983 from the Secretariat of the Chief Martial Law Administrator advising them to seek relief in a civil Court.

6. The plaintiff-opposite parties as such filed the instant suit on 13.5.84 stating further that the defendant-petitioners by a Gazette Notification No. DA-72/71/355 dated 25.6.73 purporting to be under section 5(7) of Act-XIII of 1948 allegedly acquired the suit land. The plaintiff-opposite parties contended that service of the alleged copy of the old notice dated 21.6.60 and the notice under section 5(3) on 23.4.73 and the subsequent Gazette Notification dated 25.6.73 purporting to acquire the suit property under section 5(7) are all without jurisdiction, illegal and void. The plaintiff-opposite parties, therefore, prayed for:

(a) for a decree declaring that required and valid notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) of Act- XIII of 1948 have not been issued or served in L.A. Case No. 63/59-60 in respect of the suit property as per provisions of law;

(b) for a declaration that Gazelle Notification No. DA-72/71/355 dated 25.6.73 has no legal basis or validity or binding force;

(c) for a declaration that the notice under section 5(3) along with enclosed copy of notice under section 5(1) served on the plaintiffs on 23.4.73 are fraudulent. defective, invalid and without any legal effect and as such the title and ownership of the suit land has always rested and continues to rest with the plaintiffs and has never been vested with the defendants:

(d) for an order of mandatory injunction directing the defendants to perform their statutory duties by making proper and lawful assessment for the period of requisition through requisition order dated 21.6.60 till the filing of the suit for use and occupation of the suit land as well as start valid acquisition proceeding afresh under Part-II, section 3 of the Acquisition & Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 and other provisions of law in force for ex- pressed intent of acquisition within 3 months failing which the possession of the suit land be restored to the plaintiffs.

7. The defendant-petitioners filed a written statement and contested the suit. It was stated that there was no cause of action for the suit; that the suit was not maintainable in its present form and manner; that the suit was barred under sections 42 and 55 of the Specific Relief Act; that it was barred by the law of limitation; that it was barred by res judicata and also barred under the provisions of Act- XIII of 1948. It was stated that the plaintiffs' land measuring an area of 6.4650 acres along with other lands was requisitioned on 21.6.60 with a view to permanent acquisition for Railway Staff Quarter under L.A. Case No.63 of 1959-60. Vacant possession of the land in question was handed over to the requiring body on 2.7.60 and since then the Railway Board is possessing the suit land after constructing their buildings except approximately an area of 0.16 acre of land which is still under the occupation of the plaintiffs. The land in question has already been acquired and vested in the Government vide Gazette Notification No.DA-72/71/355 dated 25.6.73. From the office record of the office of Additional Deputy Commissioner (Land Acquisition) it appears vide order sheet at page 20 dated 30.12.60 that the notice under section 5(la) and 5(3) was issued to the plaintiffs in the year 1960. It was further stated that as per order of the then Additional Deputy Commissioner (Development) on the body of the report of the then Kanungo, the Ministry of Land Administration & Land Reforms was informed Vide T.O. No. 2095- L.A. dated 14.6.72 for a fresh requisition and acquisition of the land in question of the plaintiffs. The Ministry thereupon issued instructions along with the Attorney-General's minutes dated 15.3.73 where- upon the office of the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Land Acquisition) served upon the plaintiffs a fresh notice under section 5(3) fixing 30.4.73 for filing objection, if any, against acquisition along with the true copy of the notice under section 5(1a) as already served in the locality in the year 1960. It is claimed that the said Gazette Notification is quite legal, valid and binding upon the plaintiffs and the suit land vested in the defendants absolutely and free from any encumbrances with the publication of the aforesaid Notification. Fresh notice or fresh acquisition proceedings under the Acquisition & Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 is neither necessary, nor can be conceived of in respect of the suit land which has already vested in the defendants. The object of filing of the suit is to get a fresh notice for fresh assessment of compensation causing loss and injury to the defendants.

8. The trial Court found that prayer (a) is superfluous and redundant because the plaintiff-opposite parties had already obtained a decree from a competent Court with the declaration that notices under section 5(la) and 5(3) were not served on the plaintiffs. The first prayer, therefore, deserves no consideration.

9. The trial Court was of the view that if the disputed acquisition was invalid and ineffective in the eye of law, then the plaintiff-opposite parties were entitled to recovery of possession of the suit land at the time of institution of Title Suit No. 36 of 1968. But since they omitted that claim in the said suit, they have subjected themselves to the mischief of Order 2, Rule 2(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. They have also invited the hurdle of limitation provided in Article 142 of the Limitation Act.

10. The trial Court, however, was clearly of the view that the subsequent fresh service of old notice cannot have any effect of legalizing an illegal acquisition. The disputed acquisition continued to be an invalid acquisition in spite of a ridiculous attempt on the part of the Government to validate it by a fresh service of an old notice. The Gazelle Notification dated 25.6.73 is devoid of any legal effect and, as such it had no effect of vesting the suit land with the Government under section 5(7) of Act-XIII of 1948, but the decree will be of no use to the plaintiffs in the absence of consequential relief in the form of recovery of possession etc. The plaintiffs have not sought any consequential relief. So the suit was barred under the proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The prayer No. (c) is practically covered by prayer No. (b). Hence, the prayer (c) also cannot be given. The prayer No. (d) is vague, indefinite and cumbrous. When there is no valid acquisition of the suit land, there cannot be any question of assessment of compensation. The plaintiff-opposite parties could seek recovery of possession of the suit land with mesne profits.

11. With these findings the trial Court dismissed the suit.

12. The appellate Court below agreed with the trial Court and held that prayer No. (a) was unnecessary, because the plaintiff-opposite parties had already obtained a declaration to the same effect in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968. Prayer No. (a) is also barred by res judicata.

13. The appellate Court below concurrently held with the trial Court that the service of an alleged copy of the old original notice under section 5 (1) dated 21.6.60 after 13 years on 23.4.73 fixing 30.12.60 as the date of hearing under section 5(5) is completely unreasonable, impracticable and impossible. The intention of service of notice is not fulfilled thereby. Hence, it is invalid and illegal in the eye of law. Without serving a notice under section 5(1a) there cannot be any assessment of compensation for acquisition of land. The appellate Court below concurrently held with the trial Court that giving 7 days notice instead of 15 days in the notice under section 5 (3) is defective and illegal. The subsequent Gazette Notification issued in pursuance of an illegal and invalid course of action is also illegal and invalid. The appellate Court below then noticed some decisions and held that the entire acquisition proceeding was illegal, without jurisdiction and invalid. As such, the suit was decreed in so far as plaintiff-opposite parties prayer Nos. (b), (c) and (d) in the plaint were concerned.

14. Mr. A.Y. Salehuzzaman, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the defendant-petitioners submits that the Court of appeal below has not adverted to the reasonings and decision of the trial Court while reversing its judgment and decree. In particular, nothing has been said by the appellate Court below as to the trial Court's reasoning that the plaintiff-opposite parties ought to have prayed for recovery of possession of the suit land in the earlier Title Suit No. 36 of 1968 and having omitted to so pray for, their present prayer for recovery of possession in prayer No. (d) is barred under Order 2, Rule 2(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

15. Mr. M. Gholam Rabbani, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties, submits on the other hand that the trial Court's concept of the earlier and the present suit was so misconceived that it was not necessary for the appellate Court below to advert to its reasonings. The defendant-petitioners admittedly took over possession of the suit land not as a trespasser, but as a requisitioning authority under section 3 of Act-XIII of 1948 on 21.6.60. Their present possession is, therefore, not that of a trespasser. They are possessing the suit property validly, legally and under the cover of law. Therefore, the question of recovery of possession from the defendant-petitioners need not be prayed for. The question of limitation under Article 142 of the Limitation Act and the question of bar of suit under Order 2, Rule 2(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure also docs not arise.

<u>16. Faced with this submission of Mr. M. Gholam Rabbani the learned Deputy Attorney-General has not pressed this point further. We also hold that it was not necessary for the plaintiff- opposite parties to pray for recovery of possession, because the Government-petitioners are not trespassers. The plaintiff-opposite parties acknowledge in paragraph 2 of their plaint that the suit property has been requisitioned under section 3 of Act No. XIII of 1948. They have not challenged the order of requisition. Therefore, the possession of the defendant- petitioners in the suit properly is not an unauthorised and illegal possession. The question of limitation under Article 142 of the Limitation Act and the question of bar of suit under Order 2, Rule 2(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure do. not arise.</u>

17. The learned Deputy Attorney-General next submits, that the Court of appeal below has failed to evaluate the true meaning and import of the judgment and decree in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968. It is stated in the judgment, "it is the definite case of the plaintiffs that no notices under section 5(1 a) and 5(3) of the East Bengal (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 were served on the plaintiffs before the alleged acquisition". It is also the finding that notices under section 5(la) and 5(3) "were not served on the plaintiffs" and as such there was no valid acquestion of the disputed property. Mr. Salehuzzamaa submits that this declaration conferred no real benefit to the plaintiffs and as such the copy of the original notice dated 21.6.60 was rightly served on them on 23.4.73.

18. On 21.6.60 when the notice under section 5(1) was allegedly served in the locality by public notice, section 5(1) stood as follows:

"(1). The District Magistrate may, if he thinks fit, acquire any requisitioned property and if he proposes to so acquire he shall cause 11 public notice to be given at convenient places on or near the property to be acquired stating that he intends to acquire the property."

By East Pakistan Ordinance No. XL of 1961 sub-section (1) and (1a) were substituted for the former sub-section (1) as follows;

"5. (1) The Provincial Government may, if it thinks fit, acquire any requisitioned property on the proposal of the Deputy Commissioner in the manner hereinafter provided in this section.

5.(1a) The Deputy Commissioner shall, if he considers that the acquisition of any requisitioned property is expedient for a public purpose or in public interest, cause a public notice to be given at convenient places on or near the requisitioned property stating that the property is proposed to be acquired."

19. Mr. Salehuzzaman submits that the public notices under former section 5(1) and the subsequent section 5(1a) are not required to be served personally or individually upon the owriers of the suit land under requisition. In both cases it is required to be served by a public notice to be given at convenient places on or near the requisitioned property stating that the property is proposed-to be acquired. In contradistinction to a notice under section 5(1a), a notice under section 5(3) is to be served personally on the owner of the suit property or on interested persons. Section 5(3) is as follows:

5.(3) Notice shall also be served to the above effect on the Owner of such property and on all such persons known or believed to be interested therein or to be entitled to act for persons so interested as reside or have agents authorised to receive service on their behalf within the revenue district in which the property is situated."

20. Mr. Salehuzzaman submits that in Title Suit No. 36. of 1968, all that the plaintiff-opposite parties obtained by way of a finding and by way of a decree is that notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) "were not served on the plaintiffs". The Government took the view that the aforesaid declaration of the Court did not confer on the plaintiff-opposite parties any real benefit Had there been a declaration that no notice was issued under section 5(1a) or that such notice was illegal or invalid, the subsequent acquisition proceeding would have been materially affected, because the date of notice under section 5(1a) is relevant for determination of the market value of the acquired property for compensation. The Government took the view that notice under section 5(1a) is a general notice, so it is definitely not required to be served on the owner but the notice under section 5(3) is a personal notice and is required to be served on the owner. Therefore, the declaration in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968, in so far as it relates to notice under section 5(1a) being not served on the plaintiffs, seemed to be of no real effect and of no real value to the plaintiffs. This declaration in any view of the matter did not in terms invalidate or have the effect of invalidating the notice already issued under section 5(1a) in the connected land acquisition case. However, in view of the declaration made by the Court, a copy of the old original notice under section 5(1) dated 21.6.60 was served upon the plaintiff-opposite parties along with a fresh notice under section 5(3). Mr. Salehuzzaman submits that this was done in strict compliance with the meaning and purport of the declaratory decree obtained by the plaintiff- opposite parties in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968. It is true, he submits, that the notice under section 5(3) falls short of 8 days in giving the plaintiff-opposite parties an opportunity to file objections against the acquisition, if any, but the notice was issued by a competent authority with jurisdiction and whatever defect was there was a mere irregularity and did not strike at the very jurisdiction to issue the notice. The plaintiff-opposite parties could have represented to the authority complaining of shortage of time and the defect could have been remedied but they preferred not to file any objection and, therefore, the appellate Court below ought to have considered that both the old notice under section 5(1) and the new notice under section 5(3) were served in full compliance with the decree obtained by the plaintiff-opposite parties in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968. He further submits that the plaintiff-opposite parties have not challenged the competence or jurisdiction of the authorities to issue the notices under sections 5(1a) and 5 (3) and to issue the Gazette Notification dated 25.6.73. They have also not challenged the validity of public purpose for acquisition of the suit land. As such, he submits, the suit itself is barred under section 14A of Act No. XIII of 1948.

21. Mr. Gholam Rabbani, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties, has read out to us paragraph 7 of the plaint in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968 in which the plaintiff-opposite parties clearly stated that there has been no due service of notice in the matter either in the locality or on the plaintiffs. He has also read out prayer No. (a) of the aforesaid plaint seeking a declaration that there has been no valid service of notice for acquisition under section 5(la) and 5(3) of Act No. XIII of 1948 with regard to the suit land in the connected land acquisition case. Therefore, the plaintiff-opposite parties themselves did not make out any case in the aforesaid Title Suit No.36 of 1968 that notice under section 5(1) or 5(1a) are required to be served personally on them and that they did not receive any personal notices under those sections. They were very clear in stating that notices under section 5(1) or 5(1a) are required to be served in the locality and that no such notices were served in the locality. As regards personal service; they limited their claim to the notice under section 5(3) only.

22. But the learned Munsif while delivering the judgment in Title Suit No.36 of 1968 did not make any distinction between the mode of service of notice under section 5(1) or 5(la) and 5(3). He gave a lump-sum finding that the plaintiffs did not receive notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) and he passed-a lump-sum decree declaring that the notices under section 5 (la) and 5(3) "were not served on the plaintiffs."

23. The question is, can the defendant- petitioners taking advantage of the phraseology employed, by the learned Munsif honestly argue that this decree does not confer any real benefit on the plaintiff-opposite parties?

24. As we see it, section 5(1) or 5(1 a) speaks of a public notice to be given at convenient places on or near the requisitioned property stating that the property is proposed to be acquired. This does not mean that this public notice is not meant to be a service of notice. It is to our mind a mode of service of notice upon al\ the owners of the requisitioned property indicating the mind and intention of the requisitioning authority to acquire the property. That a public notice under section 5(1 a) is also "a service of notice" is clear from the language of the proviso (1) of section 7(e) of the said Act which provides as follows:

"(i) the market-value of any immovable property for the purpose of this section shall be the "weighted average value, calculated in the manner prescribed by the rule made by the Government and after excluding abnormally high and low sale figures" of the properties of a similar description and, with similar advantages in the vicinity, during the twenty-four months preceding the date of the service of notice under sub- section Clause of section 5.

25. So, causing a public notice to be given under section 5(la) is a "service of notice" acknowledged by the Act itself. Service upon whom? Service upon the owners of the requisitioned properties which are sought to be acquired. A public notice is also a mode of service of notice upon the owners the requisitioned properties. It is not a personal notice, but a collective notice meant for the owners also. So when a decree declares that the notice under section 5(la) was "not served on the plaintiffs", it cannot be understood to mean that a personal notice on the plaintiffs under section 5(la) was not served The decree will be understood to mean that the mode of service prescribed in section 5(1a) was not resorted' to as a result of which the plaintiff-opposite parties were not served with the notice under section 5(1 a).

26. Besides, both the Courts below have concurrently held that the prayer No. (a) in the instant suit is unnecessary. The appellate Court below held that this prayer is barred by res judicata. In paragraph 3 of the present plaint the plaintiff-opposite parties stated that at the time of requisition or thereafter no notice under section 5(la) and 5(3) was served "either in the locality or on the plaintiffs as required by law for acquisition". The plaintiff- opposite parties never averred that they were entitled to a personal notice under section 5(la). Their prayer No.(a) in the present suit was for a decree declaring that required, legal or valid notices under section 5 (Ia) or 5(3) have not been issued or served in L.A. Case No.63/59-60 in respect of the suit property as rape) visions of law. Surely, this prayer means that no notice under section 5(1a) was served in the manner provided by law itself, i.e. by . causing a public notice to be given at convenient places on or near the requisitioned property stating that the property is proposed to be acquired.

<u>27. Both the Courts below have found that prayer-(a) has already been decided in favour of the plaintiff-opposite parties in the earlier Title Suit No. 36 of 1968. This means that the issue of service of notice under section 5(1 a) in the locality, as required by law, has already been decided. It is barred by res judicata. It has nowhere been agitated in the civil revisional application and has not at all been argued by the learned Deputy Attorney General that the aforesaid concurrent finding is either bad in law or on facts. In other words, the present revisional application has proceeded on the assumption that this con- current finding is unassailable.</u>

28. It has next been contended by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the plaintiff-opposite parties have not led any evidence in the suit that no public notice was given under section 5(1a) in 1960. P. W. 1, the only witness examined by the plaintiff-opposite parties, has not uttered a word regarding lack of public notice under section 5(1a). The trial Court has taken into account the opinion of the Minister, opinion of the Law Ministry and the note made by the Additional Deputy Commissioner, but these papers were not formally proved by any witness. The makers of these statements were not examined and no one was examined to prove that those were statements made by them. As such, this opinion evidence is absolutely inadmissible and there can be no finding that there was no public notice under section 5(la) in 1960 on the basis of these opinion. Further, the plaintiff-opposite parties could file an application under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure for correction of the decree in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968 so as to rectify the decree to the extent that no public notice was given under section 5(1a) and since they failed to do so, they cannot now re-open the matter and they are barred to do so under Order 2, Rule 2(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

29. As the concurrent finding of the Courts below is that the question as to whether public notice was served under section 5(la) or 5(1) in 1960 has been decided already in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968, the question of proving the said fact afresh in the present suit does not arise. It is true that opinion etc. of certain official have been marked as exhibits without examining the makers thereof or without proving them in the manner provided by the Evidence Act, but the absence of notice under section 5(la) or 5(1) in 1960 is a matter already decided in Title Suit No. 36 of 1968 and, therefore, it needs no further proof in this suit.

<u>30. Now coming to the concurrent finding by the Courts below that service in 1973 of an alleged copy of an old notice dated 21.6.60 under section 5(1) is no service of notice at all and service of a notice under section 5(3) giving only 7 days’ time to file any objection against acquisition is also no notice under the said Act, we do not find any reason to differ from the concurrent findings of the Court below. The service of the alleged copy of the old notice is no compliance with the provisions of section 5(1a) which is mandatory in nature. Giving 7 days’ notice, when the statute itself provides for 15 days’ notice, is also no notice in terms of the Act itself. Both the notices were issued not defectively or irregularly, but without jurisdiction. A statutory authority required to act by following a set procedure given in the Act itself cannot be said to act with jurisdiction if he deviates therefrom in material particulars. The impugned notices in prayer No.(c) are, therefore, no notices at all in the eye of law, far less notices under Act No. XIII of 1948 and, therefore, we hold that the bar of section 14A has no application in the present case. When a statutory authority acts without jurisdiction or acts in a manner without following a procedure provided in the statute itself, then it is not an act under the statute and the bar of suit does not apply.</u>

31. A ground has been taken in the civil provisional application that the validity of acquisition of immovable property under Act No. XIII of 1948 is not dependent upon prior issuance of notice under section 5(la) and 5(3) of the said Act and as such the Court of appeal below committed an error of law in holding that the Gazette Notification dated 25.6.73 was illegal and without jurisdiction.

32. We arc of the opinion that it is too late in the day to argue that notices under section 5(1a) and 5(3) of the said Act are not a sine qua non for the validity of the acquisition proceedings under section 5 (7). The Government docs not take a decision to acquire a requisitioned property unless it receives a report from the Deputy Commissioner containing his recommendations on the objections received. The Deputy Commissioner in his turn receives objection from the owners after service of notice in the manner provided under section 5(1 a) and 5(3). He has to hear the objections and has to make further enquiry if any. If notices under section 5(la) and 5(3) are not mandatorily required to be served before the Deputy Commissioner submits his report and the Government takes a decision to acquire the requisitioned properties, then the whole game of compulsory acquisition of private land will be left to the ipse dixit of the executive. A notice under section 5(1a) and 5 (3) is mandatory before the Government can at all decide to acquire any requisitioned property, far less publish a notification to that effect. If no such notices were received or if notices were invalid or illegal then the subsequent acquisition under section 5(7) is also illegal. We concur with the Courts below that the Gazette Notification dated 25.6.73 has no legal basis or validity or binding force and that it is illegal and void. The bar of section 14A is also not applicable to this Gazette Notification

33. It has been finally argued by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that the prayer No. (d) in so far as it seeks a mandatory injunction requiring the defendant-petitioners to start a valid acquisition proceeding afresh under Part-Il of section 3 of the Requisition and Acquisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 and other provisions of law in force for acquisition within three months failing which the possession of the suit land be restored to the plaintiffs, is not maintainable and, therefore, the Court of appeal below committed an illegality in granting the plaintiff-opposite parties the said prayer.

34. We find that the defendant-petitioners stated in paragraph 11 of their written statement in the present suit that the plaintiff-opposite parties land measuring an area of 6.4650 acres along with other lands was requisitioned 'on 21.6.60 "with a view to permanent acquisition for Railway Staff Quarter under L.A. Case No. 63/59-60". It has also been stated that the "vacant possession of the land in question was handed over to the Railway Board on 2.7.60 and since then the requiring body is possessing the land after constructing their buildings."

35. When it is the defendant-petitioners' own case that the suit land was requisitioned with a view to permanent acquisition for Railway Staff Quarter and when it is their own case that the requiring body is possessing the suit land after constructing their buildings thereon, then they have no right to possess the property as a mere requisitioned property for an indefinite period. They have either to de-requisition the property, dismantle the buildings constructed thereon and hand over the vacant possession thereof to the owners in the same condition in which they came into possession thereof, giving a goodbye to their desire for acquisition, or they have to complete the acquisition proceedings in accordance with the 'law of acquisition as it stands in present, not in accordance with the law as it stood in 1960. The mandatory injunction thus given under the circumstances is the most appropriate and correct decree. The defendant-petitioners cannot Just sit over the property and continue to deny the plaintiff-opposite parties their rightful claim of a proper notice of acquisition of the suit property followed by necessary consequences thereof.

36. These are all the arguments advanced by the learned Deputy Attorney General and no other point has been canvassed.

For all the above reasons, we do not find any ground to interfere with the judgment and decree of the appellate Court below.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs

End.
