full_judgment:
Latifur Rahman, J.:-These three Rules are heard together and are disposed of by this Judgment as they arise out of the same judgment passed by the Member. Arbitration Appellate Tribunal and District Judge, Dhaka in Arbitration Appeal Nos. 1/87 and 2/87 allowing in part and modifying the Award passed by the Arbitrator and Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Arbitration Revision Case No. 4 of 1986.

<u>2. It appears that 0.52 acres of land belonging to late Mir Basharatullah, the father of the petitioner in plot No. 1363 of mouza Faidabad under P.S. Gulshan, Dhaka was requisitioned on 19.3.58 in L.A. Case No. 66/57-58. Thereafter Basharatullah filed Title No. 193 of 1969 in the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and obtained a decree declaring the requisition as illegal and void. In consequence of the said decree the land was released from requisition and symbolic possession was given in favour of the said Basharatullah. Subsequently, the Government decided to acquire the land afresh under Ordinance No. II of 1982 for the Civil Aviation Authority, the opposite party No. 2 and after service of notice under section 3 of the Ordinance, the Government assessed the value of the land and submitted an estimate to the requiring body for placement of the fund and fund was not placed by the opposite party No. 2 and instead raised an objection as to the assessment of the Award. Accordingly the land acquisition proceeding abated under section 12(1) of the Ordinance. Thereafter the land being in urgent need of the opposite party No. 2 a fresh land acquisition proceeding was started and the Government took steps for acquiring the land. Thereafter the petitioner being the eldest son of late Basharatullah accepted the compensation and filed an application under section 28 of the Ordinance and consequently the Arbitration proceeding started. According to the petitioner the Award that was passed by the Deputy Commissioner is inadequate and not based on matters to be considered in determining the assessment of the award under section 8 of the Ordinance.</u>

3. The Government as well as the requiring body appeared and challenged the assessment of compensation as inflated and high. Both the opposite parties submit that under an agreement the amount of compensation was reduced to Tk. 22 lakhs and the amount having been accepted on agreement between the parties the arbitration proceeding is not maintainable.

4. The Arbitrator on hearing the parties awarded a total sum of Tk. 1,04,50,000/- and on appeal the Member, Appellate Tribunal reduced the award of the Arbitrator and made it at Tk. 61,02,000/- for the aforesaid land in question. Being aggrieved by the decision of the Member, Appellate Tribunal, these three Civil Revisional Cases have been filed by the Awardee, the requiring body and the Government.

5. Mr. A.Y. Salehuzzaman, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the Government submits that the Revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not maintainable as the Member Appellate Tribunal is not a Court but a persona designata and the decision of the Arbitration Appellate Tribunal being final, the revision case is not maintainable in law but the petitioner may file writ.

6. Mr. Gazi Abdur Rashid, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the requiring body submits that the petitioner's father, namely, Basharatullah having accepted Tk. 22 lakhs on agreement between himself and the requiring body, the application under section 28 of the Ordinance challenging the Award is not maintainable.

7. Mr. M. Golam Rabbani, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the eldest son of the Awardee, late Basharatullah submits that the decision of the Appellate Tribunal need be reconsidered as the member has failed to assess a fair and reasonable compensation in accordance with section 8 of the Ordinance and the relevant materials on record.

<u>8. At the outset we will consider as to whether a revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is maintainable or not. A reference to section 34(3)(4) of the Ordinance shows that an Arbitration Appellate Tribunal shall consist of a Member who shall be appointed by the Government from amongst persons who are or have been District Judges and the decision of the Arbitration Appellate Tribunal shall be final. Sub-section 2 of section 34 speaks that the Government shall, by notification in the official Gazette, constitute one or more Arbitration Appellate Tribunals for such areas as may he specified therein. From the Gazette notification No.S.R.O.184-L/83/VII-21/83 it appears that in pursuance of the provision of sub-sections (2) of section 34 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (II of 1982), the Government is pleased to constitute an Arbitration Appellate Tribunal for district and has appointed the District Judge of that District to be the member of the said Tribunal. Thus it appears that the District Judge of a District is a Member, Appellate Tribunal for hearing of the appeal from the decision passed by the Arbitrator appointed under section 27 of the Ordinance. Thus, we are called upon to see whether the function which the Member, Appellate Tribunal dis-charges in deciding an appeal from the decision of an Arbitrator is a Judicial one or a function in his private capacity. If the function is a judicial one then it is amenable to the jurisdiction of this court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, other-wise not.</u>

<u>9. In the decision reported in 38 DLR (AD)-172, the learned Judges of the Appellate Division have held the legal position in an elaborate manner. We will be guided by the reasonings given by the Appellate Division at paragraph 35 of that reported decision. Their Lordships further held that there is no conflict between the two expressions 'persona designata' and 'Court'. If the function of the designated person is judicial in character then he is a Court even though he is not described as a Court. The real test is the power and function which the person discharges. Thus if the function is a judicial one then the authority discharging the function is a Court although he is not described as Court by official designation. Thus in view of the reasoning given by their Lord-ships in Appellate Division we are of the view that the Member Appellate Tribunal in deciding the appeal over the decision of Arbitrator certainly exercises a judicial function and the Member Appellate Tribunal is a Court and for that matter the decision of the Member Appellate Tribunal under Ordinance No. II of 1982 is amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of this Court. Mr. Salehuzzaman, the learned Deputy Attorney-General in course of his argument submitted the decision reported in 40 D.L.R. 232, that was a case relating to drawing up of a contempt proceeding for not paying the compensation amount. There the Division Bench held that Arbitrator is not a Court and as such interference in a contempt of Court proceeding is not maintainable.</u>

<u>10. In this proceeding we are precisely called upon to decide as to whether the Member Appellate Tribunal who sits over the judgment of the Arbitrator is a Court or not. The Appellate Tribunal sits over the Judgment of the Arbitrator in appeal in doing so the Tribunal must judge whether the decision has been rightly given within the frame of the Ordinance and the evidence on record and in doing so certainly the Tribunal exercises a judicial function and we have no hesitation in holding that the Appellate Tribunal is a Court.</u>

11. In the present case the payment of the compensation was received by the eldest son of late Basharatullah on 7.4.86 on protest as contemplated in section 28 of the Ordinance on the basis of General Power of Attorney dated 24.3.86. The case of the Government and the requiring body is that Basharatullah agreed to receive the compensation of an amount of Tk. 22 lakhs and he entered into an agreement by way of confirmation as per verbal under standing with Civil Aviation Authority to receive the said amount of Tk. 22 lakhs as compensation in L.A. Case in respect of the land acquired and as such the Arbitration case is not maintainable and the Petitioner is not entitled to the amount as decreed.

<u>12. It is to be stated here that under section 7 of the Ordinance, the Deputy Commissioner is to make the award and while making the award the Deputy Commissioner must determine the compensation on matters as mentioned in section 8 of the Ordinance. The question of agreement as set up by the opposite party between the Awardee and the requiring body is not very relevant within the scheme of the Ordinance. Herein we may refer to the Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 where section 7 authorises the Deputy Commissioner to determine the Award as per section 7. Section 7(a) and (aa) speaks that compensation can be fixed by agreement and the same is also subject to the approval of the Provincial Government. The Emergency Requisition of Property Act, 1948 speaks of agreement but in the present Ordinance there is no such provision of agreement and on the contrary the assessment of Award is to be made by the Deputy Commissioner and the requiring body is to place the amount for the proposed acquisition. It appears from the record that Basharatullah has confirmed his verbal understanding between himself and the requiring body, this agreement is not contemplated between the awardee and the requiring body within the Ordinance. Thus learned Member Appellate Tribunal has also correctly found that this agreement is not contemplated within the scheme of the Ordinance and the question of agreement is not relevant in this case. This being the legal position we cannot accept the argument of the learned D.A.G. and the learned Advocate of the requiring body that the petitioner is not entitled to more than Tk. 22 lakhs in this Arbitration case.</u>

13. Both the Courts below also found that the application for Arbitration was rightly filed under section 28 of the Ordinance and the application does not suffer from any defect of parties.

14. The Appellate Tribunal further found that under sub-section 3 of section 10 of the Ordinance the petitioner is entitled to claim the amount as he accepted the amount on protest and as such he is entitled to make the application under section 28 of the Ordinance.

15. Now coming to the question on merit, it is found that the Appellate Tribunal as a Court of fact has considered the claim of the respective parties, the nature of land, the evidence both oral and documentary and the law and has come to an independent assessment of fact in this case. The Appellate Tribunal has also considered the evidence that was led with regard to the nature of land as to whether it is a bhiti land or a chala land.

<u>16. The Appellate Tribunal in its decision has given cogent reasons for reducing the amount as awarded by Arbitrator in respect of each of the items, namely market value of the property, the question of damage by severance of the property from the other properties of the petitioner and on other necessary considerations as contemplated under section 8 of the Ordinance.</u>

17. In that view of the matter, we do not find that there is anything to interfere in the judgment of Member Appellate Tribunal. The Appellate Tribunal on consideration of the materials on record has given correct findings and we do not feel that he has committed any illegality which occasioned any failure of justice calling for our interference by this court in these cases. Consequently these Rules are discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Abdul Quayum ------ For the Petitioner.
 P.C. Guha ------ For the Opposite Party No. 1.
parties:
Abdul Majid Akon ------ Petitioners.
Vs.
Satya Bhoma Nath & ors ------ Opposite Parties.
case_source: In the matter of an application for stay.
full_judgment:
This Rule arises out of an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and is directed against the Order dated 28.5.80 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Barisal in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 15 of 1977 reversing that of the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Pirojpur in Miscellaneous Case No. 7 of 1973 dated 30.11.76.

2. In this application the petitioner has challenged the order of the learned Subordinate Judge allowing the application for pre-emption filed under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 which arose in the following circumstances:

The Opposites parties No. 1 and 2 filed the aforesaid Miscellaneous case under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the Act for preempting 0.97 acres of land appertaining to C.S. plot Nos. 430 and 431 corresponding to S.A. plot Nos. 796 and 792 and C.S. Plot Nos. 425 and 430 corresponding to S.A. plot No.773 of Mouja Panthadubi which was transferred to the petitioner for consideration of Taka 2,300 by a registered kabala dated 16-8-72 by the predecessor-in-interest of opposite parties No. 3(a) to 3(d) on the allegations, inter alia that they were owners of land contiguous to the land under pre-emption, that they were bona-fide cultivators, that the petitioner was neither a co-sharer of the holding nor a tenant holding land transferred and that they had no knowledge of the transfer earlier than the date alleged in the application.

3. The said Miscellaneous Case was contested by the petitioner by filing written objection denying the material allegations made in the application contending, inter alia, that the application was barred by limitation; that it suffered from defect of parties and was not maintainable under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act that the lands transferred were non-agricultural lands; that they incurred expenses of Taka 1500 for improvement of the land.

4. The said Miscellaneous case has got a chequered career. It was first allowed by the learned Munsif by his order dated 3-6-74 on the finding that case was not bad for defect of parties and that there was no improvement of the land. Against the aforesaid order the petitioner filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 139 of 1974 in the court of District judge. The appeal, however, on transfer was allowed by the learned subordinate Judge who sent the case back on remand for fresh trial by the learned Munsif with a direction to decide the question as to whether application under sub-section (1) of section 96 of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was maintainable. It may be noted here that after remand the petitioner filed and additional written objection on 4-7-1975 wherein for the first time he alleged that transferred was non-agricultural land. The case after remand was allowed on contest against the petitioner with costs and exparte against rest with the finding that the case was maintainable under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, that it was not barred by limitation, that there was no defect of parties, that the petitioner could not prove improvement and the opposite party Nos. 1-2 were contiguous land holders and the petitioner was neither a co-sharer tenant nor a boundary man. The petitioner against the aforesaid order for the second time preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 28 of 1976. The appeal, however was allowed and the case again was sent back on remand to the trial court for fresh hearing. Thereafter the case was heard for the third time by the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Pirojpur. This time the learned Munsif by his order dated 30-11-76 dismissed the case and rejected the pra for pre-emption holding that the case was not maintainable under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act on the finding that land was non-agricultural one. Against the aforesaid order of the learned Munsif dismissing the case the opposite parties Nos. 1 and 2 preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 15 of 1977 in the Court of District Judge, Bakerganj which, however on transfer was heard by the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Bakerganj. The learned Subordinate Judge by his judgment and order dated 28-5-80 allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the learned Munsif holding that the application under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the Act was maintainable.

5. In support of the present Rule Mr Abdul Quayum appearing on behalf of the petitioner assails the judgment of the court of appeal below on several counts. Firstly, he submits that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in holding that the application under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the Act was maintainable. His next contention is that the lower Appellate Court committed an illegality in allowing pre-emption at the instance of a contiguous holder of land against a co-sharer. His third contention is that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in not awarding improvement cost to the petitioner who improved the land by incurring cost of Taka 1,500. His next contention is that the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error in allowing pre-emption in respect of all the plots in dispute although the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 were not owners of land contiguous to disputed plot No.797. He also urges that the lower appellate court was wrong to hold that the application was not barred by limitation under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Now let me consider the contentions one by one.

6. Mr PC Guha, appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 submitted that in the appeal before the learned Subordinate Judge only the question of maintainability of the application under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the Act fell for consideration as all other points had been decided earlier by the courts below and as such the learned Subordinate Judge was not to consider those points afresh and in that view of the matter the contentions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners on other points except question of maintainability could not be gone into at this stage. As these points arise out of the order of Lower Appellate Court I find no bar in urging those points by the learned Advocate for the petitioner.

7. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has taken me through the judgments of both the courts below and very strenuously argued that there being existence of dwelling huts, bagan and ditches as it appears from the record of right viz. the C,S. Khatian and the SA Khatian the land transferred is non-agricultural land and application for pre-emption lies in this case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act 1949 and not under sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. He also submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in reversing the finding of the learned Munsif that the land was non-agricultural. From perusal of the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge it appears that while he came to the finding that the land was agricultural land and not non-agricultural land he considered both documentary and oral evidences. He took into consideration CS Khatian, Ext. 5, SA Khatian, Ext. 6, kabala Ext. 1 written objection filed by the petitioner on 31-3-73 wherein the petitioner himself described the disputed land as agricultural land, and the additional written objection filed after the case was remanded by the appellate court. So far as the additional written objection is concerned the learned Subordinate Judge observed that "After the case was sent back on remand the Opposite party No. I filed an Additional Written objection as on 4-7-75 alleging for the first time that part of the case land is not an agricultural land. Evidently this was done in order to frustrate the purpose of pre-emption". After considering the evidences of the witnesses adduced by both the parties he also came to the finding:

"I find that the case land is an agricultural land and as such the case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is quite maintainable".

<u>8. From the evidence on record it appears that the land admittedly situates outside the Municipal Area, section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act provides for filing application for pre-emption in respect of non-agricultural land within a Municipal Area. This section has got no manner of application to case of an agricultural land situated outside the Municipal Area. In the present case the land being admittedly situated outside Municipal area provisions of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act has little application. Moreover, under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act a contiguous owner of land has no right of pre-emption. We may profitably refer to the case of Md Abdur Rouf and others vs Ahmuda Khatun and others reported in 33 DLR (AD) 323, Delivering the judgment of the report his Lordship Fazle Munim (as his Lordship was then) observed;</u>

<u>"Moreover, the ingredients of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are different. Some of these distinctions, are that while section 96 confers right of pre-emption on such holder of land contiguous to the land transferred, no such holder of land can exercise the right of pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act which merely confers the right of pre-emption on a non-agricultural tenant in respect of non-agricultural land."</u>

<u>9. Mr Quayum relying on CS Khatian and SA Khatian also submits that the land in question was not agricultural one. Whether land was an agricultural one or non-agricultural has to be determined by the purpose for which the predecessors-in-interest of the petitioner took settlement of the land. The determinant factor for deciding the nature of the land, whether the land is agricultural or non-agricultural, is the initial purpose either for taking settlement of land or for purchase of the same. This view finds support in the decision of a Division Bench of Dhaka High Court in the case of Lutfun Naher vs Syeda Hashmat Ara reported in 21 DLR 633 wherein it has been held that:</u>

<u>"The position in law, therefore, is that the Character of the land is determined by the purpose for which lease is taken and not by subsequent use of some of its part".</u>

<u>10. In that case an application under section 96(1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was filed for pre-empting some land by a contiguous owner of the land. The said application was resisted by the purchaser on the ground that land was not an agricultural but non-agricultural land and used for residential purpose and as such cannot be pre-empted under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. On reading the original deed by which lease was granted mainly for "purpose not connected with agriculture" their Lordships made the above observation and dismissed the appeal rejecting the prayer for pre-emption under section 96 of the Act. The learned advocate for the petitioner was unable to show in the case before us from the record that the original owner used this land for non-agricultural purpose. Rather it appears from the kabala. Exhibit-1 itself that both the vendees of the kabala were agriculturists and there was nothing in the document itself, namely, the kabala Exhibit 1 to show that the petitioner purchased the land for non-agricultural purpose. To attract the provision of section 34 Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act it has to be proved that a non-agricultural tenant himself has also erected a dwelling structure thereon. But in this case evidences also show that there was no structure whatsoever on the disputed land itself. Mere entry in a record of right showing hut, bagan, ditch or pond in plot does not make the land a non-agricultural land unless it can be shown that the initial purpose for which the land was leased out or sold was non-agricultural one. The learned Subordinate Judge also took into consideration the evidences of opposite party Nos. 5, 6, and 7 in order to ascertain the character of the land and considering the evidences in this respect the learned Subordinate Judge as already quoted above found that the land was agricultural land. There is nothing on record to show that this finding is perverse. Therefore, I do not find any reason to hold that this, finding of the learned Subordinate Judge as to the nature of land suffers from any error.</u>

11. Learned Advocate for the petitioner next contends that the petitioner being a co-sharer tenant by purchase of plot No. 530 in the holding the application for pre-emption at the instance of the opposite parties Nos. 1 and 2, owners of the land contiguous to the land transferred, cannot be maintained against the petitioner. In support of his contention the learned Advocate relied upon the case of Abdul Haque Miah and others vs Abdul Rashid & others reported in 35 DLR 54(A). But the decision is of no assistance to the learned Advocate as the facts of that case are different from the facts of the instant case before me. In that case the transferee was a co-sharer by inheritance and the pre-emptor was a co-sharer by purchase. But here the petitioner is not a co-sharer by inheritance; he claims to be a co-sharer by purchase. Their Lordships in the aforesaid case on interpretation, of sub-section (10) of section 96 of the Act held that an application under sub-section (1) of section 96 at the instance of a co-sharer by purchase cannot be allowed against a co-sharer by inheritance. The learned Advocate also placed reliance upon the decision in the case of Md Azimuddin Pramanik & others vs Sree Satya Narayan Pramanik & others reported in 37 DLR (AD) 220 in support of his above contention. In the aforesaid case cited before the petitioner for pre-emption was resisted by a co-sharer tenant by purchase. But in the instant case the petitioner is not a co-sharer tenant by purchase as it appears from the finding of the Lower Appellate Court to effect. Whereas admittedly the opposite party No. 1 is neither a co-sharer not a boundary man. "In that view of the matter the principle of law as enunciated in the case reported in 37 DLR (AD) 220 has got no manner of application in this case also. Therefore I held that the learned Subordinate Judge was correct in the facts and circumstances of the case, in holding that the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was maintainable."

12. So far as the contention regarding improvement of the land is concerned the learned Advocate for the petitioner very strenuously argue that the petitioner had incurred cost of Taka 1,500 for improvement of the land and he was entitled to get improvement cost. But the learned Subordinate Judge did not allow the petitioner to urge this point merely on the ground that the petitioner without filing any cross-objection under Order XLI, rule 22 of the Civil Procedure Code was not entitled to urge this point. The learned Advocates submits that the court of appeal below on an erroneous view of law did not allow to raise this point and decide the same although there was sufficient evidence on record to show, that the petitioner incurred expenses for improvement of the land. The learned Advocate submits that the petitioner could urge this point before the lower Appellate Court without preferring cross-objection under Order XLI, rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure. I find force in this contention. The learned Subordinate Judge was wrong in taking the view that the question of improvement of the land could not be agitated in the appeal preferred by the opposite parties No. 1 and 2 as the petitioner did not file any cross-objection. Although a plaintiff or a defendant-petitioner does not file any cross-objection under Order XLI, Rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the appeal filed by his opponent he cannot be debarred from urging a point which if accepted by trial court would have necessitated an order favourable to him. It appears from the record that there was appointment of an Advocate Commissioner in the instant case to ascertain as to whether the petitioner incurred any cost for improvement of the land. The Advocate Commissioner after holding local enquiry found that as a matter of fact the petitioner incurred Taka 1,200 by way or improvement cost but this material aspect did not receive due consideration by the learned court of appeal below no an erroneous view that the petitioner without preferring a cross-objection was not entitled to raise this point before him. Non-consideration of this report of the learned Advocate Commissioner namely, Exhibit. A dated 17-8-73 has seriously resulted in error in his decision. In view of the above discussion I hold that the petitioner is entitled to get the improvement costs of Taka, 1200 and the learned court of appeal below was not legally justified in disallowing the petitioner to raise the question of improvement of the land and in not deciding the same in favour of the petitioner.

13. He next submitted that the opposite parties pre-emptors were not boundary men of plot No. 797 and as such the learned sub ordinate Judge was wrong to allow the pre-emption with regard to all plots. Now let us examine this contention of the learned Advocate vis-a-vis the concurrent findings of both the courts below in this respect. From perusal of the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge it appears that he came to the following finding in this respect:

"But undisputedly their land appertaining to the plot Nos. 775 and 795 is situated to the contiguous to case land and as such they are boundary man".

On this point the finding of learned Munsif also runs:

"The petts, are admittedly boundary persons holding land contiguous to the disputed land measuring .97 acres in the plot Nos. 775, 797, 796."

In view of the aforesaid findings of both the courts below I do not find any substance in the contention of the learned Advocate. The learned Subordinate Judge has not committed any error in allowing pre-emption in respect of all the plots as sought for.

14. Now so far as the question of limitation is concerned the learned Subordinate Judge also held that the application was not barred by limitation under section 96 of the Act on the finding that pre-emptors had no prior knowledge of transfer. This finding as to limitation was based on evidence on record and I do not find any substance in the contention of the learned Advocate of the petitioner as both the courts below came in this finding on proper consideration of evidences.

15. For the reasons stated above, the order of the court of appeal below is modified to the extent as indicated above.

In the result, the Rule is disposed of. However, there will be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. AR Yusuf with Mr. Manzur-Ur-Rahim, Advocates  ------- For the Plaintiff. 
Mr. Rafiq-Ul-Huq with Mr.Md. Fazlul Hoque and Ms. Anjumanara Shelee, Advocates ------- For the Defendants.
parties:
Sadharan Bima Corporation  ------- Plaintiff 
Vs.
M V Birba and others  ------- Defendants
full_judgment:
The plaintiff instituted the present suit for the following declarations:

"(a) a declaration that the declaration of General A verge by the Principal Defendants is illegal and not binding on the plaintiff and/or anybody;

(b) a declaration that the plaintiff is not liable to contribute any sum in respect of general average of the ship or vessel Birba, her cargo and freight and is entitled to the cancellation and return of bonds or guarantees given to the principal defendants by the insured consignees and/or on behalf of the plaintiff by way of general average security as detailed in Annexure 'B'."

2. Bangladesh Pharmaceutical Industries, proforma-defendant No. 9, wanted to import certain goods from abroad and the present plaintiff Sadharan Bima Corporation was its insurer. Proforma-defendant No. 9 placed order to import 132 drums of RBD Palm Oil under bill of lading No. S/CTG-2, 527 drums of RBD Palm Oil under bill of lading No. S/CTG-I, 57 cartons of Polyester Textured Yarn under bill of lading No. S/CTG-5 and 25 cartons of Electric Fans under bill of lading No. S/CTG-23. The aforesaid goods were loaded in defendant No. 1, the vessel M V Birba, at Singapore for Chittagong. It was in the contract as well as in the invoices and the bills of lading that the defendant No. 1 vessel MV Birba would carry those cargoes direct from Singapore to Chittagong, But instead of coming to Chittagong direct the aforesaid vessel, violating the terms of the contract, went to Madras and there it met with an accident. It is alleged that in order to save the vessel, it had to jettison 100 drums of palm oil and then after about 8 months and few days it reached Chittagong. The owner of the vessel, after the alleged jettisoning, declared general average. The present plaintiff met up the claim of the proforma- defendant No. 9 and being subrogee instituted the present suit for the aforesaid declaration. It is not' disputed that the cargoes of the importer were loaded at the port of Singapore and then the vessel went to Madras and thereafter general average was declared and then after about 8 months and few days the vessel arrived at Chittagong.

3. In the instant case the defendant No. 1 MY Birba through its local agent filed an application for return of the plaint on the grounds that the plaintiff in this suit has challenged the validity of the declaration of General Average in question and has sought declaration to the effect that declaration of general average is illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff. But this Court in its Admiralty Jurisdiction is not competent to adjudicate the validity of the general average declaration and has no jurisdiction to make the declaration sought by the plaintiff herein. The authority of this Court in its Admiralty Jurisdiction is conferred and limited by the provisions of Admiralty Court Act, 1861. But the said Act does not confer any jurisdiction to this Court to decide any dispute arising out of the General Average Act and as such this Court has no jurisdiction to entertain and try the present suit in its Admiralty Jurisdiction. In a word, the prayer of defendant No. 1 is that there is no cause of action for institution of such a suit and a suit for such a declaration does not come within the purview of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. I have heard the arguments of both sides on this preliminary point of maintainability of the present suit instituted in its present form.

4. At the very outset, Mr. Aminur Rahman Yusuf (AR Yusuf) has read out before me section 135A of the Transfer of Property Act and with it he has referred to a decision reported in 16 DLR (SC) 61 (East and West Steamship Co. Vs. Queensland Insurance Co.) showing the locus standi of the present plaintiff to institute the present suit. In that decision their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan held that in a case of Marine Insurance the Insurer having paid up loss sustained by the assured and being subrogated to the position of the assured is entitled to sue tortfeaser ie the person who has caused the loss, in his own name. Mr. Yusuf has cited another decision of this Court reported in 43 DLR 548, Sadharan Bima Corporation Vs. Bangladesh Shipping Corporation, wherein this Court held that the insurer being not the owner or assignee or consignee of the goods is not entitled to file a suit under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. It appears that at the time of hearing of that case this provision of section 135A of the Transfer of Property Act and the decision reported in 16 DLR (SC) were not placed before this Court. However, on some other grounds that suit was found not maintainable. So, in the present case the plaintiff insurance corporation being subrogee is entitled to file the suit under the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, as the right as well as remedy gets transferred to the subrogee by operation of law.

5. The plaintiff being subrogee has invoked the jurisdiction of this Court under Admiralty Court Act. Mr. Rafiq-Ul-Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for defendant No. 1 M. V. Birba, submits that the present suit in its present form having no cause of action cannot be entertained either under section 6 or any other sections of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. Mr. Yusuf, on the other hand, has referred to different sections, namely, sections 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12, particularly; he has referred to section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act. Section 6 of the said Act runs as follows:

"The High Court of Admiralty shall have jurisdiction over any Claim by the Owner or Consignee or Assignee of any Bill of Lading of any Goods carried into any Port in England or Wales in any Ship for Damage done to the Goods or any Part thereof by the Negligence or Misconduct of or for any Breach of Duty or Breach of Contract on the part of the Owner, Master, or Crew of the ship, unless it is shown to the Satisfaction of the Court that at the Time of the Institution of the Cause any Owner or Part owner of the Ship is domiciled in England or Wales: Provided always, that if in any such Cause the Plaintiff do not recover Twenty Pounds he shall not be entitled to any Costs, Charges, or Expenses incurred by him therein unless the Judge shall certify that the Cause was a fit one to be tried in the said Court."

<u>6. Mr. Yusuf submits that being subrogee of the owner of the goods the present plaintiff has lodged a claim before this Court as contemplated under the above section. He further submits that on breach of contract the owner of the vessel has done damage to the goods which were imported by the defendant No. 9, Since there was damage done to the goods carried by the defendant No. 1 and since there was breach of contract on the part of the owner, master or crews of the vessel, the present suit is maintainable. Mr. Rafiq-Ul-Huq, on the other hand, submits that mere breach of contract is not enough. The breach of contract must lead to the damage done to the goods imported and for compensation of that damage a suit under section 6 is maintainable. But in the present case no cause of action arose for claiming any damage done to imported goods and no compensation for any damage to goods is claimed in the prayer of the plaint; rather the plaintiff prayed for a declaration that the declaration of the general average is illegal and not binding upon the plaintiff. It is just like a declaratory suit in civil nature which is not contemplated under section 6 of the said Act.</u>

7. Mr. Yusuf has referred to the case of Albert David (Bangladesh) Limited Vs. M/s NedIloyd Lijnen BV, Rotterdam, 34 DLR 356. He placed reliance upon the observation of his Lordship that the Admiralty Jurisdiction of High Court Division can be traced back to clause 26 of the Charter of 1774 by which power was given to the Supreme Court of Bengal to hear, examine, try and determine all causes, civil and maritime and "all pleas of contracts" and ''all matters and contracts" which in any manner whatsoever relates to freight or money due for ships hired and let out, transport-money, maritime usury, trespass, injuries, complaints, damages and matters, civil and maritime, whatsoever, between merchants, owners and proprietors of ships and vessels, employed or used within jurisdiction or between others contracted 'done, had or commenced contracted, in, upon or by the sea, or public rivers, or ports. He further submits that jurisdiction of High Court Division is derived from the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act of 1891 and the Court of Admiralty Act of 1861 of England. But in the same decision it is held by his Lordship that under the Act of 1891 the High Court Division of this Court was declared as Court of Admiralty.This Court exercised the same jurisdiction as the High Court of England exercised in 1890 under the Admiralty Court Act of 186l. In order to understand the matter more clearly let me quote his Lordship's observation which runs as follows:

"So far as the present action for non- delivery of the plaintiffs cargo is concerned the jurisdiction of this Court is not derived from the Letters Patent of 1862 or that of 1865, but from the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India) of 1891 and the Court of Admiralty Act, 1861 of England. The latter Act is not on our statute book but it is administered in view of the combined operation of sub-section (2) of section 2 of the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act 1890 of the British Parliament and the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India) 1891, the latter Act being revised by the Bangladesh Laws (Revision and Declaration) Act, 1973 (Act VIII of 1973) is now on our statute book. It is true that if the revised Court of Admiralty Act of 1891 is read in isolation then it would not give any idea as to the nature and extent of the Admiralty jurisdiction of this Court, but it is to be read in its historical perspective. Under the Act of 1891 the High Court Division of this Court was declared as the Court of Admiralty. This Court exercises the same jurisdiction as the High Court of England exercised in 1890 under the Admiralty Court Act of 186l."

8. In that case the suit was instituted for a claim for non-delivery of the cargo that was to be carried by the ship which was amenable to the jurisdiction of this Court. This decision, in my view, does not help Mr. Yusuf, rather it supports Mr. Rafiq-Ul-Huq. In the present case no cause of action was shown as regards damage done to the goods and no compensation was claimed and prayed for any alleged damage to the goods carried by the defendant No. 1 MV Birba.

9. Mr. Yusuf has further referred to the case of At-Sayer Navigation Co. Vs. Delta International Traders Ltd., 34 DLR (AD) 110. In that case the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court held that for loss of market due to longer voyage through breach of contract, the owner of the goods is entitled to sue for damages. It has further been held that for damages on account of late delivery of goods carried by the ship, the principle of calculating loss for late delivery as in the case of transit by land will be applicable. Relying upon this decision Mr. Yusuf has referred to paragraphs 7 and 8 of the plaint, Mr. Yusuf stated that in bill of lading No. 2, out of 132 drums of palm oil the importer got only 15 drums; in bill of lading No. 1, out of 527 drums the importer got delivery of 48 drums; in bill of lading No. 5, out of 57 cartons of Polyester Yarn the importer got 52 cartons and in bill of lading No. 23, the importer got 19 cartons out of 25 cartons. In these two paragraphs Mr. Yusuf has tried to show the short delivery of the cargoes, but nowhere the value of these alleged short-delivered goods was assessed and nowhere any assessment was made as regards the quantum of damage for long delay in discharging the goods. No prayer was made for a decree for any compensation for any alleged damage.

10. Mr. Yusuf submits that the claim of the plaintiff as well as short delivery of the imported goods are very much there in the plaint and as such the claim of the plaintiff comes under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act. This contention of Mr. Yusuf has no basis inasmuch as no claim for damage and compensation with regard to damage or short-delivered imported goods is made in the plaint itself, which is the main ingredient of section 6 of the above Act for invoking jurisdiction of this Admiralty Court. So, the decision reported in 34 DLR is not in any way helpful to Mr. Yusuf.

11. Mr. Rafiq-Ul-Huq has referred to section 1(q) of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956. In that section the provision of general average was specifically inserted. Though that Act is not applicable in our country, yet Mr. Rafiq-Ul-Huq submits that since Admiralty Court Act of 1861 docs not contemplate and include the provision of general average, the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 inserted specifically that declaration of general average in section 1 (g). So, by reference, he wanted to submit that general average is not contemplated under the Admiralty Court Act, 1861.

12. In this case I do not like to mention anything on merit although Mr. Yusuf argued it at length. In two other Admiralty suits, namely, Admiralty Suit No. 4 of 1982 and Admiralty Suit No. 6 of 1982 this Court recently delivered judgments decreeing the suits. In those two suits the plaintiffs prayed for decree for damages and compensation against the self-same defendant No.1 the vessel which loaded the goods of the plaintiffs from Singapore and, violating the terms of the contracts, the vessel went to Madras and thereafter the defendant No. 1 vessel reached Chittagong after about 8 months and few days and those two cases were decided on their own merits. Fundamental difference in between the instant suit and other two suits decreed is that damage and compensation were assessed and the specific prayer were made for a decree for damage done to the goods by the carrier. But in the present case there is no assessment of any damage or compensation and there is no prayer for decree for any amount as regards damage and compensation of goods damaged. In view of the above, I am of opinion that the suit as framed in the plaint of the present case and the prayer made in the plaint are quite distinguishable from the above two admiralty suits, and as such I find that the present suit is not maintainable either under section 6 or any other sections of the Admiralty Court Act of 1861. There is no cause of action shown as regards any damage done to the goods and there was no prayer for decree for compensation for the damaged goods. Decree claiming for damage and compensation must be prayed for in an admiralty suit, and a prayer for declaration that the declaration of general average is illegal and void may be made as additional, supplementary or ancillary or consequential prayer along with the main prayer for decree for compensation for the damage done to goods by the carrier during the voyage. But such a declaration as made in the present case does not independently come within the purview of any of the provisions of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. So, I find no substance in the contention of Mr. Yusuf.

13. Mr. Yusuf further submits that if the present suit is not directly maintainable under section 6 or any other sections of the Admiralty Court Act, the plaintiff is entitled to institute such a suit under clause 26 of the Charter establishing the Supreme Court at Fort William in Bengal dated 6th March, 1774. Clause 26 of the said Charter of 1774 has given wide jurisdiction to this Court 10 entertain any suit regarding any maritime claim and crime. In reply, Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq submits that the contention of Mr. Yusuf is absolutely erroneous. He has referred to section 9 of the Act establishing High Court of Judicature at India dated 6th August. 1861. By section 9 of the above Act the jurisdiction given to the Supreme Court by the Charter of 1774 was abolished. In 1861 the Admiralty Court Act came into force. On 14th May 1962 the Letters Patent for the High Court of Judicature at Fort William in Bengal came into force. Here, by section 31 the Admiralty Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court as Admiralty Court was taken away. On 28th December, 1865, the Letters Patent for the High Court of Judicature at Fort William in Bengal came into being and in this Letters Patent, 1865 the High Court of Judicature was given all powers civil, criminal and admiralty. Section 32 of the Letters Patent of the year 1865 has given to the High Court of Judicature at Fort William the jurisdiction to exercise all civil and maritime powers as may be exercised by the High Court of Admiralty or Vice-Admiralty and also such jurisdiction for other maritime cases arisen in India as may be exercised by the said Court, Mr. Huq has then referred to section 3 of Law Reforms Ordinance of the year 1978. Under section 3 of the Law Reforms Ordinance, 1978, the Letters Patent of 1865 was totally repealed. Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq submits that under these circumstances, even if, before 1978, that is before promulgation of Law Reforms Ordinance, Mr. Yusuf could have faintly argued that such a matter regarding declaration of maritime claim is maintainable before this Admiralty Court but after the repeal of Letters Patent vide Law Reforms Ordinance of 1978, Mr. Yusuf has no scope to argue that under clause 26 of the Charter of 1774 this Court has jurisdiction to entertain such a suit.

14. In this connection Mr. Rafiq-Ul-Huq has referred to the case of National Co. Ltd. Vs. Asia  Mariner, MS, 72 CWN, 635. It appears that his Lordship has discussed in details touching almost all the maritime cases of the sub-continent right from the Charter of 1774, in his judgment. After considering those cases and the maritime loss his Lordship held as follows:

"There was no further extension of Admiralty jurisdiction of the High Court in England by statute or otherwise over cargo claims or over contract of carriage of goods till 1920, so that at the time when the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890 was enacted, the High Court in England in its Admiralty jurisdiction could exercise jurisdiction in those matters only under the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. Therefore, it transpires, that this Court can have jurisdiction to entertain the present action, if at all, only under the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 and under no other statute or principle."

His Lordship further held that:

"If this is the proper analysis, and I think it is, no action will lie under the section unless the action is for damage done to the goods and the cause of action in negligence or misconduct or breach of contract or breach of duty in relation to the goods."

His Lordship further held that:

"Its jurisdiction is prescribed by clause 26 of the Charter of 1774 and by section 2(2) of the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890. The jurisdiction has not been extended or modified by any statute. None of the subsequent British statutes by which the Admiralty Jurisdiction of the High Court in England has been extended or affected have been made applicable to India."

15. The upshot of the aforesaid decision is this that if damage done to the goods and if compensation for that damage is prayed for and if the cause of action and the claim arise for such compensation for damage then such a suit under the Admiralty Court Act is maintainable, and all maritime claims and disputes can be raised before this Admiralty Court only under the provisions of the Admiralty Court Act of 1861, and in no other law. I respectfully agree with his Lordship's view to the fact that the only law under which the admiralty suit is to be entertained by this Court is the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 and under no other law. So, the second submission of Mr. Yusuf fails.

16. Defendant No.1 has filed this application for return of the plaint. In the Code of Civil Procedure, Order VII. rule 10 contains the provision of return of plaint. He has not prayed for rejection of the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But under Order XLIX, rule 3(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure the return of the plaint in Admiralty Suit under Order VII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not permissible. In the case of M/s. Saleh Steel Industries Ltd. and another Vs. TSS Pacific Abeto and others, 1983, BLD (HC) 104, the Admiralty Court (MH Rahman, J.) allowed rejection of plaint on the ground that no cause of action had arisen under the provisions of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 for institution of that suit. In this connection regarding return or rejection of plaint in an Admiralty Suit under Order VII, rules 10 and 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq has referred to the case of M/s Saleh Steel Industries Limited Vs. TSS Pacific Abeto and others, 35 DLR (AD) 188. In that case their Lordships, after considering the provisions of Order VII, rules 10 and 11 read with Order XLIX, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure, held that this Admiralty Court has no jurisdiction to reject a plaint in an Admiralty Suit under Order VII, rule 11(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure. But their Lordships further held that the Admiralty Court is conferred with power to return a plaint under section 151 read with sections 117 &141 of the Code of Civil Procedure, although Order XLIX, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure puts restriction upon High Court Division for returning the plaint to the plaintiff in the exercise of its ordinary or extraordinary original civil jurisdiction. In that decision their Lordships also held that the rejection of the plaint under Order VII, rule 11 (a) by the Admiralty Court is not permissible. Since rejection of plaint is not permissible as held by their Lordships. Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq submits that for abundant caution he has prayed for return of the plaint relying upon the decision of their Lordships in that case. In this connection I may quote Order VII, rules 10 &11 and Order XLIX, rule 3(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

17. Order VII, rules 10 &II run as follows: "10.-(1) The plaint shall at any stage of the suit be returned to be presented to the Court in which the suit should have been instituted.

(2) On returning a plaint the Judge shall endorse thereon the date of its presentation and return, the name of the party presenting it, and a brief statement of the reason for returning it.

11. The plaint shall be rejected in the following cases:

(a) Where it does not disclose a cause of action;

(b) Where the relief claimed is undervalued, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court, to correct the valuation within a time to be fixed by the Court fails to do so;

(c) Where the relief claimed is properly valued, but the plaint is written upon paper insufficiently stamped, and the plaintiff, on being required by the Court to supply the requisite stamp-paper within a time to be fixed by the Court, fails to do so;

(d) where the suit appears from the statement in the plaint to be barred by any law."

18. Order XLIX, rule 3(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure runs as follows:

"3. The following rules shall not apply to (High Court Division) in the exercise of its ordinary or extraordinary original civil jurisdiction, namely:

(1) rule 10 and rule II, clauses (d) and (c), of Order VII;

19. In that case leave was granted by the Appellate Division to consider as to whether the Admiralty Court was wrong in rejecting the plaint under rule 11(a) of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure. So, it appears that it was for the consideration of the Appellate Division as to whether the rejection of plaint under Order VII, rule 11(a), of the Code of Civil Procedure was legal or not, inasmuch as the High Court Division had rejected the plaint of the Admiralty Suit under Order VII, rule 11 (a) relying upon the provisions of Order XLIX, rule 3(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. KA Bakr, the learned Counsel for the plaintiff-appellant in the above case, submitted that the High Court Division was wrong in rejecting the plaint under Order VII, rule ll(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure. In that judgment his Lordship Mr. Justice Ruhul Islam held as follows:

"On careful examination of the different provisions of the Rules as referred to by the learned Counsels, it appears to me that rejection of a plaint filed in the Admiralty Jurisdiction under Order VII, rule 11(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure is not permissible under the Rules. In my opinion the learned Admiralty Judge acted without jurisdiction in entertaining the application under rule 11(a) of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure and rejecting the plaint. On this ground alone the judgment of the learned Admiralty Judge is liable to be set aside. In view of the legal provision stated above the judgment appealed from is set aside."

20. Mr. Rafiq-U1-Huq, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-petitioner here, frankly expressed his sorrow that though he appeared in that case before the Appellate Division on behalf of the respondent, he failed to point out and bring it to their lordships notice about some printing mistake in law i.e. in Rule 3(1) of Order XLIX of the Code of Civil Procedure, and that rejection of the plaint in an Admiralty Suit under Order VII, rule 11(a) of the Code of Civil Procedrue is not at all barred under law is Order XLIX rule 3(1) CPC. The judgment of the Appellate Division is binding upon all including the High Court Division. With due respect I would like to mention something below upon the submissions of Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq. In ordinary civil suits, the plaint can be returned or rejected under Order VII, rules 10 & 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure upon certain grounds. In Admiralty Jurisdiction some barring clause in returning and rejecting the plaint is imposed by Order XLIX, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Huq submits that though no bar is imposed by Order XLIX, rule 3 in rejection of the plaint in the exercise of ordinary and extraordinary original civil jurisdiction by this Court under Order VII, rule 11(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure, yet Mr. Bala, in fact, wrongly argued the case that High Court Division has no power to reject a plaint in Admiralty Suit under Order VII, rule 11(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr. Huq did not hesitate to submit that at that time he could not detect the apparent printing mistake in the law itself.

21. This apparent printing mistake lies in Order XLIX, rule 3(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Code of Civil Procedure has been modified upto 31st June, 1984 vide Government publication which has shown Order XLIX, rule 3 as "the following rules shall not apply to (High Court Division) in the exercise of its ordinary or extraordinary original civil jurisdiction, namely, (1) rule 10 and rule 11, clauses (d) and (c), of Order VII". Mr. Huq submits that this clause (d) is a mistake and it will not be clause (d), but it will be clause (b). In order to examine that mistake let me sec the Civil Procedure Code printed and published in Unrepealed Central Act of Pakistan. The Unrepealed Central Act, Volume-V contains the Civil Procedure Code. It was printed in the year 1953. It shows that Order XLIX, rule 3(1) says "rule 10 and rule 11, clauses (b) and (c) of Order VII." The volume-V of Pakistan Code contains the Code of Civil Procedure which was printed and published in 1966. In this Pakistan Code the Order XLIX, rule 3 (1) shows, "rule 10 and rule 11, clauses (b) and (c) of Order VII." Bangladesh Code, volume-VI which was published in the year 1979, contains the Code of Civil Procedure where Order XLIX, rule 3(1) shows as "rule 10 and rule 11, clauses (d) and (c) of Order VII." Then, relying on it the Government publication of Code of Civil Procedure made in the year 1984 shows this Order XLIX, rule 3(1) as "rule 10 and rule 11, clauses (d) and (c) of Order VII." Now, it appears that in Unrepealed Central Act and in Pakistan Code this Order XLIX, rule 3(1) shows as "rule 10 and rule 11, clauses (b) and (c) of Order VII." But when it was reprinted in 1979 in Bangladesh Code, volume-VI, it brings an apparent mistake like "rule 10 and rule 11, clauses (d) and (c) of Order VII." It appears to me that in an Act or Enactment there cannot be any dissimilarity or reverse arrangement in putting the numbers of sections or sub-sections or Rules or Clauses either numerically or alphabetically. It can not be clause (d) and thereafter clause (c). It must be arranged and numbered as clauses (b) and (c) or (c) and (d), but it must not be clauses (d) and (c). Unrepealed Central Act and Pakistan Code show the clauses as (b) and (c) and this clause (d) for the first time came in the Code of Civil Procedure in 1979 in Bangladesh Code, volume-VI. From 1966 to 1979 or in any subsequent year no amendment of Civil Procedure Code was made inserting clause (d) in place of clause (b) of Order XLIX, rule 3(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure. From the above, I am of the opinion that this insertion of clause (d) in place of (b) in rule 3(1) of Order XLIX of the Code of Civil Procedure is absolutely a printer's devil. If the small English letter (b) is placed in reverse way, it appears as small letter (d). From the above circumstances I find that this is absolutely a printing mistake done when the Civil Procedure Code was reprinted in Bangladesh Code, Volume VI in the year 1979.

22. However, Mr. Huq submits that in the aforesaid judgment of 35 DLR (AD) case, this rule II, clause (a) of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure was taken and considered. But clause (a) is no where in Order XLIX, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure which puts embargo in rejecting or returning plaint in Admiralty suit. Mr. Huq asserts that it must be clause (b) or at best, in a wrong way, it should be clause (d), but in no way it can be clause (a) of rule 11 of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure. Since Order XLIX, rule 3(1) does not contain any barring clause upon clause (a) of rule 11 of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure, Mr. Huq, submits, he could have prayed for rejection of the plaint under Order VII, rule 11(a) of the Code as the present case does not disclose any cause of action for instituting a suit under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act But taking abundant caution in view of the above decision of the Appellate Division he has filed this application for return of the plaint, which the Appellate Division allowed in the aforesaid reported case under section 151 read with sections 117 and 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

23. Since it is a judgment of the Appellate Division, it is a law and it will remain as law binding upon all including the High Court Division unless and until it is revised by the Appellate Division itself. As I find substance in the above submissions of Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq that the barring provision as contained in Order XLIX, rule 3(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure regarding rejection or return of plaint in an Admiralty suit does not contemplate this clause (a) of rule 11 of Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure, this Court expresses it pious desire that the learned members of the Bar, particularly, Mr. Rafiq-ul-Huq and Mr. AR Yusuf may urge this point again before their Lordships of the Appellate Division at an appropriate time and in an appropriate case and pray for reconsideration of their lordships decision on the point of rejection of plaint in an Admiralty Suit considering the correct provisions of Order XLIX, rule 3(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure in order to put an end to all probable future doubts in a matter like this.

<u>24. In two other suits against the same carrier-defendant No. 1, I have already passed decrees in favour of the plaintiffs as in those two suits the plaintiffs had shown causes of action as well as they made prayers for a decree for certain amounts as compensation of their damaged goods. The facts of the present suit are identical with those of the two other suits decreed, but as the plaintiff in the present suit has not shown any cause of action and has not prayed for a decree for any damage or compensation herein, and as the Appellate Division allowed return of plaint in an Admiralty Suit under section 151 read with sections 117 and 141 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the above judgment, I feel that ends of justice will be met if the plaintiff in the present suit is allowed to take back the plaint with liberty to file it in the appropriate forum with appropriate prayer disclosing appropriate cause of action.</u>

25. In the result, this application for return of the plaint is allowed. Let the plaint be returned to the plaintiff with a liberty to file it afresh in an appropriate forum disclosing appropriate cause of action and with appropriate prayer. This suit is thus disposed of. There will be no order as to costs.

Let a copy of this judgment be sent to the Secretary, Ministry of Law and Justice for making necessary correction in clause (1) of rule 3 of Order XLIX of the Code of Civil Procedure by inserting clause (b) instead of clause (d).

End.

lawyer:
Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed with SM Munir, Advocates ------ For the Appellants. 
Moazzen Hossain, DAG ------ For the Respondent No. 1.

Padmabati Biswas ------ Appellants

full_judgment:
Badrul Islam Chowdhury, J. : This appeal at the instance of defendant Nos. 24 and 31-38 arises out of the judgment and decree dated 19.4.62 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Khulna in Title Suit No. 5 of 1959.

2. Collector of Khulna on 16.5.59 made a reference to the Alluvial Lands Act, 1920 stating that some island chars were formed in the bed of the river Kazibacha in Mouza Tetultala within PS Batiaghata in the District of Khulna, as depicted in the sketch-map attached to the letter of reference, which had been shown as blocks 1-5 and 6-7 as prepared by khas mahals Surveyor and the chars comprising of 129.22 acres of cultivable land were being claimed by different persons including the government with the result that there were occasions for breach of peace. It was further stated that the Collector of Khulna therefore, attached the said char land in accordance with the provision of section 3 of the aforesaid Act and had appointed District Manager as receiver for management of the said land. The land were still under attachment and in possession of the receiver. As the Collector thought that rival claims of title and possession of this char land were likely to cause further breach of peace he referred the matter to the District Judge, Khulna for determining the claims of the different claimants. The District Judge under sub-section (2) of section 5 of the said Act transferred the reference to the Court of Subordinate Judge, Khulna where it was registered as Title Suit No. 5 of 1959. In the letter of reference 11 persons including the government were shown as persons claiming title and possession over the disputed land. However, after service of notice under section 5 of the said Act by the Court 40 more persons entered appearance and set up claims over the disputed land. They were added as defendant Nos. 12-51 in the suit.

3. The letter of reference of the Collector shows that the government was claiming the disputed land as island chars arising out of the bed of the river Kazibacha situated in Mouza Tetultala through which the river runs.

4. Claimant Nos. 2-51 have been treated by the trial Court as defendants in the suit and for the sake of convenience we shall also term them as such. Defendant No. 2 Abdul Haque Sarder claims that during CS operation it was found that the river Kazibacha, which is also known as Ramdashia, flowed through Mouza Tetultala comprised in the permanent settlement estate of Touzi No. 120 of Khulna Collectorate and as such the settlement authority treated the former bed of the river as Diara land. Accordingly a Diara proceeding was started, and in the CS maps (sheet Nos. 1-3) prepared in 1922-23 this diara land was demarcated and a new Touzi No. 1144 was assigned to it. The land of these diara Touzi was taken in settlement by the proprietors of Touzi No. 120. The further case of defendant No. 2 is that river Kazibacha formerly flowed by the north-south and eastern sides of Mouza Tetultala but subsequently it receded on the north and south as a result of which there was gradual and imperceptible accretion to the land of Touzi Nos. 120 and 1140. In 1940 the Government again surveyed the land of Touzi No. 1140. Along with land accreted to this touzi were delineated in the map so prepared and separate khatians were opened in the names of those who were holding the land contiguous to their Asli land. But there was no survey of the land accreted to Touzi No. 120. However, the landlords brought suits against the tenants who were holding the land in Touzi No. 120 for increase of rent on the ground of accretion and the same were decreed. In or around 1942 one island char measuring 2.55 acres was formed out of the bed of the river opposite to CS Plot Nos. 51-54. A similar island char measuring 16.60 acres arose out of the bed of river Kazibacha. Both these island chars were surrounded on all sides by deep water of the river. Government under the provision of section 4 of Regulation No. XI/1825 claimed both the chars as khas land and the Collector of Khulna started Settlement Case No. 54/46-47, got both the chars surveyed and map prepared. Initially both these two chars, one situated to the south of the other, were allotted Touzi No. 1442 which was subsequently changed to Touzi No. 1444 under Khas Mahal Officer's Order dated 27.5.48. Defendant No. 2, Abdul Haque Sarder, Kali Kanta Chatterjee, Anil Kumar Ghosh and Bupendra Nath Das who were tenure holders under the aforesaid Touzi Nos. 120 and 1142 took permanent settlement in raiyati right of both the above mentioned island chars at a rental of rupees 3.00 per acre from the government on payment of salami and by executing 4 separate kabuliyats in the year 1946 AD. Kabuliyats were accepted by the government and the tenants paid rent. The kabuliyats contained the stipulation that in case of increment to the leased out island chars, the lessees would pay enhanced rent at the stipulated rate. Lessee Kali Kanta Chatterjee settled his share comprising 4.79 acres to defendant No. 3 Sk. Nuruddin by patta dated 10.2.48. Lessee Anil Kumar Ghosh sold his 4.79 acre to one Mahbubur Rahman who in turn settled 1.50 acres out of his purchased land with defendant Nos. 5-7 in 1354 BS at an annual rent at Rupees 7-8-0 annas and sold the remaining 3.29 acres as well as rent receiving interest of the settled 1.50 acres to defendant Nos. 5-7 by kabala dated 25.10.56. Bupendra Nath Das, the other lessee, sold his share to defendant No. 4 by kabala dated 20.12.48 while defendant No. 2 remained in possession of his share of leased land. Gradually further land accreted to the northern island char and defendant No. 2 began to possess that accreted land too. There are two khals or channels on the east and west of this char. Out of the land accreted to this char seven bighas was settled with Monsur Bawali and Sariatullah Sk. by patta dated 29.5.51 with an annual rent of Rupees 14-0-0 and they arc possessing that land. Defendant No. 2 is in possession of the landaccreted to this northern island char. Thus defendant No. 2 possessed 28.00 acres land including the tenanted land and Asli land of 2.55 acres of touzi No. 1444. He also possesses 2.23 acres on the eastern side of the southern char of touzi No. 1444 by virtue of his lease taken from the government and with gradual accretion to this land by the recess of the river he had been possessing the accreted land as well. Defendant No. 2 further alleges that before attachment of the land a proceeding under section 144 CrPC was started at the instance of the Khas Mahal Depart.ment wherein it was clearly admitted that the disputed land were accret.ion to touzi 120 and 1144 and the said proceeding was ultimately dropped. Defendant No. 2 further claims that before attachment by the Collect.or the char contiguous to CS Plot No. 3 was possessed by defendant No. 3 Dwarik Mondal who is korfatenant under one Nalini Bala Chatterjee who is an under-tenant under defendant No. 2, the tenure formed under CS Plot No. 47 was being possessed by successors of Bangeshwar Chatterjee; that the lands of block No. 1 of Collector's map was in possession of defendant No. 9 and sons of Bangeshwar; that the land accreted to CS Plot Nos. 8 and 9 was in possession of defendant No. 9 Rabia Khatun along with her co-sharers; the land accreted to CS Plot No. 101 was possessed by Upendra Nath Mondal and his co-sharers and these persons were tenants under defendant. No. 2 who realised additional rent for the additional areas; that one Zohura Khatun had been possessing CS Plots No. 113 and 115 of khatian No. 24 and portion of block Nos. 6 and 7 of Collector's map as accretion to her land by purchase from Satish Chandra Bhadra. Defendant No. 2 therefore prays for declaration of his title over the land accreted to touzi Nos. 1144 and 120, for recovery of possession which are now in possession of the receiver appointed by the Collector and for cost against the government.
