23. Mr. Moazzem Hossain, the learned Deputy Attorney-General at the outset has taken the legal objection that the suit as well as the present appeal, which is the continuation of the suit, is not at all maintainable and should abate in view of the provisions of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act, 1950 as amended by PO Nos. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972. His next contention is that the islands which are the subject matter of the dispute arose out of the bed of the navigable river Kazibacha and as such those have vested in the government in accordance with the provision of law and therefore, no one else can set up any claim over the same.

<u>24. At the very outset we would like to dispose of the legal objection taken by the learned Deputy Attorney-General. Sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act as amended by PO Nos. 72, 135 and 137 of 1972 introduced radical changes in the century old law with respect to land gained by the recess of river or of the sea, as well as land reformed in situ, by providing that such accreted land or reformed land not be considered as the land of riparian or the original owner, as the case may be, but shall vest in the government free from all encumbrances, unless such accretion or reformation was finally recognised or declared by a competent authority or Court under any law for the time being in force. This provision of law was also given retrospective effect by insertion of the words "whether the loss of such land or portion by diluvion took or takes place before or after the commencement of State Acquisition &Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972. This fourth amendment is incorporated in PO 135 of 1972. In sub-section (3) similar provisions have been made with respect to land reformed in situ. Sub-section (5) of this amended section 86 further provides that all suits, applications, appeals or other proceeding with respect to any claim to the re-possession of any land lost by diluvion which has re-appeared or is alleged to have re-appeared pending before any Court or authority on the date of commencement of the said PO 135 of 1972 shall not proceed and shall abate. Mr. Moazzem Hossain relying on the provisions of this amended law as contained in sub-sections (2), (3) and (5) of section 86 contends that admittedly the disputed land are accretions as claimed by some of the defendants or reformation in situ as claimed by others and since the litigation with respect to title and possession over the said land was pending on the date of coming into force of PO 135 of 1972 the present appeal, which is a continuation of the original suit, cannot proceed and should abate. This contention of the learned Deputy Attorney-General may appear correct on the face of the provisions contained in statute itself. However, every law must be looked into not only by the language appearing in the statute book but also by its interpretation as enunciated by the superior courts of the country. Our Constitution enjoins that the decisions of the highest court i.e. the Supreme Court of Bangladesh should be followed and acted upon by all authorities and subordinate Courts. A decision given by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court is binding upon all Courts including the High Court Division. In the case of Abdul Mannan Vs. Kulada Ranjan Mowali reported in 31 DLR (AD) 195, their Lordships of the Appellate Division after discussing the history of the development of the law relating to accretion and reformation-in-situ as well as the provisions of sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act, 1950 as amended in 1972 have held:</u>

<u>"Having regard to the legal consequences flowing from the notification under section 3 of the Act, as referred to above, no retrospective effect can be given to the provision of sub-section (2) of section 87 of the Act, in any view of the matter, in most of the cases beyond 14-4-56, as the said provision read with that of sub-section (1) does not purport to extinguish or nullify any right which has been created under the provision of the very statute, of which this newly enacted section 87 is a part. It is significant that in the introductory clause of sub-section (1) of section 87, namely, "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force" there is reference only to "any other law", but there is no reference to the law as contained in the present Act. It is, therefore, reasonable to conclude that there was never any intention on the part of the legislative authority to extend the rctrospectivity of section 87 beyond 14-4-56 or such other date as may have been specified in any earlier notifications under section 3(1) of the Act."</u>

<u>The Court further held:</u>

<u>"But the manner in which sub-section (1) and sub-section (2) have been drafted, it is manifest that it was not the legislative intent to give such a wide retrospective operation to the provision of sub-section (2) of section 87. The past rights which have already accrued have not been sought to be affected by President's Order No. 137 of 1972 retrospectively, but such rights were purported to be affected only prospectively. That is to say, the right of accretion which the riparian owner has acquired in respect of the lands added to his holding before 28.6.72 ceased to be operative and to remain in force only since 4-11-72, the date of the coming into force of the President's Order No. 137 of 1972. In that sense also it would not doubt, be destructive of some vested rights, though in a prospective sense."</u>

<u>While following the above quoted decision of the Appellate Division a Division Bench of this Court in the case of the Government of Bangladesh Vs. A Wahed Sikder &others reported in BLD 1990 page 270 held:</u>

<u>"11. The expressions used in sub-section (5) of section 86 and sub-section (3) of section 87 of the Act gave rise to a great deal of controversy as to the extent of their retrospectively at one time, but the point is no longer res integra. It is laid down in the case of Abdul Mannan and others Vs. Kulada Ranjan Mowa and others, 31 DLR (AD) 195 that the suits, applications, appeals and other legal proceedings referred to in sub-section (5) must necessarily involve claims which come within the mischief of sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 86 and relate to lands which are lost by diluvion after the commencement of the Order as all lands which were lost by diluvion before the commencement of the Order but have re-appeared after coming into force of Part V of the Act. It is further laid down in that decision that sub-section (3) should be read harmoniously with sub-sections (1) and (2) and the land gained or alleged to have been gained from the recess of a river or the sea as have been contemplated in sub-section (3) must be such lands as are within the purview of sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 87 and "it will necessarily be those accreted lands which have appeared as hard soil only after the coming into force of Part V of the Act and the provision as the bar and abatement of suits, etc. as made in sub-section (3) are attracted in case of those suits where a claim of the right is asserted in respect of such land." Reference may also be made to the decisions in Makku Mia & others Vs. Ali Hossain Bhuiyan and others BCR 1984 (AD) 60, and Jafar Ali & others Vs. Sadek Ali & others BCR 1985 (AD) 29 in this connection."</u>

25. Thus after the above quoted pronouncement of the Appellate Division (31 DLR page 195) there remains no doubt about the fact that the provision of sections (2), (3) and (5) of section 87 as they stand now, can have effect only with respect to land which have accreted or re-appeared after Part V of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act, 1950 came into force in the locality in question. In the District of Khulna Part V of the Act came into force on August 29, 1963 whereas the disputed land appeared above the water of the river as hard soil due to recession of the river Kazibacha in the later part of the forties or in the early part of the fifties and attached by the Collector in 1955. In these circumstances the amended provision of sections 86 and 87 can in no way be applicable in the instant case. Therefore, the contention of the learned Deputy Attorney-General is not tenable in the eye of law.

26. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has raised objection as regards the correctness of the sketch-map prepared by the Collector and appended to the letter of reference. We find that at the time of trial the District Kanungo of Khulna ABM Moslemuddin was examined as PW 1 on behalf of the government represented by the Collector of Khulna, He deposed to the effect that after attachment of the disputed land the Collector ordered for survey of the same and accordingly Amin Abdul Masud Chowdhury surveyed and then Kanungo Monjur Ali prepared the map. On perusal of the said map it appears that the revenue survey lines as well as the channels have been depicted therein. From Ext. I, it also appears that on the application of one Haran Chand Mallik the Collector of Khulna started Misc. Case. No. 54 of 1957 and in that case the map was prepared by the Government Surveyor. Moreover, on scrutiny of the sketch map it becomes crystal clear that it contains the entire land in dispute and it has been sufficiently identified. Moreover, the original two island chars, the accreted land, khals, revenue survey lines and all other salient features of the disputed property have been clearly depicted in the map. So we find that the learned Subordinate Judge rightly came to the finding that there was no defect in the sketch map relating to the disputed land prepared under the order of the Collector and appended to the letter of reference. The law relating to chars or alluvial land is laid down in the Bengal Alluvion and Diluvion Regulations, 1825 (Regulation No. XI of 1825). The first clause of section 4 of Regulation XI of 1825 provides:

"When any land may be gained by gradual accession, whether by the recess of a river or of the sea, it shall be considered as an increment to the tenure of the person to whose land or estate it is thus annexed, whether such land or estate be held immediately from the government by a Zaminder or other superior land holder, or as a subordinate tenure by any description of under-tenant whatever."

Thus the law as it was in force at the relevant time provided that all alluvial land would be increment to the land of the Zaminder or tenant who held the main land under any superior landlord including the government. No doubt in the third clause it has been provided that if a char is thrown opened in a large navigable river the bed of which is not the property of any individual and if the channels of the river between the char and the main land are not fordable it shall be at the disposal of the government, but if the channel is fordable in any season of the year it shall be acquisition to the land of the persons whose estate may be most contiguous to it. Relying on this provision of law, the leaned Deputy Attorney-General Mr. Moazzem Hossain contends that it is admitted by almost all the contending parties in the suit that two island chars arose out of the bed of the river Kazibacha which was navigable at the relevant time and the two chars have been depicted as 'A' in the sketch map, in that view of the matter, according to him, these two chars belong to the government as per provision of clause (3) of section 4 of regulation XI of 1825 and any accretion to these two chars are accretion to government khas land and no one else can set forth claim over them. There is no doubt about the fact that PWs 1 and 2 as well as OWs 1-6 who were witnesses for defendant Nos. 2-7 in unequivocal language stated that in or around 1940 two island chars, one described as the northern char comprising of 2.55 acres, and the other as the southern char comprising 16.60 acres arose out of the bed of the river Kazibacha running through mouza Tetultala. DW 8 Mansur Bawali who is defendant No. 22, DW 9 Hatem Ahmed who deposed on behalf of defendant Nos. 9 and 12-18, DW 10 Tarek Mondal who deposed on behalf of defendant No. 21 also supported the case of the government and DWs 1-6 about the raising of these two chars out of the bed of the river which belonged to nobody. Therefore, there remains no doubt about the fact that immediately after the formation of these two island chars marked 'A' in the sketch map, those were at the disposal of the government. But it is the case of the defendant No. 2 and others that he, Kali Kanta Chatterjee, Anil Kumar Ghosh and Bhupendra Nath Das took lease of both the Chars in their totality from the government by executing four kabuliyats. The kabuliyat executed by Kali Kanta Chaterjee has not been produced in Court as because in spite of being called for the government who is supposed to be in custody of the same, did not file it. But the other three kabuliyats executed in the year 1946 have been filed in Court and marked as A, A(1) and A(2). These three documents prove that defendant Abdul Haque Sarker, Anil Kumar Ghosh and Bhupendra Nath Das executed kabuliyat in favour of the government for 4.79 acres of land each of the two island chars. Mr. Moazzem Hossain tried to argue that mere execution of the kabuliyats cannot create tenancy in favour of these executants unless the same were accepted by the government and the executants were recognised as tenants. But the documents Ext. A, A(I) and A(2) show that these were accepted by Khas Mohal Officer, Khulna and the said Officer also attested the same as witness. Moreover, these sets of defendants filed series of dakhilas to prove that they paid rent to the government for their leased land. So there cannot be any doubt about the fact that the two chars after becoming cultivable, were leased out by the government to defendant No. 1 Abdul Haque Sarder, Kali Kanta Chatterjee, Haran Kumar Ghosh and Bhupendra Nath Das in 1946 and subsequently rent was also accepted from them. With the leasing out of the land these four persons became tenure holders under the government and therefore on and from date of their acquisition of lease hold right over the two island chars clause (1) of section 4 of Regulation XI of 1825 became operative and by virtue of that provision of law they became entitled to anyadditional land which was gained to the two original island chars by recession of the river as increment to their tenure. Under the circumstances the plea taken by the government that since the two original chars marked 'A' in the Collector's sketch map, belonged to the government any accretion to them would automatically vest in the government is unacceptable. These accretions by operation of law as was in force at the time of such accretion, went to the tenure holders and their under tenants as well as the transferees as increment to their holdings. Of course, if the other set of defendants namely defendant Nos. 24-25, 26, 27, 30, 31-37 and 38-39 could show that these newly risen lands were reformation in situ of their land which previously were diluviated, then their claim would get preference. The documents filed in the trial Court show that by Ext. B one of the lease holders Kali Kanta Chatterjee, leased out his share to defendant No. 3, Sk. Nuruddin, that defendant No. 4, Emdad Ali Khan purchased the share for Buhpendra by kabala Ext. F and one Mahbubur Rahman purchased this interest of Anil Kumar by Ext. F(2) who in turn sold it to defendant Nos. 5-7 by Ext. F(1). These persons possessed their respective land in the islands and paid rent to the government and obtained dakhilas marked Ext. B series. The sketch map also shows that the accreted lands which are subject matter of the dispute depicted as blocks 1 to 5, surround the original northern island char of 2.55 acres while block Nos. 6 and 7 are contiguous to original southern island char of 16.60 acres and those have been attached by the Collector, being subject matter of contention between the parties and cause of apprehension of breach of peace. It may also be mentioned here that the kabuliyats marked Ext. A to A(2) contained the stipulation that in case of increase in the area of four lease hold lands the lessees would be liable to pay increased rent. This stipulation in other words means that the lessees would be entitled to any accretion that may happen to the areas of the original leased out land. In the Collector's map two khals or channels have been shown, one running between the block Nos. 2 and 3 and the other one between the block Nos. 6 and 7. PW 1, the District Kanungo tried to make out a case that these khals were navigable but he could not give the exact depth of the khals and on the other hand, he admitted that he had no personal knowledge of the origin of the khals or if they were fordable or not. On the other hand, DW 1 categorically stated that the khals were fordable at the time of formation of the disputed chars and that subsequently those have further silted up. Defendant Nos. 2-11, 12-18 and 21 and 23 claimed the disputed land as accretion to their tenancies. It. has been already stated that kabuliyats dated 18-10-46, 6-9-49 and 26.5.46 show that 4.79 acre of lands were taken settlement by each of DW 1 Abdul Haque Sarder, Kali Kanta Chatterjee and Anil

Kanta Ghosh at a rental of Rs. 3.00 per acre. It has also been shown that defendant Nos. 3-7 acquired the interest of Kali Kanta, Anil Ghosh and Bhupcn Das. Defendant No. 2 Abdul Haque Sarker claims 2.55 acres in the northern island and 2.23 acres in the southern island and also 28.00 acres as accretion to his original leased land. Out of these lands he has let out some to tenants who are parties in the suit and who support him. On the other hand, defendant Nos. 24-39 claim reformation in situ. Defendant Nos. 24-27 claim that disputed land originally were in mouza Jalma which was to the west of river Kazibacha while Tetultala was on the east, that during CS operation the river receded towards the north, south and was causing diluvion of some land of Jalma. Their further case is that the diluviated land subsequently re-appeared in their original sites, that Nanibala and others were tenure holders of mouza Jalma and on reformation these tenure holders brought Title Suit No. 5 of 1939 which was subsequently renumbered as 20/41 for the recovery of khas possession of these re-appeared land and obtained part decree in respect of the land described in schedule "kha" to the plaint of that suit and that their claim with respect to schedule "Ka" was dismissed. Their further case is that after obtaining decree these tenure holders settled the land with different tenants including defendant Nos. 24-27. So the sheet anchor of the claim of the these defendants is the decree obtained by their superior landlords in TS No. 20 of 1941. Admittedly the suit was with respect to the land of Jalma. But these defendants in the present suit did not take any attempt to relay the map attached to the decree passed in TS No. 20/41 in order to ascertain that the decretal land of that suit are identical with any portion of the present disputed land as shown in blocks No. 1-7 of the Collector's map. There is no dispute about the fact that in the CS map the whole of the river Kazibacha was included within mouza Tetultala while the eastern boundary line of both Jalma and Rangiamari was the western bank of the river. It is also not disputed that even after the change of course of the river there runs a channel in between the accreted land and the two villages Jalma and Rangiamari. Therefore, without relying the connected village maps it cannot be said that the disputed land are contiguous part of village Jalma and Rangiamari or that these char lands have re-appeared in the old sites which were originally depicted as part of Jalma or Rangiamari. Moreover, in Title Suit No. 20 of 1941 the government and some of the present claimants were not made parties and as such the decree passed in that suit is not binding upon them. Defendant No. 30 as DW 14 claims possession over the land. But from his deposition it transpires that he has no idea about the land and has no paper to show his possession. In that view of the matter, the trial Court has rightly held that the document Ext.A(9) is a spurious one. Defendant Nos. 31-37 claim 49.88 acres under the patta dated 13th Falgoon, 1354 BS marked Ext. A(7) purported to have been executed by Bhaigyadhar and Rajeshwar. The identity of this land has not been established by relaying the map. The Pleader Commissioner DW 18 said that he visited the land but in the next breath he said that plot No. 101 was under water at the time of his visit. On scrutiny of his deposition it appears that this Commissioner prepared his report Exts B(7) and C(7) sitting in his house without visiting the locality. Moreover, the map and the report in question were prepared by him in connection with Title Suit No. 155 of 1951 which suit is still pending and the report and the map of the Commissioner have not been accepted by the Court as yet. Kiran Biswas as DW 13 claimed that up to Kartick, 1355 BS Bhaigyadhar and defendant Nos. 31-37 possessed the land but could not produce any documentary evidence to substantiate his contention. He did not know if defendant Nos. 2, 3 and others took settlement of the land from government by executing four kabuliyats. Again, in a proceeding under section 145 CrPC this very witness claimed some land appertaining to mouza Tetultala. Thus he himself destroyed his credibility by saying one thing at one time and another at another time. Moreover, these defendants also did not take any step to get the land surveyed for the purpose of establishing their identity. Amrit Lal Guha who is said to have cultivated the land from 1362 BS has not been produced as witness. Moreover, DW 13 could not say who possessed plot Nos. 1009, 1015, 1045 and 1046 of block No. 2. From his cross-examination it transpires that the land of Rangiamari mouza is still under water and the entire land of block Nos. 1, 2 and 3 do not appeartain to that mouza. So he has virtually destroyed the case of this defendant that these three blocks reformed in the old situ and appertaining to Rangiamari mouza. Defendant Nos. 38 and 39 also did not give sufficient description of their land in their written statement. Defendant No.

33 as DW 15 said that defendant No. 39 claimed 63 bighas from block Nos. 6 and 7 but could not say how much of these 63 bighas are in block No. 6 and how much in block No. 7. He had no personal knowledge as to the diluvion and the formation of these blocks nor can say their boundaries. These lands were not recorded in their names either in the CS or in Diara or petty settlement. DW 7 admitted that many tenants possessed the northern land of mouza Tetultala. No one of their alleged bargadars have come forward to support their case, nor they produced any dakhila to prove that they paid rent.

<u>27. Regulation XI of 1825 has not made any specific provision regarding the reformation in situ. Sub-section (5) of section 4 of the said Regulation provides that in case of claim which are not provided for by the rules laid down in section 4(1) to 4(4) the Courts shall be guided by a local usage, if there be any, and in the absence of such usage by the general principle of equity and justice. In the case of Lopez Vs. Mudun Tahakur, 13 MIA 467 the Privy Council laid down the principle that when an estate is gradually swallowed by the river or the sea and afterwards re-appeared on the old site and is capable of identification it is the property of the original owner and not an accretion to the estate to which it is attached unless there has been an abandonment by the original owner. Thus the cardinal principle is that in order to succeed on a claim of reformation in situ the identity of the land must be established by satisfactory evidence and that original owners cannot claim title if they after diluvion, had abandoned their rights by remission of revenue or by adverse possession. Keeping this principle in mind if we scrutinise the evidence on record as adduced by defendant Nos. 24-25, 26, 27, 30, 31-37 and 38-39 it become clear that they have miserably failed to establish their claim to the satisfaction of a reasonable mind. It has been stated earlier that they did not take any step to relay the disputed land so as to establish their identity with the alleged diluviated land. There is practically no credible evidence to prove that they resumed possession of these lands immediately on reformation without abandoning their claim. The plea of reformation in situ cannot be sustained unless it is proved that the land appearing as char is the same land which was lost by diluvion and that the claimants possessed the same land both before diluvion and after reformation. The above mentioned defendants miserably failed to prove these two points. It may be mentioned here that witness Nos. 11-14 could not even say accurately as to how and when defendant Nos. 24-27 and 30 to 39 possessed the disputed land or that these defendants paid rent before the diluvion and after reformation. A single dakhila Ext. A(5) of the year 1366 BS has been rightly termed as spurious by the trial Court. Defendant Nos. 40-51 whose claims have been dismissed by the trial Court have not come forward with any appeal. Similar is the case with defendant No.8. Under the circumstances the learned Subordinate Judge after discussing the evidence of DWs 2-6 and 9 who stated that no tenant of Rangiamari or Jalma ever possessed the disputed land since their appearance, has rightly come to the conclusion that defendant Nos. 43-55 abandoned their right, if any, by non-payment of rent and by not possessing the same for more than 12 years.</u>

28. Considering the evidence on record both oral and documentary, we hold that the learned Subordinate Judge on proper sifting of the evidence on record has rightly come to the conclusion that defendant Nos. 2-7, 9, 12-18 and 21-22 have successfully proved their claim of title and possession over the disputed land, while defendant Nos. 8, 19, 24-27 and 30-51 could not prove their claim and defendant Nos. 20, 28 and 29 did not come forward to lay any claim over the disputed land at the time of trial.

29. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed lastly contended that in the decree the learned Subordinate Judge has not specifically ascertained the quantum of land which the successful defendants could get out of the accreted land and as such the decree suffers from vagueness. We are unable to agree with him. The Court has passed decree in favour of defendant Nos. 2-7, 9, 12-18 and 21-23 declaring their title and recovery of possession jointly. So these defendants can in future file a suit for partition amongst themselves and in that event the quantum of the accreted land to which each of them would be entitled will be ascertained by the Advocate Commissioner.

In the result, we find that the present appeal has no merit and there is nothing to disturb the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed on contest against respondent No. 1 and ex parte against the rest considering the circumstances there shall be no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Naimuddin Ahmed, J: This Rule, obtained on a revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, is directed against an order passed by Mr. Md. Habibur Rahman, District Judge and Appellate Election Tribunal, Narayanganj on 12.11.89 in Election Tribunal Appeal No. 5 of 1989 admitting the said appeal preferred against an order passed by the Election Tribunal, Narayanganj, in Election Tribunal Case No. 2 of 1988 on 30.9.89 condoning the delay in filing the appeal by applying section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908.

2. The facts of the case are that the election for electing the Chairman and Members of the Siddhirganj Union Parishad was held and ultimately the result of the election was notified in the Bangladesh Gazette declaring the opposite party No. 1 as the elected Chairman. The petitioner of this revisional application, Md. Iqbal Hossain, challenged the said election before the Election Tribunal, Narayanganj, by filing an application under section 29(4) of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 disputing the said election. After hearing the parties the Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Narayanganj and Election Tribunal, by a Judgment and order dated 30.9.89, set aside the election and declared the present petitioner, Md. Iqbal Hossain, as the elected Chairman. As against the aforesaid order dated 30.9.89 passed by the Assistant Judge, 2nd Court, Narayanganj and Election Tribunal in Election Tribunal Suit No. 2 of 1988, the opposite party No. 1 of this revisional application, Abdur Rab who had been elected as Chairman and was unseated by the order of the Election Tribunal dated 30.9.89, preferred an appeal before the Appellate Election Tribunal, Narayanganj, on 12.11.89, being Election Tribunal Appeal No. 5 of 1989 and the learned Appellate Election Tribunal, Narayanganj, admitted the said appeal by recording the following order:—

“অদ্য দাখিল করা হইয়াছে। রেজিষ্ট্রিভুক্ত করা হউক। ইহা নারায়নগঞ্জ ২য় সহকারী জজ আদালতে নির্বাচনী ২/৮৮ নং মোকদ্দমায় নির্বাচন ট্রাইবুনাল জজ, জনাব আবুল হোসেন খন্দকার কর্তৃক ৩০-৯-৮৯ ইং তারিখে প্রদত্ত রায় ও আদেশের বিরুদ্ধে আপীল। আপীল মোকদ্দমাটি নির্ধারিত সময়ের পরে দাখিল করিয়াছেন। আপীলকারী হলফ নামা সহকারে এক দরখাস্ত করিয়া অত্র আপীল মোকদ্দমা নির্ধারিত সময়ের পরে দাখিল করার বিলম্বের দিনগুলি কর্তন করার প্রার্থনা করিয়াছেন।

আপীল্যান্ট প্রতিপক্ষের বিজ্ঞ কৌশলীর বক্তব্য শ্রবন করিলাম। আপীল্যান্ট দরখাস্তকারী পক্ষ হইতে দাখিলী তমাদি আইনের ৫ ধারার দরখাস্ত ও তৎসমর্থনে দাখিলী শফথনামা ২টি পর্যালোচনা করিলাম। দরখাস্তে ও শফথনামায় উল্লেখিত কারনে অত্র আপীল দায়ের করিতে বিলম্ব হইয়াছে দেখা যায়। উল্লেখিত কারন সমূহ আপাততঃ অবিশ্বাস করিবার কোন হেতু দেখিনা কাজেই অত্র আপীল দায়ের করিতে বিলম্ব এতদ্বারা মওকুফ করা হইল। আপীলটি শুনানীর জন্য তালিকাভুক্ত করা হউক।”

3. As against the aforesaid order whereby the Appellate Election Tribunal admitted the appeal, the petitioner obtained the present Rule by filing this revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

4. Mr. TH Khan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, has challenged the impugned order of the learned Appellate Election Tribunal whereby the appeal was admitted by condoning the delay under section 5 of the Limitation Act, on the ground that sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 prescribed the period of limitation for filing an appeal against an order passed by the Election Tribunal within 30 days from the announcement of the decision of the Election Tribunal and as this period of limitation provided in sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 is a period of limitation provided in a special law, the general provision of section 5 of Limitation Act could not be applied for condoning the delay in filing the said appeal and as such, Mr. TH Khan has argued, by applying section 5 of the Limitation Act and thereby by condoning the delay in filing the appeal the Appellate Election Tribunal has committed a serious error of law.

5. The next ground taken by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that before passing the impugned order no notice was issued on the present petitioner who was the respondent in the Election Tribunal Appeal before the learned Appellate Election Tribunal and without affording the petitioner any opportunity of being heard a right already vested in the petitioner has been taken away by the impugned order and as such, the principle of natural justice has been violated and on this ground alone the impugned order can not been sustained.

6. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate, appearing for the opposite party No. 1, has, on the other hand, contended that by operation of section 29 of the Limitation Act, applicability of section 5 of the Limitation Act in case of an application under sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 has not been excluded and as such, the Appellate Election Tribunal was justified in condoning the delay in filing the appeal against the order of the Election Tribunal in the facts and circumstances of the case.

7. It appears that in Election Tribunal Suit No. 2 of 1988 in which the election of the opposite party No. 1 was challenged by the petitioner of this revisional application, the Election Tribunal, Narayanganj, found the election as illegal and by its judgment and order passed on 30.9.89 allowed the application of the petitioner, set aside the said election of the opposite party No. 1 and declared the present petitioner of this revisional application as the elected Chairman of Siddhirganj Union Parishad. It also appears that the appeal against this order of the Election Tribunal was filed on 12.11.89 before the Appellate Election Tribunal and this appeal was registered as the Election Tribunal Appeal No. 5 of 1989. It also appears that the appeal was filed before the Appellate Election Tribunal 13 days after the expiry of 30 days from the date of the order of the Elec-tion Tribunal in contravention of sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 providing the limitation for an appeal against an order of an Election Tribunal as follows:—

"(4). Any person aggrieved by a decision of the Election Tribunal may, within thirty days of the announcement of the decision, prefer an appeal to the District Judge within whose jurisdiction the decision in dispute was held; and the decision of the District Judge on such appeal shall be final.

Provided that in the case of a decision announced before the commencement of the Local Government (Union Parishads) (Amendment) Ordinance, 1984 (XLIV of 1984), such appeal may be preferred within thirty days of such commencement."

8. It is not disputed that the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983, is a special law. It appears that sub-section (4) of section 29 of the aforesaid Ordinance prescribes a special period of limitation of 30 days against an order or decision of the Election Tribunal from the date of announcement of such order or decision. It is also not disputed that the appeal before the Appellate Election Tribunal in the present case was filed by the opposite party No. 1 beyond 30 days from the date of the judgment and order of the Election Tribunal.

9. Mr. TH Khan has mainly relied on section 29(2) of the Limitation Act in order to emphasise his argument contending that by this provision the application of section 5 of the Limitation Act to Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983, is excluded. It is, therefore, necessary to refer to sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act which runs as follows:—

"29(2). Where any special law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule, the provisions of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefor in that schedule, and for the purpose of determining any period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special or local law—

(a) the provisions contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18, and section 22 shall apply only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special law; and

(b) the remaining provisions of this Act shall not apply."

10. Mr. TH Khan appears to have placed reliance on clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act in excluding section 5 of the Limitation Act from the purview of an appeal under sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads), Ordinance, 1983. Mr. Khan has also cited a number of decisions in support of his contentions that by operation of clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act, the applicability of section 5 of the Limitation Act, to an appeal under sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983, has been excluded. A plain reading of section 29 of the Limitation Act indicates that if the special law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule of the Limitation Act, the provisions of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefor in that schedule, and for the purpose of determining any period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special or local law, the provisions contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18 and 22 shall apply only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special law and the remaining provisions of the Limitation Act shall not apply. It, therefore, appears that as section 5 of the Limitation Act is not included in clause (a) of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act, section 5 of the Limitation Act cannot, in view of clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section 29 thereof, be made applicable for filing an appeal under sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983. It is, however, true that there is no provision in the Local Government (Union Parishads), Ordinance, 1983 excluding section 4, sections 9 to 18 and section 22 of the Limitation Act and, as such, by operation of clause (a) of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act, section 4, sections 9-18 and section 22 may be said to be applicable to an appeal under sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983. It, therefore, appears that since section 5 of the Limitation Act is not included in clause (a) of sub-section (2) of section 29 thereof clause (b) thereof governs section 5 and as such, section 5 cannot apply for purpose of determining any period of limitation for appeals under sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983.

11. In support of the above proposition Mr. TH Khan has cited a number of decisions. In the case of Aftabuddin Vs. Sajjad Ali and others reported in 1986 BLD (HC) page 235, the question before a Division Bench of this Court was whether an appeal under section 417(2)(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Act V of 1898) could be condoned by applying section 5 of the Limitation Act. In that case an appeal under section 417(2)(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was filed beyond 60 days prescribed as the period of limitation under the said section, and it was held that although the Code of Criminal Procedure was normally to be considered under the general law of limitation, an appeal under section 417(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure has to be treated as a special law prescribing special limitation and as such, in an appeal under section 417(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure filed beyond the period of 60 days from the date of the judgment, the delay in filing the appeal could not be condoned by invoking section 5 of the Limitation Act in view of clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act.

12. In Sirajuddin and others Vs. Ahmed Fazlur Rahman and another reported in 1986 BLD at page 258 a Single Bench of this Court also held that section 5 of the Limitation Act was not applicable for condonation of delay in filing an appeal against the decision of the Administrator of Wakf as special period of limitation had been provided under the Wakf Ordinance, (Ordinance No. 1 of 1962) for such an appeal. It was also held that since sections 35 and 50 of the Wakf Ordinance, prescribed special limitation, section 5 of the Limitation Act could not be applied in view of clause (a) of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act in condoning the delay in filing the application under the said sections of the Wakf Ordinance, 1962.

13. Mr. Khan then cited Authorised Officer CDA Vs. The State reported in 38 DLR (HC) page 27. The facts of this case were almost similar to those of the case reported in 1986 BLD page 235 and in this case also it was held that an appeal under section 417(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure could not be filed beyond the period of 60 days which was prescribed as the limitation for an appeal under the said section in view of clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act.

14. Mr. Khan cited another decision, Syed Mahmud Alam Vs. Syed Mehdi Hussain and others reported in PLD 1970 (Lahore) page 6. In this case an appeal was filed under section 18 of the Land Settlement Act (XLVII of 1958) beyond the period of limitation prescribed therefor under the said section before the Appellate Authority by condoning the delay in filing the appeal under section 5 of the Limitation Act and it was held that the Appellate Authority was not competent to condone the delay in filing the appeal by applying section 5 of the Limitation Act in view of clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act.

15. Mr. Khan also cited a decision reported in 1941 AIR (Allahabad) page 207, Chheda Lal Jain Vs. Officer Commanding, Station Meerut Cantonment. In this case, an appeal was preferred under section 29 of the Cantonments (House Accommodation) Act of 1923 beyond the period of limitation prescribed in the said Act and the question arose whether the appeal could be admitted by condoning the delay by applying section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1908. It was held that since the Cantonments (House Accommodation) Act of 1923 was a special law and provided special period of limitation section 5 of the Limitation Act was not applicable to condone the delay in filling the appeal under section 29 thereof in view of clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act.

16. In addition to the above decisions, Mr. Khan, last of all, cited a decision of this Court reported in 39 DLR page 164, Elahi Bux Vs. State. In this case an appeal was filed against the decision of Special Tribunal constituted under the Special Powers Act, 1974 beyond the period of limitation prescribed therefor under section 30 of the Special Powers Act, 1974 and it was held by a Division Bench of this Court that the delay in preferring the appeal beyond the period of limitation prescribed therefor under section 30 of the Special Powers Act, 1974, which was a special law, could not be condoned under section 5 of the Limitation Act in view of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act.

17. As against the aforesaid long series of decisions Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has, first of all, cited a decision of the Calcutta High Court in Province of Bengal Vs. Amulya Dhan reported in 54 CWN page 297. In this case, an appeal was preferred against the decision of a Tribunal constituted under the Calcutta Improvement Act (V of 1911) before the Calcutta High Court beyond the period of limitation and the question arose whether the delay could be condoned by applying section 5 of the Limitation Act.

18. After elaborate discussion of section 29 of the Limitation Act the Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court classified 4 categories of cases falling under section 29 of the Limitation Act as follows:—

(1) Where the local or special law is silent on the matter of limitation in respect of suits, appeals or applications contemplated or authorised by it, and some Article of Schedule I of the Limitation Act would cover them.

(2) Where some Article of that schedule would have covered such suits, appeals or applications, but the local or special law had prescribed a period of limitation different from that prescribed in the relevant Article of Schedule I, either by altering the period of time mentioned in the second column of the relevant Article of Schedule I or by prescribing a starting point different from that indicated in the third column thereof.

(3) Where none of the Articles of Schedule I would have covered such appeals or applications and the local or special law itself prescribed limitation. In this head and the next we are omitting Reference to suits for the reason that the residuary Article, namely 120 of Schedule I, would in any event cover any class and every class of suits contemplated or authorised by the local or special Act, and so would fall either within type (1) or (2). We are however including applications because of the view taken in some cases that Article 181 of Schedule I has restricted application.

(4) Where none of the Articles of Schedule I would have covered such appeals or applications and the special or local law prescribed none."

19. In the case before the Calcutta High Court the Calcutta Improvement Act (V of 1911) did not provide any special provision for limitation for an appeal against the decision of the Calcutta Improvement Trust Tribunal and Article 156 of the First Schedule of the Limitation Act governed such an appeal. It was held that the case fell under the first type and as such, section 5 of the Limitation Act was applicable. It was further held in the said case that in cases falling within the third type (as the case before us) "secs. 4, 9 to 18 and 22 were made applicable unless the special or local law excluded any of them, and the remaining sections namely, 5 to 8, 19 to 21 were not to apply unless they were made applicable by special or local law" in view of clause (b) of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act. So, apart from the fact that in the case before the Calcutta High Court the special law did not provide any limitation and an Article of the First Schedule of the Limitation Act provided the limitation as distinct from the present case in which the limitation is provided in the special law different from the First Schedule of the Limitation Act, the above interpretation put by the Calcutta High Court in Amulya Dhan's case reiterates the views expressed by Mr. Khan.

20. Mr. Ahmed appears to have laid stress on the following words appearing in sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act:—

"Where any special law prescribed for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation  different from the period prescribed therefor by  the first schedule the provisions of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefor in that schedule, and for the purpose of determining any period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special or local law....."

21. Mr. Ahmed has argued with reference to the words underlined above that since in the first schedule no limitation has been prescribed for an appeal under sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983, section 29 of the Limitation Act cannot be attracted. It appears from the trend of this argument that he wants to say that when a period of limitation is prescribed by a special or local law and a period of limitation for the purpose of filing similar nature of case is also prescribed in the first schedule of the Limitation Act, and the period of limitation prescribed in the special law is different from that provided in the first schedule of Limitation Act the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act can be attracted. It is difficult to accept this contention of Mr. Ahmed. If a period of limitation is prescribed by a special or local law and no such period of limitation is prescribed by the first schedule of the Limitation Act, sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act is attracted. This is clear from the decision cited by Mr. Ahmed reported in 54 CWN page 297.

<u>22. In the next place, Mr. Ahmed has cited a decision of this Court in the case of Rokeya Begum Vs. Radha Gobinda reported in 27 DLR page 418. In this case, the question arose whether the period of limitation for an application under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act was three years from the date of the non-notified co-sharer's knowledge of the transfer of a portion or share of a holding or a period of limitation as prescribed in section 26F of the Ben-gal Tenancy Act, and it was held by a Single Bench of this Court as follows:—</u>

<u>"Where a special or local law prescribes a special period of limitation, the excluded provisions of the Limitation Act shall not apply. For instance, it has been held that under section 20, Madras Act IV(4) of 1936, a special period of limitation is laid down for the filing of an application under section 19 by a person who has obtained a stay under section 20 and consequently section 5 of the Limitation Act cannot be applied to extend the period therefor prescribed under the Special Law. In section 25A, newly introduced into this Act, though a right of appeal is given, no period of limitation different from the period prescribed by Schedule I, Limitation Act, is indicated. Therefore the provisions of section 29(2) have no application, so as to exclude the provisions of section 5, Limitation Act, from being applied to appeals under the special law.</u>

<u>It is thus quite clear that the provision of section 29(2) has no application to a case where no different period of limitation has been prescribed by a special or local law for an application which may be filed to enforce a right created or declared under the said law and the person making such an application is entitled to the benefits of those provisions of the Limitation Act which operate to extend the period of limitation for such an application in certain cases."</u>

23. It, therefore, appears that in this case also the law has been clearly stated that where a special law prescribes a period of limitation for an appeal or application section 29(2) of the Limitation Act comes into operation.

24. Mr SS Haider, who also appeared for the opposite party No. 1, has advanced a different line of argument relying on certain decisions and arguing that an Appellate Election Tribunal has been held to be a civil court within the meaning of the Civil Courts Act, 1887, and as such, the general provisions of the Law of Limitation are applicable in respect of an appeal filed before the Appellate Election Tribunal.

<u>25. It has been well settled by the decision in the case of Ruhul Amin Vs. District Judge and Appellate Election Tribunal, Bhola, and others reported in 38 DLR (AD) page 172 that while the District Judge acts as the Appellate Election Tribunal he acts as a Civil Court within the meaning of the Civil Courts Act, 1887. The decision which Mr. Haider, first of all, cited is Gonapathi Vs. N. Kumaraswami reported in 1975 AIR Madras page 383. In this case, the question was whether section 5 of the Limitation Act would apply against the order of the Rent Controller as the Rent Controller was not a Court. The applicability of section 29(2) of the Limitation Act was considered and it was held that when a period of limitation was prescribed by a special law section 5 of the Limitation Act could not be applied. This decision is of no assistance to Mr. Haider.</u>

<u>26. Mr. Halder then cited Ulahannan Chacks and others Vs. Pareed Marakkar and others, reported in AIR 1978 (Kerala) page 161. In this case arising out of an appeal under the Kerala Rent Control Act, the question was whether section 5 of the Limitation Act could be applied in condoning the delay in filing an appeal before the Appellate Authority constituted under the said Act and it was held 41t the appellate authority not being a court section 5 of the Limitation Act could not be applied. Mr. Halder, however, drew our intention to an observation in this case to the effect that section 29(2) of the Limitation Act did not exclude Mt applicability of section 5 of the Limitation Act. This aspect and the applicability of this observation will be taken up presently. For the present, it can be said that Ulahannan Chacks's case is hardly relevant to the issue involved in the present case.</u>

27. In order to emphasize that section 5 of the Limitation Act is not excluded by sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act, Mr. Haider produced Kantibai Vs. Kawal Singh Thakur reported in 1978 AIR (Madhya Pradesh) page 245. It was held in this case that section 5 of the Limitation Act could be applied for condoning the delay in filing an appeal under section 28 of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, since there is no provision in the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, excluding the operation of section 5 of the Limitation Act although the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, also provided special limitation for an appeal under section 28 thereof. Unfortunately, Mr. Halder overlooked that the above decision was made after enactment of the Indian Limitation Act, 1963, which made an important departure from the Limitation Act, 1908, which still held good in this country. In the Indian Limitation Act, 1963, section 29 as it stood in the Limitation Act, 1908, which applies to this country, was replaced and in sub-section (2) of section 29 all the sections 4 to 24 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1963, were included and made applicable to any suit, appeal or application where special or local law provided a special period of limitation as distinct from the Limitation Act, 1908, in section 29(2)(a) whereof only sections 4, 9 to 18 and 22 were included and made applicable and in section 29(2)(b) whereof all other sections were excluded and made inapplicable. Consequently, so long as section 29 of the Limitation Act, 1908 is on the statute book in this country, Kantibai's case has no relevancy.

28. From a consideration of all the above decisions and the provisions of section 29 of the Limitation Act, 1908, it, therefore, emerges that section 5 of the Limitation Act has been completely excluded from application in case of limitation prescribed by any special or local law by operation of clauses (b) of sub-section (2) of section 29 of the Limitation Act. The provision of section 5 of the Limitation Act cannot, therefore, be invoked in condoning the delay in filing an appeal against the decision of an Election Tribunal in an election dispute. The Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 is a special law and this special law under sub-section (4) of section 29 has prescribed a special period of limitation different from the First Schedule of the Limitation Act for preferring an appeal. It, therefore, appears to me that in the face of the well-settled principle of law established by a long series of decisions as cited above, the learned District Judge acting as the Appellate Election Tribunal committed an error of law by applying section 5 of the Limitation Act for condoning the delay in filing the appeal being No.5 of 1989 before him against the order of the Election Tribunal in Election Case No.2 of 1988, and this has resulted in an error of decision occasioning a failure of justice.

<u>29. It now remains to be seen what is the period of limitation prescribed under sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983. Sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 lays down that "any person aggrieved by a decision of the Election Tribunal may, within thirty days of the  announcement of the decision, prefer an appeal to the District Judge "</u>

30. It appears that under sub-section (4) of section 29 of the above Ordinance the words "announcement of the decision" have been specifically used and such words as "the date of the judgment or order of the Election Tribunal," etc., have been deliberately avoided. It remains for this court to interpret the words "announcement of the decision."

31. It is true that the normal interpretation is that the date of the judgment or the order passed by the court is usually presumed to be the date of announcement of the decision, but, there may be extreme cases in which the judgment and order may be signed on a date but may not be announced immediately. There may also be more extreme instances, as has been alleged in the present case by the opposite party No. 1 in his petition for condonation of delay before the Appellate Election Tribunal, in which there may be an antedated judgment by the Election Tribunal. In such circumstances what should be accepted as the date of announcement of the decision in terms of sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983? In ouch extremes cases where the judgment is not announced on the date on which it is signed or in cases where the judgment is antedated and disclosed after the period of limitation, the person aggrieved by a decision of the Election Tribunal cannot have any remedy before the Appellate Election Tribunal if the date of the judgment is deemed to be the date of announcement thereof. Such cannot be the intention of the legislature in enacting sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983. It, therefore, appears to me that in extreme cases where the judgment or decision of an Election Tribunal is not announced according to law on the date on which the judgment or decision, as the case may be, is signed, the period of limitation should be determined with reference to the exact meaning of the word "announcement" occurring in sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 i.e. on the date on which the decision is notified to the party concerned according to law. It also appears to me that no other interpretation of the words "announcement of the decision" can be made for ends of justice.

32. Consequently, I am of the opinion that the starting point of limitation for an appeal under sub-section (4) of section 29 of the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 is the actual date of announcement of the judgment and decision.

33. In the light of the above findings and observations this revisional application will succeed with the direction to the Appellate Election Tribunal to ascertain as to when the decision of the Election Tribunal was actually announced. He should compute the period of limitation from the date of such announcement.

34. The result is that the revisional application succeeds. The Rule is made absolute.

<u>35. The impugned order dated 12.11.89 where-by the learned Appellate Election Tribunal admitted the Election appeal being Appeal No. 5 of 1989 is hereby set aside. The learned Appellate Election Tribunal will decide the application for condonation of delay by issuing a notice upon the parties concerned and then holding an enquiry as to on which date the Election Tribunal announced the decision in Election Tribunal Case No. 2 of 1988. If he finds that the petition of appeal was filed before him within 30 days from the date of the actual announcement of the decision of the Election Tribunal, Narayanganj, he shall admit the appeal and if he finds that the application was filed before him after the expiry of 30 days from the date of announcement of the decision of the Election Tribunal, the petition of appeal shall be dismissed as being barred by limitation.</u>

36. He shall dispose of the question of admission of the appeal in the light of the observations made above within one month from the date of receipt of this order.

37. The stay order granted by the. Appellate Election Tribunal on 12.11.89 is vacated.

There will be no order as to costs.

End.
