full_judgment:
1. This Rule is directed against Order No. 116 dated 21.4.73 passed by Mr. M.A. Rahman, Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 81 of 1968 recording abatement of the suit. 

2. The plaintiff-petitioner instituted the aforesaid suit for declaration and permanent injunction upon the averments that the petitioner as the mutwalli of two waqf estates created by his great grandfather late Chowdhury Raisuddin Ahmed Siddiky and his grand-father late Khan Bahadur Kasemuddin Ahmed Siddiky unsuccessfully challenged by Writ Petition No. 80 of 1957 the general Notification, Nos. 4836-L.R. and 4849-L.R. both dated 2.4.56 purporting to acquire en block with effect from 14.4.56 all the remaining rent-receiving interest in the District of Dhaka under section 3(1) and all khas lands under section 3(2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. Thereafter on 24.5.60 Ordinance No. IX of 1960 was promulgated amending the said Act by adding a new section l0A and on 7.2.62 Ordinance No.IV of 1962 was promulgated providing, inter alia, that the then Provincial Government having not exercised the right of possession in respect of waqf and debuttor interests after the aforesaid notification, the mutwalli or shebait shall continue and be deemed to have continued to manage such interests as the agent of the then Provincial Government till the last day of the agricultural year next following the date of publication of the notification under section 43(2) of the Act declaring that Compensation Assessment Roll in respect of such interest has been finally published. It is the plaintiffs contention that the Compensation Assessment Roll in respect of the two waqf estates in question have not been prepared in accordance with the terms of the said Act and the rules framed thereunder. The plaintiff has given particulars of non-compliance of the Act and the rules. He stated that he was still in undisturbed and unhampered possession of all the properties of the concerned waqf estates as mutwalli even after the aforesaid general notification by realising rents and tolls, except the forest lands described in schedule -III of the plaint. When the plaintiffs possession was threatened by the officers of the defendant No.1, the then Province of East Pakistan, the plaintiff again filed Writ Petition No.146 of 1964, but a Special Bench of the High Court of East Pakistan discharged the Rule on 7.4.65 by a majority decision holding that the plaintiffs waqf estates stood acquired under the notifications dated 2.4.56. The plaintiff preferred Civil Appeal No. 27-D of 1965 in the then Supreme Court of Pakistan and obtained an order of stay on 15.8.65. The appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan on 26.2.68 with the observation, inter alia, that if there be any defect in the proceedings which culminated in the publication of the Compensation Assessment Rolls, then it would still be open to the plaintiff-petitioner to agitate the matter in the proper forum. Upon these averments the plaintiffs prayer No.1 in the suit was as follows:- 

"(i) For a declaration that no valid Compensation Assessment Roll in respect of the properties in suit has been prepared and finally published within the meaning of section 43 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, and the plaintiffs right to possess and manage the said properties has not been affected by the publication of the alleged Compensation Assessment Roll as claimed by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2." 

3. The plaintiff-petitioner made some further averments in paragraphs 14-16 of the plaint. He averred that from a book written by Syed Qamrul Ahsan, an M.N.A. and Member of the Provincial Assembly in East Pakistan from 1954-58, one Syed Majid Baksh came to know that Mr. A.K. Fazlul Hoque the then Governor of East Pakistan did not at all sign the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance No. III of 1956 and on this ground the said Syed Majid Baksh filed a suit against the defendant No. 1. The plaintiff collected the judgments passed in the said suit and the appeal arising therefrom and also obtained certified copy of the High Court's order dated 19.5.65 passed in Second Appeal No. 445 of 1962 and came to know all about the case. The trial Court decreed the suit in favour of the said plaintiff Syed Majid Baksh and the Second Appeal of the Province of East Pakistan was dismissed for default by the High Court's order dated 19.3.65. 

4. The present plaintiff-petitioner, therefore, contended that East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance No. III of 1956 was not a valid piece of legislation but the plaintiffs Writ Petition No.98 of 1968 containing the aforesaid contention was rejected on 10.4.68 by a Division Bench of the High Court on the ground that it involved disputed questions of fact. As such, the plaintiff filed the suit also for a determination of the question as to whether the said Ordinance was a valid piece of legislation or not. These allegations are the basis of the plaintiffs second prayer in the suit which was as follows :- 

"(ii) For a further declaration that the plaintiff has the right to continue with the maintenance and management of the religious institution of waqf in respect of the properties described in the schedules below and that the defendants have no right to interfere with the plaintiffs said right of maintenance and management of the wakfs."

5. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2, i.e. the then Province of East Pakistan and the Deputy Commissioner of Dhaka entered appearance and contested the suit by filling a written statement. It is not necessary to go into the details of the written statement for purposes of this Rule. 

6. Thereafter the suit was heard on different dates and taking of evidence on both sides was completed. Only arguments could not be heard on both sides. The suit, therefore, remained pending till after liberation of the country. 

7. On 6.6.72 the Bangladesh(Legal Proceedings)(Second) Order, 1972, President's Order No. 69 of 1972, was promulgated. Read with the amendment thereof by President's Order No. 97 of 1972 dated 15.8.72, it provides as follows :- 

"4.(1) Subject to clause (2), any legal proceedings which are pending by or against the erstwhile Government of Pakistan or the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan in any Court or Tribunal or before any arbitrator, tax authority or other authority in Bangladesh shall be continued by or against the Government of Bangladesh and the government of Bangladesh shall be deemed to be substituted for the Government of Pakistan or, as the case may be, the Government of East Pakistan as a party to such proceedings. 

(2) The Government of Bangladesh may, at any time before the final hearing of any legal proceedings mentioned in clause (1) submit a written application to the Court, Tribunal, arbitrator, tax authority or other authority in or before which such legal proceedings are pending stating that the Government of Bangladesh shall not be a party to the proceedings and with effect from the date of submission of such application the Government of Bangladesh shall cease to be a party to such proceedings and, if such proceedings cannot continue in the absence of the Government of Bangladesh, the proceeding shall abate." 

8. On 3.8.82 the Bangladesh (Legal Proceedings) (Third) Order, 1972, President's Order No. 90 of 1972, was promulgated, section 2 whereof was as follows :- 

"2. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, on the commencement of this Order, all suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings pending or continuing or deemed to be pending or continuing in any Court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (E.B. Act No. XXVIII of 1951), or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 (E.B. Ord. No. III of 1956), or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act, or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate, and all orders, including orders of injunction and other interlocutory orders, passed in such suits, appeals, applications and other legal proceedings shall cease to have any effect and no court shall entertain), and no person shall bring any fresh suit,appeal, application or other legal proceeding's in which the legality or validity of any such law or acquisition is challenged or called in question." 

9. On 30.8.72 the learned Advocate for the defendant Nos. 1 and filed an application stating that under Article 4(2) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972 the Government of Bangladesh has got an option and right for not being a party to the above suit. The Government of Bangladesh, therefore, docs not like to be a party in the above suit. The suit cannot continue in the absence of the Government of Bangladesh as a party and, therefore, the suit abates. Memo No. 5591-Rev-XII/72 dated 22.8.72 signed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dhaka to the Special Government Pleader containing the aforesaid decision of the Government was also annexed with the application. 

10. Further, on 29.9.72 by another application the Special Government Pleader submitted that since in the suit in question the plaintiff has challenged the legality, validity and even the very existence of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance No. III of 1956, therefore, under Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 the suit has abated. 

11. By the impugned order dated 21.4.73 the learned Subordinate Judge disposed of the aforesaid two applications of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 in the following manner :- 

"It appears that in view of the above stated provisions of law the petitions of the plaintiffs party cannot be entertained. Therefore the prayer for amendment of the plaint impleading the Government of Bangladesh ipso facto stands added as a party in this suit (sic). The prayer for time is also rejected. Considering the provisions of law as referred to above, this suit does abate against the defendant." 

12. Thereafter the plaintiff-petitioner obtained this Rule against the aforesaid order of abatement. 

13. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits from a reading of the order of abatement that it is not clear as to under which provision of law the learned Sub-ordinate Judge has recorded the abatement of the suit. He has assailed the order of abatement both under President's Order No. 69 of 1972 and President's Order No. 90 of 1972. 

14. On President's Order No. 69 of 1972 Mr. Ahmed first submits that the suit was finally heard before the liberation of the country. Therefore, the Government of Bangladesh had missed the opportunity to opt out of the suit. 

15. This argument has no legs to stand. Whatever hearing took place before the liberation of Bangladesh was between the plaintiff-petitioner and the Province of East Pakistan. The Government of Bangladesh substituted itself as a party to the suit by a fiction of law under Article 4(1) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972, but that does not mean that the Government of Bangladesh became a successor of the Province of East Pakistan in terms of the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Government of Bangladesh acquired the right to have the suit heard de novo, because it was a new party and not a successor-defendant. Secondly, the final hearing was not over. Under Order XVIII, Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure the party who has the right to begin states his case and produces his evidence and the other party then states his case and produces his evidence. The other party may then address the Court generally on the whole case. The party beginning may then reply generally on the whole case. This right of the parties to address the Court generally on the whole case is what is known in common parlance as argument. I have gone through' the order sheet of the suit and I find that both the sides wanted to exercise their right of addressing the Court generally on the whole case and, therefore, it cannot be said that the "final hearing" was over in the suit. The words "final hearing" are nowhere to be found in the Code of Civil Procedure, but when the Legislature chooses to use an uncommon word with regard to civil proceedings it should be interpreted so as to bring it in harmony with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. I do not find any justification for holding that the "final hearing" means the stage when evidence is led by the parties. On the contrary, the words "final hearing" in the context of the Code of Civil Procedure embrace the entire period during which evidence is given and the arguments are concluded. 

16. Mr. Ahmed next submits that with the subsequent introduction of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 the Government of Bangladesh lost the option to opt out of the suit under President's Order No. 69 of 1972, because, in any view of the matter, a later law abrogates earlier laws clearly inconsistent with it. 

17. I find that Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 starts with a non-obstante clause, namely, "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". President's Order No. 69 of 1972 came into force on 16.6.72 and President's Order No. 90 of 1972 came into force 003.8.72 . It seems to be very clear that Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 also refers to Article 4(1) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972 by mentioning suits etc. "deemed to be pending or continuing in any Court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh". Needless to say, suits etc. were "deemed to be pending or continuing in any Court against the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh" only by virtue of Article 4 (1) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972. Therefore, Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 obviously makes a new provision of abatement in regard to some particular suits. It is well-established that when a non-obstante clause is used it has first to be ascertained what the enacting part of the section provides on a fair construction of words used according to their natural and ordinary meaning and the non obstante clause is to be understood as operating to set aside as no longer valid anything contained in relevant existing law which is inconsistent with the new enactment. The plain meaning of Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 is that suits in which the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act or to the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof is challenged or called in question shall abate. Suits answering this description, therefore, fall under a second category of automatic abatement and it is neither necessary for or open to the Government to prefer an application under Article 4(2) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972 to opt out of suits of such nature. President's Order No. 69 of 1972 and President's Order No. 90 of 1972 are mutually exclusive in respect of suits of the above description. 

18. Therefore, it seems to me to be quite reasonable to take the view that the Government's application under Article 4(2) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972 was not maintainable, because in any view of the matter the later law (president's Order No. 90 of 1972) has abrogated the earlier law (President's Order No. 69 of 1972) in so far as suits of the category mentioned in Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 are concerned, because the provisions' of the two Acts with regard to such suits are mutually inconsistent. I am of the opinion that both the two remedies in respect of such suits are not available to the Government. Suits answering the description of Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 can abate only because of the provisions of the said Article. 

19. I, therefore, hold that application of the Government under Article 4(2) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972 was not maintainable. 

20. In respect of the application under President's Order No. 90 of 1972, it is patently obvious that the plaintiff in paragraphs 14-16 of the plaint has categorically challenged the very existence, validity and legality of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy(Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 and his prayer (ii) inevitably follows from that challenge. It is clear that under Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 the averments of the petitioner in paragraphs 14-16 of th6 plaint and his. prayer No. (ii) in the plaint are hit by the mischief of the said Article and, therefore, the suit must abate in so far as those averments and the said prayer are concerned.

21. But Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed has submitted that the suit can legitimately be severed, in that the plaintiff has neither challenged the legality and validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 or of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 or of any other law making any amendment in the said Act, or of the acquisition of any property made under any provision thereof, when the plaintiff-petitioner averred that the Compensation Assessment Roll was not prepared in terms of the Act and the rules and that he is entitled, therefore, to possess and manage the waqf properties till the Compensation Assessment Roll is validly prepared, because that is a right given to him under section 10A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. 

22. The substance of Mr. Ahmed's contention is that the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 having been amended by incorporation of a new section 10A by Ordinance No. IX of 1960, whereby possession of a waqf property which has been acquired under section 3(1) and 3(2) of the Act by its mutwali has been protected till after the final publication of the Compensation Assessment Roll, the plaintiff-petitioner has a right under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act itself to agitate that there has not been a valid Compensation Assessment Roll lawfully prepared and that there has not been a lawful final publication thereof within the meaning of section 42. Therefore, any notification purported to be issued under sub-section (2) of section 43 declaring such publication of the Compensation Assessment Roll is a nullity and of no legal effect. The Government does not acquire in that view of the matter any right to take over possession of the waqf property from the mutwalli who is deemed to be in possession of the waqf properties as an agent of the Government. Mr. Ahmed contends that in order to en-force the mutwalli's right of existing possession as against the Government in terms of section 10A of the Act, he need not challenge the legality or validity of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 or the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 or the acquisition of the aforesaid property under any provision thereof. Therefore, he submits that the question of abatement of the suit under the provision of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 does not arise so far as the first prayer for decree, as stated in the plaint, is concerned.

23. In reply to this submission of Mr. Ahmed, Mr. Mashuk Hossain Ahmed, the learned Assistant Attorney General has cited the case of People's Re-public. of Bangladesh. Vs. Sri Sri Madan Gopal Jew Bigraha and others, 33 DLR (AD) 13, in which, in a suit for declaration of title and for permanent injunction along with the prayers that the suit property had not been acquired and the notification dated 2.4.56 under section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act are null and void, a further declaration was also sought for, namely, that no compensation assessment roll with regard to the plaintiff debuttor estate have been prepared or published in terms of the Act or rules thereunder. The Appellate Division has held that the directive in the law is clear. On the coming into operation of President's Order No. 90 of 1972 notwithstanding any other earlier view of law on the subject, a pending proceeding or a proceeding which is sought to be instituted challenging or calling in question the acquisition of any property under any of the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act shall abate and no proceedings shall be instituted in any Court. The Appellate Division further held in the facts and circumstances of the said suit that the plaintiff-respondent in clear language challenged the notification of 2nd April, 1956 as null and void and claimed immunity of the debuttor estate from acquisition. The Appellate Division further held that all other prayers are consequential prayers following therefrom. The plaint as it stands cannot but abate being hit by President's Order No. 90 of 1972. 

24. Mr. Mashuk Hossain Ahmed, the learned Assistant Attorney General submits that in the present suit the plaintiffs main prayer is prayer No; (ii), but prayer No. (i) is not the main prayer. It ancillary or consequential or subsidiary to the main prayer No. (ii). As such, Mr. Mashuk Hossain Ahmed submits that the whole suit abates and the order of the learned Subordinate Judge cannot be taken exception to. 

25. I have carefully considered the decision reported in 33 DLR (AD) 13 and have compared the facts of the case with the present case. In the aforecited case the plaintiff-respondent very clearly wanted to challenge the very acquisition of the debuttor property by notices of wholesale acquisition. This challenge came within the mischief of Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972. The further prayer for a declaration that no Compensation Assessment Roll with regard to the plaintiff debuttor estate have been prepared or published in terms of the Act and rules thereunder does appear to be a consequential prayer flowing from the main prayer, because there is no averment and no prayer that the plaintiff-respondent wants to protect his possession till the Compensation Assessment Roll is lawfully prepared and published. In the present suit, however, the plaintiff has candidly stated that all his efforts to declare the general notification of wholesale acquisition to be null and void has ended in failure, but he now wants to protect his possession under the provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 itself till the Compensation Assessment Roll is lawfully prepared and published. Rather it appears to, me that he challenges the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956 in a speculative manner, devised as an after-thought, formulated upon a chance information. This challenge does not appear to me to be the main burden of the plaintiffs suit. The suit can well proceed without this challenge. Therefore, I am of the opinion that the whole suit does not abate. It is only the plaintiffs averments in paragraphs 14-16 of the plaint and his prayer No. (ii) which abate in the facts, and circumstances of the case. 

26. Mr. Mashuk Hossain Ahmed next submits that the Government of Bangladesh may in any case opt out of the remaining portion of the suit under Article 4(2) of the President's Order No. 69 of 1972 and, therefore, this Court may not make an order which will be rendered infructuous. 

 27. I really do not know how the Government will view .its participation in the remaining portion of the suit and as to whether the Government will at all exercise its option under Article 4(2) of President's Order No. 69 of 1972. When that option is exercised it will be for the parties to take such steps as they are advised. 

28. In the result, the Rule is partially made absolute without, however, any order as to costs. The impugned order in so far as recording abatement of the whole suit is set aside and it is ordered that only paragraphs 14-16 of the plaint and the prayer No. (ii) of the plaint stand abated under Article 2 of President's Order No. 90 of 1972, but the rest of the suit survives and may be proceeded with in accordance with law. 

End.

 Vs. 
Bangladesh through the Secretary, Ministry of Agriculture and others ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J.: This Rule Nisi obtained under Article 102 of the Constitution calls upon the respondents to show cause as to why a direction should not be issued upon them to comply with the order dated 3.11.85 passed by the Administrative Tribunal, Dhaka in Case No. 36 of 1985.

2. The petitioner is a Subject Matter Officer, Upazila Krishi Office, Habiganj in the Ministry of Agriculture, Government of Bangladesh in the New National Scale of Pay of Tk. 750-1470/-. He filed an application before the Administrative Tribunal under section 4 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 (Act No. VII of 1981) being Case No. 36 of 1985, challenging Notification dated 5.2.85 issued under the signature of respondent No.2, the Joint Secretary (Extension and Research), Ministry of Agriculture, promoting 170 officers of the petitioner's rank to posts in the New National Scale of Pay of Tk. 1400~2225/-without first preparing any Gradation List on the basis of inter se seniority and totally ignoring the petitioner's seniority over all such promotes except No. 14.

3. The Government of Bangladesh contested the case by filing a written statement.

4. After hearing the parties and considering the evidence and records of the case the Administrative Tribunal passed the following order on 3.11.85 :-

"So, in view of the Government commitment that the Gradation List is going to be published within 2 months and also of the fact that sufficient posts are still vacant to which incumbents senior to the O.Ps. may be promoted with retrospective effect, it would I think not be in the interest of justice and administration to set aside the order at the moment, even though on a fair consideration the seniors should not be made to wait and juniors promoted on the plea of want of Gradation List

From the above facts and circumstances of the case I am inclined to hold that the impugned order dated 5.2.85 of promotion of O.Ps. 3 to 172 is not liable to be. set aside but that the applicant is entitled to get a direction upon the O.Ps. 1 and 2 to finalize without delay the seniority list of the officers of his cadre. In the result the applicant succeeds in part Accordingly the case is allowed on contest but without cost. O.P. Nos. 1 and 2 are directed to finalise and publish the seniority list of the officers of the applicant's cadre without delay."

5. The opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 in the said Case No. 36 of 1985 are respondent Nos. 1 and 2 in this writ petition. These respondents have not finalised and published up to this day the seniority list of the officers of the petitioner's cadre, although the Administrative Tribunal directed them to do so "without delay" as far back as on 3.11.85.

6. The petitioner thereafter obtained the present Rule Nisi in the aforesaid term on 10.2.86.

7. An affidavit-in-opposition has been filed on behalf of the respondent No.1 in which practically the judgment of the Administrative Tribunal has been dissented from by reiterating the old contentions made earlier before the Administrative Tribunal. It is on record, however, that the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 did not prefer any appeal from the decision of the Administrative Tribunal before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal constituted under section 5 of Act No. VII of 1981.

8. In order to appreciate the point involved in this Rule, it is necessary to recount briefly the constitutional and legal position with regard to administrative tribunals.

9. Article 117 of our Constitution, contained in Part VI, Chapter III deals with Administrative Tribunals. Article 117 is as follows:-

"117.( 1) Notwithstanding anything herein before contained, Parliament may by law establish one or more administrative tribunals to exercise jurisdiction in respect of matters relating to or arising out of-

(a) the terms and conditions of persons in the service of the Republic, including the matters provided for in Part IX and the award of penalties or punishments;

(b) the acquisition, administration, management and disposal of any property vested in or managed by the Government by or under any law, including the operation and management of, and service in any nationalized enterprise or statutory public authority;

(c) any law to which clause (3) of Article 102 applies.

(2) Where any administrative tribunal is established under this article, no Court shall entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunals: Provided that Parliament may, by law, provide for appeals from, or the review of, decisions of any such tribunal."

<u>10. Sub-article (2) of Article 117 is relevant for purposes of exercise of jurisdiction by this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution, because the Constitution uses the word "Court" to mean "any Court of law including Supreme Court." (Article 152(1). The plain meaning of Sub-article (2) of Article 117 is that this Court is constitutionally debarred from exercising any jurisdiction over any matter covered by the jurisdiction of administrative tribunals when any such tribunal is established under Article 117.</u>

<u>11. The Parliament enacted the Administrate : Tribunals Act, 1980 (Act No. VII of 1981) precisely and expressly under Article 117 of the Constitution and it came into effect on 1.2.82 by Notification No. S.R.O.30-L/82/J-IV/lT-3/81 dated 12.1.02, published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary on 16.1.82. By section 4 of the Act, an Administrative Tribunal was given the exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine applications made by any person in the service of the Republic in respect of the terms and conditions of his service including pension rights, or in respect of any action taken in relation to him as a person in the service of the Republic. Pro- vision was also made for the establishment of an Administrative Appellate Tribunal (section 5) to hear and determine appeals "from any order or decision" of an Administrative Tribunal (section 6). For the purposes of hearing an application or appeal, a Tribunal was given all the powers of civil Court, while trying a suit under the Code of Civil Procedure, in respect of some specified matters (section 7) and the Tribunal's decisions and orders were given a binding effect in the following terms in section 8 :-</u>

<u>"8. Binding effect of Tribunal's decisions and orders. - (1) All decisions and orders of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal shall be binding upon the Administrative Tribunals and the parties concerned.</u>

<u>(2) All decisions and orders of an Administrative Tribunal shall, subject to the decisions and orders of Administrative Appellate Tribunal, be binding on the parties concerned."</u>

12. Section 10 provides that subject to this Act, no proceedings, order or decision of a Tribunal shall be liable to be challenged, reviewed, quashed or called in question in any Court. Section 11 provides that the provisions of this Act shall have effect not- withstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. Section 12 gives the Government the power to make rules for carrying out the purposes of this Act. In exercise of the powers under Section 12, the Government has in fact made the Administrative Tribunals Rules, 1982, by Notification No. S.R.O.92-L/82-JIV /IT -3/81 dated 12.3.82, which have been published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary on 12.3.82. Rule 7 of the Rules pro- vides as follows:-

"7. Execution of decisions and orders of a Tribunal. - A Tribunal shall, for the purpose of execution of its decisions and orders, follow, as far as practicable, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (IV of 1908), relating to the execution of a decree."

13. A question has arisen in the past, as it has arisen in the present Rule, as to what a person in the service of the Republic shall do if the Government- respondent simply ignores or fails to implement the decisions and orders of the Administrative Tribunal. Here is a case where the Administrative Tribunal has directed the Government-respondent to prepare a Gradation List "without delay." The order was passed as far back as on 3.1l.85. Even today, the Government- respondents have not complied with this direction.

14. Article 102(2)(a)(i) of our Constitution empowers the High Court Division, if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law, to make an order on the application of any per- son aggrieved, inter alia "to do that which he is re- quired by law to do." Persons in the service of the Republic who have had their successful applications before the Administrative Tribunal rendered nugatory and frustrating by the continued inaction, silence and even tacit refusal by the judgment-debtor Government-respondents have found their refuge in Article 102(2)(a)(i) of the Constitution and have preferred writ petitions with the object of getting a direction from this Court to do that which the Government- respondent is required by law to do, namely, to implement the decision of the Administrative Tribunal, which is "binding on the parties."

15. Inevitably, the Government-respondents have come up with the preliminary objection, as Mr. Delwar Hossain, learned Assistant Attorney-General has unfailingly done in this Rule as well, that the application itself is not maintainable, because Rule 7 of the Rules (fully quoted earlier) provides an equally efficacious remedy and, as a corollary, it follows that when a remedy is provided in Rule 7, the Supreme Court is barred under sub-article (2) of Article 117 of the Constitution from entertaining any matter relating to the execution of the decision and order of the Administrative Tribunal because the Administrative Tribunal has to take its own decisions under Rule 7 with regard to the execution of its own decisions and orders.

16. The argument of Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the petitioner, follows the language of Article 102(2)(a)(i) of the Constitution, resting with the submission that this remedy remains the only available remedy for a frustrated person in the service of the Republic.

17. Section 12, the rule-making power, of the Act is relevant for our purpose, especially section 12(2)(f), which may be quoted as hereunder

"12. Power to make rules-t l) The Government may, by notification in the official Gazette make rules for carrying out the purposes of this Act. (2) In particular, and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power, such power may provide for all or any of the following matters, namely:- (f) execution of decisions and orders of Tribunal ;

18. We are therefore satisfied that Rule 7 of the Rules (fully quoted earlier) has been framed in full conformity with the powers given to the Government.

<u>19. The petitioner has not explained why he did not file an application before the Administrative Tribunal for execution of the Tribunal's decision and order dated 3.11.85 under Rule 7 of the Rules.</u>

<u>20. The Constitution, as we have seen, has de- signed the Administrative Tribunal as an exclusive forum. Not to speak of the ordinary Courts, even the Supreme Court is debarred under Article 117(2) of the Constitution to "entertain any proceedings or make any order in respect of any matter falling with- in the jurisdiction of such tribunal."</u>

21. How an Administrative Tribunal will execute its own decisions and orders, is very much a matter within the exclusive and unencroachable jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal itself. It is the Administrative Tribunal which is the sole arbiter of the method and procedure with regard to the execution of its own decisions and orders. Rule 7 enjoins upon the Tribunal to-follow. as far as practicable, the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, relating to the-execution of a decree. A decision and order directing payment of money to an applicant may thus be enforced by following the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure relating to the execution of a decree. But the rule-making authority was fully aware that there may be a variety of decisions and orders of the Tribunal which may not by capable of being enforced by following the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure relating to execution of decree. Rule 7 docs not say that the Tribunal is barred from following any other procedure. It will follow the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure relating to the execution of a decree "as far as practicable", but as and when it is not practicable to do so, the Tribunal is not powerless. It will not be a lame duck. Its decisions and orders are not meant to be meaningless decorative art pieces. Section 8 of the Act says that its decisions and orders are "binding on the parties". This is not a mere pious legislative wish. The Administrative Tribunal has the fullest jurisdiction to devise its own method and procedure to execute its own decisions and orders, when the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure cannot be followed. In the present case, for example, it can pass an order in execution (based upon the judgment) giving the respondents a certain period within which to prepare the Gradation List and submit the same to the Tribunal. In this way, no decision or order of the Tribunal will remain inexecutable. The Administrative Tribunal is functioning under a Constitutional mandate and the legislation has armed it to the teeth to be an effective body. This Court, exercising its jurisdiction under Article 102, will not tell the Tribunal in each case whether the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable or not. The Tribunal will take that decision itself. If it is wrong in its decision, the Administrative Appellate Tribunal will correct it, for an appeal lies against "any order or decision of an Administrative Tribunal." All questions and problems relating to execution will have to be answered and resolved by the Administrative Tribunal or the Administrative Appellate Tribunal within the periphery of the Act and the Rules.

<u>22. After exhausting the procedure laid down in Rule 7 the aggrieved party has, it appears, a further remedy before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, for it has been provided in the Administrative Tribunals (Amendment) Act, 1988, enacted on' 24.5.88; that the Administrative Appellate Tribunal shall have the power to punish for contempt of itself and the Administrative Tribunal. The new section 10A inserted by the said amending Act is as follows:-</u>

<u>"10A. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal shall have power to punish for contempt’s of its authority or that of any Administrative Tribunal, as if it were the High Court Division of the Supreme Court. (2) No appeal shall lie from any decision of the Administrative Appellate Tribunal under sub-section (I), but the Tribunal may review any such decisions."</u>

<u>23. Mr. Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed submits that the petitioner obtained the Rule Nisi on 10.2.86. Section 10A of the Act was introduced at a much later date in 1988. That may be so, but the present Rule Nisi will be disposed of in the light of the law as it stands today, and not in the light of the law as it existed on the date of issuance of the Rule Nisi. As of today the AdministrativeTribunals Act, 1980 is a self-contained and composite legislation. Both the execution of the decisions and orders of a Tribunal and violation thereof are well taken care of by the legislation. It does not need the additional umbrella of this Court's jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution for implementation of the decisions and orders of the Administrative Tribunal.</u>

24. Besides, if, in spite of the existence of Rule 7 and section 10A of the Act, it is made a practice to additionally invoke the jurisdiction of this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution for purposes of implementing a decision and order ofthe Administrative Tribunal, then the affected parties will themselves be the losers. Respondents against whom an adverse order has been passed by the Administrative Tribunal will not care to execute the Tribunal's decisions and orders, until and unless they get an additional Rule Nisi from this Court under Article 102 of the Constitution. They will wait with impunity till such a Rule Nisi is received and such a practice will render the Administrative Tribunal into a most ineffective and useless body. We are firmly of the opinion that the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1980 ought to be interpreted in such a manner that ) consistent with the constitutional provision and legislative intent it may provide for a complete and self- sufficient remedy to the affected parties.

25. For the above reasons we do not think that the petitioner can avail of the remedy provided under Article 102 of the Constitution. If not otherwise barred he can still go to the Administrative Tribunal for the execution of its own decision and order dated 3.11.85 under Rule 7. The Administrative Tribunal is quite competent to come to a decision how it will implement its own decision and order. Failing this remedy the petitioner has been given a further remedy under section 10A of the Act. His interests being well-protected by legislation the present application is not maintainable.

26. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

27. Let a copy of this judgment be forwarded to the Ministry of Law and Justice at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Sultan Hossain Khan, J: The plaintiff has filed a suit in Admiralty jurisdiction for realisation of Tk. 17,87,363.18 against the principal defendants for loss and damage to the cargo owing to short delivery and damage caused to it.

2. The plaintiff has alleged that it delivered to and shipped on board the vessel MV VICEROY belonging to defendant No. 1 a consignment of 399 metric tons skimmed milk powder under 8 Bills of Lading for carriage and delivery to the plaintiff at Chittagong. It has been alleged that the consignment was partly damaged and a part was not delivered to the plaintiff due to negligence, misconduct and lack of duty on the part of the Master, Officers and crews of the said, vessel and as a result the plaintiff has suffered loss to the tune of Tk. 17,87,363.18 as has been detailed item wise in the plaint. Since the plaintiff allegedly has suffered loss due to short delivery and damage of the goods on account of negligence, fault and misconduct of the defendant No. 1, the master, officers and crews of the vessel, he is entitled to realise the claim from the principal defendant and accordingly, he has instituted the suit in the Admiralty jurisdiction of this Court for realisation of the aforesaid amount, He also has filed an application for arrest/attachment of ship "MY CHERRY ORIENT", a sea going vessel allegedly owned by defendant No. 1 which was berthed at Chittagong port: the plaintiff has alleged that if the aforesaid sister ship MV CHERRY ORIENT is not arrested or attached and it leaves the port of Chittagong the plaintiff would have nothing within the jurisdiction of this Court to recover the loss suffered by him. Except the ship MV CHERRY ORIENT, the defendant No. 1 has no other property in Bangladesh from which the claim of the plaintiff could be satisfied. On that application this Court on 28-5-85 passed an order of attachment/ arrest of the aforesaid ship MV CHERRY ORIENT then lying in the port of Chittagong. The Court also ordered that the ship might be released on furnishing a bank guarantee to the tune of Tk. 15,00,000.

3. The defendant Nos. 2 and 3 i. e. the ship and the Master of the ship appeared and they furnished a Bank guarantee for Tk. 15,00,000 upon which the ship has been released from attachment/arrest. The said defendants however, have filed an application for vacating the order of arrest/attachment of the ship and a written objection against the application filed by the plaintiff praying for attachment/ arrest of the ship.

4. The defendants in their objection have alleged that the suit and the application for arrest of MV CHERRY ORIENT is not maintainable in the Admiralty jurisdiction of this Court. They have alleged that the cause of action of the suit relating to the allegation of damage and loss of the cargo admittedly being against the vessel MV VICEROY and not against MV CHERRY ORIENT the latter ship cannot be arrested/attached or proceeded against in an action in rem. They have denied that MV CHERRY ORIENT was owned by the defendant No. 1 or the owner of MV VICEROY; it could not be arrested because it was not concerned in the cause of action. The defendants have alleged that under the Court of Admiralty Act, 1861 in order to render the ship MY CHERRY ORIENT to be arrested or detained or to be proceeded against in an action in rem the said MV CHERRY ORIENT itself must be instrumental in giving rise to the cause of action if any, and that the alleged remedy of the plaintiff cannot be enforced against any other ship other than that in which the goods were carried to Bangladesh, and as such admiralty action in rem against vessel MY CHERRY ORIENT is not maintainable in law and the order of arrest is liable to be vacated and the Bank Guarantee furnished may be returned.

5. As regards the ownership of the vessel MV CHERRY ORIENT it has been alleged that it is owned by M/s. Bunga Shipping Co. Pte Ltd. Singapore, whereas the vessel . MV VICEROY is owned by M/s Container Feeders Singapore Pte Ltd. Singapore. The plaintiff in their affidavit-in-reply has asserted that both the ships are owned by M/s LS Line (Member of Lian Soon Group of Companies). The plaintiff has also alleged that the documents filed by it would show that MY CHERRY ORIENT is controlled, managed, and possessed by the defendant No. 1 and that it is interested in the ship and, as such, the said arrest of MV CHERRY ORIENT though it has not carried the consignment of the plaintiff but it being a property over which the defendant No 1 is interested and exercised full control and management and it possessed the ship, its arrest has been made legally in exercise of the admiralty jurisdiction of this Court. As regards the questions whether both the ships belonged to the defendant No. 1 or the same owner or that the defendant No. 1 exercises full control and management over MV CHERRY ORIENT these need not be answered at this stage without going into full evidence which may be led by the parties to substantiate their respective case in this regard. Moreover, for the reasons I am proceeding to give on a main question, it need not be answered.

6. Now the principal question in this application is, assuming that both the ships are owned by defendant No. 1, whether this Court in Admiralty jurisdiction can arrest/attach a ship within the tidal waters of Bangladesh for assuring satisfaction of a claim of the plaintiff in a suit though it was not concerned with cause of action, or whether the ship MV CHERRY ORIENT" could be the 'res' connected with the cause of action Admittedly MV VICEROY a sea-going vessel carried the consignment of the plaintiff from Singapore to Chittagong. Now whether a remedy in rem can be exercised in Admiralty jurisdiction of this Court against MV CHERRY ORIENT which is unconnected with the cause of action. Assuming that MV CHERRY ORIENT is owned by defendant No. I whether any action in rem can be directed against any property of the said defendant No. 1 other than that in respect of which cause of action has arisen.

7. Mr Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff has made elaborate submissions to press his contentions that under the Admiralty jurisdiction of this court a suit both in personam as well as in rem against a ship or its owner, carrier and agent of the ship or against any person who is interested and exercises control, management over the ship is maintainable and that in an action in Admiralty jurisdiction any property of the defendant or a sister ship owned by the defendant within the jurisdiction of the court can be arrested or detained. He has submitted that this court having derived its Admiralty jurisdiction from the practice and procedure of High our of Admiralty of England and the English Statutes, namely, the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, 1890 and the amendments thereof as made by British Parliament, the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 or at least its principles as regards the Jurisdiction of the High Court of Admiralty of England as has been vested by the said Act can be applied while exercising jurisdiction of this Court of Admiralty. According to him even before the enactment of Administration of Justice Act, 1956 the High Court of Admiralty in England exercised jurisdiction over the properties and ships of the owner which was not connected with the cause of action. In support of his contention that a sister ship can be arrested in an action in rem or in personam, he has referred to the passage in Note Nos. 88 and 90 at pages 48 and 49 of Halsbury's Laws of England, Volume, I (Third Edition) and the observations made in AIR 1437 Calcutta 122 (123). The learned Advocate has also referred to the observations made by the Hon'ble Appellate Division of this Court in the decision reported in 34 DLR (AD) 110 (paras 9-10). According to the learned Advocate even before the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 High Court of Admiralty of England ordered arrest/detention of any property belonging to any defendant within the tidal waters of England when the defendant failed to appear or the offending ship could not be arrested.

8. The contention that any ship of the defendant or a sister ship owned by the defendant which was not concerned in the cause of action can be arrested is possibly founded on some observations made in the case of Henrich Biorn (1885) (5 Aspinall's Maritime Law Cases 391). In that case the court of appeal of England has said with regard to a procedure in rem:

"The arrest need not be of the ship in question, but may be of any property of the defendant within the realm". It will be appropriate to mention, this view has been disapproved by the same court of appeal after 50 years in the famous case of 'Beldis' reported in 18 Aspinall's Maritime Law Cases 598. I shall refer to the judgment of the case of Beldis in detail when I proceed to deal with the question thoroughly.

<u>9. At the outset it should be stated that this Court in exercising Admiralty Jurisdiction has derived its jurisdiction from the Admiralty Court Act, 1861, Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, 1890 and Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India). 1891. It is not disputed that this Court would exercise the same jurisdiction after the enactments of the said Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, (India) 1891 as the High Court of Admiralty of England exercised in 1890 under Admiralty Court Act of 1861. In England originally a suit in a Court of Admiralty and the jurisdiction of the Court was based on practice and the judgments of the Judges. But after the enactments of laws governing Admiralty jurisdiction since 1840, i.e. with the passing of Admiralty Court Act, 1840 the field of jurisdiction was defined. Thereafter with the passing of Admiralty Court Act, 1861 the Jurisdiction of the High Court of Admiralty in England appears to be based more on statute than on practice. These enactments of the statutes in England was possibly due to conflict of jurisdiction between the country Courts and the Court of Amorally. However by virtue of the provision of section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act. 1861 the jurisdiction of High Court of the England was statutorily assigned to that Court over any claim of account of damage done to the goods by negligence or misconduct or for breach of any contract on the part of the owners, master, crews, etc. of the ship. Section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 was, however, repealed by section 21 of the Administration of Justice Act, 1920 which was again repealed by section 226 of the Supreme Court of Judicature Act, 1925. Thereafter by section 49 of the Admiralty Jurisdiction Act, 1956, section 226 of 1925 Act was repealed. It is not disputed that by section 3 of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court in England was enlarged empowering the High Court of Admiralty of England to arrest any ship of the defendant in an action before it although that ship was not concerned in the cause of action. Before passing of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 the Court of Admiralty in England, however, did not exercise in any action in rem by arresting of a ship of the defendant other than that which was not involved or connected in the cause of action.</u>

<u>10. The practice of the High Court of England to arrest the defendant or any property of the defendant within the realm fell in disuse definitely after the passing of Administration of Justice Act, 1840 and the same practice as will appear from the Halsbury's Laws of England, Third Edition, Note No. 89, became obsolete and the Admiralty Court never arrested the property which was not the subject matter of the dispute for the purpose of enforcement of the judgment against the property so arrested. In the case of Beldis reported in 18 Aspinall's Maritime Law Cases, the court of appeal has noticed that for the last 100 years Admiralty Court of England never exercised jurisdiction in an action in rem by arresting any other ship than the one to which 'the cause of action related. Their Lordships of the Court of Appeal in this connection has observed;</u>

<u>"The complete absence of any reported case in the last 100 years, in which the present attempt to arrest a ship or property unconnected with the cause of action has ever been made before, is indeed, of itself almost conclusive that the procedure in rem was not regarded in the Admiralty Court as extending to such other ships or property and from this fact, too, I draw the inference that it had ceased to be permissible."</u>

<u>11. As I have referred to above excepting the case of Hainrich Biorn which has been held by their Lordships in the case of Beldis to be erroneous, there is no case in the English jurisdiction for the last 100 years to support the view that a ship which was not concerned with the cause of action can be arrested because it was owned by the defendant. In this connection it would be appropriate to refer to a passage from Carver's Carriage by Sea, 12th Edition (1971) (Volume-2) in Note 1390 page 1176 dealing on the question whether remedy in rem can be exercised against property unconnected with cause of action. Carver quoting .the aforesaid decision in the case of Beldis says as follows:</u>

<u>"Historically the jurisdiction of the Admiralty Court was originally exercised by employing either of two methods of procedure for bringing the defendant before the Court, (1) the arrest of his person, (2) the seizure of his goods which might be goods other than the goods or ship concerned in the particular cause of action. But both methods had fallen into disuse before the beginning of the nineteenth century. Probably as it result of the incessant war of jurisdiction waged by the common law courts on the Admiralty Court in the sixteenth and seventeenth century."</u>

12. The Beldis made it clear that (subject now to section 3(4)(b) of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 as regards ships) an action in rem can be brought only against the actual ship or other property which is the rem in respect of or out of which the cause of action arises procedure in rem either in the High Court or in the county court does not generally permit the arrest of a ship or other property of the defendant unconnected with the cause of action."

<u>13. Admittedly after the passing of Administration of justice Act, 1956 by English Parliament, by virtue of section 3(4) of the Act, the Court of Admiralty of England rem exercise admiralty jurisdiction in an action in rem by arresting any vessel or property of the defendant whether or not that was concerned in the cause of action. But a Court of Admiralty in Bangladesh in my opinion cannot by virtue of section 3(4) of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 of England in an action in rem or in personam arrest any vessel or property not concerned in the cause of action on basis of the aforesaid English enactment.</u>

14. Mr Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff has submitted that though the Administration of Justice Act, 19515 is not a law of Bangladesh but since the Admiralty Court of Bangladesh has been exercising the jurisdiction on basis of English laws beginning from the Admiralty Court Act of 1861, though the provision of that Act which was the foundation of the jurisdiction of Admiralty Court of Bangladesh had been repealed and never enacted in Bangladesh and Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, 1890 of British Parliament which is not a law of Bangladesh, this Court similarly can exercise jurisdiction on the basis of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 by arresting the ship of the defendant though it was not concerned with the cause of action.

In support of his contention be has referred to the decisions reported in 20 DLR 25 and 2 All ER 274 (277). I am unable to agree with the learned Advocate' "for 'the plaintiff that this court can exercise jurisdiction on the principle of the aforesaid English' Act 'of 1956 on the ground that this Court on the basis of laws of British Parliament' and the repealed section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861 had been exercising admiralty jurisdiction. The learned Advocate in this connection has referred to the observations of the Hon'ble Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh reported in 34 DLR (AD) 110 (114) wherein the Hon'ble Judges have observed thus:

"Thus the jurisdiction was enlarged and all that is required is that the claim must arise out of an agreement of carriage of goods, it is evident there-has been a sea change in the law since 1861. In 1861 Act the words damage done to the goods occupied a central place and the words 'breach of duty' or 'breach of contract' were related to the goods carried into any port in England or Wales but in 1956 Act jurisdiction was conferred to hear and determine any claim arising out of any agreement relating to the carriage of goods in ship".

15. This observation appears to me that the Appellate Division has noticed with reference to the facts of that case the change of Admiralty law in England. In that decision I do not find anything to show that the Appellate Division has taken a view that the Admiralty Court in Bangladesh can exercise the same jurisdiction as has been extended or conferred upon the High Court of Admiralty in England by the aforesaid English Act of 1956.

<u>16. Be that as it may, as regards the submission of the learned Advocate that the principles of the Administration of Justice Act, 1956 extending jurisdiction of the High Court of Admiralty of England can be followed by this Court, it appears to me that by virtue of Colonial Court of Admiralty Act (India) 1891, the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has been vested with the same powers as were exercised by the High Court of Admiralty of England. The High Court Division of this Court exercises the same jurisdiction as was conferred upon the High Court of England or the High Court of Admiralty of England by virtue of the provisions of section 2(2) of the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890. The jurisdiction under section 6 of Admiralty Court Act, 1861 of this High Court Division is being exercised by virtue of the provisions of Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, 1890 and Colonial Court of Admiralty (India) Act, 1891.</u>

<u>17. It will appear that this court exercises admiralty jurisdiction by virtue of specific legislation of Imperial Parliament and the Indian Legislation Council; the High Court of Bengal or the High Court of East Pakistan or the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has never exercised Admiralty jurisdiction on the basis of practices or the uncodified laws upon which the Court of Admiralty of England exercised its jurisdiction before the law relating to Admiralty jurisdiction of England were defined and extended by Administration of Justice Act, 1840. Following of practices and unmodified laws by the Admiralty Court in England was discontinued long before the advent of the nineteenth century. The Admiralty Court of England exercises jurisdiction on the basis of statute laws. This Court similarly exercises jurisdiction as has been given to it under section 6 of the Act of 1861 by virtue of the provision of section 2(2) of Colonial Court of Admiralty Act, 1890 and as such Administration of Justice Act, 1956 is not applicable in Bangladesh. In view of my above discussion I hold that this court exercising Admiralty jurisdiction has no power to arrest any property or ship of the defendant No. 1 than the one which was concerned in the cause of action. Thus for the consignment having been allegedly carried by MY VICEROY the arrest of MV CHERRY ORIENT cannot be maintained.</u>

18. As regard the submission of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff that this suit both in rem and in personam is maintainable, I hold that there is no defect in framing of this suit. The present suit in personam is maintainable notwithstanding the fact that the suit in rem cannot proceed. The suit in rem against Cherry Orient, its Master, agent, etc. cannot be maintained. The plaintiff may however amend the plaint accordingly.

19. Mr. Siddique Ahmed Choudhury, has lastly argued that if a suit in personam is maintainable, this Court can exercise jurisdiction under Order 38, rule 5, CPC in arresting before judgment a sister ship inasmuch as that rule of Code of Civil Procedure would be applicable even if a remedy in rem is not available to a suit or under the Admiralty Rules.

<u>20. The Admiralty Rules specifically provide arrest of a ship before judgment in an action in rem. In paragraph 4 of the Admiralty Rules it has been provided that in a suit in rem warrant of arrest of property may be issued at the instance of the plaintiff. Admiralty Rules having specifically provided arrest of a ship in an action in rem and that being the only remedy available to a suit or in an action in rem before judgment is made, the procedures under Order 38, rule 5, CPC for attachment before judgment of any property of the defendant would not be available to the Admiralty Court. The procedures governing action in Admiralty jurisdiction in England are separate than those governing action in Chancery of County Courts. This Court has also a separate set of Rules for admiralty jurisdiction. An arrest of the concerned ship in admiralty jurisdiction having been provided in Rule 4, attachment before judgment of any property of the defendant under Order 38, rule 5 CPC cannot be held to be applicable in an action in personam. In this view I hold that the submission of the learned Advocate that in a suit in personam this Court can exercise jurisdiction to attach any property of the defendant under Order 38, rule 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure is clearly untenable.</u>

21. In the result the attachment or arrest of the ship MV CHERRY ORIENT is vacated and the Bank Guarantee for Tk. 15,00,000 (Taka fifteen lacs) furnished by the defendants Nos. 2 and 3 be returned to the concerned bank for cancellation.

Mr. Siddique Ahmed Choudhury, the learned Advocate prays that the order may be stayed for one month. This order is, therefore, stayed for one month.

End.

parties:
Dr Md Abdullahel Based Shah ----- Petitioner
vs
Secretary, Ministry of Health & Population Control, Government of Bangladesh & others ----- Respondent.
full_judgment:
Amin-ur-Rahman Khan J : In this rule the petitioner has sought a declaration that the order dated 12-3-1981 passed by the Government dismissing him from service, and the orders passed by the Administrative Tribunal and the Administrative-Appellate Tribunal dismissing the petitioner's appeal are without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

2. The petitioner's case was as follows: The petitioner had been serving as Medical Officer at Balialcandi Thana Health Complex, District Faridpur (now District Rajbari) till 21-7-1980 when he was transferred to Dighinala Thana Health Complex, Chittagong Hill Tracts (now District Khagra Chari) by an order dated 24-6-80 and was directed to report for duty to the Civil Surgeon, Chittagong Hill Tracts by 20-7-80. The petitioner handed over his charge on 21-7-80. Then he fell ill. On recovery from the illness he obtained fitness certificate on 10-2-81 and reported for duty on 13-2-81 to the Civil Surgeon, Chittagong Hill Tracts who accepted his joining report and posted him as Medical Officer in Dighinala Thana Health Complex, Chittagong Hill Tracts. The petitioner was asked to hand over charge to the Assistant Surgeon of Dighinala Thana Dispensary through a Radiogram dated 28-5-81 but having no substitute the petitioner handed over charge to one Dr. Qazi and was released on 13-7-81. The petitioner preferred an appeal on 20-5-81 for his re-instatement in service against the now impugned order of the Government dated 12-3-81. That was rejected and the petitioner made an application before the Administrative Tribunal. The Administrative Tribunal dismissed his application by order dated 23-12-82. The petitioner then preferred appeal before the Member, Administrative Appellate Tribunal and the appeal was dismissed by order dated 18-3-85. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid orders of the Government, Administrative Tribunal and the Administrative Appellate Tribunal he has made this writ petition.

3. On behalf of the Government Mr Md Delwar Hossain, the learned Assistant Attorney-General submitted that the present writ petition against the orders of the Administrative Tribunals is not legally maintainable being barred by Article 102 as well as by Article 117 of the revived Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.

4. So the question that now calls for determination is whether the present writ petition challenging the legality of the order of the Administrative Tribunal and in respect of the matters falling within the jurisdiction of the Administrative Tribunal is maintainable or is barred by Articles 102 and 117 of the Constitution.

5. Mr Md Roushan Ali, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that Article 1022 of the Constitution has defined the word 'person' in sub-Article (5) of Article 102 and that the said definition does not exclude the Administrative Tribunal from the meaning of the word 'person' as contained in Sub-Articles (1) and (2) of Article 102 of the revived Constitution.

6. Article 102(1) provides that on the application of any person aggrieved High Court Division may give such direction or orders to any person or authority and Article 102(2) provides that the High Court Division may, if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law, on the application of any person aggrieved make an order directing a person performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do or to do that which he is required by law to do or declaring that any act done or proceeding taken by a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority has been done or taken without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and requiring a person holding or purporting to hold a public office to show under what authority he claims to hold that office. The 'person' stated in Article 102 on whom the High Court Division can give directions or orders and about whose act the High Court Division can make declaration has been defined in Article 102(5) of the Constitution as has been revived by substituting the original Article 102(5) of the Constitution. According to the Article 102(5) which is now in force in view of the Constitution (Partial Revival) (Second) Order, 1985 which came into force on 15th January, 1985 reads as follows:—

"(5) In this article, unless the context otherwise requires, "person" includes a statutory public authority and any court or tribunal, other than—

(a) a court or tribunal established under a Martial Law Regulation or Order.

(b) a court or tribunal established under a Law relating to the defence services of Bangladesh or any disciplined force, or.

(c) an administrative tribunal, but does not include a person performing or purporting to perform any function in exercise of any power derived or purported to have been derived from the Proclamation of the 24th March, 1982, or from any Martial Law Regulation or Order or Instruction or Notification or in execution of or in compliance with any order made or sentence passed by any court, tribunal or authority in the exercise or purported exercise of such power".

<u>7. On a plain reading of the aforesaid sub-article (5) of Article 102 it is found that the word 'person' as contained in Article 102 (1) and Article 102(2) includes a statutory public authority and any court or tribunal other than three classes of courts, tribunal as has been specified under clauses (a), (b) and (c) of Article 102 (5) of the Constitution as revived by amendment. As clause (c) is an administrative tribunal and this falls within the category of exclusion from the definition of 'person' which has been denoted by the words "other than" as contained in Article 102 (5) of the Constitution. Besides that Article 102 (5) has further excluded by the terms "does not include" a person performing or purported to perform any function in exercise of any power derived or purported to have been derived from the Proclamation of the 24th March, 1982 or from any Martial Law Regulation or Order or Instruction or Notification or in execution of or in compliance with any order made or sentence passed by any court, tribunal or authority in the exercise or purported exercise of such power. Thus, reading Article 102 (1), Article 102 (2) and Article 102 (5) together it is clearly found that by Article 102 (5) the Administrative Tribunal has been excluded from the word "person" as contained in Article 102 (T) and Article 102 (2) of the Constitution. The consequence of this exclusion is that according to the Article 102 of the Constitution as revived the High Court Division cannot give directions or orders on the Administrative Tribunal and also can not declare any acts done or proceeding taken by the administrative tribunal as having been done or taken without lawful authority as being of no legal effect. In other words, the administrative tribunal is not under the writ jurisdiction of Article 102 of the Constitution.</u>

<u>8. In the present writ petition, as we have already mentioned, the, petitioner has alleged to have been aggrieved by the order of the administrative tribunal and administrative appellate tribunal who by their impugned orders had dismissed his appeals against the order of his dismissal from service by the Government. So we find that the present application under Article 102 is not entertainable according to the express and clear provision of Article 102 of the Constitution.</u>

<u>9. Mr Roushan Ali, the learned Advocate for the petitioner contended that Article 117 (2) only provides that no court shall entertain any proceeding or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal and that by the word no court" it does not contemplate the High Court Division of the Supreme Court. We pointed out to Mr. Roushan Ali the definition of the word 'court' as has been contained in Article 152 of the Constitution which provides as follows: "In this Constitution except where the subject or context otherwise requires  court" means any court of law including Supreme Court". So by reading the provision of Article 117(2) with reference to the definition provided in Article 152 (1) the constitutional provision in that regard means that where any administrative tribunal is established under Article 117 no court including the Supreme Court shall entertain any proceeding or make any order in respect of any matter falling within the jurisdiction of such tribunal. In the present writ petition is a matter which fell within the jurisdiction of the administrative tribunal. In the same Article 117 (2) it was also provided that Parliament may, by law, provide for appeals from, or the review or, decisions of any such tribunal. It is evident that the administrative tribunal and the administrative appellate tribunal have been already formed in pursuance of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980 (Act VII of 1981) and in fact the present petitioner has already put up though unsuccessfully his grievance before both the administrative tribunal and the administrative appellate tribunal.</u>

<u>10. Lastly, Mr. Roushan Ali, the learned Advocate argued that since the administrative appellate tribunal's impugned order was a final order so this Court was competent to look into the legality of the said order in exercise of its power under Article 102 of the Constitution. But as we have already observed Article 102 as well as Article 117 of the Constitution have barred the Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in express terms and in that position this Court cannot assume Jurisdiction which in expressly barred on the ground as was pleaded by Mr. Roushan Ali. Of course if the Administrative Tribunal or the Administrative Appellate Tribunal would not have been properly and legally constituted or acted without jurisdiction or acted malafide then only inspite of the barring provision the superior court's power under Article 102 may be exercised in appropriate cases.</u>

<u>11. In other words an order or action of the excepted authority mentioned in Sub-Article (5) of Article 102 is immune from challenge in writ jurisdiction unless it was coram non judice or malafide. This has been so held in the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Iqbal vs Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR (AD 154 and in the case of Jamil Huq vs Bangladesh reported in 34 DLR (AD) 125.</u>

12. In the present case there was no representation by the petitioner or by his learned counsel that the Administrative Tribunal acted without authority or acted malafide. In that position we have no scope to entertain the writ petition or to interfere with the impugned order of the Administrative Tribunal.

In the result, we find that this writ petition is not entertainable and consequently it will not be proper to go into the other point relating to the factual merit of the petitioner's case. The rule is accordingly discharged without any order as to costs.

End.
