Moulana Abdul Haque ----- Petitioner
vs
Fazlul Huq and others ----- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
Mustafa Kamal, J: This Rule arises out of an election petition. The petitioner was elected as the Chairman of No. 11 Gandharbapur Union Parishad within Hajiganj Upazila, District Chandpur on 2-1-84, having secured 2649 votes. Nine other contestants also contested the said election. The opposite party No. 1 polled the 2nd highest number of votes, i.e. 2224 votes. The result was duly published in the official gazette on 23-1-84.The opposite-party No. 1 instituted Election Tribunal Case No. 2 of 1984 in Court of Election Tribunal and Munsif, Hajiganj. The petitioner contested the case by filing a written objection. The opposite-party No. 1 examined 6 witnesses including himself and the petitioner examined 5 witnesses including himself. The ballot boxes were opened and ballot papers were recounted by the Election Tribunal. By judgment and order dated 7-5-84 the Election Tribunal set aside the election of the present petitioner and declared the opposite-party No. 1 to be the legally elected Chairman of the concerned Union Parishad. On appeal Mr. M.A. Quddus, the learned District Judge, Chandpur affirmed the judgment and order of the Election Tribunal by his judgment and order dated 19-3-85 in Election Tribunal Appeal No. 1 of 1984.

2. The opposite-party No. 1 founded his election petition on a number of material allegations, prominent among which are as follows:-

i) In violation of election Rules the petitioner and his people canvassed for votes throughout the night previous to the day of poll and also in the morning of the day of poll over mike.

ii) At the polling centre of Ward No. 3, i.e. Datra Primary School Polling Centre, polling was started 11/2 hours late.

iii) The Presiding Officers and the Staff were lodged in the house of the Petitioner in the night previous to the day of poll when the petitioner threw a feast for the voters, the Presiding Officer and the Polling Officers of the Datra Primary School Polling Centre.

iv) Before the polling started at Datra Primary School Polling Centre the Polling Officers did not show empty ballot boxes to the opposite-party No. 1 and the other candidates,

v)  When polling was in progress some of the relatives and canvassers of the petitioner freely entered into the polling centres and persuaded the voters to cast their votes in favour of the petitioner. The opposite-party No. 1 protested in writing to the Presiding Officer who expressed his helplessness in the matter and returned the petition to the opposite party No. 1 Supporters of the petitioner were men of dangerous character. They forced the supporters of the opposite-party No, 1 to leave the Datra Primary School Polling Centre without casting their votes and there was no security of voting in the said polling centre. The petitioner bribed the voters openly. The Presiding Officer acted in connivance with the petitioner.

vi) Datra Primary School Polling Centre was opened very near the house of the petitioner so that the petitioner may directly control the polling station by his hired goondas.

vii) At the Datra Primary School Polling Centre the petitioner in connivance with the Presiding Officer cast the votes of dead and absentee voters by false personation.

viii) No allegation was made regarding the counting of votes in the body of the petition but in ground No. VI of the election petition it was urged that the polling and counting of votes were not fair and correct and for ends of justice the votes cast in favour of the candidates are required to be recounted.

The opposite-party No. 1 prayed, inter alia, that the ballot papers, ballot boxes, seal, counterfoil and all other connected papers be taken into judicial custody.

In his written objection the petitioner denied all the material allegations and contended that the election was held peace fully and without any incident. The result of the election has been declared lawfully.

3. The Election Tribunal did not utter a word as to what parties' evidence was with regard to the material allegations of the opposite party No. 1. The evidence of 6 PWs and 5 OPWs were left completely untouched by the Election Tribunal. The Tribunal opened the ballot boxes in presence of the learned Advocates of the petitioner and the opposite-party No. 1 and recounted the same. It found that in the polling station of Ward No. 3, i.e. Datra Primary School Polling Centre the petitioner obtained 780 votes. The Returning Officer had shown that the petitioner had obtained 12222 votes in this centre. The difference is of 442 votes. The Tribunal also recounted the ballot papers of the Union Parishad Members of the Datra Centre. The same number of ballot books and ballot papers were found to have been used and cast as those of the candidates for Chairmanship. In the election of Chairman and Members, 8 ballot books were found to have been used in full and only one book was partly used. The Tribunal found it impossible that out of 1414 total votes at Ward No. 3, the petitioner could have secured 1222 votes. From the recounting it drew the "presumption" that the petitioner had made a new polling station at Datra with a view to exercising undue influence over the voters.

The Tribunal also held that the petitioner being the Vice-Principal of a Government Madrassa is disqualified to contest for Chairmanship.

4. On recounting of ballot papers of all the centres the Tribunal found that the opposite-party No. 1 got 2236 votes and the petitioner got 2208 votes. He therefore, declared the opposite-party No. 1 to be the legally elected Chairman. The appellate Court below only affirmed the judgment and order of the Election Tribunal. The appellate Court also limited its inquiry into recounting results, PWs and OPWs were not event mentioned.

5. The first point urged by Mr. M. A. Karim, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, is that the Tribunal's finding regarding the eligibility of the petitioner to contest the post of Chairman is based on wrong facts. He submits that the petitioner was the Vice Principal of a private Madrassa. He has himself deposed to that effect and there was no challenge to his statement.

In view of what has been submitted 1 hold that the Tribunal's finding on the petitioner's eligibility was based on no evidence and cannot be sustained.

6. The next point urged by MA Karim is that the election petition was barred by limitation. He submits that the result of the election in dispute was published in the official gazette on 23-1-84. As per rule 44(1) of the Union Parishads Election Rules, 1983, hereinafter referred to as the said Rules, an election petition shall be presented to the Tribunal within 30 days next after the publication of the names of the returned candidates in the official gazette under rule 41. Mr. Karim submits that the election petition should have been filed on 22-2-84.

7. Mr Abu Taher Khan, the learned Advocate for the opposite-party No. 1 submits that the opposite-party No. 1 filed the election petition on 22-2-84. The office of the Election Tribunal affixed the seal of the Tribunal on each page of the election petition and it clearly shows that the petition was filed, received and stamped by the said office on 22-2-84. Mr. Abu Taher Khan also points out that Order No. 1 dated 22-2-84 clearly shows that the application was registered as an Election Tribunal Case and was No on that date fixing 15-2-84 for service return. Mr MA Karim submits that the election petition itself contains the verification of the opposite-party No. 1 bearing the date 23-2-84. Subsequently the date 23-2-84 was changed to 22-2-84 by overwriting, but no initials have been put. He submits that both the order-sheet and .the verification portion of the election petition and the seals of Election Tribunal have been manipulated at a later stage. Mr. Karim further submits that under Rule 44(3) of the said Rules every election petition shall be accompanied by a receipt showing a deposit of Tk. 500/- to any branch of the Sonali Bank or Government Treasury in favour of the Returning Officer for the cost of the election petition. The opposite-party No. 1 filed the original chalan in the Tribunal showing deposit of Tic. 500/ on 23-2-84. This chalan was entered and kept at page 30 of the Tribunal's records. Some malicious hands have removed the chalan containing the evidence on the date of payment. Before the appellate Court the opposite-party No. 1 submitted a photostat copy of the original chalan showing the deposit to have been made on 22-2-84. Mr MA Karim submits that the photo-stat copy is not receivable in evidence. In the present revisional application the petitioner has annexed a certificate from the Manager, Sonali Bank, Chandpur Branch stating that the opposite-party No.1 deposited Tk. 500 on 23-2-84. Mr Abu Taher Khan submits that this certificate cannot be entertained in the provisional application. The question of limitation was raised for the first time before the appellant Court which has held, after considering fresh evidence, that the election petition was not barred by limitation.

8. From the foregoing arguments of the parties it is obvious that the question as to obvious that the question as to whether the election petition was barred by limitation or not is not a pure question of law in the facts and circumstances of the present case. It is a pure question of fact. If the election petition itself contained 23-2-84 as the date of verification and if the chalan kept at page 30 of the Tribunal's record contained 23-2-84 as the date of deposit, then the petitioner had a clear notice of late filing of the election petition, but lie did not allege in his written objection that the petition was barred by limitation. No such issue was framed by the Tribunal. It was at the appellate stage that he raised the issue for the first time. Whether the Tribunal's order-sheet was interpolated or whether the chalan was removed from the Tribunal's record by a malicious hand or whether the verification portion of the election petition was interpolated are matters which cannot be decided in this revisional Court. His grievances on this score could not have been fully adjudicated even by the appellate Court below because the said Court could not have come to a decision for the first time as to whether the Tribunal's record were interfered with or not. The Tribunal itself was the best authority to so determine.

9. I shall revert to this subject later on. Mr Karim next submits that the Tribunal, as also the appellate Court below, set-aside the election on recounting of votes without reference to the evidence tendered by the witnesses and there-fore the two Courts below acted illegally resulting in a miscarriage of justice.

10. Mr Abu Taher Khan, on the other hand, supports the view of the appellate Court below that the Local Government (Union Parishads) Ordinance, 1983 and the said Rules empower the Election Tribunal to recount the votes in order to come to a correct conclusion.

<u>11. It is quite clear that the learned District Judges as also the Election Tribunal did not fully comprehend the powers of the Election Tribunal vis-a-vis the recounting of votes. Nowhere in the four corners of the said Ordinance and the said Rules has an express power been given to the Election Tribunal to re-open the ballot boxes and recount the votes. That power has been given to the Election Tribunal by judicial decisions. In other words, it is a judge-made law which empowers the Tribunal to reopen the ballot boxes and to re-count the ballot papers. The Tribunal's jurisdiction to reopen and recount the ballot boxes is therefore, circumscribed by the various conditions laid down in various judicial decisions of our Courts.</u>

<u>12. In the case of Abul Basher Chowdhury vs Habibur Rahman Mia and others, 31 DLR (AD) 296, the Appellate Division observed as follows:</u>

<u>"We have no manner of doubt that in an appropriate case the Election Tribunal has authority to make a recounting of the votes in order to satisfy itself that the counting made by the Presiding Officer on the basis of which the result of the election has been declared was properly made."</u>

<u>What is an "appropriate case" has been elucidated in various other decisions.</u>

<u>In the case of Azimuddin Ahmed vs Election Tribunal, Narayanganj and others, 27 DLR 594, a Division Bench of the High Court Division observed as follows:</u>

<u>"The Election Rules do not provide for recounting ballot papers by the Tribunal and the power to recount ballot papers has been given under Rule 41 to the Presiding Officer only. But if recounting of ballot papers is a material issue before the Tribunal and the election petition cannot be determined without such recounting, only then the Tribunal has got power to re-open the ballot boxes and recount the ballot papers in presence of parties. Before doing so it must come to a finding by evidence on oath that this recounting is indispensably necessary."</u>

<u>Subsequently this view was endorsed by the Appellate Division in the case of Afzal Khan vs The Election Tribunal and Munsif 3rd Court, Comilla and another 1980 BSCR 69.</u>

<u>13. The Appellate Division held as correct the following views of the High Court Division:</u>

<u>(a) that the counting was not asked for before the Presiding Officer.</u>

<u>(b) foundation for the exercise of jurisdiction of the Tribunal merely for recounting was not laid.</u>

<u>(c) In the facts and circumstances to that particular case the High Court Division was justified in recounting the votes itself of the other 14 centres.</u>

<u>The Appellate Division further observes ;</u>

<u>"Normally mere counting of votes may not be a sole issue before any Election Tribunal unless sufficient foundation for such exercise is laid by evidence. In the present case no allegation was made before the Returning Officer specifically regarding the error in counting but this was raised before Tribunal along with the allegation of corrupt practice."</u>

<u>The Appellate Division further observes,</u>

<u>"The jurisdiction of counting eminently lies elsewhere and even the Election Tribunal cannot count the ballot papers, unless the recounting becomes a necessary part of the case itself which has been brought on the basis of certain allegations of corrupt and illegal practices. It is well settled that if recounting of ballot papers is a material issue before the Tribunal in connection with all election petition which cannot be determined without such recounting, then only the Tribunal has got power to reopen the ballot boxes and recount the ballot papers provided sufficient foundation has been laid to come to the finding that the recounting is indispensably necessary for adjudication of the election petition."</u>

<u>14. In the case of Nurul Islam Talukder vs Munsif, 28 D.L.R 375 a Division Bench of the High Court Division laid down the manner in which the evidence of election officers has to be weighed, the effect of not lodging any complaint with the relevant authorities alleging irregularity in the counting of polls, etc.</u>

<u>15. I have already noticed that the opposite-party No. 1 examined 6 P.ws. including himself and tile present petitioner examined 5 O.P.Ws. including himself. Not a word has been said about their evidence by either the Tribunal or the appellate Court below. There is no knowing whether the material allegations of corrupt and malpractices against the petitioner and others has at all been substantiated. Without discussing the oral evidence on record the Tribunal and the appellate Court below straightaway discussed the reopening of ballot boxes and recounting of ballot papers, as if that was the only issue before them. As I noticed earlier, there was no complaint in the election petition that the counting of votes was unfair and that the opposite-party No. 1 raised the issue with the concerned Officer before or immediately after the election. A general ground was taken that the counting of votes was not fair and correct. Upon these averments it was incumbent upon tile Tribunal to discuss the oral evidence on record and come to a finding as to whether the substantive allegations of the opposite-party No. 1 against the petitioner and others have been proved or not. The Tribunal was also required to weigh the evidence of election officers, if any, in the light of the guidance given in the case reported in 28 DLR 375 It is only when the Tribunal comes to a definite decision against the elected candidate and others on the substantive issue of corrupt and Malpractices or it is only when the Tribunal cannot come to a firm conclusion about the alleged corrupt and malpractices of the elected candidate and others on the basis of the oral and documentary evidence on record, that it has to fall back upon its findings on recounting in order to come to a just decision in the matter. But without adverting to the oral evidence on record the Tribunal cannot come to any finding on a mere recounting of votes. The Tribunal has not been given the power to recount for the sake of recounting only. The Tribunal is not a mere second counting body.</u>

<u>16. Under similar circumstances a Division Bench of the High Court Division held in tile case of Nawsher Ali Molla vs Election Tribunal and Sadar Munsif; Faridpur and another, 33 D.L.R. 344, that the Election Tribunal acted illegally in not at all referring to the oral and documentary evidence on record and, as such, setting aside of the election was wrong.</u>

<u>As already noted 6 P.ws. and 5 O.P.ws have been examined and there is ample evidence on record for the Tribunal to conic to a decision as to whether the allegations of the opposite party No. 1 against the petitioner and others have been substantiated or not. I am of the opinion that the Tribunal should follow the well-settled path of discussing the oral and documentary evidence on record and then dwell on the result of recounting, if necessary. The Tribunal has already reopened the ballot boxes and whatever it has already found after recounting the ballot papers it will discuss after discussing the other evidence on record. The Tribunal, however, is not precluded from receiving further evidence if it considers necessary for arriving at a decision. The petitioner shall also be at liberty to raise the question of limitation and adduce evidence in respect thereof. The opposite-party No. 1 will also be entitled to give evidence to the contrary. The petitioner shall also be entitled to file an additional written objection so as to question the election petition on the ground of limitation.</u>

<u>In the result, the Rule is made absolute but without any order as to costs. The judgment and order of the appellate Court below are set-aside and the election petition is sent back on remand to the Election Tribunal for re-hearing in the light of observations made above and in accordance with law. The Election Tribunal is further directed to dispose of the petition within 2 months from the date of arrival of the records in his Court.</u>

Let the lower Court's records be sent down expeditiously.

End.

caseno: Appeal from Original Order No. 334 of 1988 with Civil Rule No. 84 (F.M.) of 1988.
lawyer:
Rafiqur Rahman with Nurul Huq, Matiur Rahman and Serajur Rahman, Advocates  -------- For the Appellant.
 No one  -------- For the Respondents.
parties:
Muhammad Raushan Ali -------- Appellant
Vs.
Bangladesh Bar Council & Ors ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Mozammel Haque, J.: This First Miscellaneous Appeal under Article 36(1) of the Bangladesh Legal Practitioners and Bar Council Order, 1972 (P.O. No. 46 of 1972) is directed against the judgment and order dated 26.11.88 passed by the Bar Council Tribunal No. 11 in Complaint Case No. 5 of 1985.

2. Respondent No. 3 Mohammad Moslemuddin was the complainant-petitioner and the appellant Mr. Raushan Ali was the Advocate-opposite party in the above complaint case before the Tribunal. On 26.4.84 the complainant filed a petition of complaint before the Bangladesh Bar Council against the present appellant under Rule 41 of the Bangladesh Legal Practitioners and Bar Council Rules, 1972, alleging, inter alia, that the complainant's wife Mrs. Angur Begum had purchased a house being holding No. 10-A/L-11/12, Mirpur, Dhaka from one Abdul Hamid by a registered sale deed dated 25.12.80. The complainant was living in the purchased house with his family long before registration since 1975. The complainant's wife received a notice on 20.6.83 from the office of the Abandoned Property Management Board, Dhaka City, with a direction to appear before it on 22.6.83 with papers and documents in support of their ownership of the above house. The complaint appeared before the aforesaid Management Board on 22.6.83 and submitted his papers. From there he came to know that a suit being T.S. No. 805 of 1981 in respect of the said house of his wife was filed in the 4th Court of Sub-Judge, Dhaka. But in fact the above Title Suit related to plot No. 5, lane No, 3, Block-A, Section-6, Mirpur Housing Estate, Dhaka and in that suit Most. Mahmuda Begum was the plaintiff and one Tosaddeque Hossain Siddiqui and two others were the defendants. It was a suit for specific performance of contract. Thereafter the complainant along with one Chand Miah, contacted the opposite party (Appellant) at his residence-Chamber. The complainant showed the plaint of Title Suit No. 805 of 1981 to the opposite party and it was found that the above house of his wife was shown as the residential address of the defendant No. 1 of the aforesaid suit. After seeing it the opposite party advised the complainant that his wife should be added as a party in the suit. Being so advised the wife of the complainant executed a Vokalatnama on 14.8.83 and an application was drafted on behalf of his wife for addition of party in the aforesaid suit under Order 1, rule 10 C.P.C.

3. The complainant further alleged that the opposite party realised Tk. 15,000/- as fees for filing the aforesaid application although there was no necessity for filing such an application, because no suit was filed in respect of the above property of his wife. The opposite party played another trick by filing an application in the said suit with the help of another Advocate namely, Mr. Mohiuddin. The property in the aforesaid Title Suit No. 805 of 1981 had no connection with the property of his wife and the opposite party, in utter violation of professional ethics, gave him the false advice that his entire property was in danger. Through misrepresentation he managed to extort Tk. 15,000/- from him stating that his wife was to contest the aforesaid suit. When the complainant later realised the true position, he demanded refund of the said amount which the opposite party refused. He took back his papers from the opposite party. On the above allegation of professional misconduct the complainant prayed for disciplinary action against the opposite party.

4. The Advocate-opposite party who is now the appellant before this court filed a written reply against the allegations made by the complainant. He totally denied all the allegations made in the complaint-petition. He further stated that the complainant-petitioner had no locus standi to file this complaint case because the property in question stands in the name of his wife who executed the vokalatnama in his favour. The complainant himself was not his client. His further case is that the house of the wife of the complainant was enlisted as an abandoned property and for that matter the complainant came to his chamber for consultation and legal advice. From the certified copy of the plaint of the aforesaid suit it appeared that the defendant No. I Tosaddeque Hossain Siddiqui was shown to reside in the residence of the wife of the complainant which is holding No.10-A/L-11/12, Mirpur, Dhaka, The complainant was nervous and apprehensive because of the fact that, on the one hand, the property in question was listed as an abandoned property and, on the other hand, in the aforesaid Title Suit the defendant No. 1 had shown his residential address which is actually the house of his wife and the residence of the complainant and his wife. The defendant No. 1 Tosaddeque Hossain never stayed there and he was not known to the complainant and his wife. Unless and until the address is corrected by adding the wife of the complainant as a party in the suit, there might be some complication in future over the property of his wife. Apprehending that, the complainant instructed him to take steps in the aforesaid title suit and for that reason he filed an application under Order 1, rule 10 C.P.C. for addition of party. He further stated that he did not receive Taka 15,000/- from the complainant or his wife. He received Tk. 3,400/- from the complainant as his fees.

5. After considering the petition of complainant and the written objection of the Advocate-opposite party the Tribunal framed the following issues:-

"1. Whether Mr. Mohammad Roushan Ali, Advocate is guilty of professional misconduct by intentionally involving the complainant's wife Angur Begum in Title Suit No. 805/81 of the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka and for realisation of Tk. 15,000/- from the complainant and his wife Angur Begum under false pretext and on misrepresentations of facts?

2. What relief, if any, is the complainant entitled to?"

6. In the hearing the complainant and his wife examined themselves as P.Ws. 1 and 2 and the opposite party-Advocate examined himself as D.W. 1. The parties have also produced some documents in sup-port of their respective cases. After hearing the parties and perusing the materials on record the Tribunal passed the impugned judgment and order on 26.11.88 finding the Advocate-opposite party guilty of professional misconduct under Article 32(1) of P.O. No. 46 of 1972 and suspending him from practice for a period of 5(five) years.

7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order the Advocate-opposite party namely, the present appellant preferred this appeal.

8. The complainant examined himself as P.W. 1. In his deposition he has reiterated what he stated in his petition of complaint. He further stated that in four instalments he paid the entire amount of Tk. 15,000/- to the opposite party. In order to appreciate his evidence the following portion of his deposition may be quoted:-

"Myself and Chand Mia went to the chamber of Mr. Roushan Ali at 44, Siddheswari, Dhaka at about 8 in the evening. I showed Mr. Roushan Ali the notice issued by Abandoned Property Management Board and Chand Mia told the O.P. that a Suit being T.S. 805/81 was pending in the 4th Sub-Judge Court regarding my property. Barrister Shahib told me that the certified copy of the plaint of T.S. No. 805/81 is to be obtained and demanded Tk. 1000/-(one thousand) for the purpose which I paid to Roushan Ali then and there. I left his Chamber. On 5.7.83 I again went to the chamber of Mr. Roushan Ali who showed me the certified copy of the plaint asked for earlier and told me on perusal of the paper that there is a serious case pending in the court with regard to your property and told me that if I do not contest the suit and take steps my property will be lost. Then I told him how my property can go ? Then Mr. Roushan Ali told me that your property will not go. You are to contest the case and an amount of Tk. 20,000/-(Twenty thousand) will be needed for that purpose. Ultimately I agreed to pay him Taka 15000/- and he also agreed on this. On that date I paid him Taka 2000/-. During the conversation Mr. Roushan Ali made me understand that a case Musammat Masuda Khatun Vs. Tossadiq Siddiqui is pending where though your name is not appearing in the case but your home address is the address of said Tosaddiq Hossain. Mr. Roushan Ali said that this house is not yours but it is the house of Tosaddiq Hossain. On seeing the papers he told me that the paper shows that Tosaddiq Hossain Siddiqui is staying in your house. I told him no, I am staying in my house. Then Mr. Roushan Ali told me that if you say it is your house it will not do. Tosaddiq Hossain will take away your house from the Court, you will not know. Then Mr. Roushan Ali suggested that you are not a party to the case but you are to be added as party to the case. Then I left his residence and again went to his residence on 14.8.83, according to his suggestion."

9. His wife Angur Begum also examined herself as P.W. 2. She in fact corroborated the statement of P.W. 1.

10. The Advocate-opposite party examined himself as D.W. 1. In his deposition he stated that after getting notice from the Abandoned Property Management Cell the complainant came to his chamber on 20.6.83 and asked him to appear before the Abandoned Property Management Cell at Motijheel as his engaged lawyer For the aforesaid purpose he went to the office of the abandoned property cell but without any vokalatnama and came to know that a Title suit was also pending in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka in respect of the self-same property of Angur Begum. The complainant apprehended that the property in question might be taken over by one Altaf Hossain whose wife was the plaintiff in the aforesaid title suit. The defendant No. 1 in that title suit was a fictitious person and the address of defendant No. 1 as given in the aforesaid Title Suit No. 805 of 1981 was also fictitious, which was in fact the address of the complainant and his wife. For this reason the complainant instructed him to get the said address of defendant No. 1 corrected and deleted from the title suit. The complainant became further apprehensive that not only the aforesaid Title Suit was pending, but also his wife's above property had already been listed as abandoned property and the plaintiff of the suit might claim the defendant No. 1's alleged house in future. Being apprehensive of the above, the complainant engaged him as a lawyer and instructed him to make his wife a party in the aforesaid suit to delete the address of the defendant No. 1. Under such instruction he appeared before the court and filed an application under Order, 1 rule 10 C.P.C. for adding Angur Begum as a party in the above suit. He further stated that he actually received Tk. 3,400/- and not Tk. 15,000/- from the complainant. The aforesaid statement of D.W. 1 had not been challenged at all in the cross-examination.

11. Together with the oral evidence there are other evidence on record. One is the application for compromise dated 30.5.86 signed by Angur Begum and the Advocate-opposite party Mr. Roushan Ali. Another application was filed by Angur Begum on 12.7.86. She filed the application by herself and on behalf of her husband Moslemuddin stating that since there was a compromise she received the entire amount of Taka 10,000/- and she did not like to proceed with the case. Ext. 'Ga' shows that the Manager, Sonali Bank, Supreme Court Branch, Dhaka issued a certificate stating that the complainant Moslemuddin encashed Taka 10,000/- by cheque No. 295921 dated 31.5.86 issued by Mr. Roushan Ali in favour of Moslemuddin. These are more or less the oral as well as the documentary evidence in the present case.

12. Though the notices were duly served upon the respondents, yet neither of them has appeared and contested the present appeal.

13. In the background of the aforesaid oral as well as the documentary evidence Dr. Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the appellant, submits that the findings of the Tribunal to the effect that the conduct and attitude on the part of the practising Advocate of the highest Court is against professional ethics, responsibility and etiquette and that Mr. Roushan Ali deliberately involved a simple litigant in an unwanted litigation and realised fees for doing nothing worthy, are contrary to the evidence on record, and as such the judgment is not tenable in law.

14. To consider the above point it may be stated that the said property of Angur Begum had admittedly been enlisted as an abandoned property and for that reason the complainant with one Chand Mia went to the chamber of the appellant-Advocate and admittedly had consultations with him on several occasions. Thereafter, from the office of the Abandoned Property Management Cell they came to know that a Title suit was pending in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka in respect of the same property. After obtaining the certified copy of the plaint it was found that the address of the defendant No. 1 was shown as the address of the complainant and his wife. The defendant No. 1 had given a fictitious ad-dress in that suit which clouded the mind of the complainant. He, being apprehensive that his wife's above property might be in some danger in future, instructed the learned Advocate to take steps in the matter, namely, deleting the address of the defendant No. 1 from the cause title. Unless and until she becomes a party in the suit an application from a third party to delete the address of a party to the suit can-not be accepted by the court and for this reason the learned Advocate advised him to file an application to add his wife as party first. Thereafter he will file an application for deletion of the address of defendant No. 1 wherein the house of Angur Begum was involved. For the reason that the property had been listed as an abandoned property and also for the additional reason that a title suit was pending involving the same property in some way, the complainant at-tended the chamber of the learned Advocate on several occasions and took his legal advice and the learned Advocate also had admittedly taken some steps in the aforesaid title suit in order to protect the interests of his client and to remove any future complication and possible danger to the house of Angur Begum.

15. From the aforesaid facts and circumstances and the evidence on record we find that the learned Advocate apart from holding consultations in his Chamber had performed some professional duties on the instruction of the complainant and his wife both in the office of the Abandoned Property Management Cell as well as in the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. The complainant failed to prove that Mr. Roushan Ali deceived him of a sum of 15000/- on false representation and thereby committed gross professional misconduct. On the contrary the evidence of the complainant himself as quoted above clearly shows that the complainant engaged Mr. Roushan Ali as his lawyer and Mr. Roushan Ali had done his professional works bonafide in order to safeguard the interest of the complainant and his wife. So, the Tribunal is completely perverse in its finding that without doing any professional work and through misrepresentation the appellant extorted Tk. 15000/- from the complainant.

16. Dr. Rafiqur Rahman further submits that realisation of fees allegedly high, cannot be a ground of misconduct for an Advocate of the Supreme Court with 18 years' standing. Because to realise such amount of fees is neither contrary to nor violative of any provision of law, Mr. Roushan Ali being a member of the English Bar is an Advocate of 18 years' standing. Evidence on record shows that he had consultations with his client in his chamber on several occasions. He had been instructed by his client to appear before the Abandoned Property Management Cell as well as before the 4th Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka to take all necessary steps to protect the interest of his client. Regarding the professional fees of a lawyer, there is no schedule of fees either in P.O. No. 46 of 1972 or in the Rules framed thereunder. In Chapter II Paragraph (10) of the 'Canons of Professional Conduct and Etiquette' framed by the Bar Council some guidelines have been given as to how an Advocate is to realise fees from his clients.

It is stated that-

"(10)" In fixing fees, Advocates should avoid charges which overestimate their advice and services as well as those which undervalue them. A client's ability to pay cannot justify a charge in excess of the value of the service, though his poverty may justify a lesser charge or even none at all. The reasonable requests of a brother Advocate should also receive special and kindly consideration. In respect of the widows and orphans of an Advocate, all Advocates shall assist them free of charge.

17. In determining the amount of fee, it is proper to consider: (i) the time and labour required, the novelty and difficulty of the questions involved and the skill requisite properly to conduct the case; (ii) whether the acceptance of employment in a particular case will preclude the Advocate's appearance for others in cases likely to arise out of the transaction about which there is a reasonable expectation that otherwise he would be employed, or will involve the loss of other business while employed in a particular case; (iii) the customary charges of the Bar for similar service; (iv) the amount involved in the controversy and the benefits resulting to the client from the service (v) the contingency or the certainty of the compensation, and (vi) the character of the employment, whether casual or for an established and constant client. Of these considerations, none in itself is the controlling factor. These are mere guidelines in ascertaining the real value of the service. In fixing fees, it should never be forgotten that the profession is a branch of the administration of justice and not a mere money-making trade."

<u>18. Excepting such a guideline there is no other provision as to how an Advocate is to realise fees from his client. Hence the observation of the Tribunal as regards extortion of exorbitant fees from the complainant has no basis at all. Since there is no schedule of fees to be realised from the client, the Tribunal had no yardstick with which to judge the abnormality of fees. Professional misconduct has not been defined in P.O. No. 46 of 1972. The Tribunal a has no jurisdiction to decide the amount of fees an Advocate should realise from a client. The canons of Professional Conduct and Etiquette are there for the learned Advocates to follow, but every breach thereof cannot attract the mischief of professional misconduct.</u>

<u>19. Fees of a lawyer vary from lawyer to lawyer. It depends upon many factors, namely, long experience in the legal profession, depth of understanding and knowledge, reputation and goodwill in the profession, etc. Further, bona fide mistake or a well intentioned but wrong advice of a lawyer cannot be a ground of professional misconduct. Depth of know- ledge of law and understanding of procedure are not b equally possessed by legal practitioners. If it is argued that the appellant had given the complainant wrong advice in this case, it will not ipso facto amount to any professional misconduct inasmuch as the complainant has failed to make out a case that with an evil design or malafide motive for some gain the appellant entangled him in an unnecessary litigation where no interest of the complainant was involved. On the contrary, we find that the appellant had correctly advised the complainant that unless his wife becomes a party to the suit, the wrong address of the defendant No. 1 cannot be deleted upon a mere application by a stranger to the suit.</u>

<u>20. In the absence of any specific provision of law regarding realisation or fixation of fees for legal service, it appears to us that to realise or fix fees is nothing but a contract between the lawyer and the client.</u>

21. The most important factor in this case is' the compromise effected between the parties during' the pendency of the case. For consideration of this aspect we may quote the orders dated 31.5.86, 12.6.86, 19.6.86 and 28.6.86 from the order sheet of the Tribunal which are as follows:-

"31.5.86 Parties present. Complainant has filed an application stating that the case is being compromised out' of Court. Hence, he does not want to proceed with the case. The complainant's wife present in Court arid she has voluntarily shown us an NC crossed cheque on Sonali Bank dated 31.5.86 in favour of complainant Mohammad Moslemuddin for Taka 10,000/- only given by the O.P. Mr. Roushan Ali, Advocate, not to be encashed on or before 10.6.86. This is a good gesture of compromise out of Court. Let the matter stand over till 12.6.1986.

Sd/- Siddique Ahmed Ch.

Sd/- Mohammad Habib Ahmed.

12.6.86. Parties present. The O.P. has filed an application praying for one week's time to enable him to create facilities in the Bank for encashing the cheque in question. Prayer allowed. To 19.6.86 as prayed for.

Sd/- Siddique Ahmed Ch.

Sd/- Mohammad Habib Ahmed.

19.6.86. Put up this matter on 28.6.86 for necessary order.

Inform the parties immediately.

Sd/- Siddique Ahmed Ch.

Sd/- Mohammad Habib Ahmed. 28.6.86. Let this matter come up on 12.7.86. Inform the parties with R.P. also.

Sd/- Siddique Ahmed. Ch."

22. From the aforesaid orders it appears that on 31.5.86 both the complainant and his wife Angur Begum as well as the appellant Mr. Roushan Ali were present and the parties had effected a compromise between them and as per term of the compromise the appellant Mr. Roushan Ali had given a crossed cheque dated 31.5.86 on Sonali Bank in favour of the complainant Moslemuddin for a sum of Tk. 10,000/- not to be encashed on or before 10.6.86. The Tribunal in the said order stated that this is a good gestures of compromise out of Court. So, it appears that with the consent as well as within the knowledge of the Tribunal the parties had effected the compromise. From Ext'. Ga' it appears that the complainant Moslemuddin encashed the aforesaid NC payee cheque-amount of Tk. 10,000/- in fulfilment of the terms of compromise.

<u>23. Dr. Rafiqur Rahman submits that there is no legal bar in effecting such a compromise in a case before the Bar Council Tribunal. In a case like this the grievances of a client can be compensated generally in terms of money. It is not like a noncompoundable criminal offence. If a lawyer is found guilty of professional or other misconduct, a Tribunal may reprimand him or suspend him for some period or remove him from practice. Except the above, the Tribunal has no other power to award any other punishment. It is not a criminal Court. It is an investigative authority like an inquiry committee in c a disciplinary proceedings with the added power to award certain specific and limited punishment if it finds the Advocate to be guilty. There is no legal bar either in P.O. No. 46 of 1972 or in the relevant Rules made thereunder to effect a compromise between the parties before the Tribunal since the misconduct complained against is not a non" compoundable criminal offence. The parties, therefore, may effect a compromise in a case of this nature before the Tribunal provided it is made bonafide with the consent of the parties and the Tribunal and it is not against any law or public policy. Article 35 of P.O. 46 of 1972 provides that for the purpose of inquiry the Tribunal shall have the same powers as are vested in a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure in respect of only 3 specific matters and every such inquiry shall be deemed to be a judicial d proceeding within the meaning of sections 193 and 228 of the Penal Code and a Tribunal shall be deemed to be a Civil Court for the purposes of sections 480 and 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. These indicate that the proceeding before a Tribunal is of a civil nature and as such there appears to be no bar to effect a compromise between the parties in a proceeding before the Tribunal.</u>

24. In the present case, the most unfortunate thing is that the former members of the, Tribunal could not pass a formal and final order before 12.7.86 accepting compromise and dismissing the v. petition of complaint in terms of compromise. On 28.6.86 the previous members of the Tribunal No. II passed their last order. On 19.11.86 the new members of the Tribunal took up the case for necessary order. From the order sheet it appears that the new members of the Tribunal directed to issue notices under registered post-with AID on 19.11.86, 13.12.86 and 27.1.87 upon the complainant asking him to appear. The order dated 13.12.86 shows that the appellant Mr. Roushan Ali appeared before the Tribunal and prayed for recording the. compromise. The complainant was not present and did not take any further interest in the matter, but the new Tribunal did not accept the compromise and again notice under registered post was issued upon the complainant. In spite of the issue of the above registered notices the complainant did not care to appear before the Tribunal on 12.2.87, 22.3.87, 27.4.87 and 6.6.87. Ultimately he was made to appear on 21.6.87 when he engaged a different Advocate, gave him power and filed an application stating that he was not a party to the compromise as it was not signed by him, but it was signed by his wife and the appellant-Advocate Mr. Roushan Ali. Further, he claimed refund of the remaining sum of Taka 5,000/- from the appellant.

<u>25. The property in question is in the name of the complainant's wife Angur Begum. Angur Begum executed vokalatnama in favour of the appellant, but it is the husband of Angur Begum, namely, the complainant Moslemuddin who filed this complaint petition before the Bar Council. So, the complainant in fact had no cause of his own. He was defending the interest of his wife before the Tribunal. In fact, if the Tribunal wanted to be technical, it could return the petition of complaint to the complainant, asking him to submit proper petition of complaint from his wife. When the said Angur Begum herself comes and files an application for compromise stating that she received Tic. 10,000/- from the appellant Mr. Roushan Ali and that she will not proceed with the case and when the complainant Moslemuddin is also present in the proceedings, raising no objections, we find no illegality in the matter of compromise and it ought to have been accepted by the Tribunal. Further, the order dated 31.5.86 clearly shows that on that date the complainant Moslemuddin and his wife Angur Begum were both present before the Tribunal and Angur Begum received the crossed cheque dated 31.5.86 of Tk. 10,000/- from the appellant Mr. Roushan Ali and that cheque was issued in favour of the complainant Moslemuddin who himself encashed the same subsequently as per Exhibit 'Ga'. Though the complainant himself did not put his signature in the compromise petition, he was very much a party to the compromise as well as a direct beneficiary of the compromise. The compromise was acted upon. Ext'. Ga' shows that the crossed cheque issued in favour of the complainant Moslemuddin was encashed by Moslemuddin himself. By order dated 21.6.87 the Tribunal rejected the petition of compromise recording the complaint statement that he wants Tk. 5,000/- more, the balance sum. The Tribunal behaved rather strangely. Fees paid to a lawyer for professional services is not a loan. The complainant was not entitled to receive back from the appellant a single farthing. He did not file a Money suit for Tk. 15,000/- before the Tribunal. He received Tk. 10,000/- from the appellant, not as a refund of money paid, but as a compromise sum. The Tribunal failed to realise that the complainant was blowing hot and cold at the same time. He was allowed by the Tribunal to approbate and reprobate. We cannot help finding that it is the new members of the Tribunal who gave the complainant this new-found indulgence. The matter was nearly over. The new members of the Tribunal dug it up and carried it to an extreme.</u>

26. The Tribunal further found that payment of Tk. 10,000/- to Moslemuddin by the appellant Mr. Roushan Ali as a matter of compromise further proved the misconduct of the appellant by admission. Such a finding cannot stand the legal test. When a compromise is effected between the parties out of Court, its terms, conditions or merit or demerit should not be questioned inasmuch as it is done by the consenting parties out of their free will without prejudice to their respective cases and the Tribunal is only to sec whether it is done bonafide or not. It is indeed unheard of that the terms of an amicable compromise reached between the parties out of Court and without prejudice to their respective cases were taken by a Tribunal as an evidence and a proof of commission of offence by one of the parties to the compromise.

27. In view of the above Dr. Rahman lastly submits that he does not like to argue about the malafide intention of the members of the Tribunal, but he will not be wrong if he argues that the members of the Tribunal were not at all fair in dealing with the matter of compromise in this particular case. In order to consider this point we may pose the following questions.

(a) What led the Members of the Tribunal to reject the compromise showing total disrespect to the former members of the Tribunal, as expressed in their order dated 31.5.86 and 12.6.86.

(b) What interests prompted the Members of the Tribunal to issue notices again and again upon the complainant and drag the proceeding for several months while the complainant did not care to appear before the Tribunal ignoring the prayer of Mr. Roushan Ali for disposing of the case in terms of compromise?

(c) Why did the Members of the Tribunal after rejecting the compromise, not compel the complainant to refund Tk. 10,000/- to Mr. Roushan Ali when the complainant repudiated the compromise and wanted to proceed with the case? Who will now be responsible for refund of Tk. 10,000/- to the appellant with interest?

28. From the records it is found that with the knowledge and consent of the Tribunal (while the former members were sitting) the compromise was effected and the Tribunal encouraged such compromise, but owing to some technical difficulty it could not record the final order. In spite of the fact that the complainant was a consenting party as well as a direct beneficiary to the compromise, the Members of the Tribunal illegally rejected the compromise for no reason or for reasons best known to them. Again, the order-sheets of the case show that the Members of Tribunal were waiting and waiting for the complainant and they were in fact bent upon making him appear before the Tribunal while the complainant himself had lost all interest in the case. Further, when the Members were successful in bringing the complainant before the Tribunal, how could they allow him to repudiate the compromise and proceed with the case on the face of Ext "Ga' which shows that the complainant personally received Tk. 10,000/- through cheque from the appellant in fulfilment of the terms of compromise. All these unmistakably lend support to the last contention of Dr. Rahman that the Members of the Tribunal had not fairly dealt with the present case, particularly the compromise chapter. In our view, after effecting the compromise there was nothing for adjudication in the present case and the Members in fact made a mountain out of a molehill for no reasons whatsoever.

29. In view of the facts and circumstances and the evidence on record, we find that the findings of the Tribunal are totally perverse and the judgment and order of the Tribunal based on such findings are liable to be set aside and the appellant should be exonerated from the charge of misconduct.

30. In the result, the appeal is allowed but without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order of the Tribunal are hereby set aside and the petition of complaint is dismissed. The connected Rule being infructuous is discharged without costs.

End.
